en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Pāṭika Chapter of the Dīgha Nikāya.
1. Commentary on the Pāṭhika Sutta:

Commentary on the Account of Sunakkhatta Thus have I heard... [as usual] "...dwelling among the Mallans": this is the Pāṭhika Sutta. Herein, this is the commentary on the words not previously explained.
"He dwells among the Mallans": the Mallans were royal princes of a certain district;
their residence, though it was but a single district, is called "the Mallans" by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhīsadda*). [The phrase] "in that district of the Mallans" refers to this.
"Anupiya, a market town of the Mallans": Anupiya is the name of a market town belonging to the district of the Mallans; he made that his alms-residence village.
The meaning is: having done so, he dwelt in a certain forest grove endowed with shade and water. *Anopiyaṃ* is also a reading. *Pāvisi* means "he entered.
However, the Blessed One had not yet actually entered; rather, because he had set out with the intention, "I shall enter," he is said to have "entered. How so?
Just as a man who has set out with the thought, "I will go to the village," is said to be "where? even though he has not yet reached that village.

When it is said, "So-and-so," it is replied, "He has gone to the village"; it is just so. "This thought occurred to him" means that while standing near the village, as he was looking at the sun, this thought occurred to him:
"It is indeed too early; the rice-gruel and meal have not yet been finished in the families.
But did the Blessed One set out without knowing the time? No, he did not go without knowing. It was at the very time of dawn.
For the Blessed One, having spread out the net of his knowledge and surveyed the world, saw the wanderer Channa of the Bhaggava clan caught within that net of knowledge;
and he thought: "Today, having brought together the reasons for what I have done for this wanderer in the past, I shall preach the Dhamma to him;
that discourse on the Dhamma will bear fruit for him by way of his gaining confidence in me."
Having understood this, desiring to enter the wanderers' park, he set out very early in the morning. Therefore, with the sole intention of entering there, he gave rise to such a thought. 2.
"He said this": having seen the Blessed One, and without being stiff with pride, he went out to meet the Teacher and spoke as follows.
He spoke these words beginning with, "Let him come, venerable sir. "This turn" (*imaṃ pariyāyaṃ*) means this occasion; the sense is, "today is this occasion for his arrival.
But had the Blessed One gone there previously as well? He had not gone there before;

however, he spoke thus in accordance with worldly convention. For when worldly people see someone of a pleasing nature arrive—even if they have not come in a long time or have never come before—[they speak in such a manner].
They say things such as, "From where have you come? It has been a long time since you arrived. How did you know the way here? Are you lost?
Therefore, it should be understood that this person also spoke thus by way of worldly convention.
"This seat" refers to him speaking thus while offering his own seat after clearing and preparing it. "Sunakkhatta, son of the Licchavis."
Sunakkhatta was the son of a Licchavi king. It is said that he was his [the Buddha’s] lay companion and would go to him from time to time.

"Renounced" means: having been thus rejected, dismissed, and abandoned with the words, "Venerable sir, I renounce you; from now on, venerable sir, I shall no longer live as one who has the Blessed One as his guide."
"3. 'Having designated the Blessed One' means: having made this reference, thinking, 'The Blessed One is my teacher; I am fulfilling the Blessed One's instruction.
'Who being, what do you reject?'—would a beggar reject what has been begged from him, or would one who has been begged from reject the beggar?
But you are neither a beggar nor one who has been begged from. This being so, O foolish man, who being..."
"Who are you, and whom do you reject?"—this shows [what he said]. "Behold, you vain man! means "behold, you empty man.

"And to such an extent as this you have offended"—this shows that Bhaggava, "I attribute to him a fault exactly equal to the extent of your offense; however great your transgression, however great your fault, to that same extent I attribute the fault."
4. *Uttarimanussadhammā* means: superior to the human states (*manussadhamma*) consisting of the five precepts and the ten precepts.

*Iddhipāṭihāriyaṃ* means a miracle that has become a supernormal power (*iddhi*). *Kate vā* means "or when it has been performed. *Yassatthāya* means for the sake of which, namely, for the sake of the destruction of suffering.
*So niyyāti takkarassā*ti means that Dhamma leads the one who practices it, according to how the Dhamma has been taught by me. Thus...

He asks: "Does it lead, or does it not lead; does it conduce, or does it not conduce, for a person who has practiced rightly, to the destruction of all the suffering of the round and to the realization of the deathless Nibbāna?"—in this regard, Sunakkhatta, concerning that Dhamma taught by me which, for one who practices it, conduces to the complete destruction of suffering.
"What is the point of performing a miracle of supernormal power (*iddhipāṭihāriya*) that transcends the human condition? What purpose is served by its performance?
For whether it is performed or not performed, there is no decline for my teaching;

indeed, I fulfilled the perfections (*pāramitā*) for the sake of leading gods and humans to the deathless *nibbāna*, not for the sake of performing miracles. Having thus shown the pointlessness of the miracle, [he spoke].
“Behold, you foolish man!”—with these words, he leveled the second charge.

5. Regarding “the foremost”: this refers to the world’s conventional designation. He says that even though one ought to know what is the “foremost”—that is, the limit of the world as “this indeed is the foremost of the world”—he does not proclaim such a limit. The rest here should be understood according to the immediately preceding discourse.
6. As for the phrase “in many ways”: why was this begun? It is said that Sunakkhatta thought, “I shall disparage the Blessed One’s virtues.”
Having rambled on thus far, thinking, “I will point out his fault,” Sunakkhatta stood listening to the Blessed One’s words without support and without a sound.

Then the Blessed One said, beginning with the words, “Sunakkhatta, standing thus in a state of malice, you yourself will incur blame,” in order to show the danger of such malice through many discourses. Therein, “through many discourses” means:
For many reasons. "In the Vajjian village" means in the village of the Vajjian kings; "at Vesālī" means in the city of Vesālī. "He was not able" means he was incapable.

"Being unable"—that Sunakkhatta, who previously could not even face the one who spoke in praise of the Three Jewels, now speaks dispraise with that very same mouth; certainly, being unable and incapable, he [abandoned] the holy life.
"Because of his own foolishness, he spoke dispraise of himself and returned to the low life. But the Buddha is truly enlightened, the Dhamma is well-expounded, and the Saṅgha is practicing rightly.
Thus, by praising the Three Jewels, people will see only your faults.
"In this way, Sunakkhatta, they will speak of you. And so it was.

It shows that you cannot say: "Even though the Teacher possesses unimpeded knowledge regarding the past and the future, he did not speak beforehand, even though he knew, 'Such a fault will arise in me.
*Apakkameva* means "he departed indeed," or the meaning is "he passed away. *Yathā taṃ āpāyiko* means as a being who is destined for rebirth in a state of misery (*apāya*) would depart.
In the same way, "he departed" is the meaning.
Regarding the commentary on the account of the Koliyan Khattiya:
what does this [sutta] show by the words "Ekamidāhaṃ"? This sutta is bound together by two phrases: the miracle of psychic power (*iddhipāṭihāriya*).
"He does not perform miracles" and "he does not proclaim the first beginning.

Of these, the phrase "he does not proclaim the first beginning" he will show at the conclusion of the sutta. However, this teaching was commenced by way of showing the connection for the phrase "he does not perform miracles."
In this context, *ekam-idāham* means "on one day. *Samayaṃ* means "at a time"; the sense is "on one occasion I [was there].
*Thūlūsu* refers to a district named Thūlū; I was dwelling there. *Uttarakā nāma*:

by way of the feminine gender, *Uttarakā* is the name of a market town (*nigama*) in the Thūlū district; the meaning is that I made that market town my alms-residence village (*gocaragāma*). *Acela*: [meaning "naked"].
"Nagga" means naked. "Korakkhattiya" means a khattiya with inwardly curved feet. "Kukkuravatika" means one who has adopted the dog-vow;
like a dog, he sniffs and eats, lies down amidst the cooking pots, and performs other such canine actions.
"Catukkuṇḍika" means one who is joined at four points; having placed both knees and both elbows upon the ground.
He wanders about. "Scattered upon the ground" means strewn, cast down, or placed upon the earth.

"Food" (*bhakkhasa*) refers to any kind of edible thing, whether solid food (*khādanīya*) or soft food (*bhojanīya*). "With the mouth alone" means that without touching it with the hand, he eats solid food with his mouth alone, and he also consumes soft food with his mouth alone.
"One of good form" (*sādhurūpa*) means one of beautiful appearance. "This is a recluse" (*ayaṃ samaṇo*).
“This ascetic is one of the Arahants. In this context, *vatā* is a particle used in the sense of aspiration.
It is said that such was his aspiration: “There is no other ascetic equal to this ascetic;
for he does not wear a robe due to his fewness of desires, and thinking ‘this is a mere distraction,’ he does not even carry an alms-bowl, [eating] only what is scattered upon the ground.”
"He eats; this one is indeed called a 'samaṇa. But what kind of samaṇas are we?
Thus, even while walking behind the All-Knowing Buddha, he conceived this evil thought.
"He said this," [the Buddha replied], for the Blessed One thought: "This Sunakkhatta has an evil disposition; what could have made him see this?"
"...thought thus? While he was thinking in this way, [the Blessed One], having understood his underlying intention, thought:
"This foolish man, following behind an omniscient one such as myself, imagines he is worthy of the naked ascetic; right here, this fool deserves rebuke.
Without turning back, he spoke these words beginning with, "Even you, by name... In that context, "even you, by name" means:
The particle *pi* has the sense of reproach (*garaha*). For the Blessed One spoke thus, “Even you indeed,” while reproaching him.
The intended meaning here is: “Even you, being so base in your inclinations, will claim, ‘I am a recluse, a son of the Sakyans’?
But when he asks, “But what, venerable sir, [is there] in me?,” he is asking: “Venerable sir, seeing what in me is censurable did the Blessed One speak thus?”
Then the Blessed One, explaining it to him, said: “Is it not so for you? and so forth. “He is jealous” means:
“May no one else attain Arahantship”—does he ask, “Does the Blessed One likewise feel such jealousy toward Arahantship?
[The reply is: “Indeed I do not, O foolish man; rather, I desire only the attainment of Arahantship for the world with its devas, and it is for this very purpose.”
“By performing many difficult deeds, I have fulfilled the perfections (pāramitās). Indeed, O foolish man, I am not stingy regarding arhatship.
‘An evil view’—this refers to the view that arose in him, thinking: ‘One who is not an arhat is called an arhat, and one who is an arhat is not called an arhat.
It was with reference to this that he said, ‘an evil view. As for the phrase ‘whatever...’”
Regarding this naked ascetic whom you think thus: "On the seventh day" means on the seventh day. "By indigestion" means by the disease of *alasaka*.
"He will die" means he will die with a bloated belly.
"The Kālakañjakas" is the name of those asuras; it is said that their bodies are three *gāvutas* in height and lack flesh and blood.
Resembling withered leaves, their eyes protrude from their heads and remain fixed there;
their mouths are like needle-pincers and are located right on the head, by means of which they stoop down to seize their prey. Regarding the term *bīraṇatthambaka*:
there was a stalk of *bīraṇa* grass in that charnel ground, and for that reason it is called *bīraṇatthambaka*.

"He approached him" means that after the Blessed One had said this much, having wandered for alms in that village and returned to the monastery, [Sāriputta] went forth from the monastery and approached him.
"For which reason you" (*yena tvam*) means: because of which reason you; the sense is: because of that which was prophesied by the Blessed One.
"Measure by measure" (*mattaṃ mattaṃ*) means: appropriate in measure, appropriate in measure. It is also read as "counsel by counsel" (*mantā mantā*).
"Reading" means having examined and re-examined with wisdom. "Just as for the ascetic Gotama" means:
"You should act in such a way that the words of the ascetic Gotama would be false.
When this was said, the naked ascetic, who was lying like a dog in the place of the hearth, raised his head, opened his eyes, and looked about.
“What are you saying? ‘The ascetic Gotama is our enemy, one of a different faction;
ever since the ascetic Gotama appeared, we have become like glow-worms when the sun has risen.
The ascetic Gotama might speak of us in this way or otherwise. But the talk of an enemy is never true. Go, I [shall remain] here.”
Having said, "I shall know what must be done," he lay down once again.
"One, two" (*ekadvīhikāya*): having said this, he counted. "In the manner of the tradition" (*yathātan ti*): he counted in the same way that someone who does not believe might count.
And having approached him three times on one day, [he thought], "One day has passed; two days have passed."
He reported this. Regarding the "seventh day," it is said that having heard Sunakkhatta’s words, he remained without food for seven days.
Then, on the seventh day, one of his attendants, thinking, "Today is the seventh day since our family preceptor ascetic has not come home;
has some ailment arisen? had pork cooked and took the meal [to him].
Having gone there, he set it down on the ground before him. Seeing this, the naked ascetic (Acela) thought:
"Whether the words of the ascetic Gotama be true or false, death is better for me than to eat food and become satiated.
Placing both hands and his knees upon the ground, he ate until his belly was full. During the night, he was unable to digest it.

Being unable [to eat], he passed away from dysentery. For even if he had thought, "I shall not eat," he would still have eaten on that day and died of dysentery; for the words of the Tathāgatas are never double-dealing. Regarding the *bīraṇatthambaka*:
it is said that the sectarians, having heard that "King Korakkhattiya has passed away," counted the days [until his funeral].

This much was indeed true; but now, having discarded it elsewhere, they went thinking, "We shall subdue the ascetic Gotama with a lie," and binding his body with creepers, they dragged it along, saying, "We will throw it here, we will throw it there.
Yet wherever they went, it was only an open courtyard. As they continued dragging it, they reached the Bīraṇatthambaka cemetery itself.
Having gone there and recognized it as a charnel ground, they thought, "We will discard it elsewhere," and so they dragged it along.
Then their rope broke, and afterwards they were unable to move it; they departed from that very spot. Therefore it is said: "They discarded it in the Bīraṇa-thicket charnel ground.
9. "He approached him": why did he approach? It is said that he thought: "First, let me [examine] the remainder of the ascetic Gotama..."
"His speech is consistent; however, since one who is dead has no way of rising to converse with another, let me go and ask him.
If he speaks, it will be well; if he does not speak, I shall rebuke the ascetic Gotama with a falsehood.
For this reason, he approached. "He struck him" means he hit him. "I know, friend," refers to the dead body.
"There is no one capable of speaking after rising; how then did he speak this? [The answer is: "By the power of the Buddha.
It is said that the Blessed One brought the Kora kṣatriya from the womb of an asura, projected him into a body, and made him speak.
Or rather, he made that very [original] body speak; for the domain of the Buddhas is inconceivable.

10. *Tatheva taṃ vipākan* (‘The result of that speech was exactly so’): the word order has been inverted; it means “the result (*vipāka*) was exactly so,” or rather, “it was not [otherwise]. Some, however, read it as *vipakka*, meaning “it came to pass.
Standing upon this, the miracles (*pāṭihāriya*) should be brought together. All of these indeed constitute the five miracles.
It was said, “He will die on the seventh day,” and he died exactly so; this is the first miracle.
It was said, “By indigestion”; he died indeed from indigestion—this is the second. It was said, “He will be reborn among the Kālakañjika hell-beings”;
he was reborn right there—this is the third. It was said, “They will discard him at the Bīraṇatthambaka cemetery”;
he was discarded right there—this is the fourth. Having come from the place of rebirth, by means of Sunakkhatta...
When told, "Let us discuss this together," he indeed discussed it; this was the fifth miracle.
Regarding the account of the naked ascetic Kaḷāramaṭṭaka:
"Kaḷāramaṭṭaka" means one whose teeth have merely fallen out, or that is simply his name. He had attained the pinnacle of gain.
"Attained the pinnacle of gain" means he attained the highest possible gain. "Attained the pinnacle of fame" means he attained the pinnacle of fame, that is, an excellent retinue.
"Vow-terms" (*vatapadāni*) refers simply to the vows themselves, or the constituent parts of the vows. "Fully undertaken" (*samattāni*) means they were accepted;
"undertaken" (*samādinnāni*) is a synonym for the same. "To the east of Vesālī" means in the eastern direction, not far from Vesālī. "Cetiya" [means a shrine].
The site of the Yakkha Shrine. This same method applies everywhere.
12. Having performed the customary duties toward the Blessed One, he approached where the naked ascetic Kaḷāramaṭṭaka was;
he asked a question—that is, he asked a profound question struck by the three characteristics. He did not comprehend—that is, he did not correctly understand.
He proceeded with his knowledge as if he were blind stumbling here and there in uneven terrain; he saw neither the beginning nor the end.
Alternatively, “he did not proceed” (*na sampāyāsi*) means he did not manage it; having failed to prepare himself, he was unable to speak.
“Not proceeding” (*asampāyanto*) refers to him looking about by turning his eyes like a wild beast: “You have been ordained in the presence of one who is untrained.”
"Even though you have gone forth, you wander about asking questions even in an improper place;

go away, do not stand in this spot," he said, manifesting anger, hatred, and resentment—making manifest the state of being angry (*kopa*), the state of being hateful (*dosa*), and the state of dissatisfaction known as dejection (*appaccaya*). "We were looking forward to it... (*āsādimhasa*)... [etc.]
We have offended, we have struck him. "Mā vata no ahosī" means "O, may it not be so for us.
There is also the reading "mā vata no ahosī," where "maṃ" is used in the accusative case with the sense of the genitive; thus the meaning is "O, may it not have happened to me.
Having thought this, he sat down in the *ukkuṭika* posture and asked his forgiveness, saying, "Forgive me, venerable sir. He too [from here...]
"From this day forward, you shall not ask any further questions. "Yes, I shall not ask," he replied.
"If that is so, go; I forgive you," he said, and dismissed him. 14.
*Parihita* means "clad," referring to one who has put on his lower garment (*nivāsana*). *Sānucārika*—here *anucārikā* refers to a wife.
“Together with his followers” means accompanied by his retinue; “having abandoned that holy life together with his wife” is the meaning.

“Rice and sour gruel” means eating even rice and sour gruel in addition to liquor and meat. “Fallen from fame” means having fallen away from the pinnacle of gain and the pinnacle of fame he had attained.
“A superhuman state, a wonder of psychic power, has been performed” is used here [in this context].
The seven wonders should be understood by way of the transgression of the seven points of conduct.
Commentary on the Story of Acela Pāṭikaputta (15):
"Pāṭikaputta" means the son of Pāṭhika. "With a declaration of knowledge" means together with a declaration of knowledge. "Halfway" means...
"If it were one *yojana* apart, Gotama would go half a *yojana* and I would go half a *yojana*. This same principle applies to distances of half a *yojana* and so forth.
Even if we move beyond a single step, victory will belong to the one who goes forward and defeat to the one who does not.
"There" (*tattha*) means "in that place where we have met. "Twice as much" (*taddiguṇaṃ*) means "twice as much from there [to here]."

"I shall perform double [the miracle]. Although he knew that he was incapable of performing a miracle together with the Blessed One, he spoke thus, knowing that "one who engages in a contest with a Supreme Person is praiseworthy even if they are unable to succeed.
When the city-dwellers heard this, they thought, "One who is truly incapable does not roar like this; certainly, this one too must be an Arahant."
They paid him great honor. [The Buddha thought:
"I shall go to where he is. He heard that Sunakkhatta Pāṭikaputta was saying this. Then, because of his low disposition and inferior outlook, a thought arose in him.
Having performed the duties for the Blessed One, when the Blessed One had entered the Perfumed Chamber, he went into the presence of Pāṭikaputta.
Having gone there, he asked, "Is it true that you are speaking such words? "Yes, we are," they replied. "If that is so, do not be afraid;
speak with confidence again and again. I am the attendant of the ascetic Gotama; I know his domain.
He will not be able to perform a miracle together with you. I [will deal] with the ascetic..."

Having spoken thus to Gotama and instilled fear in him, he took him away elsewhere and departed, saying, “Do not be afraid,” and having thus comforted him, he went into the presence of the Blessed One. Therefore it is said: “I approached where he was.
Regarding the words “That speech,” and so forth: “While being a non-Buddha, I wandered about saying ‘I am a Buddha’; what I spoke was untrue; I am not [a Buddha].”
When one says, "I am a Buddha," one is said to abandon that speech.

Sitting in seclusion and reflecting, thinking, "For so long a time I have wandered about thinking, 'Though not yet a Buddha, I am a Buddha,' but from this moment on, I am no longer a Buddha," one is said to abandon that thought.
[Thinking], "I was wicked for so long a time, saying, 'Though not yet a Buddha, I am a Buddha'..."
"Having held this view, I have wandered; from now on, I abandon this view"—by abandoning in this way, one is said to relinquish that view.
However, one who does not do so is said to have "not abandoned that speech, not abandoned that mind, and not relinquished that view.
"Should fall down" means like a palm fruit released from its stalk.
He might fall from his neck, or he might even split into seven pieces.
"Let him protect this" means let him guard this. "Categorically" means without any alternative formulation. "Uttered" means spoken.
"And if, venerable sir, the naked ascetic Pāṭikaputta"—thus, if the naked ascetic Pāṭikaputta [should hear] these words of the Blessed One uttered categorically.
"By means of a hideous form" (*virūparūpena*) means by means of a form that has departed from its [usual] appearance, a form whose essential nature has vanished;
that is, having abandoned his own natural form, he would appear with an invisible body. Or, he might manifest in various forms such as a lion or a tiger.
"That would be a lie for the Blessed One"—if this were the case, that statement of the Blessed One would be false; thus he rebukes him with the charge of speaking falsehood. Setting aside...
It is said that the Blessed One had never before been refuted by anyone else through false speech.

18. "Leading to the two" means leading to existence in its literal sense and to non-existence in its actual sense; thus it leads to the two. This is a designation for speech that is false, empty, and fruitless.
19. "Ajita, the commander-in-chief of the Licchavis": he, it is said, was an attendant of the Blessed One, and he passed away.
Then, after the people had performed the funeral rites for his body, they asked Pāṭikaputta, "Where has the general been reborn?
He replied, "He has been reborn in the Great Hell. Having said this, he spoke again:
"Your general came to me; yet, instead of following my word, he established the doctrine of the ascetic Gotama."
"I have been reborn in hell," he cried out. Regarding the phrase "He approached for the sake of the midday rest":
why does one not say here, "for the sake of performing a miracle"? Because it was impossible. For there was no face-to-face encounter with him; how then could a miracle be performed?
Therefore, instead of saying that, he said, "for the sake of the midday rest."
Commentary on the Discussion of the Miracle of Psychic Power (Iddhipāṭihāriyakathāvaṇṇanā) 20.
"Householders who were wealthy" (*gahapatinecayikā*) means householders of great fortune. For they possess a vast accumulation of wealth and grain; therefore, they are called "wealthy" (*necayikā*).
"Many thousands" (*anekasahassā*) refers to a number that is immeasurable even by thousands. It is said that he had thus assembled such a great assembly.
There was no one else capable of gathering Sunakkhatta; for that very reason, the Blessed One traveled about taking Sunakkhatta with him for all this time.

21. "Fear" (*bhaya*) refers to the fear of mental trepidation. "Trembling" (*chambhitatta*) refers to the shaking of the entire body. "Horripilation" (*lomahaṃsa*) refers to the state of the hairs standing on end. He, it is said, thought:
"I have spoken a discourse that is far too great for the world with its devas..."
He has entered into hostility with the Supreme Person; yet within me there is neither the attainment of *arahatta* nor any motive for performing a miracle.
However, the ascetic Gotama will perform a miracle, and when the great multitude sees his miracle, they will say:
"Since you are now unable to perform a miracle, why did you, without knowing your own measure, [challenge] the Supreme Person in the world?"
"Thinking, 'Having become my rival, he will roar,' he will harass me with sticks, clods of earth, staffs, and so forth.
Upon hearing of that great gathering of people and the arrival of the Blessed One, fear, trepidation, and horripilation arose within him.
Desiring to be freed from that suffering, he went to the Tinduka-wood ascetic hermitage.
To demonstrate that meaning, the Blessed One spoke the passage beginning with "Then... and so forth. In this context, "he approached" does not mean merely that he approached;
rather, having approached, he entered the wanderers' park located half a *yojana* away.
Even there, finding no satisfaction for his mind, he searched from end to end until he discerned a secluded thicket on the outskirts of the park, whereupon he sat upon a stone slab.
He sat down. Then the Blessed One thought: "If this fool should come here having taken up some instruction from someone, let him not perish.
He resolved: "Let the stone slab on which he is sitting adhere to his body.
Simultaneously with that resolving mind, it adhered to his body. He became as if bound by great iron fetters and as if his feet were severed.
"Assosi" means: a group of people, searching for Pāṭikaputta here and there, followed his tracks and learned where he was sitting.
When a certain man who had arrived asked them, "Whom are you searching for? they replied, "Pāṭikaputta.
He heard this statement: "He is sitting in the Tinduka-Staff Ascetic’s Park."
22. "It crawls" means it sinks down; it moves about right there. "Pāvaḷā" refers to the pelvic bone. 23.
"One whose form is ruined" means one who is defeated, or one whose form is destroyed.

25. "By teams of oxen" means by yokes consisting of a hundred or a thousand oxen. "We would pull" means we would drag. "They would break" means they would snap; or Pāṭikaputta would break at the point of binding.
26. *Dārupattikantevāsī* means the pupil of Dārupattika. It is said that this thought occurred to him:
"Let the miracle be for now; the ascetic Gotama has said, 'The naked Pāṭikaputta will not rise from his seat.
Come now, I shall go and by some means or other cause him to rise from his seat. And in this way, [I shall show] the ascetic Gotama..."
“There will be defeat. Therefore he spoke thus. 27. “Of lions”:
there are four types of lions—the grass lion, the black lion, the pale lion, and the maned lion. Among these four lions, the maned lion is preeminent;
it is this one that is intended here. “King of beasts” refers to [the lord] of all quadrupeds.
Of the king. "They lie down" means they take up residence. "A lion's roar" means a roar of fearlessness.
"They would set out for the sake of their range" means they would set out for the sake of food. "The best of the best" means the most excellent;
the meaning is "the fattest of the fat. "Tender flesh" means soft flesh. There is also a reading, "sweet flesh," which means "delicious flesh. "I would approach" means I would go near.
"Having roared a lion’s roar" means: having roared out of compassion based on his own courage, thinking, "Let those creatures who are weak flee.
"Reared on scraps" (*vighāsasaṃvaḍḍha*) means: reared by scraps; grown by eating scraps, that is, by eating leftover meat. "Haughty" (*ditta*) means: arrogant, with a stout body.
"Powerful" (*balava*) means: endowed with strength. "Why did this thought occur? Because of the fault of the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*).
In this regard, this is the sequential account: One day, it is said, that lion, while returning from his foraging grounds, saw the jackal fleeing in fear.
Filled with compassion, he said, "Friend, do not be afraid; stop! What is your name?
"I am named Jambuka, sir," he replied. "Friend Jambuka, from now on, will you be able to attend upon me?"
"I shall attend upon you. From that time forth, he attended upon him. Whenever Sīha returned from his hunting grounds, he would bring back a large piece of meat;
having eaten it, Sīha would rest on a stone slab not far away.
Within a few days, [the jackal] became stout-bodied and possessed great shoulders. Then Sīha said to him: "Friend, jackal, when I am stretching my limbs..."
"Standing nearby, will you be able to say, 'Shine forth, Master'? "I can, Master," he replied.
When the lion yawned, the jackal did so as well. Because of this, the lion developed an excessive pride of self.
Then one day, an old jackal, while drinking water in a pool, saw his own reflection.
Seeing his own fat body and large shoulders, he did not think, "I am an old jackal," but instead imagined, "I too have become a lion. Then he said this to himself: "O age, O jackal!
Is it indeed fitting for you, with such a physical form, to eat the leftovers of another's meat? Are you not a man?"
“You are a lion! A lion has four feet, two tusks, two ears, and one tail; you too have all those very same things, with the sole exception that you lack the mane.
As he reflected in this way, his conceit (*asmimāna*) increased. Then, due to the fault of that conceit, the thought “Who am I?
and so forth arose as a delusion (*maññita*). In that context, “Who am I? means:
The intention is: "Who am I? Who is Sīha, the king of beasts? He is neither my kinsman nor my master; why should I perform an act of service for him?
*Siṅgālakaṃ yeva* means "nothing but the howling of a jackal. *Bheraṇḍakaṃ yeva* means "nothing but a sound that is unpleasant and disagreeable.
*Ke ca chave siṅgāle* means "what is this wretched jackal? *Ke pana sīhanāde* means "and what is this 'lion's roar' of a jackal?"
The intended meaning is: "And what is the connection between [this] and the lion’s roar? Regarding the "footprints of the Sugata" (*sugatāpadānesu*), this refers to the characteristics of the Sugata.
It refers to the three trainings that have arisen from the teaching of the Sugata. But how does he live there?

For when people give the four requisites, they give them thinking, "We give to the Fully Enlightened Ones who are endowed with virtues such as moral discipline (*sīla*). Thus, although he is not a Buddha, [he lives by means of those requisites].
One who makes use of requisites dedicated to the Buddhas is said to live upon the footprints of the Sugatas. Regarding "the remnants of the Sugatas":
it is said that those who give food to them first offer it to the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddhas, and afterwards give what remains in the evening;
in this way, one is said to eat the remnants of the Sugatas. "Tathāgata" refers to the Tathāgata.
The Fully Enlightened One, the Arahant, should be provoked or challenged. Alternatively, "tathāgate" and so forth are simply plural accusative forms.
"Āsādetabbaṃ" (should be provoked) is also plural, though it is stated in the singular form.
"Āsādanā" (provocation) means the act of challenging with the thought: "I shall perform a miracle together with the Buddha."
29. *Samekkhiyānā* means having scrutinized; the meaning is "having reflected. *Amaññī* means he again reflected—[namely] Kotthu, the jackal. 30.
*Attānaṃ vighāse samekkhiyā* means having seen his own gross physical form in the remains of the meal, [specifically] in the leftover water in the snout.
*Yāva attānaṃ na passatī* means as long as he does not see himself truly as he is, thinking: "I am an old jackal who has grown fat on the remains of the lion's meal."
"He does not see himself. "He thinks, 'It is a tiger'" means he thinks, "I am a lion," or he thinks, "I am indeed a tiger equal in strength to a lion.
31. "Having eaten a frog" means having eaten a frog from a pit. "And mice in the threshing floor" means having eaten mice in the threshing floors.
Having eaten corpses (*koṇapa*) cast away in the *kaṭasī*— that is, corpses discarded in the charnel grounds—
and having grown up in the great forest (*mahāvana*), in the empty forest (*suññavana*), he was thus brought to maturity. Even though he had grown up in that way, that king of beasts,
although thinking "I am the king of beasts," remained just as he was before in his time as a weak jackal.

In the same way, he let out only the cry of a jackal. Even with this verse, like a jackal that has grown fat by eating frogs and other creatures, he—greedy for gain and honor—only harassed Pāṭikaputta.

"By elephants" means by means of elephants. "From the great bonds" means having released them from the great bonds of the defilements (*kilesa*). "From the great abyss" refers to the four floods (*ogha*), which are called the "great abyss"; having pulled them out from there and established them on the ground of *nibbāna*.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Exposition of Primordiality (Aggaññapaññatti-kathāvaṇṇanā): 36.

Thus, having shown the connection for the phrase, "The Blessed One does not perform a miracle by means of this much method of discourse," he now shows the connection for the phrase, "He does not proclaim a primordial beginning," by saying: "And as for 'primordiality'..."
He began his teaching. Therein, "And I, Bhaggava, understand the beginning" means that I, Bhaggava, understand both the beginning and the lineage of the world's origin and conduct.
"I understand that" means not only the beginning, but I understand that beginning;
furthermore, I understand everything from the higher levels of virtue and concentration up to omniscience. And while understanding that, I do not misapprehend it.
And even though I understand that, I do not misapprehend it by way of craving, views, or conceit, thinking, "I understand this.
This shows that there is no misapprehension in the Tathāgata. "The extinction has been personally realized" means that the extinction of defilements has been realized within oneself by oneself.
"That which the Tathāgata, having directly known... refers to that extinction of defilements which he knows.
"The Tathāgata does not fall into misfortune" means that, unlike the non-Buddhist teachers who are ignorant of Nibbāna, he does not fall into misfortune, suffering, or calamity.
Now, showing what those non-Buddhist teachers proclaim as the "primordial beginning," the Blessed One said: "There are, Bhaggava...
and so forth. In this context, "made by Īśvara" or "made by Brahmā" means created by Īśvara or created by Brahmā; "fashioned by Īśvara" or "fashioned by Brahmā."
The meaning is as follows. Here, it should be understood that Brahmā himself is the "lord" (issara) by virtue of his sovereign authority (*ādhipaccabhāva*).
"The teacher’s doctrine" (*ācariyaka*) refers to the state of being a teacher and the teacher’s teaching. In this context, the "teacher’s doctrine" is the theory of primordial beginnings (*aggañña*).

Since it is taught here as the primordial beginning, it is specifically called "the theory of primordial beginnings. How was it formulated? By whom was it formulated, and in what manner was it formulated? The rest is as in the *Brahmajāla Sutta*.
It should be understood according to the method already explained in detail.
41. *Khiḍḍāpadosika* means the root of those corrupted by play.
47. *Asata* means by what that does not exist; the sense is "by way of being non-existent. *Tuccha* means by what that is empty, [that is,] by what is devoid of internal essence.
"By 'lying' (musāti) is meant by false speech (musāvādena). By 'untrue' (abhūtena) is meant that which is devoid of the actual fact.
'Misrepresenting' (abbhācikkhantīti) means they speak over and beyond [the truth]. 'Perverse' (viparīto) means one who has perverted perception and a perverted mind.

And 'the monks' (bhikkhavo ca) means not only the ascetic Gotama, but also those who carry out his instructions; those monks too are perverse. Thus, it is with reference to this that he says 'perverse.'"
In order to demonstrate that [which they say], it is said: "The ascetic Gotama," and so forth.
"The beautiful liberation" refers to the color-kasina. "Only the foul" means he understands both the beautiful and the foul as being only foul.
"At that time, only the beautiful" means that at that time he understands it only as beautiful, not as foul. And "those bhikkhus" refers to those who...
They speak thus; but their disciples and co-ascetics, O monks, are mistaken. "Pahoti" means capable and competent. 48.
"Difficult indeed" refers to what this wanderer said, namely, "I am thus confident, venerable sir," and so forth;
he said that out of deceit and hypocrisy. For it occurred to him: "The ascetic Gotama has [seen] so much of me..."
He delivered a discourse on the Dhamma, yet even after hearing it, I was unable to go forth;
I thought, ‘It is fitting that I should become like one who has entered upon this teaching. Then, out of deceit and hypocrisy, he spoke thus.
Thereupon, as if striking him where it hurts, the Blessed One said: “This is indeed difficult for you, Bhaggava, being of a different view,” and so forth.
This has the same meaning as what was stated in the *Poṭṭhapāda Sutta*. "Guard it well" means guard it thoroughly.
Thus the Blessed One exhorted the wanderer to guard even a mere measure of faith.
Although he heard such a great discourse, he was unable to bring about the destruction of the defilements; nevertheless, this teaching became a condition for his future mental impression (*vāsanā*).
The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
The commentary on the Pāṭhika-sutta in the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*,
the commentary on the *Dīghanikāya*, is finished.
2. Commentary on the Udumbarika Sutta:
Commentary on the Background Story of the Paribbājaka Nigrodha 49.
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Udumbarika Sutta. Herein, this is the commentary on the previously unexplained words: *paribbājako* means a wandering ascetic (*channa-paribbājaka*).
"At Udumbarikā’s Wanderers’ Park" means at the wanderers’ park belonging to Queen Udumbarikā.

"Sandhāna" was his name. Furthermore, this man of great power, the foremost among the five hundred lay followers who wandered about surrounding him, was an Anāgāmī (Non-returner) who was thus extolled by the Blessed One in the midst of a great assembly:
“Bhikkhus, endowed with six factors, the householder Sandhāna lives having reached certainty regarding the Tathāgata and the true Dhamma.

What are the six? With unwavering confidence in the Buddha, unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha, noble virtue, noble knowledge, and noble liberation. It is with these six factors, bhikkhus, that he lives.”
“Endowed with these qualities, the householder Sandhāna has reached certainty regarding the Tathāgata and conducts himself within the true Dhamma.
Having resolved upon the factors of the Uposatha at the very break of dawn and having given an alms-offering to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha during the morning,
when the monks had departed for their dwellings, he was disturbed by the noise of the small and large children in his house.
He set out from the presence of the Teacher with the thought, "I shall hear the Dhamma. Therefore it is said: "In the middle of the day, he departed from Rājagaha.
In this context, "in the middle of the day" (divā divassa) means the passing of midday; the meaning is that he departed as soon as midday had become the "middle of the day" for that particular day.
"Secluded" (paṭisallīno) means [withdrawn] from here and there from the range of objects such as forms and so forth.

Having withdrawn the mind, he became secluded and attained a state of oneness through the practice of delighting in *jhāna*. "Those who are to be cherished by the mind" (*manobhāvanīyānaṃ*) means those who increase the mind.
And those whom one approaches with attention and mental engagement, whose minds become free from hindrances, and who rise up and increase [in virtue].
50. The terms beginning with "those who shout out" (*unnādiniyo*) are to be understood according to the method explained in detail in the *Poṭṭhapāda Sutta*.
51. *Yāvatā* means as many as there are. *Ayaṃ tesaṃ aññataro* means this one among them, a single disciple within their midst.
It is said that five hundred householders who were non-returners (*anāgāmin*) lived in Rājagaha as disciples of the Blessed One.

Each of them had a retinue of five hundred lay followers; it was with reference to them that he said, "this one among them. *Appeva nāma*... [means] perhaps... [or even... (the remainder of the phrase follows).
Desiring to approach him, he spoke thus. The reason for his aspiration has already been stated in the *Poṭṭhapāda Sutta*. 52.
"He said this" means that because he had heard their conversation while on the road as he was coming, he spoke these words beginning with, "But otherwise, these...
In that context, "those of other sects" refers to them by way of appearance, dress, conduct, and behavior.
"Other sectarians" (*aññatitthiyā*) refers to those belonging to other religious orders, whether by their monastery or by their mode of conduct.

"Having gathered together" (*saṅgamma samāgamma*) means having come together and assembled, sitting in a place where they have formed a group. "Forest and woodland tracts" (*araññavanapatthāni*) refers to forest and woodland tracts situated far from the vicinity of villages, serving as remote dwellings.
"Remote" (*pantāni*) means even further away, devoid of the presence of people. "Quiet" (*appasaddāni*) means...

They are "with little sound" because they are quiet even with the noise of travelers passing by on the monastery grounds. They are "with little noise" because they have little clamor due to the absence of manifest sounds.
They are "free from the wind of people" because they are devoid of the movement of air caused by people walking inside.
They are "suitable for human seclusion" because they are appropriate and fitting for the performance of private matters among humans. They are "conducive to retreat."
“They are suitable for the state of oneness. Thus, the householder Sandhāna, thinking, “Oh, my Teacher, who uses such lodgings as these!
raised his joined palms, placed them upon his head—the highest part of the body—and sat there uttering this inspired utterance (udāna). 53.
When it was said thus: when this had been said by the householder Sandhāna while he was uttering the inspired utterance, the wanderer Nigrodha...
"Even though this householder is sitting in my presence, he praises and extols his own teacher alone;
he does not even think that we exist. 'I shall cast the anger he has aroused against him upon the ascetic Gotama,' thinking thus, he said this to the householder Sandhāna."
*Yaggha* is a particle used in the sense of an exhortation. *Jāneyyāsi* means you should understand, perceive, or see.

*Kena samaṇo Gotamo saddhiṃ sallapati* means for what reason or with what person does the ascetic Gotama converse, speak, or address himself? What is meant [by this]? "If there were some cause for conversation, or if there were someone..."

“If he were to go into the presence of the ascetic Gotama seeking conversation and engage in discussion, there would be no reason for anyone else to go into his presence; so with whom does this ascetic Gotama converse?
Without conversing, how could he be one who makes a loud noise?”

They converse and discuss. "Discernment of wisdom" (*paññāveyyattiya*) refers to the state of clarity of knowledge through the method of question and answer. "Lost in empty huts" means they have perished in empty huts;

for even that small measure of wisdom attained by the ascetic Gotama at the foot of the Bodhi tree has perished as he sits alone in empty huts. But if we were like those who dwell in the company of a group...
It shows that if one were to sit having done so, one’s wisdom would not perish. "One who does not frequent assemblies" means that, due to lack of confidence, he is unable to enter an assembly.
"Not fit for conversation" means he is incapable of engaging in discourse.

"Only the most remote corners" means that, fearing questions such as "Someone might ask me a question," he frequents only the most remote and secluded lodgings. "A bull with a broken horn" (gokāṇa) means—
A one-eyed cow is struck in one eye. It is said that she wanders along the boundaries and frequents only the edges.
Indeed, because of her blindness in one eye, she is unable even to face toward the forest edge. Why?
Because she fears a blow from a stone, a branch, or a thorn. She is also unable to face toward the cattle. Why?
Because he fears a blow with a horn, an ear, or a tail. "Inggha" is a particle used in the sense of an exhortation.
"We would cause him to sink" means we would cause him to reach a state of despondency by the mere asking of a single question. "Like an empty jar" means like a vessel that is void.
"We would block him up" means we would bind him; for a jar filled [with water] [cannot move] here and there.
Once it has been turned over, it cannot be bound securely. Just as an empty vessel can be bound as one pleases after being turned over,
so he says, "We shall bind the ascetic Gotama on all sides with the binding of debate, for he is like an empty jar due to his destroyed wisdom."
Thus, not seeing the Teacher’s gold-colored forehead-circle, the wanderer—
displaying his own strength in the absence of the One Possessed of Ten Powers, provoking a noble youth of unblemished lineage like a son of a *caṇḍāla*,
and challenging the king of beasts, the lion with unbroken manes, by force like an old jackal— addressed him in various ways.
He let out a hollow roar. The lay follower also thought: "This wanderer roars excessively;
he exerts himself in vain, like one stretching out his foot to touch the Avīci hell or extending his hand to grasp the peak of existence.
If my Teacher were to come to this place, he would [cut down] this wanderer’s banner of pride, which has been raised as high as the peak of existence."
“...one could easily fall into a pit.
The Blessed One also overheard that conversation between them; therefore it is said, “He heard this conversation.
At Sumāgadhā means: there is a lotus pond named Sumāgadhā, on whose bank a certain man was sitting among the stalks of lotuses.
He saw the army of asuras entering the asura realm. "Moranivāpa" (peacock-feeder): "nivāpa" refers to food;
the meaning is that it is a place where food is given to peacocks along with a guarantee of safety. "Abbhokāse" means in an open courtyard.
"Assāsapattā" means those who have attained satisfaction, those who have attained joy. "Ajjhāsayaṃ" means the supreme basis. "Ādibrahmacariyaṃ" means...
The Noble Path, which is designated as the ancient holy life (*purāṇabrahmacariya*). This is what is meant:

"Venerable sir, what indeed is that Dhamma by which the Blessed One’s disciples, having fulfilled the Noble Path consisting of the holy life of aspiration and so forth, claim to have attained comfort through the realization of Arahantship?"
55. Regarding the "Praise of the Discourse on Aversion to Asceticism":

"Left unfinished" means it remained uncompleted due to my arrival; [the Buddha] invited [the monk to speak], saying, "Speak; I shall complete this, bring it to its conclusion, and show it to you," thus offering an invitation to his omniscience.
56. "It is indeed difficult to know," the Blessed One said, having heard the words of the wanderer: "This wanderer [is one whom] I [have designated as] for my disciples..."
He asks about the Dhamma that should be taught and the practice that should be fulfilled by them;
if I were to explain it to him from the very beginning, he would not understand even what was explained. However, this is a discourse on loathing evil through energy;
well then, let me have him ask a question on this very subject and demonstrate the pointlessness of the views of the various recluses and brahmins.
Then, thinking, “I shall answer this question later,” he said, “This is indeed difficult to understand,” and so forth.
In that context, *sake ācariyake* means in one’s own teacher’s doctrine. *Adhijegucche* refers to the state of loathing evil through exertion (*vīriya*).
*Kathaṃ santā* means being of what nature. *Tapojigucchā* is the loathing of evil and the avoidance of evil through exertion.
“Complete” means “pure. He asks thus: “How is it incomplete? How does it become impure?
Regarding the phrase “yatra hi nāma”: this means “he who indeed. 57.
“Having made little noise” means having made it noiseless and quiet. It is said that he thought: “The ascetic Gotama [is one]...”
“He does not even engage in debate; he has very little conversational discourse.
Yet these people, from the very beginning, have been following and praising the ascetic Gotama. Well then, let me silence them and speak for myself.
He did exactly that. Therefore it is said: “having silenced them. Regarding the phrase “those who preach austerity and self-disgust,” and so forth:
The meaning is: "We speak of self-mortification through austerity; we wander about having grasped that very thing as essential even with our minds;
we are attached to that very thing even with our bodies; we dwell devoted to various kinds of self-torment.
This concludes the commentary on the defilements (*upakkilesa*).
58. *Tapassī* means one who relies on austerity (*tapa*). Terms such as "naked ascetic" (*acelaka*) are to be understood according to the method already explained in detail in the "Lion's Roar.
"He undertakes austerity" means he correctly adopts and firmly grasps austerities such as the state of being naked.
"He becomes elated" means he becomes joyful in mind, thinking, "Who else in this world is like me in this austerity? "He has fulfilled his intention" means...

"Enough with this much"—thus his intention is brought to completion. This has been presented by way of the sectarians (tīrthikas), but it should also be illustrated by one who follows the Dispensation (sāsana).

For someone might undertake an ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) and, through that very practice, become self-satisfied and fulfilled in his intention, thinking, "Who else is like me, a bearer of ascetic practices? This is a defilement for the ascetic.
This is a defilement for this ascetic of two kinds. To this extent, I say, this austerity is defiled.

"He exalts himself" means he exalts and elevates himself, thinking, "Who is there who is my equal? "He disparages others" means he derides and deprecates others, thinking, "This person is not like me.
"He becomes intoxicated" means he becomes intoxicated by the production of the intoxication of pride. "He becomes infatuated" means he is infatuated, gripped, and obsessed.

"He falls into negligence" means he regards this very thing as essential and thus falls into negligence. Even though he has gone forth in the Dispensation, he is one who purifies himself through the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), not one who purifies himself through the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). He perceives the ascetic practices themselves as the essence, just like Arahantship.
59. "Gain, honor, and renown": here, the four requisites are obtained, hence they are called "gains" (*lābha*); these very things, when excellent...
"Honour" means having performed and prepared [offerings], one receives hospitality; "praise" means verses of eulogy.
"Produces" means that by relying on the state of being a naked ascetic (*acelaka*) and so forth, or by undertaking the thirteen ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), great gain arises;
therefore, it is said "produces. The rest here should be understood according to the method of the previous section, in terms of both types of ascetics.
60. "He falls into a state of expectation" means he falls into two parts; he makes two portions. "It is agreeable" means it is pleasing. "It is not agreeable" means it is not pleasing.
"He abandons with longing" means he abandons while still possessing craving. How so? Suppose one has eaten milk-rice early in the morning, and then meat is brought to him.
It occurs to him: "When shall we ever obtain such a thing again?"
"If we had known this, we would not have eaten our milk-rice even at dawn; what could we possibly do?
Go, sir, you eat it yourself," saying this, he abandons it with longing, as if giving up his very life. *Gadhitō* means "one who has become greedy.
*Mucchitō* means "one who is infatuated by powerful craving," having become one whose mindfulness is lost. *Ajjhāpannō* means "one who is excessively attached to material things."
Without making even a mere invitation to the Dhamma, saying, “Eat, friend,” he makes very large mouthfuls.

“One who does not see the danger” means he does not see even a slight danger. “One whose wisdom lacks the means of escape” means here he does not perform even a minimal enjoyment that reflects upon moderation as the means of escape.
“For the sake of craving for gain, honor, and renown” means due to the cause of craving for gain and so forth.
61. "He devours" means he chews. "A thunderbolt-wheel" refers to the thunderbolt itself in the shape of a wheel.
This is what is meant: "The tip of his teeth is like a thunderbolt-wheel; there is nothing among root-seeds and the like that it does not consume.
And yet, they perceive him as a 'recluse' (samaṇa) by way of the designation 'recluse. Thus he disparages and reviles him. This...
This has been presented by way of the non-Buddhist sectarians (titthiya). However, here is the application by way of a bhikkhu:
he himself is a bearer of the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), yet he disparages another thus: "What kind of recluses are these who claim to be 'recluses'?

They do not possess even a mere fraction of the ascetic practices; seeking out meals by invitation and the like, they wander about as those who indulge excessively in the requisites. [The term] "one who lives a coarse life" (lūkhājīvī) refers to this.
"Living on coarse means of subsistence" refers to [living] by way of being naked (acelaka) and so forth, or by way of the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga).

"Envy and avarice" (issā-macchariyaṃ): envy has the characteristic of grumbling at the success of others, such as honor and so forth; avarice has the characteristic of being unable to endure the giving of honor and so forth to others.
"He sits in the line of sight" (āpāthakanisādī hoti): he sits in the range of vision of people, in a place where they can see him. Wherever they look, [he is there].
Staying there, he practices the ascetic discipline of the *vagguli* (the "bat"), endures the fivefold heat, stands on one foot, and pays homage to the sun.
Even though he has gone forth in the Teaching and undertaken the *dhutaṅga* observances, he sleeps through the entire night and performs his penance within the range of vision of people;
he makes his robe-shed right at the great gateway and withdraws it once the sun has risen, [leaving it] for the sake of people.
Knowing that [the time] had arrived, he struck the gong, placed his robe upon his head, and descended to the walking path;
taking up a broom, he swept the courtyard of the monastery.
Regarding the phrase "not displaying himself," here the syllable *a-* is a mere particle; the meaning is "displaying" (*dassayamāno*).
"Idampi me tapasmiṃ" means "this action of mine also is asceticism," or using the locative case in apposition, it means "this too is my asceticism.
For he, having heard that in such-and-such a place there is a naked ascetic (acelaka) who practices the vow of nudity (muttācāra), and so forth, says, "This is our asceticism;
he is our pupil," and so on. Or else, [hearing] that in such-and-such a place there is a wearer of rag-robes (paṃsukūlika)...
Having heard such things as "there is a monk," he says, "This is my asceticism" or "He is my pupil.
"Something" means some fault or a particular view. "He practices in secret" means he practices in such a way that others do not know.
Regarding one who is unwilling, he says, "It is acceptable," meaning he says, "I like it," even though he does not actually like it. By himself...
He proclaims even a very grave fault as being merely trifling; he shows even a mere transgression of a *dukkaṭa* committed by another as being equivalent to a *pārājika*.
"Anuññeyya" means that which should be permitted, that which should be consented to, or that which should be approved. 63.
"He is prone to anger and is resentful" means: by means of anger characterized by the act of becoming angry, and by means of resentment characterized by the non-relinquishing of enmity.
"And he is possessed of malice. He is possessed of "slander," which is characterized by the slandering of the virtues of others, and "stubbornness," which is characterized by taking sides.

He is "envious" and "miserly": [he is envious] through envy, which is characterized by resentment toward the honors and so forth of others; and [he is miserly] regarding dwellings, families, gains, beauty, and the Dhamma.

He is possessed of the fivefold stinginess characterized by the nature of avarice. He is "crafty and deceitful," meaning he is possessed of craftiness characterized by the nature of hypocrisy (*kerāṭika*) and by deceit (*māyā*) characterized by the nature of concealing what has been done.
He is "obstinate and arrogant," meaning he is possessed of stubbornness (*thambha*) characterized by the nature of being devoid of affection and compassion, and having transgressed...

He is possessed of conceit characterized by the act of imagining and by excessive pride. "He has evil desires" means he is possessed of the state of having evil desires, which is characterized by the longing for honor that is not deserved.
"Under the sway of those very evil desires" means being under the influence of those same base cravings.
"Holding wrong views" means being endowed with a view that does not correspond to reality, proceeding in such a manner as "there is no gift," and so forth. "Of those that grasp at extremes":
That very view is called "clinging to extremes" because it grasps at the extreme of annihilation;
the meaning is that one is possessed of such a view. Regarding the terms *sandiṭṭhiparāmāsī* and so forth: one's own view is *sandiṭṭhi*;
one who clings to (*parāmasati*) that very *sandiṭṭhi*, having grasped it and asserted it, is a *sandiṭṭhiparāmāsī*. *Ādhāna* is said to mean firmly and well-established; likewise...

"One who takes [the robe] after having [made a formal resolve]" is one who takes it by means of a formal act (*ādhāna*). "One who is difficult to make relinquish" is like Arittha, in that he cannot be made to give it up.
*Yadime* means "if these. 64. Commentary on the Discussion of Reaching the Stage of Pure Sprouts:
"In this case, Nigrodha, there is an ascetic..."—thus the Blessed One spoke regarding the doctrine held by those of other sects and protected by them.
Having shown the text on defilements (*upakkilesa-pāḷi*) by stating that "all asceticism (*tapa*) is indeed defiled," he now began the teaching for the purpose of showing the text on purity, saying:
"In this case, Nigrodha... and so forth. Therein, the phrases "not pleased" and so on should be understood by way of the opposites of what was previously stated.
And in all instances, the application [of the meaning] should be made with reference both to one who practices harsh asceticism and to one who maintains the ascetic virtues (*dhutaṅga*).

It should be understood thus: "In this way he is pure in that respect. In this manner, by reason of that state—namely, the absence of dissatisfaction and the fulfillment of his intention—he becomes pure and free from defilement;
and by striving further, becoming one who purifies the meditation subject, he reaches Arahantship.
The meaning in all sections should be understood according to this method.
"69. 'Certainly, venerable sir,' [Nigrodha replied]. Thinking, 'This being so, the doctrine of loathing evil through energy alone is entirely pure,' he acknowledged it.
Beyond this, not knowing its preeminence or its essence, he said, 'It has reached the summit; it has reached the core.
Then the Blessed One, refuting his claim that it had reached the core, said, 'Not so, Nigrodha,' and so forth."
“Has reached the outer bark” means it shows that, having passed beyond the heartwood, the sapwood, and the inner bark of a tree possessing a core, it has become like the outermost layer of bark.
70. Regarding the commentary on the discussion beginning with “has reached the pure bark”:
“Let him reach the summit” means let him teach by reaching the summit through the method of teaching; “let him teach by reaching the core” refers to the One of Ten Powers.
He requests. "Restrained by the fourfold restraint" means enclosed by the fourfold restraint. "He does not take life" means he does not kill a living being.
"He does not covet what is cultivated" means that what is called "cultivated" refers to the five strands of sensual pleasure according to their conventional designation;
the meaning is that he does not long for them, nor does he indulge in them.
"He possesses this" means that he now possesses the characteristic about to be described, beginning with "he brings it forward.
"By way of asceticism" means he exists through the state of being an ascetic. In this context, "he brings it forward" means he brings that virtue forward; he increases it further and further.
He does not relinquish his energy, thinking, "My virtue is perfected, my asceticism has been undertaken; enough of this much. "He does not revert to the low" means...
He does not turn back toward the inferior state of a householder. He exerts energy for the sake of attaining further distinction beyond mere virtue;
acting in this way, he resorts to a secluded lodging. The terms "forest" (*arañña*) and so forth have already been explained in detail in the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta*.
The terms "accompanied by loving-kindness" (*mettāsahagatena*) and so forth are described in the *Visuddhimagga*. "Reaching the bark" (*tacappattā*) means [reaching] inside the outer bark.
“...it has reached the bark. “It has reached the inner bark” means that it has reached the inner bark from the outer bark; the meaning is that it becomes like the inner bark.
(74) “To this extent, Nigrodha, austerity and self-reproach have reached the pith and have reached the heartwood”—this the Blessed One said with reference to the sectarian teachers.
For the gain and honor of the sectarian teachers is like the branches and foliage of a tree.
The mere five precepts are like the outer bark. The mere eight attainments are like the inner bark.
The higher knowledges (abhiññā) ending with the knowledge of past lives are like the softwood. However, these [wanderers] take divine-eye to be Arahatship and travel about with that;
therefore, for them, that is like the heartwood of the tree. But in the Dispensation, gain and honor are like the branches and foliage. Perfection of virtue—

The outer bark is like the preliminary stages; the meditative attainments (*jhāna-samāpatti*) are like the inner bark; the mundane superknowledges (*lokiyābhiññā*) are like the softwood; and the Path and its Fruit (*maggaphala*) are the heartwood.
Thus, the Blessed One compared his own dispensation to a tree heavily laden with the weight of fruit that has bent and drooped under its own burden.
Because of his skill in teaching and because of the excellence of its inner bark and heartwood, my dispensation is both superior and more sublime than that.
In order to show the excellence of his own teaching by asking, "When will you come to know that?", he began the instruction with the words, "Thus indeed, Nigrodha.
"Those wanderers" refers to those three hundred wanderers who were his followers.
"We shall perish here" means in this regard—namely, in the Acelaka-pāḷi and so forth; what is meant is: "Even our mere Acelaka-pāḷi..."
It does not exist; how, then, could there be a pure textual tradition? For us, there is not even a pure textual tradition;

how, then, could there be the fourfold restraint and so forth? There is no fourfold restraint; how, then, could there be dwelling in the forest and so forth? There is no dwelling in the forest; how, then, could there be the abandoning of the hindrances and so forth?
There is no abandoning of the hindrances; how, then, could there be the divine abodes and so forth? There is not even the divine abodes; how, then...
"Regarding past lives and so forth: we do not possess even the mere knowledge of past lives; how then could we have the divine eye?
In this matter, we, together with our teachers, are lost. By "anything further superior to this," they mean:
"Beyond this attainment of the knowledge of the divine eye, we know of no other superior or distinguished attainment, even by way of what we have heard."
The Commentary on the Praise of Nigrodha’s Repentance (75).
Then, regarding the words "the wanderer Nigrodha," it is said that this thought occurred to him: "These wanderers are now desirous of hearing the Blessed One’s speech;
yet by this Nigrodha, in the absence of the Blessed One, harsh and insolent words were spoken."
"It has been said; now this man too has become desirous of hearing. This is the time for me to cast down his banner of pride and cause him to take up the teaching of the Blessed One.
Then he spoke thus to the wanderer Nigrodha. Furthermore, it occurred to him:
"If I do not speak to him, he will not ask the Teacher for forgiveness; that will lead to his harm and suffering in the future."
"But when I have spoken, he will ask for forgiveness, and that will lead to his welfare and happiness for a long time.
Then he said this to the wanderer Nigrodha: "But make him one who does not move in circles" (*aparisāvacaraṃ*). Here, *pana* is a particle;
thus the meaning is, "then make him one who does not move in circles. There is also a reading, *aparisāvacare taṃ*, which means "make him one who does not move in circles."
"Or do this to him," means "or do it to one such as Gokāṇa. Regarding "Gokāṇa," the meaning here is also:
"treat him like Gokāṇa, who was restricted to walking within boundaries. "Became silent" means having entered into a state of silence.
"Became abashed" means having fallen into a state of lack of luster. "With shoulders drooping" means with neck bent down. "With face cast downward" means with the face turned toward the ground.
76. "He is a Buddha, a Blessed One, for the sake of awakening": he himself has awakened, and he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of the awakening of beings to the Four Noble Truths.
"Tamed" means tamed even in the eye... [and so on] ...tamed even in the mind. "For the sake of taming" means solely for the sake of taming others, not for the sake of debate.

"Peaceful" means peaceful through the pacification of lust, peaceful through the pacification of hatred and delusion, and peaceful through the pacification of all unwholesome states and all volitional formations.
"Santo" means he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of calming—namely, for the purpose of pacifying lust and other defilements in the great multitude.

"Tiṇṇo" means he has crossed over the four floods. "Taraṇāya" means for the purpose of enabling the great multitude to cross over the floods. "Parinibbuto" means he has attained final Nibbāna through the Nibbāna of the defilements.
"Parinibbānāya" means he teaches the Dhamma for the purpose of bringing about the final Nibbāna from all defilements for the great multitude as well.

The Commentary on the Conclusion of the Holy Life (Brahmacariyapariyosāna), etc., [Section] 77. "Transgression" and so forth are stated in the *Sāmaññaphala* [Sutta]. "Upright by nature" means one whose natural disposition is straight, being free from crookedness of body and so forth.
"I instruct such a person" means: I instruct that kind of individual; I teach him the Dhamma. "For seven days"—[etc.]
"For seven days"—the Blessed One said all this with reference to a person of dull wisdom;
however, one who is not deceitful, free from guile, and upright by nature will be able to attain Arahantship in that very moment.
Thus, by the words beginning with "not deceitful," the Blessed One—showing that one who is deceitful and crookedly crooked cannot even be instructed by him—seized the wanderer by the feet.
He threw [the stone] as if onto the foot of Mount Mahāmeru. Why? Because this man was exceedingly crafty and crooked-minded;
even while the Teacher was speaking thus, he had no conviction in the Buddha, the Dhamma, or the Saṅgha, nor did he lend an ear for the sake of conviction.
Remaining in hypocrisy, he sought to appease the Teacher. Therefore, the Blessed One, knowing his disposition, said: "Let the wise one come..."
He said, "A man who is not deceitful," and so forth. However, he thought, "I am not able to instruct one who is deceitful.
(78) "Antevāsikamyatā" means by way of desiring us as pupils; thus he said, "Let a wise man come," and so forth.
"Yo eva vo ācariyo" means whoever is your natural teacher. The recitation...
"No one wishing to cause [you] to fall away" means: having caused you to accept his own instruction, he does not wish to cause you to fall away from your own recitation (*uddesa*).
"Let that very recitation be yours" means: let that which is your natural recitation remain yours alone; we have no need for your recitation.
"From livelihood" means: from the way of life. "Designated as unwholesome" means: the category known as unwholesome (*akusala*).
"Attained. "Unwholesome states" refers to the twelve types of unwholesome consciousness-arising, or specifically craving alone;
for it is called "leading to renewed existence" because it produces further becoming. "Accompanied by distress" means associated with the distress of the defilements.
"Subject to birth, aging, and death" means being the condition for birth, aging, and death. "Defiled states" refers to the twelve types of unwholesome consciousness-arising.
“Purifying” (*vodāniya*) refers to the states of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*). For they purify beings; therefore, they are called “purifying.
“The fulfillment of wisdom” (*paññāpāripūri*) means the fulfillment of path-wisdom (*magga-paññā*). “And its abundance” (*vepullatta*) means the abundance of fruition-wisdom (*phala-paññā*);
or both of these are simply synonyms for one another. This is what is meant: “Therefore, you [should develop] both path-wisdom and fruition-wisdom.”
“Having realized it for yourselves through direct knowledge in this very life, you shall enter upon and abide in it.
Thus the Blessed One, referring to the wanderers, concluded his teaching with the pinnacle of Arahantship, demonstrating the fruit of his own instruction and exhortation.
79. “Just as if their minds were possessed by Māra”—just as they would sit with minds overwhelmed by Māra, even so they sat silent... [and so on] ...speechless.
Māra thought, "The Teacher, indeed, is preaching the Dhamma to these wanderers while roaring exceedingly and manifesting the power of a Buddha;
perhaps there will be an penetration of the Dhamma by them. Come now, I shall overwhelm them. Thus he overwhelmed their minds.
For the mind of those who have not abandoned the perversions is subject to Māra to do with as he pleases. They too—
With their minds possessed by Māra, they sat silent and speechless, as if their limbs and members were paralyzed.
Then the Teacher, reflecting, "These wanderers are sitting here in extreme silence; what can be the cause?
understood that they were possessed by Māra. However, had there been a cause for the arising of the path and its fruits in them, he would have warded off Māra.
The Blessed One would teach the Dhamma, yet they did not have it. He realized, "All these are empty men.
Therefore it was said: "Then it occurred to the Blessed One: 'All these are indeed empty men,'" and so forth.
In that context, *phuṭṭhā pāpimatā* means touched by the Evil One, Māra. *Yatra hi nāma* means "in whom indeed. *Aññāṇatthampi* means even for the sake of ignorance.
"Even knowing this, what will it matter? What will those seven days determined by the ascetic Gotama do for us?
This is what is meant: "The ascetic Gotama has said, 'Having realized it through my own direct knowledge, I shall dwell having attained [it] in seven days';
what discomfort will those seven days cause us? Come now..."
“Whether we are able to realize this Dhamma within seven days or not, we shall nevertheless lead the holy life for the sake of that very knowledge.
Or alternatively: “Let us know this Dhamma for a while. On a single day and at a single time, their minds did not arise even for the sake of that knowledge;
but what will those who are indolent do in seven days? Will they be able to achieve it?
"To fulfill for seven days" is the intended meaning here. "Lion's roar" means having roared a fearless roar that shatters the arguments of opponents and uplifts one's own doctrine.
"He stood present" means he established himself [there]. "At that very moment" means at that precise instant.
"He entered Rājagaha" means he entered Rājagaha itself. Now, as for those wanderers, although this sutta...
Having heard it, no distinction was produced; however, it will serve as a condition for their future mental impression (*vāsanā*).
The rest is self-evident everywhere.
[Thus ends] the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, the commentary on the *Dīghanikāya*.
The commentary on the Udumbarika-sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Cakkavatti-sutta: Explanation of the State of Being One’s Own Island and Refuge.
80. Thus have I heard: this is the Cakkavatti Sutta. Herein, this is the commentary on the words not already explained:
*Mātulāyaṃ* means in the city of that name. Having made that city his alms-resort village, he dwelt in a grove nearby.
Regarding the passage, “There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus,” this is the sequential narrative: [text continues].
It is said that at the time this sutta was first occasioned, during the hour of dawn, the Blessed One emerged from the attainment of great compassion and surveyed the world.
Seeing that eighty-four thousand living beings residing in the city of Mātulā would attain the realization of the Dhamma through this discourse on the Suttanta which illuminates the future lineage,
he set out for the city of Mātulā early in the morning, accompanied by a retinue of twenty thousand bhikkhus.

He arrived. When the Kṣatriyas residing in the city of his maternal uncle heard that "the Blessed One has come," they went out to meet him, invited the One of Ten Powers, and having conducted him into the city with great honor, prepared a place for him to sit.
Having seated the Blessed One upon a magnificent couch, they gave a great alms-offering to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha.
After the Blessed One had finished his meal, he thought:
"If I were to teach the Dhamma to these people in this place, it would be crowded;
there would be no room for people to stand or sit, and yet a great assembly must surely gather."
Then, without even offering words of thanksgiving for the meal from the royal families, he took his bowl and departed from the city.
The people thought: "The Teacher is going away without even giving us a blessing; surely the dining hall was unpleasant.
It is indeed impossible to grasp the minds of the Buddhas; making friends with the Buddhas is truly difficult."
"It is like seizing a venomous snake with its hood raised by the neck. Come now, friends, let us ask the Tathāgata for forgiveness.
All the inhabitants of the city set out together with the Blessed One.

As they were going along, the Blessed One saw a certain mātuḷa tree standing in the Magadha country, possessed of branches and foliage, casting a spreading shade, and covered knee-deep in leaf-litter.
Seeing this, and thinking, "If I sit at the foot of this tree while the Dhamma is being taught,
there will be room for the great multitude to stand and sit," he turned back, descended from the path, approached the foot of the tree,
and looked toward the Elder Ānanda, the treasurer of the Dhamma. By the mere sign of his look, the Elder, knowing that "the Teacher wishes to sit," [prepared] the Sugata’s great robe.
Having had it prepared, he gave it [to the Blessed One]. The Blessed One sat down on the seat that had been prepared. Then people sat down in front of him;
on both sides and behind him was the community of monks; in the sky stood the deities.
Thus, surrounded by this great assembly, the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"Those monks" refers to the monks who have entered there as recipients of the Dhamma. "Be islands unto yourselves" means:
dwell having made yourself an island, a refuge, a shelter, a resort, a final goal, and a foundation. "Self-refuge" is a synonym for that very same thing.
