"Not another refuge" is a statement that precludes any other refuge; for indeed, one person cannot be the refuge for another.
It is a refuge because, through the effort of one person, another is not purified.
And this has been said: "The self is indeed its own protector; for who else could be the protector? Therefore he said, "having no other refuge. But what here is called the "self"?
It is the mundane and supramundane Dhamma. Therefore he said: "Having the Dhamma as their island, having the Dhamma as their refuge, having no other refuge. [In the passage on] the body...
“Contemplating the body,” and so forth, are explained in detail in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta.
“In his own range” means in a place suitable for wandering. “His own” means belonging to himself. “In the ancestral domain” means in the sphere inherited from his father.
“Of those wandering” means of those who are wandering. There is also a reading “carantaṃ,” which has the same meaning. “He shall not obtain” means he will not obtain.
"He will not see [it]. "Māra" refers to the Māra of the sons of gods, the Māra of death, and the Māra of the defilements.

"An opening" means a flaw, a fissure, or a vulnerability. This meaning, however, should be illustrated by the story of the bird Pakkhandasena, who, having emerged from his perch on a clod of earth and sat upon a gateway arch, seized a quail that was brooding in the morning sun. For it has been said:
“Once upon a time, monks, a hawk suddenly swooped down and seized a quail.
Then, monks, as the quail was being carried off by the hawk, he lamented thus:
‘We are indeed unfortunate, we are of little merit, we who have wandered outside our own range, into the territory of others. Had we today been in our own range—’”
‘We shall roam in our own ancestral domain; this hawk will not be able to fight us.
‘But what, Lāpa, is your own ancestral domain as a feeding ground? ‘It is the place where the ploughing is done and clods of earth are thrown.
Then, monks, the hawk, overconfident in its own strength and disregarding its own strength, [approached] the Lāpa.
“Go, Lāpa bird, release the other bird; even having gone there, you shall not escape,” he said.
Then, monks, the Lāpa bird went to a place where ploughing was being done and clods were being thrown;
having climbed upon a large clod, it stood there calling out to the hawk: “Come now, hawk, come!”

"Indeed, he is now a falcon for me. Then, monks, that falcon, overconfident in her own strength and not measuring herself against her own strength, folded both wings and suddenly swooped down upon the lapwing bird.
When the lapwing bird, monks, realized, "This falcon has come at me with great force," then, right there—
The opening of the clod was revealed. Then, monks, the hawk struck its breast right there.
For this is what happens, monks, to one who wanders in a non-range, in another’s domain.
Therefore, monks, do not wander in a non-range, in another’s domain; for those wandering in a non-range, monks—
Māra will find an opening; Māra will find an object. And what, bhikkhus, is the non-range, the foreign domain of a bhikkhu?

It is these five cords of sensual pleasure. Which five? Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust; sounds cognizable by the ear that are desirable, lovely, agreeable... [and so on].
Odors cognizable by the nose that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust;
tastes cognizable by the tongue that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust;
tangibles cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.
“Monks, this is not the proper resort, the domain of others, for a monk.
Monks, you should move within your own resort... Māra will find no foothold there.
And what, monks, is the proper resort, the ancestral domain of a monk? It is the four foundations of mindfulness. What are the four? Here, monks,” [he said].
A bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world;
he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world;
he dwells contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.

He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world—this, monks, is the bhikkhu’s own domain, his ancestral sphere.
"Skilful" means characterized by blamelessness. "On account of undertaking" means on account of acting after having undertaken [the practice]. Thus is this merit.
"It increases" means that in this way this mundane and supramundane fruit of merit increases;
and by "fruit of merit," both further merit and the ripening of merit are to be understood.
Commentary on the Story of King Daḷhanemi the Wheel-turning Monarch.
81. Therein, wholesome [kamma] is twofold: that which leads to the round of existence (*vaṭṭagāmī*) and that which leads to the cessation of the round (*vivaṭṭagāmī*).

Therein, what is called wholesome leading to the round is a mind of softness and gentleness arising from affection toward one's mother and father for their children, or toward one's children for their mother and father.

What is called wholesome leading to the cessation of the round consists of the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*), classified as "the four foundations of mindfulness" and so forth.
Among these, the culmination of merit leading to the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) is the glory and power of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*) in the human world.

The culmination of skillfulness leading to the turning away from the round (*vivaṭṭa*) is the attainment of the path, the fruit, and Nibbāna. In that regard, he will demonstrate the result (*vipāka*) of skillfulness leading to the turning away at the conclusion of the Sutta.
However, here, for the purpose of demonstrating the result of skillfulness leading to the round of existence, [it is said]: "Monks, when sons and daughters [behave] toward their mother and father..."
When they did not abide by the instruction, they then declined in lifespan, in beauty, and in sovereignty; but when they did abide by it, they increased.

Having said this, he began the teaching with the words, "In the past, monks," by way of connecting the discourse to the wholesome factors leading to the round of existence (*vaṭṭagāmikusalānusandhi*).
Therein, the terms such as "wheel-turning monarch" (*cakkavattī*) have already been explained in detail in the *Mahāpadāna Sutta*.
82. "Ossakkati" means it has subsided even slightly. "Cuta from its place" means it has departed entirely from that position.
It is said that the Wheel-Treasure stood in the air at the gate of the inner palace as if struck by an axle-pin.
Then, having driven two acacia-wood pillars into the ground on both sides, they tied a cord upon the Wheel-Treasure, facing the rim.
In the lower portion as well, they fastened one [rope] facing the rim. Among those, if even a tiny fraction of the wheel-treasure descends below the upper rope, it is said to have "slipped back";
if the position of the lower rope has moved beyond its upper limit, it is said to have "fallen from its place.
This occurs only when there is an exceedingly powerful fault; even a mere thread [would not slip] by a measure of one or two finger-breadths.
Or it has slipped from its place; it has indeed fallen from its position. It was with reference to this that it was said: "It has receded, having fallen from its place.
Then you should report this to me: "Dear one, starting from today, go three times a day to attend upon the Wheel-Treasure (cakkaratana).
While going thus, whenever the Wheel-Treasure has receded even slightly, having fallen from its place—"
“If you see it, then you should inform me; for my life is placed in your hands. “I have seen it,” he replied.
Being diligent, he went three times a day to look, and one day he saw it.
“Then, monks,” said the Blessed One, “then King Daḷhanemi [thought], ‘The Wheel-Treasure has receded.’”
Having heard this, overcome by a powerful surge of grief, he thought: "I shall not live much longer now; my life is but short.
This is no time for me to enjoy sensual pleasures; it is now the time for me to go forth.
Having wept and lamented, he summoned his eldest son, the prince, and said to him: "Samuddapariyantaṃ" means precisely that which is bounded by the single ocean as its limit.
For this belongs to his family. However, that which has arisen by the power of his merit, extending as far as the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*), cannot be given away.
But when offering what belongs to his family, he said, "extending as far as the ocean.
Regarding "hair and beard": even those going forth into the ascetic life (*tāpasa-pabbajjā*) first shave off their hair and beard; from that point on, when the hair has grown back...
They wander about having bound [him]. Therefore it is said:
“Having shaved off his hair and beard. “Kāsāyāni” means dyed with an astringent taste. Having first done thus, they later wear even bark garments.
“Pabbajī” means he went forth (was ordained). And having gone forth, he dwelt right there in his own Maṅgalavana park. “Rājisimhi” means among the royal sages.
For those who have gone forth as brahmins are called "brahmin-sires" (*brāhmaṇisaya*). But those who have gone forth from royalty, having abandoned the white parasol, are "royal-sires" (*rājisaya*).
"It vanished" means it disappeared, having reached non-existence like the flame of an extinguished lamp.
"He experienced" means he made himself known while weeping and lamenting. "Inherited from his father" means it was not a paternal inheritance; it could not [be obtained].
It is impossible for one who is indolent and lacking in energy, having undertaken and practicing the ten unwholesome courses of action, to attain this.
Rather, it is shown that this must be attained by fulfilling the twelvefold or tenfold duty of a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti), relying upon one’s own well-performed deeds.
Then, urging him toward the practice of his duties, he said, "Come now," and so forth. In that regard:
"Ariya" means faultless. "Cakkavattivatta" refers to the conduct of wheel-turning monarchs. [In the commentary on the noble conduct of wheel-turning monarchs:
"Dhamma" refers to the dhamma of the ten courses of wholesome action.
"Nissāya" (relying upon) means by means of a mind that has that very [dhamma] as its object.
Having made it one's reliance. "Honoring the Dhamma" means acting in such a way that the Dhamma, once undertaken, becomes well-performed.
"Revering the Dhamma" means honoring it through the arising of respect for it.
"Loving the Dhamma" means dwelling having made that very Dhamma dear and worthy of cultivation. "Worshiping the Dhamma" means...
Referring to that [Dhamma], he performs worship of it by means of offerings such as perfumes and garlands.
"Honoring the Dhamma" means acting with humility toward that very Dhamma through gestures such as joining the palms in reverence.

"Having the Dhamma as his banner and the Dhamma as his crest" means that because he proceeds having placed that Dhamma before him like a banner and raised it aloft like a crest, he is one who has the Dhamma as his banner and the Dhamma as his crest.
The meaning is "having sacrificed. *Dhammādhipateyyo* means having become one for whom the Dhamma is predominant;
that is, by virtue of having arrived through the power of the Dhamma and by performing all activities solely on the basis of the Dhamma, he becomes one for whom the Dhamma is predominant.

*Dhammikaṃ rakkhāvaraṇaguttiṃ saṃvidahassū* means: that which possesses the Dhamma is "dhammika" (righteous). Protection (*rakkhā*), warding off (*āvaraṇa*), and guarding (*gutti*) constitute "protection, warding off, and guarding. In this regard:
Because of the statement, “Protecting others, one protects oneself,” patience and the other [virtues] are forms of protection. For this has been said:
“And how, monks, does one protecting others protect oneself? By means of patience, non-violence, a mind of loving-kindness, and compassion.
An enclosure is the warding off of clothing, coverings, houses, and so forth; it is a guarding for the purpose of warding off calamities such as thieves.
"Gutti" means: "arrange all of that well; cause it to proceed and establish it"—this is the meaning.
Now, showing where that [protection] must be arranged, he said: "Among your own people," and so forth.
Herein, this is the summarized meaning: establish your children and wife, who are designated as "your own people," in the restraint of virtue (*sīla-saṃvara*).
Give him clothing, perfumes, garlands, and so forth, and ward off all calamities from him. The same method applies to the army and the other [categories].
However, this is the distinction: the army should be supported by providing food and wages without letting the time lapse.
The consecrated nobles (*khattiya*) should be won over by the gift of excellent treasures such as thoroughbred horses and noble elephants. The subordinate nobles...
They should be satisfied by providing them with suitable vehicles and conveyances; the brahmins, with gifts of food, drink, clothing, and so forth;
the householders, with the provision of meals, seed-corn, ploughs, hoes, and oxen; likewise the *negamas*, who dwell in market towns, and the *jānapadas*, who dwell in the countryside;
and the ascetics and brahmins, who have stilled evil and cast out evil, with the provision of requisites for ascetics.
They should be honored. Wild animals and birds should be comforted with the gift of fearlessness.
"In his own domain" means in the place where his authority prevails. "An unrighteous act" means an unrighteous deed. "Let it not proceed" means:
practice in such a way that it does not proceed; this is the meaning. "Ascetics and brahmins" means those who have stilled evil and cast out evil.

“Abstaining from the intoxication of pride” means they abstain from the ninefold intoxication of conceit (*māna-mada*) and from negligence (*pamāda*), which consists of the mind’s indulgence in the five strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*).
“Established in patience and gentleness” means they are firmly grounded in the patience of endurance (*adhivāsana-khanti*) and in the state of being well-disposed (*suratabhāva*).
“Taming themselves alone” means they tame and pacify themselves alone through the taming of their own lust and other defilements.
"They are said to cause [beings] to attain final Nibbāna. "From time to time" means at various times.
"You should avoid" means you should avoid it thoroughly, as one would avoid excrement, poison, or fire.
"Taking it up" means you should practice by correctly taking it up, as one would take up a garland of fragrant flowers or as one would [seek] the Deathless.
Standing here, one should fulfill the duties: one toward the household, one toward the army, one toward the nobles,
one toward the followers, one toward the brahmins and householders, one toward the townspeople and countryfolk, one toward the recluses and brahmins, one toward the beasts and birds,
one toward the prohibition of unrighteous acts, and one toward the bestowing of wealth upon the destitute— these are the duties toward the recluses and brahmins.
Having approached, there is the asking of questions; thus, this is tenfold.
However, for one who counts by making the householder and the bird-born beings separate, it becomes twelvefold.

Or, for one counting what was not mentioned before, it should be understood as twelvefold by way of the abandoning of unrighteous passion (*adhammarāga*) and improper greed (*visamalobha*). "This, dear sir, is the tradition (*tanti*); this..."

The tenfold and twelvefold duty of the noble wheel-turning monarch is what is called the *ariyacakkavattivatta*. "While he is conducting himself" means while he is fulfilling [the duties] and conducting himself.
"On that very day, on the Uposatha," and so forth, is stated in the *Mahāsudassana Sutta*.
(90) "By his own judgment" means by his own intelligence. *Sudam* is merely a particle. "He rules" means he instructs. This is what has been said.
There was one who, having abandoned the ancient royal lineage, the royal succession, and the duties of kings, ruled the realm relying solely on his own wit.
Thus, he appeared as the final person who, like the one who produced the *kaḷāra* (barren) offspring for the Maghadeva dynasty, brought about the severance of the Daḷhanemi dynasty.
"The later being like the earlier" means that it was in the later period similar to what had been in the earlier period.

"The districts do not increase" means they do not expand. "As was the case with former kings" means that just as under former kings they increased, being exactly the same both before and after, so too they do not increase. In some places they become empty, plundered and destroyed;
the meaning is that even the nutritive essence (*ojā*) in oils, honey, molasses, and so forth, as well as in rice-gruel and meals, has diminished.
"Ministers and courtiers" (*amaccā pārisajjā*) means those who are both ministers and members of the royal assembly.

"Accountants and high officials" (*gaṇakamahāmattā*) means those who are accountants of the *acchiddaka* and other texts, as well as the great ministers. "Military officers" (*anīkaṭṭhā*) refers to elephant trainers and others. "Doorkeepers" (*dovārikā*) are the guards of the gates.
"Those who live by counsel" (*mantassājīvino*): "Counsel" (*manta*) is said to be wisdom (*paññā*); this is the name for those wise high officials who live depending upon that [wisdom].
Commentary on the Discourse on the Decline of Life-span, Beauty, and So Forth (91):
"But he did not give wealth to the poor"—this means that because of his powerful greed, he did not bestow wealth upon poor people.
"When it was not being bestowed" (*nānuppadiyamāne*) means when it was not being given; or rather, this is the reading itself. "Poverty" (*dāliddiya*) is the state of being poor.
"Live yourself" (*attanā ca jīvāhi*) means "sustain your own life yourself. Regarding the terms *uddhaggikā* and so forth:

it is called *uddhaggikā* because its course is directed upward (*uddhamagga*) by way of yielding fruit in successively higher planes. It is called *sovaggikā* because it is beneficial for heaven (*sagga*), producing rebirth there.

It is called *sukhavipākā* because its ripening (*vipāka*) is pleasant in the place where it is produced. [It is called *visuddhippavāhā*] because of the excellent, supreme celestial forms and so forth.
Because it brings about ten special qualities, it leads to heaven; the meaning is that one establishes such a meritorious gift.
92. "It will increase" means it will grow and become abundant. "One should suppress it well" means one should thoroughly restrain it.
"Root-and-destroy" means destroyed at the root. "With a harsh sound" means with a rough noise. "With a drum" means with a drum for execution.

93. “We shall cut off their heads”—meaning that for whomever we take even a handful of radishes, we shall cut off their heads in such a way that no one will even know they have been stolen. “Now what is this to us?
Even the king rises up and kills others in this manner!”—this was their intention. “They set about it” means they began. “Robbing the road.”
“Robbery on the road” means committing theft by standing upon the road.

94. “Certainly not, Your Majesty,” he thought: “If this king kills me because I have given my word ‘yes’ to the truth, I shall instead speak a falsehood. Out of fear of death, he said, “Certainly not, Your Majesty.
96. “Ekidaṃ”: here *idaṃ* is merely a particle; the meaning is “some beings. “Cārittaṃ” means misconduct.
Covetousness and ill will (*abhijjhā-byāpāda*) refer to covetousness and ill will. Wrong view (*micchā-diṭṭhi*) refers to the extremist and contrary views such as "there is no giving," and so forth.
Unrighteous passion (*adhamma-rāga*) is passion for inappropriate objects, such as one's mother, maternal aunt, paternal aunt, or maternal uncle’s wife.

Inordinate greed (*visama-lobha*) is excessive greed even toward objects that are appropriate for use. Unrighteous conduct (*micchā-dhamma*) is the desire and passion of men for men and of women for women.

Regarding "lack of filiality" (*amateyyatā*) and so forth: one who is beneficial to his mother is "filial" (*matteyyo*); the state of being such is "filiality" (*matteyyatā*), which is a name for proper conduct toward one's mother.
The absence of that, as well as its opposite, is "lack of filiality. The same method applies to "lack of paternal respect" (*apetteyyatā*) and the others.
"Not honoring the elders in the family" (*na kule jeṭṭhāpacāyitā*) refers to the state of not performing the act of honoring—that is, acting with humility—toward those who are senior in the family.
Commentary on the Time of the Ten-Year Life Span:
"Of these" (*imesaṃ*) means "of these [beings] at that time. "Worthy of being given to a husband" (*alaṃpateyyā*) means fit to be given as a wife to a husband.

"These flavors" (*imāni rasāni*) refers to the supreme flavors in the world. "They will shine exceedingly" (*atibyādippissanti*) means they will shine intensely; or rather, this is the reading: *ativiyādippissanti*.
“Even ‘wholesome’ will not exist” means that even the name “wholesome” will not exist;
the sense is that even a mere designation will not be discerned. “And they will be worthy of honor and praise” means they will be worthy of veneration and worthy of commendation.
At that time, it is said, people will say: “By such-and-such a person, a mother has been slain, a father has been slain, and recluses and brahmins have been deprived of life.”
Having been given away, she does not even know the existence of the elders in the family; "Oh, what a man!
they will say, honoring and praising him alone.
There will be no thought that "she was my mother," nor will there be a sense of reverence thinking "she is my mother. [This concerns] a woman in the household.
They will approach [the monk] with a lack of respect, speaking various kinds of improper talk as if they were [mere] friends.

The same principle applies to maternal aunts and the others. Here, "maternal aunt" (*mātucchā*) means the sister of one’s mother. "Maternal uncle’s wife" (*mātulānī*) means the wife of one’s maternal uncle.

"Preceptor’s wife" (*ācariyabhariyā*) means the wife of the preceptor who teaches the branches of craft (*sippāyatana*). "Wives of elders" (*garūnaṃ dārā*) refers to the wives of one’s younger father, elder father, and so forth.
Wife. "Sambheda" means mixing together, or the breaking of boundaries.
"Intense resentment will be present" means that a powerful anger will be present by way of repeated arising.
The other two terms are synonyms for this very same state. For anger is called "resentment" (āghāta) because it causes the mind to be resentful. One's own...
"Malice" (*byāpāda*) is so called because it intends harm toward the welfare and happiness of oneself and others; it is also called "corruption of mind" (*manopadosa*) because it defiles the mind.
"Intense murderous intent" (*tibbaṃ vadhakacittaṃ*) refers to the murderous mind directed toward killing another, even one who is dear.
To show the basis for this, it is said: "even toward one's mother or son," and so forth. "Of the hunter" (*māgavikassa*) means of the deer-trapper.

104. "A weapon-intervening aeon" (*satthantarakappa*) means an intervening aeon by means of weapons. It is the destruction of the world that occurs in the interval before reaching the aeon of dissolution (*saṃvaṭṭakappa*).
This intervening aeon is of three kinds: the weapon-intervening aeon, the disease-intervening aeon, and the famine-intervening aeon.
Among these, when beings abound in greed, there is a famine-intervening aeon; when they abound in delusion, there is a disease-intervening aeon.

The aeon of the interval between teachers (*satthantarakappa*) is for the purpose of causing corruption. Among these, those destroyed by the aeon of famine (*dubbhikkhantarakappa*) are mostly reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts (*pettivisaya*).

Why? Because of the strength of their attachment to food. Those destroyed by the aeon of disease (*rogantarakappa*) are mostly reborn in heaven (*sagga*). Why? Because they [think], "O, may such a disease not befall these beings!"
"A mind of loving-kindness arises. Most of those who have perished during an interval between teachers (a *satthantarakappa*) are reborn in hell.
Why? Because of their intense mutual animosity.
"The perception of deer" means the perception that "this is a deer, this is a deer. Sharp weapons will appear in their hands.
"Whatever they touch with their hands—even down to a blade of grass or a leaf—it shall indeed become a weapon.
'May we not harm anyone' means: may we not deprive even a single person of life. 'And may no one harm us' means:
may not even a single person deprive us of life. What if we were now... This is [the thought].
"The destruction of the world has arrived; it is not possible for two to survive staying in one place," thinking thus, they reflected in this way.
"A thicket of forest" (*vanagahana*) means a dense, inaccessible place consisting of grass, shrubs, creepers, and the like, which are reckoned as forests.
"A thicket of trees" (*rukkhagahana*) means a dense, inaccessible place consisting of trees. "An impassable river" (*nadīvidugga*) refers to [places] such as the islands within rivers...
A place difficult to traverse. "Mountainous and uneven" means uneven because of mountains, or a place that is rugged even among mountains.
"They will become like me" means they will make themselves similar to oneself through friendly conversation, saying: "O beings, as I live, so do you live."
Commentary on the Discourse on Increasing Life Span, Beauty, and So Forth (105).
*Āyataṃ* means "great. *Pāṇātipātā virameyyāma* means "we would desist from taking life.
They also recite *pāṇātipātaṃ virameyyāma*, in which case the meaning is "we would abandon taking life. *Vīsativassāyukā* means "having a life span of twenty years."
Their parents were abstainers from taking life; why, then, did their sons have a lifespan of only twenty years?
It was due to the purity of the field (*khetta-visuddhi*). For their parents were born with virtuous conduct (*sīlavanta*).

Thus, because they were nurtured within a womb of virtue, through this purity of the field they became long-lived. However, those among them who passed away and were reborn right there [in that same state] became long-lived by virtue of their own perfection of virtue.

"May we not be [afflicted]"—the sections beginning with "having a lifespan of forty years" and so forth are to be understood by way of those who abstain from taking what is not given and other such evils.
106. Commentary on the Arising of the Saṅkha King:
"Icchā" (desire) is the craving that arises in the form, "Give me food. "Aṇasana" (non-fasting) means the absence of fasting, the state of being non-expansive [in consumption].
*Ālasya* (laziness) means physical weakness that arises from having eaten food and produces a desire to lie down due to the effects of drowsiness after a meal.
*Jarā* refers to manifest old age. *Kukkuṭasampātikā* means "reaching as far as a cock's flight":
the flight of a cock is defined as flying up from the roof of one village and landing on the roof of another; those [distances] which exist [within reach] are called *kukkuṭasampātikā*.

There is also a reading, “*kukkuṭasampādikā*,” which means that in these [villages] there is a “roosting of cocks,” defined as the walking from one village to another on foot by means of cocks. Both of these readings indicate nothing other than dense habitation.
“It will be as if filled with Avīci” means it will be packed without any gaps, like the great hell of Avīci.
107. When it is said, “Bhikkhus, among humans with a lifespan of eighty thousand years, a Blessed One named Metteyya will arise in the world,” this is not stated by way of an increasing [lifespan].
For Buddhas do not arise when the lifespan is increasing; rather, they arise when it is decreasing.
Therefore, when that lifespan, having increased and reached the incalculable (asaṅkheyya), begins to decrease again—
"It will stand for eighty thousand years" means that it will arise at that time.
"It will endure" is said with reference to those who will wander about surrounding it. "The pillar" refers to the palace.
"Built by King Mahāpanāda" means it was caused to be built for his sake by the divine king Sakka, who dispatched the divine artisan Vissakamma, with the king acting as the cause.
It is said that formerly two father and son reed-workers had a leaf-hut constructed for a Paccekabuddha using reeds and udumbara wood;
having settled him there, they served him with the four requisites. Having passed away, they were reborn in the world of the gods.
Of them, the father remained in the world of the gods, while the son, falling from the world of the gods, [was born] to King Suruci.
He was reborn in the womb of Queen Sumedhā. He became a prince named Mahāpanāda.
Later, having had the royal parasol raised, he became King Mahāpanāda.
Then, by the power of his merit, Sakka, the King of the Devas, sent the divine son Vissakamma, saying, "Build a palace for the king. He constructed a palace for him twenty-five yojanas in height.
It was made of the seven precious gems and had a hundred stories. With reference to this, it is said in the Jātaka:
"That king was named Panāda, whose sacrificial post was of gold;
it was sixteen cubits across and, they say, a thousand spans in height."
With a thousand shafts and a hundred joints, adorned with banners and made of gold,
six thousand gandhabbas danced there in seven groups.
Thus it was then, Bhaddaji, just as you have described.
“I was Sakka at that time, your attendant.
Having lived there for as long as his lifespan lasted, that king passed away and was reborn in the world of the devas.

When he was reborn in that world of the devas, the palace drifted down with the current of the Great Ganges. At the place where its front staircase stood, there was a landing-place for the Payāga sacrifice.
A city was built there. In the place facing the stupa, there was a village called Koṭigāma.

Later, in the time of our Blessed One, that Nalakāra devaputta passed away from the world of the gods and, having been reborn as a human being in the path of men under the name of the merchant Bhaddaji, he went forth into homelessness in the presence of the Teacher and attained arahantship. On the day he crossed the Ganges by boat, for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus...
The account of how he showed him that palace should be told in detail. But why did this palace not disappear? It was because of the power of the other.

A son of good family who, having performed merit together with him, was reborn in the world of the devas, will in the future become a king named Saṅkha. That palace will arise for his use; therefore, it did not disappear.
108. "Having raised it up" means having caused that palace to be built. "Having dwelt in it" means having lived there.

"Having given it away and relinquished it" means having given that palace by way of a gift and having relinquished it by way of total renunciation without attachment. And to whom was it given in this manner?
To recluses and others. Therefore he said: "To recluses, brahmins, the poor, the destitute, the wayfarers, the beggars, and those who ask."
"Having given a gift. But how will he give one palace to many?
It is said that such a thought will arise in him: "Let this palace be broken apart.
It will then break into pieces. Without being attached to it, he will release it as a gift, saying: "Let whoever desires as much as they wish take that much."

Therefore it was said: “Having given a gift to the Blessed One Metteyya... [he] will dwell. By this much, the Blessed One has shown the connection for the skillful person who goes toward the round of existence (*vaṭṭagāmikusalassa*).
Now, showing the connection for the skillful person who goes toward the turning away from the round (*vivaṭṭagāmikusalassa*), he spoke again: “Monks, dwell as islands unto yourselves,” and so forth.
Commentary on the Discourse on Increasing a Monk’s Life-Span, etc.: 110. “This, monks, is for a monk in regard to life-span” (idaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno āyusmiṃ).

Monks, when I said to you, “You shall increase even in life-span,” therein “this is for a monk in regard to life-span” means “this is the cause of life-span. Therefore, by you, in regard to life-span...
He shows that those who desire to increase [their excellence] should develop these four bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*).
Regarding the phrase "in beauty": when I said to you, "You shall increase even in beauty," this is the cause for such beauty therein.

For in one who possesses virtue (*sīlavat*), both the physical beauty of the body increases by way of freedom from remorse (*avippaṭisāra*) and so forth, and the beauty of their qualities increases by way of their reputation.
Therefore, he shows that those who desire to increase in beauty must be endowed with virtue (*sīla*).

Regarding the phrase "in happiness": when I said to you, "You shall increase even through happiness," this refers here to the various kinds of meditative bliss (*jhānasukha*), such as the joy and happiness born of seclusion (*vivekaja-pītisukha*).
Therefore, those who desire to increase in happiness should develop these four meditative absorptions (*jhāna*).

Regarding "wealth": when I said to you, "You shall increase by means of wealth," this refers to the eleven benefits such as a comfortable bed and so forth, which bring about non-repulsiveness for immeasurable beings—the wealth of the divine abodes (brahmavihāra) that has radiated throughout all directions.
Therefore, those of you who desire to increase through wealth must develop these divine abodes.
"As to what I said to you, 'You shall increase by strength,' this refers to the strength known as the fruit of Arahantship that arises at the conclusion of the destruction of the taints (*āsava*).
Therefore, you who desire to increase by strength must apply yourselves to the attainment of Arahantship.
'As to this, monks, the power of Māra'—this refers to the Devaputta-Māra, the Māra of Death, and the Māra of Defilements."
"Power that is difficult to overcome and difficult to attain—thus I do not see even a single other power in the world comparable to it.
Even that [other] power is surpassed, overcome, and overwhelmed by this very power of the fruit of Arahantship. Therefore, he shows that 'herein alone should effort be made.

Thus, 'this is merit'—meaning that even this supramundane merit increases until the destruction of the taints (āsava)—[he establishes] the connection to the wholesome states leading to the turning away from the round of existence."
Bringing it to completion, he concluded the teaching with the pinnacle of Arahantship.
At the conclusion of the sutta, twenty thousand bhikkhus attained Arahantship, and eighty-four thousand living beings drank the drink of the Deathless.
Thus ends the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya.
The commentary on the Cakkavatti Sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Aggañña Sutta:
The commentary on Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja.
111. "Thus have I heard" refers to the Aggañña Sutta. Herein, this is the explanation of the words not [already] clear: "In the Eastern Park, at the Mansion of Migāra’s Mother.

Regarding this, the following is the sequential narrative. In the past, at the end of a hundred thousand aeons ago, a certain female lay devotee invited the Blessed One Padumuttara and, having given alms to a hundred thousand monks headed by the Buddha, [addressed] the Blessed One...
Prostrating at his feet, she made this aspiration: "In the future, may I be the foremost attendant of a Buddha such as you.

After wandering through the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, during the time of our Blessed One, she was born from the womb of Queen Sumanā in the household of the merchant Dhananjaya—the son of the merchant Meṇḍaka—in the city of Bhaddiya.
She took rebirth. At the time of her birth, they gave her the name Visākhā.
When the Blessed One arrived at the city of Bhaddiya, she went out to meet him along with five hundred female slaves; at that very first sight, she became a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*).
Later, she went to the house of Puṇṇavaḍḍhana Kumāra, the son of the merchant Migāra, in Sāvatthī. There—
The merchant Migāra placed her in the position of his mother; therefore, she is called Migāramātā.
As she was going to her husband’s family, her father had a great jeweled ornament called Mahālatāpiḷandhana made.
In that ornament, four *nāḷis* of gold were used, eleven *nāḷis* of pearls, twenty-two *nāḷis* of coral, and thirty-three [of gems].
...and *nāḷi*s. Thus, it reached completion with these and other seven kinds of gems.
When fastened upon her head, it hung down as far as the back of her feet. Only a woman capable of bearing the strength of five elephants could carry it.
Later, having become the foremost attendant of the One Possessing Ten Powers (*dasabala*), she gave away that ornament.
While having a monastery built for the Blessed One at a cost of nine crores, she constructed a palace on a plot of ground measuring one *karīsa*.
On its upper floor there were five hundred chambers, and on the lower floor likewise five hundred; thus it was adorned with a thousand chambers.
Thinking, "A bare palace does not shine," she surrounded it with five hundred and fifty dwellings.
He caused five hundred small palaces and five hundred long halls to be built. The festival for the monastery reached completion in four months.

Just as there was no one else in the female form comparable to Visākhā in her relinquishment of wealth for the Buddha’s teaching, so too there was no one else in the male form comparable to Anāthapiṇḍika; for he [spent] forty-five koṭis...
Having given this away, she had the Jetavana Mahāvihāra built on the southern side of Sāvatthī at a site similar to the Mahāvihāra of Anurādhapura.
Visākhā had the Pubbārāma built on the eastern side of Sāvatthī at a site similar to the monastery of Uttarā Devī.
Out of compassion for these two families, the Blessed One dwelt in dependence upon Sāvatthī.
He lived in a fixed residence in these two monasteries: he spent one rainy season in Jeta’s Grove and one in the Eastern Park.
At that time, however, the Blessed One was dwelling in the Eastern Park; therefore it is said, “in the Eastern Park, in the Mansion of Migāra’s Mother.
“Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja” refers to the novice Vāseṭṭha and the novice Bhāradvāja. “Were staying among the bhikkhus” means...
They were neither observing the probation for heretics (*titthiyaparivāsa*) nor the probation for an offense (*āpattiparivāsa*);
rather, they lived there because they were less than ten years old and desired the status of a monk. For this very reason, it says: "desiring the status of a monk.
Both of them were born into prominent brahmin families of great wealth, possessing forty crores each, were masters of the three Vedas, and [had studied] the Vāseṭṭha Sutta of the Majjhima Nikāya.
Having heard [the teaching], they went for refuge; having heard the *Tevijja-sutta*, they went forth and now dwell here desiring the state of a bhikkhu.

"He walks in the open air" means that in the shadow of the palace—which extends north and south—at the eastern side of the palace, he walks as if it were a golden pinnacle a hundred ratana high being drawn along by mechanical ropes.
Radiant with the six-colored rays of a Buddha streaming through the path of the wind, he walked back and forth.
"They followed him walking" means that, having raised their hands in reverential salutation and with bodies bowed low, they walked along following him.
He addressed Vāseṭṭha because he was the wisest among them and knew what should be accepted and what should be rejected. Therefore...
He addressed them: "Tumhe khvattha" means "you indeed are. "Brāhmaṇajacca" means those born of the brahmin caste.

"Brāhmaṇakulīnā" means those of noble birth among the brahmins, endowed with a [good] family lineage. "Brāhmaṇakulā" means from a brahmin family; the meaning is, having left behind a brahmin family endowed with wealth and so forth.
"Na akkosanti" means they do not revile [him] by means of the tenfold grounds for abuse.

“They do not revile” means they do not revile with various kinds of disparaging speech. Thus the Blessed One, although he already knew that “these brahmins are abusing and reviling these novices,” nevertheless asked the question. Why?
Because, if he did not ask them first, they would not speak; and since no discourse can arise unless it is spoken, he asked for the purpose of initiating the discourse.
"Taggha" is a particle used for emphatic affirmation; it means, "Indeed, Bhante, the brahmins revile and abuse us.
"Attarūpāya" means "suitable to themselves. "Paripuṇṇāya" means "fulfilled," having been completed by repeatedly adding words and syllables according to their own preference.
"No aparipuṇṇāya" means "not incomplete," that is, not interrupted but proceeding without break.
But why did the brahmins revile these novices? Because they were without support.
For these novices were the sons of preeminent brahmins, masters of the three Vedas, renowned and highly esteemed among the brahmins of Jambudīpa;
because they had gone forth, other sons of brahmins also went forth. Then the brahmins thought, "We have been left without a standing."
Because of this lack of a secure foundation, even at the village gates or within the villages, people would see them and revile them, saying such things as those recorded in the Canon:

"You have broken the tradition of the brahmins! You wander about greedy for flavors, following after that shaveling ascetic," as well as saying, "The brahmin caste alone is the best caste," and so forth. Even while they were thus reviling them, the novices—
Without harboring anger or malice, they simply reported to the Blessed One when asked:
"Truly, Bhante, the brahmins revile and abuse us. Then the Blessed One, wishing to ask about the manner of their abuse, asked them:
"In what way, however? As they explained it, they said: "The brahmins, Bhante... and so forth.
In that context, they show that regarding the designation of birth, clan, and so forth, the Brahmin alone is the best;
they say that the other three castes are inferior and base. "White" means pale; "black" means dark.
"They are purified" means they are purified in the designation of birth, clan, and so forth. "Sons of Brahmā" refers to the Great Brahmā.
Sons: "Orasā" means born from the breast; having dwelt in the breast, they emerged from the mouth, or alternatively, they are "orasā" because they were nurtured while being held against the breast.
"Brahmajāti" means born from Brahmā. "Brahmanimmitā" means created by Brahmā.
"Brahmadāyādā" means heirs of Brahmā. "Hīnamattha vaṇṇaṃ ajjhupagatā" means they have indeed entered upon a lowly state.
"Muṇḍaka" and "samaṇaka" are spoken of by those who revile and loathe them; it does not refer merely to the state of being shaven-headed or the mere outward appearance of an ascetic.
"Ibbha" refers to householders. "Kaṇha" means black ones. "Bandhu" refers to those who are kinsmen of Māra, belonging to Māra’s faction.
"Pādāpacca" means those who are descendants from the feet of Mahābrahmā; the intended meaning is that they were born from his feet.
114. “*Taggha vo*, Vāseṭṭha, *brāhmaṇā porāṇaṃ assarantā evamāhaṃsu*”: here, *vo* is merely a particle, or it is a genitive case;
the meaning is “of you, O Brāhmaṇas. *Porāṇaṃ* means the ancient *Aggañña* account of the origin of the world and the lineage of conduct. *Assarantā* means not forgetting. This is what is meant:
“Certainly, Vāseṭṭha, the Brāhmaṇas [have spoken thus] regarding the ancient...”
"It is said that those who do not recollect and do not know the origin of the world speak thus.

The passage beginning with "But they are seen," and so forth, was spoken for the purpose of refuting their tenets. In this context, "brāhmaṇī" refers to women brought into families through marriage for the sake of obtaining sons by Brāhmaṇas;
such women are indeed seen. Furthermore, at another time, these very women...
They are those who have reached their season; the meaning is that they have produced flowers [in the womb].
"Pregnant" means having conceived a fetus. "Giving birth" means producing sons and daughters. "Nursing" means suckling children with breast milk.
"Being born from the womb" means being born through the urinary passage of Brahmin women. "Thus they say" means they speak thus. How so? "The Brahmin alone is the best..."

“Complexion... [and so on] ...heirs of Brahmā. If, however, that word of theirs were true, the womb of the brahmin women would have to be the chest of Mahābrahmā, and the urinary passage of the brahmin women would have to be the mouth of Mahābrahmā;
yet this is not to be viewed in such a way. Therefore he said: “And they misrepresent the Brahmas,” and so forth.
The Explanation of the Purity of the Four Castes:
At this point, having uttered this "mouth-sealing" statement— "Let it not be said that we lived in the breast of Mahābrahmā and emerged from his mouth"—
the four castes once again proceeded by undertaking wholesome qualities.
He spoke the words beginning with “Vāseṭṭha, these four castes... for the purpose of showing those who are purified.
“Designated as unwholesome” means they are reckoned as unwholesome, or they constitute a portion of the unwholesome. This method applies everywhere.

“Not fit for the noble state” means they are incapable of attaining the state of an Ariya. “Dark” means naturally black. “With dark result” means their result is also dark, which is to say, suffering. This applies even to a khattiya.
"Those [same] two [types of persons] exist even among the khattiyas. "In some" means in one instance. This method applies everywhere.
"Bright" (*sukka*) means pure due to the absence of defilements. "Having bright fruition" (*sukkavipāka*) means that their fruition is also bright; such is the meaning. 116.
"While both are occurring mixed together" means while both are occurring having become intermingled and combined.
"In which two? In black and white phenomena—those censured by the wise and those praised by the wise.

"Regarding this, the brahmins say thus" means that even while existing amidst these black and white phenomena, the brahmins say such things as, "The brahmin caste alone is the best," and so forth. The wise do not approve of that which they say.
The meaning is that those who are wise in the world do not rejoice in this, nor do they praise it. For what reason?
This is the summary of the meaning beginning with the words, "Of these, Vāseṭṭha... Why is it said that they do not approve of it?
Because, among these four castes, whichever bhikkhu is an arahant... [as before] ...liberated through right knowledge, he is declared their chief.
And they are not of such a nature; therefore, the wise do not approve of them.

Furthermore, regarding the terms beginning with "Arahant": one is an *arahant* because of being far from (*āraka*) the defilements and for other such reasons. One is a "destroyer of the taints" (*khīṇāsava*) because of the destruction of the taints (*āsavas*).
The seven types of trainees (*sekkhā*) and the noble worldlings (*puthujjanakalyāṇaka*) are said to dwell in the holy life (*brahmacariya*). This...

But "one who has completed the residence" (*vutthavāso*) means one who has lived [the holy life]. "One who has done what was to be done" (*katakaraṇīyo*) means that the task consisting of the full comprehension of the four truths by means of the four paths has been accomplished.

"One who has laid down the burden" (*ohitabhāro*) means that both the burden of the defilements (*kilesa-bhāra*) and the burden of the aggregates (*khandha-bhāra*) have been set down. "Set down" (*ohita*) means abandoned.
"The goal of one's own welfare" (*sadattha*) refers to a beautiful goal or one's own goal; "one who has attained his own goal" (*anuppattasadattho*) means one by whom that goal has been reached.
The fetter of existence (*bhava-saṃyojana*) is said to be craving; one for whom that has been completely destroyed is "one whose fetter of existence is destroyed.
"Liberated through perfect knowledge" means liberated by knowing correctly through the cause and reason.

"In this generation" (*janetasmin*) means in this generation, that is, in this world. "Both in this very life and in the future life" means in this present state of being and in a future state of being.
117. *Anantarā* means those who are without interval; the meaning is those who are similar to one’s own family. *Anuyuttā* means those who exercise authority.
*Nipaccakāraṃ* refers to the elder ones showing respectful service (*nipaccakāra*), while the younger ones perform such acts as salutation and so forth.
In this context, *sāmīcikammaṃ* is the appropriate action, such as performing the respective duties and so on.
118. “Fixed” means firmly established and immovably situated. For whom, then, does such faith exist? For the stream-enterer. For he possesses fixed faith;

even if his head were being cut off with a sword, he would not say, “The Buddha is not the Buddha,” “the Dhamma is not the Dhamma,” or “the Saṅgha is not the Saṅgha. He is one whose faith is firmly established, like Sūrambaṭṭha.
It is said that after hearing the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, he became a stream-enterer and returned home.
Then Māra, having conjured up a form of the Buddha adorned with the thirty-two supreme marks, stood at his house door and sent word: “The Teacher has arrived.
Sūrambaṭṭha thought: “I have just now come from hearing the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher; what could this be?”
Having approached and paid homage with the perception that it was the Teacher, he stood there. Māra said: "Ambaṭṭha, as for what I told you—that 'form is impermanent...
[and so on]... consciousness is impermanent'—that was ill-spoken.
For I spoke thus without having reflected. Therefore, you should take it that 'form is permanent... [and so on]... consciousness is permanent. He thought:
“It is impossible that the Buddhas would say anything without having reflected upon it or without direct knowledge;
surely this Māra has come here for the purpose of creating a rift between us. Then he said to him, “Are you Māra?
He was unable to speak a lie and confessed, “Yes, I am Māra. “For what purpose have you come? “To shake your faith.”
He said: “Kanha Pāpima, you stand there alone; even a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand Māras like you are unable to shake my faith.
Faith that has arrived by way of the Path is firm; it is immovable like Sineru established upon the stone earth.
What business do you have here? Having said this, he snapped his fingers. Unable to remain, he [fell] right there.
It disappeared. It is with reference to such faith that this was said:
"established. "Rooted and settled" means: because the root of the path has arisen, it is settled by means of that root of the path.
"Firm" means stable. "Unshakable" means: like a well-planted pillar, it cannot be moved by anyone. This is its [meaning].
"It is fit to say" means that it is appropriate for that noble disciple to say such things as: "I am the legitimate son of the Blessed One.
For he is the Blessed One’s son because he was born upon the plane of the noble ones in dependence upon the Blessed One.
He is a "legitimate son" (orasa) because, having dwelt in the Blessed One’s breast, he was established in the paths and fruits by way of the sound of the Dhamma issuing from His mouth.
He is "born. Because he is born from the noble Dhamma and fashioned by the noble Dhamma, he is "born of the Dhamma" (dhammaja) and "fashioned by the Dhamma" (dhammanimmita).

He is "an heir to the Dhamma" (dhammadāyāda) because he is worthy of the inheritance of the ninefold supramundane Dhamma. Regarding the question, "For what reason?", this refers to the statement made after saying, "I am the son of the Blessed One," namely, that he is "born of the Dhamma and fashioned by the Dhamma.
If one asks why that was said, the Teacher now explains its meaning by saying, "Because of the Tathāgata... and so forth.

In this context, why is the Tathāgata called the "Dhamma-body" (*dhammakāya*)? Because the Tathāgata, having contemplated the word of the Buddha contained in the Three Piṭakas with his heart, brought it forth through speech.

Therefore, because his body consists of the Dhamma, his body is indeed the Dhamma. Thus, since the Dhamma is his body, he is the "Dhamma-body. Precisely because he is the Dhamma-body, he is the "Brahma-body," for the Dhamma is supreme in its ultimate sense.
It is called "Brahmā. "Dhammabhūta" means having the nature of *dhamma*. Precisely because he has become *dhamma*, he has become Brahmā.

119. Having thus far shown the doctrine of the supreme annihilator, the Blessed One now spoke the passage beginning with "There comes a time, Vāseṭṭha," in order to show the doctrine of the supreme annihilator by another method as well.
In that regard, the discourse on the contraction and expansion [of the world] is found in the *Brahmajāla Sutta*.
[The details are] already explained. "Coming to this state" means they come to this human existence (*itthabhāva*).
They are called "mind-made" (*manomaya*) because even when being reborn here in the human world, they are born spontaneously (*opapātika*) and are produced by mind alone.
Just as in the Brahma-world, here too their function of nutriment is accomplished by rapture (*pīti*) alone; thus they are "rapture-feeders" (*pītibhakkha*).
In this same manner, the terms "self-luminous" and so forth should also be understood.
Commentary on the Manifestation of the Earth of Taste (Rasapathavipātubhāvavaṇṇanā):
"Ekodakībhūtaṃ" means that the entire world-system (cakkavāḷa) had become one single mass of water. "Andhakāro" means darkness. "Andhakāratimisa" means the pitch-blackness of darkness.
Thick darkness is that which causes blindness by obstructing the arising of visual consciousness.
It settled evenly and spread out all around. "Of hot milk" means of hot milk.
"Endowed with color" means endowed with color; for its color was like that of a *kaṇikāra* flower. "Endowed with fragrance" means endowed with fragrance.
It wafts a divine fragrance. "Endowed with flavor" means it is perfected in taste, as if divine seeds had been added to it.
"Honey made by small flies" means honey produced by tiny bees. "Unstinging" means faultless, being devoid of the stingers of flies.
"Of a greedy nature" means one whose very character is greed; he was greedy even in the immediately preceding eon. "Ambho!"—he said this out of wonder. "What is this? [he asked].
"It will be"—the meaning is: "Its color and its fragrance will be pleasing; but what will its taste be like?
Whatever greed arose therein, he tasted the earth of flavor with his finger; having taken it with his finger, he placed it on the tip of his tongue.

"It covered" means that as soon as it was placed on the tip of the tongue, it spread over the seven thousand flavor-carrying channels and remained there, being pleasing. "And craving descended upon him" means that craving arose in him regarding that [taste].
**Commentary on the Manifestation of the Moon, Sun, and Other Phenomena** 121.

“They began to consume food by making mouthfuls” means that they began to consume it by dividing it into morsels and cutting it into individual lumps. “The moon and the sun” refers to the moon (*candimā*) and the sun (*sūriyo*).
“Became manifest” means they appeared. But which of them appeared first? Which one dwells in what? What is the size of each? Which is above?
Who moves faster? How many paths do they have? How do they travel? And over how great a distance do they provide light?
Both appear together, yet the sun becomes visible first.
For those beings, as their own radiance had vanished, darkness had set in; terrified and trembling, they thought, "It would indeed be wonderful if light were to appear!"
They thought thus. Then the solar disc rose, inspiring courage in the great multitude;
for that very reason, its name became "Sūriya" (the Sun). When that [disc] had made light for that day and set, darkness returned once more.
They thought, "How wonderful it would be if another light were to arise! Then, their desire—
Having recognized the moon-disk, he rose up; for that very reason, his name became "Canda" (the Moon).
Among them, Canda dwells within a palace made of jewels; it is encircled on the outside with silver, and both are cool.
Suriya dwells within a palace made of gold; it is encircled on the outside with crystal, and both are warm.

In length, the moon is forty-nine *yojanas*; in circumference, it is one hundred and fifty *yojanas* less three. The sun is fifty *yojanas* in length and one hundred and fifty *yojanas* in circumference.
The moon is below and the sun is above; between them there is one *yojana*. From the lower limit of the moon to the upper limit of the sun, there is one hundred *yojanas*.
The moon moves slowly in its direct course, but swiftly across the transverse path. On both sides, the lunar mansions and stars move along.
Just as a cow approaches her calf, the moon approaches each respective constellation; however, the constellations do not abandon their own positions.
The sun’s direct movement is swift, while its transverse movement is slow.
From the full moon day of the dark fortnight, on the first day of the waxing moon (pāṭipada), it moves away from the lunar disc by a hundred thousand yojanas.
Then the moon appears like a mere streak. On the second day of the lunar fortnight, it recedes by one hundred thousand [yojanas];
in this manner, until the Uposatha day, it continues to recede by a hundred thousand each time. Then, having gradually increased in size, the moon becomes full on the Uposatha day.
Again, on the first day of the waxing moon (pāṭipada), it runs forward and takes up another hundred thousand yojanas. On the second day...
"By the hundred thousand"—in this way, until the day of the Uposatha, it runs and seizes [the moon] by the hundreds of thousands.
Then, the moon gradually diminishes until on the Uposatha day it is no longer visible at all.
With the sun above and the moon below, the lunar disk is covered as if a small vessel were placed inside a large bowl.
At midday, the moon’s shadow is not perceived, just like the shadow of a house.
When its shadow is not perceived, it itself is not seen even by those standing at a distance, like a lamp in the daytime.
As for the question "How many paths do they have?", there are three paths: the horse path (ajavīthi), the elephant path (nāgavīthi), and the ox path (govīthi).
In that regard, the water is repulsive to goats, but pleasing to elephant-kings;

for cattle, it is comfortable because of the balance between cold and heat. Therefore, when the moon and sun enter the path of the horses (*ajavīthi*), not even a single drop of rain falls from the sky.
When they enter the path of the elephants (*nāgavīthi*), the sky pours down as if it were broken open. When they enter the path of the cattle (*govīthi*)—
When they ascend, the seasonal equilibrium is established. For six months the moon and sun move outside of Sineru, and for six months they move within it.

Indeed, in the month of Āsāḷha, they move near Sineru. Thereafter, having moved outward for two months, they pass through the center in the first month of Kattika. From there, they turn toward the Cakkavāḷa.
Having traveled for three months by way of the vicinity of the world-system (cakkavāḷa), they emerge again and travel through the middle during the month of Citta;
then, for two months, they leap toward Sineru, and in Āsāḷha, they travel once more by way of the vicinity of Sineru.
To what extent do they illuminate? They illuminate the three continents simultaneously. How so?
For when it is sunrise on this island, it is midday in Pūrvavideha, sunset in Uttarakuru, and midnight in Aparagoyāna.
When it is sunrise in Pūrvavideha, it is midday in Uttarakuru, sunset in Aparagoyāna, and midnight here.
When it is sunrise in Uttarakuru, it is midday in Aparagoyāna...
Here it is the time of setting; in Pubbavideha it is mid-watch. In the island of Aparagoyāna it is the time of rising;
here it is midday; in Pubbavideha it is the time of setting; and in Uttarakuru it is mid-watch.
"The constellations and star-forms" refers to the constellations beginning with Kattika, as well as all other star-forms, together with the moon and sun.
They appeared simultaneously. "Night and day": from the setting of the sun until the rising of the dawn was night;
from the rising of the dawn until the setting of the sun was day—thus night and day became known.
Then, fifteen nights were a half-month, and two half-months were a month—thus months and half-months became known. Then...
"Four months are a season; three seasons are a year"—thus the seasonal years became known.
122. "And the fading away of beauty": this refers to the state of beauty's deterioration. "On account of their pride regarding beauty":

on account of the pride that arose with respect to their beauty. "Of those whose nature was prone to pride and arrogance": of those whose character was such that pride and arrogance arose again and again.
"On the earth of flavors" means on the earth that received the name "flavors" because it possessed excellent flavor.
"They extolled" means they spoke in praise. "Oh, the flavor! means, "Alas! Our sweet flavor has disappeared.
"They proclaim the primordial beginning" refers to the discourse on the lineage of the world's origin. "They follow after" means they pursue it.
123. *Bhūmipappaṭakapātubhāvādivaṇṇanā* (The Explanation of the Appearance of the Earth-Crust, etc.):
"In this very way it appeared" means it arose having become such; it arose like a layer of dried mud when the water in a pond has been cut off.

124. *Padālatā*: A certain auspicious creeper with a sweet flavor. *Kalambukā*: A reed. "Ahuvata no" means: "Alas, we had a *padālatā* with a sweet flavor. "Ahāyi vata no" means: "Alas, it has now vanished from us."

125. "Grown without being cultivated" means it grows on ground that has not even been tilled. "Free from husks" means it is without the outer casing. "Free from powder" means it is without the fine dust.
"Fragrant" means it wafts a divine scent. "Having rice as its fruit" means it bears fruit that is perfectly pure and white rice.
"Ripe and immediately regrown" means that what is gathered in the evening is ripe by morning, and having ripened, it grows back again.
The place where it was grasped does not appear as it did before. "The original form does not appear" means that, having become unrecognizable, it appears without being diminished.
This is the explanation of the manifestation of the female and male signs and so forth.

126. "And for a woman": this refers to one who was previously a human being at the time of being a woman; her female characteristics (*itthiliṅga*) manifest, whereas previously, as a man, his male characteristics manifested.
For indeed, when a woman attains a male existence, she does so by gradually fulfilling the factors that serve as conditions for masculinity.
When a man attains a female existence, it is by depending upon sexual misconduct.
He obtains it. At that time, however, the female characteristic appeared for the woman by nature, and the male characteristic appeared for the man.
"Gazing upon" means while they were gazing upon or looking at one another. "Fever" means the fever of lust (*rāgapariḷāha*).
"The best" means ashes. "Being carried away" means being led away.
127. "That which was agreed upon as non-Dhamma" means that throwing dust and so forth was agreed upon as non-Dhamma.
"But now that which is agreed upon as Dhamma" means that this is now agreed upon as Dhamma; they take it up as Dhamma and carry it out.
For instance, among certain people in the countryside, women who were quarreling said, "Why do you speak? You did not even get so much as a lump of cow dung!"
They say: "To be drunk" means to be used. "Making a store" means having made a store.
"The cutting-off was seen" means that the place where it had been cut appeared as a mere stump. "In clusters" means that in each place they were like bundles tied together, forming thickets.

128. “We shall establish a boundary” means we shall establish a *sīmā*. “For indeed, [he] who” means for whoever. “They struck with their hands” means they struck with their hands because he did not accept their words after three times. “Starting from that” means making that the beginning. 130.
“One should criticize what is to be criticized” means one should proclaim what is to be proclaimed; “one should cast out what is to be cast out,” “one should remove what is to be removed.”
"He would take away" is what is meant. "Whosoever among them is a being" means whichever being among them.
But who is he? Our Bodhisatta. "We will give you a share of the rice": "We will bring from each of our fields a measure after measure and give you your share of the rice;
you need not do any work at all; you may remain in the position of our elder."
131. A syllable is produced; it is a designation (*saṅkhā*), a convention (*samaññā*), a description (*paññatti*), a worldly usage (*vohāro*) that has arisen.

"Khattiya" is what they call him for a second time as a syllable, and not merely as a syllable; moreover, they performed his consecration with three [types of] sprinklings because he was the lord of the fields (*khettasāmī*).
He "delights" (*rañjeti*) means he gladdens and pleases. "By the foremost" (*aggaññena*) means by that which is known as the foremost, or [that which is] at the head.
"By means of what was known, at the time of his appearance in the world, there was an arising.
[End of] the commentary on the *Brāhmaṇamaṇḍala* and so forth. 132.
"Without embers, without smoke": because there is nothing left to be cooked and eaten, they are free from smoke and embers. "With pestles laid aside."
“With pestles fallen” means because there was nothing left to pound and cook. “Seeking food” means searching for rice porridge and alms-food by way of wandering for alms.
“When people saw him” means when those people, having seen him...
“Unable to endure” means being unable to bear it or being incapable [of doing so]. “Making books” means composing and teaching the three Vedas.
“They dwell” (*acchanti*) means they reside; there is also a reading “they perform” (*acchenti*), which has the same meaning.
Regarding “esteemed as inferior”: Vāseṭṭha, at that time, the fact that “they memorize the mantras or teach the mantras” was esteemed as inferior.
But now, “they memorize so many mantras or teach so many mantras” has become esteemed as superior. “Of the brahmin circle” (*brāhmaṇamaṇḍalassa*) means of the assembly of brahmins.

133. "Having undertaken sexual intercourse" means having engaged in sexual intercourse. "They applied themselves to ignoble occupations" means they applied themselves to occupations such as cattle-herding or trade, which were common and widespread.

134. "Suddā, suddā" (Outcasts, outcasts): by that cruel conduct and vile behavior, they go quickly and repeatedly to a state that is contemptible; the meaning is that they perish. "Ahu kho" means "indeed there was. 135. "Reproaching his own duty":
[he realized] that one cannot be purified merely by raising a white umbrella.
Thus he censures his own status as a kshatriya. This same method applies everywhere.
By the words, "Vāseṭṭha, by these four circles," he shows this: "There is no such thing as a separate 'circle of ascetics' (samaṇamaṇḍala).
Since it is not possible to be purified by birth, purification comes through one's own respective right practice. Therefore, by these..."
"The circle of recluses arises from four circles. These circles follow the circle of recluses;
and following it, they follow only by means of the Dhamma, not by means of non-Dhamma.
For it is by coming to the circle of recluses and fulfilling right practice that they attain purity."
Commentary on the Discourse on Bad Conduct, etc. 136.
Now, demonstrating that one cannot be purified by birth alone, but is purified only through right practice, the Blessed One began his teaching with the words, "Vāseṭṭha, even a khattiya...
In this context, the phrase "on account of undertaking actions based on wrong view" means:
"By reason of the undertaking of kamma through wrong view," or "by reason of the undertaking of kamma characterized by wrong view.
(137) "One who does both": this means one who at times performs wholesome deeds and at times unwholesome deeds; thus, he is a doer of both. "He experiences pleasure and pain":
there is no such thing as the simultaneous giving of the result of both [types of kamma] in a single moment. However, for one by whom much unwholesome kamma has been performed...
When wholesome karma is weak, one is reborn by depending on that wholesome karma into a kshatriya family or a brahmin family.
Then, unwholesome karma may cause one to be one-eyed, hunchbacked, or a cripple.
Such a person is unworthy of sovereignty, or even when consecrated, is unable to enjoy wealth in such a state. At the time of another’s death—
Those two types of kamma—wholesome and unwholesome—stand before him like two powerful wrestlers. Of these two, the unwholesome is stronger;
it overcomes the wholesome and causes rebirth in the animal realm. Yet even that wholesome kamma is to be experienced in the course of existence (*pavattivedanīya*).
Consequently, they make him an auspicious elephant, or an auspicious horse, or an auspicious bull. He [enjoys] prosperity...
He experiences it. It is with reference to this that it was said: "he is one who experiences pleasure and pain.
138. Regarding the "seven factors of enlightenment":
by way of their divisions, such as the "four foundations of mindfulness" and so forth, there are seven factors of enlightenment.
But in sequence, it is by following the cultivation of the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyā dhammā).

"Following cultivation" means having pursued cultivation; the sense is "having practiced. "He attains final Nibbāna" means he attains final Nibbāna through the extinction of the defilements (kilesa-parinibbāna).
Thus, the Blessed One, having shown and turned back the four castes, [established] only one who has realized the Four Truths and whose taints are exhausted.
Having made him the best among gods and humans, he showed him [to Vāseṭṭha].

Now, in order to strengthen that same point by showing the words of Brahmā himself, who is honored by the world, he spoke the passage beginning with, "Of these four castes, Vāseṭṭha... The passage beginning with "By Brahmā also... is found in the Ambaṭṭha Sutta.

It has been explained in detail. Thus, by this line of discourse, the Blessed One demonstrated precisely the doctrine that cuts off the claim to being "best," brought the sutta to a conclusion, and completed the teaching with the pinnacle of Arahantship.

"The Vāseṭṭhas and Bhāradvājas were uplifted"—for the novice monks Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja, too, were glad at heart and joyful, exclaiming, "Excellent! Excellent! in response to the Blessed One’s speech.
They rejoiced. By reflecting upon and contemplating this very sutta, they attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
Thus ends the commentary on the Aggañña Sutta in the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, the commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya.
5. Commentary on the *Sampasādanīya Sutta*:
The Commentary on the *Sāriputta-Sīhanāda*. 141.
"Thus have I heard" refers to the *Sampasādanīya Sutta*. Herein, this is the commentary on the words not [already] explained: "At Nāḷandā."
"In Nālandā" means in the city of that name; having made that city his alms-resort village. "In the Ambavana of the Cloth-Merchant" means in the mango grove of the cloth-merchant merchant-prince.

It is said that this was his pleasure garden. Having heard the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma, he became devoted to the Blessed One and, having constructed a monastery for the Blessed One adorned with huts, caves, pavilions, and so forth in that garden, he offered it to him.
Thus that monastery came to be known as “Pāvārika’s Mango Grove,” just like Jīvaka’s Mango Grove; the meaning is that he was dwelling in that Pāvārika Mango Grove.
He said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, I am so confident in the Blessed One.
Why did he say this? It was for the purpose of making known the joy that had arisen within himself.

In this regard, this is the sequential account: it is said that on that day, the Elder, having attended to his person at an early hour, dressed himself in well-washed robes, and taking his bowl and outer robe, entered Nāḷandā for alms—inspiring faith in gods and humans with his graceful deportment such as dignified gait—and promoting the welfare and happiness of the inhabitants of Nāḷandā;
and having returned from the alms-round after his meal, he sat down.
Having gone to the monastery and performed the duties toward the Teacher, he entered the fragrant chamber while the Teacher was inside;

then, having paid homage to the Teacher, he went to his own daytime resting place. There, after performing the duties toward his co-residents and pupils, and when they had departed, he swept the daytime resting place, spread out his leather mat, and washed his hands and feet with water from his water-pot.
Having made it cool, he sat cross-legged in the triple-jointed posture, set a limit for his time, and entered the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
When he emerged from that attainment according to the predetermined time, he began to recollect his own virtues.
As he was thus recollecting his virtues, virtue came into range of his awareness; following that in sequence, concentration, wisdom, and liberation [came into range].
Knowledge and vision of liberation; the first jhāna, the second jhāna, the third jhāna, the fourth jhāna;

the attainment of the base of infinite space, the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness, the attainment of the base of nothingness, the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;

knowledge of insight, knowledge of the mind-made body, knowledge of the various supernormal powers, knowledge of the divine ear, knowledge of penetration of minds, and knowledge of recollection of past lives.
The knowledge of the divine eye... [and so on] ...the path of stream-entry, the fruit of stream-entry...

[and so on] ...the path of arhatship, the fruit of arhatship, the analytical knowledge of meaning, the analytical knowledge of phenomena, the analytical knowledge of language, the analytical knowledge of eloquence, and the knowledge of the perfections of a disciple.
From this point onward, at the feet of the Buddha Anomadassi, during the period exceeding one hundred thousand aeons beyond an incalculable eon (asaṅkhyeyya)...
Beginning with the initial resolution, as he recollected his own virtues, those qualities remained present before him until he reached the seat where he was sitting.
Thus, as the Elder recollected his own virtues, he was unable to perceive either their measure or their limit.
He thought: "Even for me, a disciple established in partial knowledge, there is no measure or limit to my virtues."
"But as for me, regarding the Teacher under whom I have gone forth, what kind of qualities does he possess?
Thus he began to recollect the qualities of the One Possessing the Ten Powers.

Relying upon the Blessed One’s virtue, relying upon his concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, and relying upon the four foundations of mindfulness and the four right efforts...
Relying upon the four bases of psychic power, the four paths, the four fruits, the four analytical knowledges,
the knowledge that delimits the four modes of birth, and the four noble lineages, he began to recollect the qualities of the One Possessing Ten Powers.
Likewise, [he recollected] the five factors of striving, the fivefold right concentration, the five faculties, and the five powers.
The five elements of escape, the five bases of liberation, the five kinds of wisdom that ripen liberation, the six qualities of endearment,
the six subjects of recollection, the six forms of respect, the six elements of escape, the six constant abodes,
the six unsurpassed states, the six kinds of wisdom pertaining to penetration, the six direct knowledges, and the six unique knowledges.
The seven factors for non-decline, the seven noble treasures, the seven factors of enlightenment, the seven qualities of a true person,
the seven bases for the wearing away [of defilements], the seven kinds of wisdom, the seven persons worthy of offerings, the seven powers of one whose taints are destroyed,
the eight causes for the acquisition of wisdom, the eight rightnesses, the eight ways of transcending worldly conditions, and the eight grounds for exertion.
The eight discourses on the inopportune moments, the eight thoughts of a great person, the eight bases of mastery, the eight liberations, the nine states rooted in appropriate attention,
the nine factors of exertion for complete purification, the nine discourses on the abodes of beings, the nine ways of removing resentment,
the nine kinds of wisdom, the nine diversities, the nine successive dwellings, and the ten qualities that make one a protector.
the ten states of Dhamma, the ten bases of totality, the ten courses of wholesome action, the ten powers of a Tathāgata,
the ten rightnesses, the ten noble abodes, the ten qualities of one beyond training, the eleven benefits of loving-kindness, the twelve modes of the Wheel of Dhamma,
the thirteen qualities of ascetic practices, the fourteen types of Buddha-knowledge, and the fifteen states that ripen for liberation;
Relying upon the sixteenfold mindfulness of breathing, the eighteen qualities of a Buddha, the nineteen kinds of reviewing knowledge,

the forty-four bases of knowledge, the fifty-one wholesome states, and the seventy-seven bases of knowledge, as well as the great diamond-like knowledge that traverses four hundred and twenty-four million meditative attainments,
he began to recollect the virtues of the One Possessing the Ten Powers.

While sitting right there in that same daytime resting place, he began to recollect those sixteen successive teachings which will follow later in the text, beginning with: "Furthermore, Bhante, this is unsurpassed:
'My Teacher is unsurpassed in the designation of the wholesome; he is unsurpassed in the designation of the sense bases; he is unsurpassed in the descent into the womb...'"
