He is unsurpassed in the methods of direct address; unsurpassed in the attainment of vision; unsurpassed in the designation of individuals;
unsurpassed in exertion; unsurpassed in the modes of practice; unsurpassed in verbal conduct; unsurpassed in the moral conduct of men;
unsurpassed in the methods of instruction; unsurpassed in the knowledge of the liberation of other persons; and unsurpassed among those who maintain eternalist views.
"Unsurpassed in the knowledge of past lives, unsurpassed in the knowledge of the divine eye, unsurpassed in the various supernormal powers,
and unsurpassed in this and that [other quality]"— thus recollecting the virtues of the One Possessed of Ten Powers,
the Elder saw neither their end nor their measure. Even regarding his own virtues, the Elder could see neither their end nor their measure.
What will one see of the Blessed One’s qualities? For whoever possesses great wisdom and clear knowledge, they believe in the greatness of the Buddha’s qualities.

Even the common people of the world, though merely coughing or sneezing, recollect the qualities of the Buddhas by standing upon their own respective spiritual supports (upanissaya), saying, "Homage to the Buddhas. From among all the common people of the world...
One stream-enterer (sotāpanna) has faith in the greatness of the Buddha’s qualities.
From among a hundred or even a thousand stream-enterers, there is one once-returner (sakadāgāmī). From among a hundred or even a thousand once-returners, there is one non-returner (anāgāmī).

From among a hundred or even a thousand non-returners, there is one arahant who has faith in the greatness of the Buddha’s qualities. Among the remaining arahants, the eighty great elders (mahātheras) [have faith] in the Buddha’s qualities...
They believe in them on a grand scale. Among the eighty great elders (*mahāthera*), four great elders [believed thus]; among the four great elders, the two chief disciples (*aggasāvaka*);
and even among those, the elder Sāriputta; and even more than the elder Sāriputta, one *paccekabuddha* believes in the qualities of the Buddha on a grand scale.
Furthermore, if within the entire interior of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*), [one were to touch] the corner of one’s outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) to the corner of another’s...

While being guarded, the Paccekabuddhas might recollect the qualities of a Buddha; yet among them all, only a single Omniscient Buddha (sabbaññubuddha) has faith in the qualities of a Buddha as something vast.
It is just as if a great multitude of people were to spin threads in order to know whether the great ocean is deep or shallow.
There, some would require a rope measuring one fathom, some two fathoms, some ten fathoms, some twenty fathoms, some thirty fathoms,
some forty fathoms, some fifty fathoms, some a hundred fathoms, some a thousand fathoms,
and some eighty-four thousand fathoms. Having boarded the ship, they [would be] in the middle of the ocean.
Or, standing on Mount Uggata or other such heights, they might each lower their own measuring-line; among them, he whose line is one fathom long knows the water only at the depth of one fathom...
and so on, up to him whose line is eighty-four thousand fathoms long, who knows the water only at the depth of eighty-four thousand fathoms.
Beyond that, he does not know how much water there is. But in the great ocean, it is not merely that much.
Water, however, is infinite and immeasurable. For the great ocean is eighty-four thousand yojanas deep;
even so, the qualities of the Buddha perceived by the worldlings should be understood as being like water known [only] from a depth of one fathom up to nine fathoms.
By one who has attained the stream-entry (sotāpanna), they are like water known at a depth of ten fathoms.
The qualities of the Buddha seen by a once-returner are like water known [to exist] at a distance of twenty fathoms by means of a twenty-fathom rope.
The qualities of the Buddha seen by a non-returner are like water known [to exist] at a distance of thirty fathoms by means of a thirty-fathom rope.
The qualities of the Buddha seen by an arahant are like water known [to exist] at a distance of forty fathoms by means of a forty-fathom rope.
The qualities of the Buddha seen by the eighty great elders are like water known [to exist] at a depth of fifty fathoms when measured with a fifty-fathom rope;
the qualities of the Buddha seen by the four great elders are like water known [to exist] at a depth of one hundred fathoms when measured with a hundred-fathom rope;
and the qualities of the Buddha seen by the elder Mahāmoggallāna are like water known [to exist] at a depth of one thousand fathoms when measured with a thousand-fathom rope.
By means of a cord eighty-four thousand *vyāmas* long, at a distance of eighty-four thousand *vyāmas*, the qualities of the Buddha were perceived by the Elder Sāriputta,
the General of the Dhamma, like water known [by its taste]. In this regard, just as that man perceives that the water in the great ocean is not merely this much,
but is infinite and immeasurable, even so did the Venerable Sāriputta, through the inference of the Dhamma...

Standing in the knowledge of the perfections of a disciple through inference based on logical sequence (*anvaya-buddhi*) and by grasping the method (*nayaggāha*), he recollected the qualities of the One Possessing the Ten Powers and had faith that "the Buddha-qualities are infinite and immeasurable.
For the Buddha-qualities yet to be grasped through the logical sequence of the Dharma are far more numerous than those already seen by the Elder. Just as:

How so? Just as if a man were to take up water with a needle’s point from the great river Candabhāgā, which flows spreading out eighteen yojanas—nine yojanas from this side and nine from that—so much more is the water not taken up than the water taken up by the needle’s point;
or just as if a man were to take up soil from the great earth with his finger.
The dust taken up by a finger is but a small portion; the remaining dust is far more abundant.
Or again, as if a man were to point his finger toward the great ocean, the water facing the finger is but a tiny portion; the remaining water is far more abundant.
And as if a man were to point his finger toward space, the portion of space facing the finger is but a small part; the rest of the expanse of space is far more abundant.
Thus it should be understood that the qualities not yet seen by the Elder are as numerous as those already seen.
And this has been said: "Even if a Buddha were to speak the praise of another Buddha for an entire eon, without speaking of anything else,"
“An eon might pass away in its long duration,
but the praise of the Tathāgata would never be exhausted.
As the elder thus recollected the virtues of both himself and his Teacher, a great flood like that of the Yamaka Mahānadī surged within him.
The rapture and joy spread through him like air filling a bellows, and like water overflowing from a great lake, it filled his entire body.
Then, as the Elder reflected, "Truly well-established is my aspiration;
truly well-gained is my going-forth, since I have gone forth in the presence of such a Teacher," an even more powerful rapture and joy arose within him.
Then the Elder, reflecting, "To whom should I announce this joy and gladness? thought:
"No other ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, or Brahmā will be able to accept this confidence of mine in a manner worthy of it;
I shall proclaim this gladness to the Teacher alone, for the Teacher alone is able to receive it."

He will indeed be able; let alone my own joy and gladness, he is capable of grasping and receiving the gladness of a hundred, a thousand, or even a hundred thousand ascetics like me as they proclaim it, winning the minds of them all.
It is just as if one were crossing the great river Candabhāgā, which flows spreading out for eighteen yojanas.
The safflower fields or the mountain caves are unable to receive it; only the great ocean receives it.
Let alone the Candabhāgā river—the great ocean receives even a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand rivers such as these, yet neither a depletion nor a filling is perceived therein.
In the very same way, the Teacher [is able to receive] one such as me.
He is able to grasp and receive the joy and gladness of a hundred ascetics, a thousand ascetics, or even a hundred thousand ascetics as they proclaim it.
Other ascetics, brahmins, and the like cannot receive my joy and gladness, just as the Canda-bhāga cave cannot hold the saffron dye. Come now, I shall [share] my own joy and gladness.

Thinking, "I shall announce this to the Teacher himself," he untied his sitting mat, shook out the piece of leather, took it with him, and at evening time—when the flowers had detached from their stalks and were dripping—he approached the Teacher.
Proclaiming his own joy, he said, "Bhante, I am one who has such faith," and so forth. In that context, *evam-pasanno* means "one in whom such faith has arisen."
"Thus I have faith" is the meaning. "Bhiyyobhiññatara" means more widely known, or possessing higher direct knowledge (*abhiññā*);
the sense is that his wisdom is superior. "In regard to full enlightenment" (*sambodhiyaṃ*) refers to the knowledge of omniscience or the knowledge of the path of Arahatship;

for it is by the path of Arahatship alone that the qualities of a Buddha are grasped in their entirety. For indeed, the two chief disciples [possess] the knowledge of the perfection of disciples (*sāvakapāramīñāṇa*) through the very path of Arahatship.
They attain it: Paccekabuddhas attain the knowledge of Paccekabodhi; Buddhas attain both omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) and all the qualities of a Buddha.
For indeed, all these are accomplished by the path of Arahantship alone. Therefore, the knowledge of the path of Arahantship is called "perfect enlightenment" (*sambodhi*).
There is no one superior to the Blessed One in that regard. Thus he said: "There is no one more highly distinguished than the Blessed One."
"That is to say, 'perfect enlightenment.
142. "Exalted" (*uḷāra*) means "supreme. For this word *uḷāra* occurs in the sense of "sweet" in such passages as, "They are eating exalted hard foods" (*uḷārāni khādanīyāni khādanti*).

It occurs in the sense of "great" in such passages as, "Indeed, Master Vacchāyana, you praise the ascetic Gotama with an exalted praise" (*uḷārāya khalu bhavaṃ, Vacchāyano, samaṇaṃ Gotamaṃ pasaṃsāya pasaṃsati*).
“Excellent” (*seṭṭhe*). In such passages as “immeasurable, sublime radiance,” it means vast; however, here it has come down as “excellent. Therefore it was said: “Sublime means excellent.

“Bull-like” (*āsabhī*) means like the speech of a bull—unwavering and unshakable. “Decided upon” (*ekaṃso gahito*) means [not established] by hearsay, or by oral tradition from teacher to teacher, or by mere rumor, or by the collection of the Piṭakas, or by logical reasoning.
Or, whether by means of contemplation of views or by way of preference, it was not taken as a categorical conclusion based on reasoning or logic;
rather, having penetrated it through direct knowledge as if seeing it face-to-face, it was grasped categorically. The meaning is that only a definitive statement was spoken.
"Lion’s roar" means the best of roars; it is the supreme roar like that of a lion, uttered neither hesitantly nor with a gurgling sound.
The meaning is "having roared. Why did he begin this teaching with the words, "What [do you think], Sāriputta"? It was for the purpose of eliciting a response.
For some, having roared a lion's roar, are unable to provide a response to their own lion's roar;
they cannot endure being tested and become like a monkey fallen into lac. Just as impure iron, when heated...
It is like a piece of charcoal from a fire; thus he is like a piece of charcoal. When one [piece of gold] is subjected to the test of a lion’s roar, it is able to endure it;
it withstands the rubbing, and when being smelted, it shines even more brilliantly like faultless native gold—such was the Elder.
Therefore, the Blessed One, knowing him as "one who can endure the test," for the purpose of subjecting him to the lion’s roar, said:
He began this teaching as well.

In that context, "all those" means all those [Buddhas] by you. In the passage beginning with "of such virtue," he asks about virtue and the other perfections (sīla-ādi) according to both the mundane and supramundane levels. A detailed exposition of these has already been given in the Mahāpadāna Sutta.
But as for the question, "What then, Sāriputta, of those who will be?"—first, those of the past have ceased and have entered the state of non-designation (apaṇṇattika-bhāva).
"Like the flame of a lamp that has gone out and is extinguished, when [the Buddha] has thus ceased and reached the state of being indefinable (*apaṇṇattika*), how will you know him?
But as for the qualities of future Buddhas, by what means have they been delimited and known by your own mind?"—asking thus, he spoke these words.
"But what of you, Sāriputta, regarding me at present?"—[this refers to] even future Buddhas who are yet unborn and unarisen.
"How will you know those that have not yet arisen? For to know them would be like seeing footprints in the trackless sky.
Now you dwell in the same monastery as me, you go for alms together with me, and at the time of teaching the Dhamma, you sit on my right side;
but have you discerned my virtues within your own mind and known them?"
While pursuing him with these questions, he spoke thus.
But whenever the Elder was questioned, he would refuse, saying, "No indeed, Bhante. Now, the Elder had both things that were known to him and things that were unknown;
did he refuse regarding those points he knew, or those he did not know?
"He does not do it in a place he knows; he does it only in a place he does not know. It is said that the Elder knew this even as the questioning had begun.
He did not refuse his own knowledge of the disciple’s perfections (*sāvakapāramīñāṇa*), saying, "This questioning is not within the scope of a disciple’s perfections;

this questioning concerns omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*)," but rather, without rejecting his knowledge of the disciple’s perfections, he rejected [the possibility of answering] regarding omniscience in a place he did not know. Therefore, this too—

He illuminates [the point] thus: “The Blessed One does not possess the omniscient knowledge capable of knowing the causes of the virtue, concentration, wisdom, and liberation of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present.

“In this regard” means among these Buddhas distinguished by their past and other periods. “Then why? means: “Since such knowledge is absent, for what reason have you spoken thus?”—this is what he says.
143. *Dhammanvaya* (logical inference) refers to the inferential knowledge that arises by following the application of knowledge regarding the Dhamma through direct perception;
it is known as the "grasping of the method. He says, "I know [the Buddha] in this very manner, standing upon the knowledge of the disciple’s perfection (*sāvakapāramīñāṇa*).
For the Elder’s grasping of the method is immeasurable and limitless, just as there is no measure or limit to the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
Or there is none; such is the method-grasping (*nayaggāha*) of the General of the Dhamma. By means of that, he knows: "By this [method] he is of such a kind;
by this [method] he is the unsurpassed Teacher. For the Elder’s method-grasping leads precisely to the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
Now, in order to make that method-grasping clear, he spoke the passage beginning with "Just as, venerable sir," etc., showing it by way of a simile. Therein, because in the middle region...
Whether the city’s foundations, ramparts, and so forth are firm or weak, or even if they are entirely absent, as long as there is no fear of thieves, it is not considered such [a fortified city];
therefore, setting that aside, he said "frontier city" (*paccantima-nagara*). "With strong foundations" means having firm bases for the ramparts.
"With strong ramparts and gate-towers" means both firm ramparts and firm battlements. Why did he say "with a single gate"?
"In a city with many gates, there must be many wise gatekeepers; in one with a single gate, only one is required.
Since there is no other equal to this elder in wisdom, he said, 'a single gate,' in order to show by way of illustration his own state of being wise. 'Wise' means endowed with wisdom. 'Clever'..."

"Endowed with proficiency" means possessed of clear knowledge. "Wise" means endowed with *medhā*, which is reckoned as the wisdom that arises on the spot (*ṭhānuppattika-paññā*). "The patrol path" refers to the wall-path known by that name.
"The breach in the wall" is the place where two bricks have come apart. "The gap in the wall" is the place where the wall has been cut through.
They defile the mind; the five hindrances defile the mind, making it turbid, afflicting it, and obstructing it.
Therefore, they are called "defilements of the mind. Regarding "weakening wisdom":
when the hindrances arise, they do not allow unarisen wisdom to arise, nor do they allow arisen wisdom to increase.

They do not give [support], therefore they are called "the weakeners of wisdom. "With minds well-established" means having established their minds well in the four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*).
"The seven factors of enlightenment according to reality" means having developed the seven factors of enlightenment in accordance with their true nature.
"Unsurpassed perfect enlightenment" indicates that they have penetrated either Arhatship or omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
Furthermore, here "foundations of mindfulness" refers to insight (*vipassanā*); "factors of enlightenment" refers to the path; and "unsurpassed perfect enlightenment" refers to Arahantship.

Thus, the foundations of mindfulness and the path are associated with the factors of enlightenment, while perfect enlightenment is Arahantship alone. However, the Elder Mahāsīva, a reciter of the *Dīgha Nikāya*, says:
"Having taken 'insight' as the foundations of mindfulness, [one understands] the path and omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) as the factors of enlightenment."
"If it were grasped in that way, the question would be excellent; but it was not grasped in this manner.

Thus the Elder demonstrates that for all the Omniscient Buddhas, there is no difference—just as there is none between refined gold and silver—in the abandoning of the hindrances, the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness, and the attainment of enlightenment.
Standing here, the simile should be correlated as follows: the Venerable Sāriputta showed the border town, he showed the rampart,
he showed the circuit road, he showed the gate, he showed the wise gatekeeper,
he showed the large creatures entering and leaving the city, and he showed the wise gatekeeper’s familiarity with those creatures.
He showed it. If one asks, "In what way is what similar to what here?"—Nibbāna is like the city;

virtue (*sīla*) is like the rampart; moral shame (*hirī*) is like the moat-path; the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*) is like the gate; the General of the Dhamma (*dhammasenāpati*) is like the wise gatekeeper;
and the Buddhas of the past, future, and present are like the coarse creatures that enter and exit the city. To the gatekeeper...

Just as those beings are manifest to him, so too is the Venerable Sāriputta manifest regarding the past, future, and present Buddhas by way of their virtue, concentration, and other qualities. To this extent, the Elder has offered his own lion’s roar, declaring:
"Standing thus in the knowledge of the perfection of discipleship, I know through the method of inference and the grasp of the guiding principle."
144. Venerable sir, for what reason did I begin this teaching with the words, "Here, venerable sir, I [approached] the Blessed One"?
It was for the purpose of demonstrating the attainment of the knowledge of the disciple’s perfection (*sāvakapāramīñāṇa*). This is the intended meaning here:

when the Blessed One attained the knowledge of the disciple’s perfection, I did not approach even a single ascetic or brahmin among the ninety-five heretical sects to obtain even that knowledge of the disciple’s perfection.
"I attained it; having approached you yourselves and attending upon you, I attained it. In this context, "here" (*idha*) is merely a particle.
"I approached for the sake of hearing the Dhamma" means that when I approached you, I did not approach for the sake of robes and such, but approached for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma.
Having approached in this manner, [I attained] the knowledge of the perfection of a disciple (*sāvakapāramīñāṇa*).

"When did the Elder approach for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma? "He approached on the day he was preaching the *Vedanāpariggaha-sutta* to his nephew, the wanderer Dīghanakha, at the Sūkarakhata Cave;
it was on that very day that he attained the knowledge of the perfections of a disciple (*sāvakapāramīñāṇa*).
For on that day, while the Elder stood fanning the Blessed One with a palm-leaf fan, he heard that teaching."

Right there, he brought the knowledge of the disciple’s perfections into his own hands. He taught by making it progressively higher and more sublime—both increasingly superior and increasingly refined.

Regarding the phrase "the dark and the bright with their counterparts": this refers to both the dark and the bright, and indeed as having counterparts; that is, having established their opposites. Having set aside the dark, [he taught] the bright; having set aside the bright, [he taught] the dark.
Having thus established the contrast by saying "the dark," he taught the dark and the bright. And while teaching the dark, he taught it as being accompanied by effort and having a result;
while teaching the bright, he also taught it as being accompanied by effort and having a result.
Through direct knowledge of that Dhamma, some here reach a definitive conclusion regarding the Dhamma among all dharmas when that Dhamma has been taught.
Having recognized a certain teaching—namely, the knowledge of the disciple’s perfections—I reached a definitive conclusion regarding those teachings. Regarding which teachings?

The teachings of the Four Noble Truths. Herein is this dialogue among the elders: first, the Elder Suma, resident of Kāḷavalli, says, "There is no reason for reaching a definitive conclusion now regarding the teachings of the Four Noble Truths. For the Great Disciple Assaji..."
"On the very day he saw [the Buddha], he reached a conclusion regarding the Dhamma of the Four Truths by means of the first path;
later, at the mouth of the Sūkarakhatā cave, he reached a conclusion regarding the Dhamma of the Four Truths by means of the three higher paths;

but in this instance, with the word 'Dhammas,' he reached a conclusion regarding the qualities of the Buddha. However, the Elder Cūḷasīva, a resident of Lokantara, said all that exactly as it was stated, and then added:
"But in this place, the term 'in the states' (dhammesu) reaches its conclusion in Arahantship," he said.
However, the Elder Mahāsīva, a reciter of the Dīgha Nikāya and master of the Tipiṭaka, stated, "Having spoken the previous position in exactly the same way,

in this place the term 'in the states' reaches its conclusion in the knowledge of the disciple's perfections (sāvakapāramīñāṇa)," and added, "But the qualities of a Buddha are included by way of implication."

They have faith in the Teacher; having thus reached a definitive conclusion regarding the qualities of the disciple’s perfections and knowledge, they develop even greater faith in the Teacher, thinking, "Truly, that Blessed One is a Perfectly Enlightened One.

They reflect: "The Dhamma has been well-proclaimed by the Blessed One"—well-expounded, well-spoken, leading to liberation, leading toward the fruit, and capable of crushing greed, hatred, and delusion.

"The Saṅgha is well-practiced": this shows that he has confidence in the Blessed One, thinking, "I have confidence in the Blessed One because even the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is well-practiced, having entered upon the right practice free from crookedness and other such faults.
145. Now, in order to show another sixteen qualities pertaining to successive lives (*aparāpariya-dhamma*) attained while sitting in the daytime resting place, [the Buddha said] further:
"But, venerable sir, this is unsurpassed," with these words he began the teaching. In this context, "unsurpassed" (*anuttariya*) means the state of being unsurpassed (*anuttarabhāva*).
"In the manner that the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma" means: in whatever way, by whatever method, and by whatever teaching the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma—that teaching of yours is unsurpassed;
thus he says. "Regarding wholesome states" (*kusalesu dhammesu*) refers to those states taught by that teaching.
He shows that the Blessed One alone is unsurpassed even among wholesome states (*kusala-dhamma*). Or, he says "among wholesome states" in order to indicate the ground for that teaching.

In that context, regarding the phrase "therein, these are the wholesome states," it should be understood that "these" refers to what are called wholesome states among those wholesome states mentioned.
Therein, they are wholesome in the sense of health, in the sense of blamelessness, and in the sense of being produced by skill.

Wholesome (kusala) should be understood in five ways: in the sense of being free from distress, and in the sense of having a pleasant result. Among these, according to the method of the Jātakas, it is wholesome in the sense of health;

according to the method of the Suttantas, in the sense of blamelessness; and according to the method of the Abhidhamma, in the sense of being produced by skill, being free from distress, and having a pleasant result.
However, in this present context, it is according to the method of the Bāhitika Sutta.
The wholesome should be understood in the sense of being blameless.

As for the four foundations of mindfulness: there is the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of the body in fourteen ways; the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of feelings in nine ways;
the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of the mind in sixteen ways; and the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of mental objects in five ways.

Thus, having analyzed them by way of various methods, the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) have been taught as a mixture of mundane and supramundane, according to the paths of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā).
However, the foundation of mindfulness as fruition (phala-satipaṭṭhāna) is not intended here.

The four right efforts (sammappadhāna) have a single characteristic in the sense of exertion, but they have different functions according to their respective tasks: "Here, a bhikkhu does not give rise to unarisen evil... [and so forth].

The four right efforts (*sammappadhāna*) are taught as a mixture of mundane and supramundane according to the method beginning with, “for the non-arising of unwholesome states,” and so forth, by way of the paths of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
The four bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*) are unified in the sense of being effective (*ijjhanatthena*), yet they possess diverse natures by way of desire (*chanda*) and the other factors.
As it is said: “Here, a bhikkhu develops the basis of psychic power endowed with concentration of desire and volitional formations of striving,” and so forth.
By way of method—that is, by way of the path of serenity and insight—the four bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*) are taught as a mixture of both mundane and supramundane.

The five faculties (*indriya*) have a single characteristic in the sense of being predominant, yet they have diverse intrinsic natures by way of their individual essences such as resolution (*adhimokkha*) and so forth.
Furthermore, the five faculties beginning with faith (*saddhā*), by way of the path of serenity and insight alone, are a mixture of both mundane and supramundane.
They have been taught. Regarding the "five powers": in the sense of being a support or in the sense of being unshakable, they are comprised as one;

yet by way of their specific characteristics, they are of diverse natures. The five powers beginning with faith, which are a mixture of mundane and supramundane, are taught precisely by way of serenity, insight, and the path.
Regarding the "seven factors of enlightenment": in the sense of leading to liberation, they are comprised as one; [yet they differ] by way of their establishment and so forth.

By their own specific characteristics (*salakkhaṇa*), they possess diverse natures. The seven factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) are taught as a mixture of mundane and supramundane, by way of serenity (*samatha*), insight (*vipassanā*), and the path (*magga*).

The Noble Eightfold Path (*ariya aṭṭhaṅgika magga*) is a single unity in the sense of being the cause (*hetu*), yet it possesses diverse natures by its own specific characteristics such as seeing (*dassana*) and so forth. The meaning is that the Noble Eightfold Path is taught as a mixture of mundane and supramundane by way of serenity, insight, and the path.

"In this case, venerable sir, a bhikkhu [sees] the destruction of the taints (*āsavānaṃ khaya*). For what purpose was this undertaken? It is for the purpose of showing the conclusion of the Dispensation (*sāsana*).
For the culmination of the Dispensation does not consist of the Path alone; rather, it consists of the fruit of Arhatship.
Therefore, it should be understood that this [sutta] was undertaken in order to demonstrate that. "This, venerable sir, is unsurpassed among wholesome states":
venerable sir, this teaching regarding wholesome states is unsurpassed. "That, Blessed One": that teaching.
The Blessed One fully and entirely knows [all things]. "From the Blessed One" means from the Blessed One who fully and entirely knows that teaching.
"There is nothing further to be directly known" means there is nothing further to be directly known beyond that;
there is no such thing as another dhamma or person whom the Blessed One does not know. "Whatever he knows... [means] whatever another ascetic... [knows].

"If there were another ascetic or brahmin who, through direct knowledge, had fully realized that which you have not yet realized, he would be more highly realized than the Blessed One and would possess superior wisdom—namely, regarding wholesome states (*kusala-dhamma*). Here, "yadidaṃ" is merely a particle;
the meaning here is: "there is no one superior to the Blessed One regarding wholesome states. Thus, it is the Blessed One alone [who is supreme] regarding wholesome states.
Showing that he is "unsurpassed among all things," he illuminates this by saying, "For this reason too, venerable sir, I am thus confident in the Blessed One.

Regarding the subsequent sections beginning with "Furthermore," we shall explain only the specific distinctions; otherwise, they should be understood in the same manner as the preceding section according to the method already stated.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Designation of the Bases (Āyatanapaṇṇattidesanāvaṇṇanā) 146.
Regarding the phrase "in the expositions of the designation of the bases" (*āyatanapaṇṇattīsū*): this means in the designations of the bases (*āyatanapaññāpanā*).

Now, in order to show those designations of the bases, he said, "Venerable sir, there are these six," and so forth. Furthermore, this discussion of the bases has been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*.
Therefore, we shall not elaborate upon that; thus, it should be understood in detail according to the method already stated therein.

"This, venerable sir, is unsurpassed among the designations of the sense bases (*āyatana-panñatti*)," refers to this teaching given by way of the classification of internal and external [bases] and so forth among the designations of the sense bases. The remainder is exactly as previously stated.
Commentary on the Teaching on Descent into the Womb (*gabbhāvakkanti*).

147. "Regarding the descents into the womb (*gabbhāvakkantīsu*)," this means in the cases of entering the womb. Showing those descents into the womb, he said: "These four, venerable sir," and so forth.
Therein, "unconscious" (*asampajāno*) means not knowing, having become deluded.

"Enters the mother's womb" (*mātukucchiṃ okkamati*) means he enters by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). "Abides" (*ṭhāti*) means he dwells there. "Departs" (*nikkhamati*) means that even when departing, he is unconscious.
He emerges as if bewildered. "This is the first": this is the first descent into the womb for ordinary worldly human beings.
"Fully aware he descends into the mother’s womb": while descending, he does so fully aware and without bewilderment. "This is the second":
this is the second descent into the womb for the eighty great elder disciples; for they know as they enter, but they do not know as they dwell or as they emerge.
“This is the third” refers to the third descent into the womb, that of the two Chief Disciples and the Pacceka-Bodhisattvas.
It is said that, due to the winds born of karma, they were cast head-downward and feet-upward at the opening of the womb as if into a precipice hundreds of fathoms deep;
and as they emerged through the narrow birth canal, like an elephant passing through the hole of a palm-leaf, they experienced boundless suffering.
They reach [this state]. Therefore, they lack the clear comprehension (*sampajañña*) that says, "We have departed.

Thus, even for beings who have fulfilled the perfections (*pāramī*), such great suffering arises in such a place; therefore, it is sufficient to become disenchanted with dwelling in the womb and sufficient to become dispassionate toward it.
This is the fourth: this is the fourth descent into the womb by way of the omniscient Bodhisattvas. The omniscient Bodhisattvas...
For even those taking rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) in the mother’s womb know it; while dwelling there they know it;
and when departing they know it. Even at the time of departure, the kamma-born winds are unable to cast them out with their feet upwards and their heads downwards;
rather, stretching out both hands and opening their eyes, they emerge as if standing still. This is the peak of existence (bhavagga).
Apart from the omniscient Bodhisattvas, there is no one else within the interval of the Avīci hell who is fully conscious throughout the three periods [of conception, gestation, and birth].
For this very reason, at the time of their descent into the mother’s womb and at the time of their emergence, the ten-thousandfold world system trembles.
The rest here should be understood according to the method already stated.
Commentary on the Modes of Direct Knowledge (Ādesanāvidhādesanāvaṇṇanā) 148.

Regarding the phrase "in the modes of direct knowledge" (ādesanavidhāsu): this means within the categories of direct knowledge. Now, showing those modes of direct knowledge, he says, "These four," and so forth.
"He declares by a sign" (nimittena ādisati) means that he speaks, saying "this will happen," based on a sign of arrival, a sign of departure, or a sign of staying.
In this regard, here is the story: A certain king, having taken three pearls, asked his chaplain, "What is in my hand, teacher?
He looked here and there. At that moment, a female sarabū leaped forward thinking, "I shall catch the fly," but at the moment of seizing it, the fly escaped;
because the fly had escaped (*muttā*), he said, "O Great King, it is a pearl (*muttā*)."
He said, "Let it be for now; how many pearls are there? He then looked at the sign.
Not far away, a cock uttered its cry three times. The brahmin said, "Three great kings. In this way, some speak by means of a sign that has appeared.
By this same method, speaking by means of signs that have passed or are stationary should also be understood.
"Of non-human beings" means of *yakkhas*, *pisācas*, and so forth. "Of deities" means of those belonging to the realm of the Four Great Kings and so forth.
"Having heard the sound" means having heard the sound of others speaking after they have known his mind.

"The sound of the diffusion of thought" means the sound of those who are prattling, produced by way of the diffusion of thought, such as those who are asleep, heedless, and so forth. "Having heard" means having heard that sound. That which...
As he applies thought (*vitakkayato*), that sound arises; by means of it, one declares, "Your mind is thus," and so forth.

"Mental formations are directed" (*paṇihitā*) means the mental formations (*cittasaṅkhārā*) are well-established. "He will apply thought" (*vitakkessati*) means one understands that he will apply thought, that he will set it in motion.
And knowing this, one knows it by way of its arrival, one knows it by way of its prior stage, and [one knows] the mind within the attainment (*samāpatti*).
One knows by observing. "One knows by the approach" means that at the very time of the preliminary work for the kasiṇa, one knows in what manner this person will bring about the first jhāna, or...
[up to] the fourth jhāna, or the eight attainments when they have commenced their kasiṇa meditation.
"One knows by the prior stage" means that one knows precisely when serenity and insight have been commenced, in what manner...
He knows: "This one who has begun insight (vipassanā) will produce either the path of stream-entry, or the path of once-returning, or the path of non-returning, or the path of arhatship.

He knows by looking at the mind within meditative absorption (samāpatti), seeing in what manner this person’s mental formations (manosaṅkhāra) have been well-established, and [recognizing] this very person.
He knows: "Immediately after this consciousness, he will think such a thought;

having emerged from this, his concentration will be either partaking of decline, partaking of stability, partaking of distinction, or partaking of penetration, or he will produce the higher knowledges."
In this regard, an ordinary person who has attained knowledge of the minds of others knows only the minds of other ordinary persons, not those of noble ones.
Even among noble ones, one who is lower does not know the mind of one who is higher, but one who is higher knows the mind of one who is lower.
And among these, a stream-enterer enters the attainment of the fruit of stream-entry; so too does a once-returner.
The non-returner and the arahant enter the attainment of the fruit of arahantship. One who is higher does not enter the attainment of one who is lower;
for those [lower attainments], each successive lower attainment results in rebirth right there. "It is just so" means it is certainly just so.
For that which is known by means of the knowledge of penetration of others' minds cannot possibly become otherwise. The rest...
It should be applied in the same manner as before.
Regarding the commentary on the teaching of the attainment of vision (dassanasamāpatti):
the passage beginning with "exerting ardor" (ātappaṃ anvāya) has already been explained in detail in the *Brahmajāla Sutta*. Here, however, is the summary: "ardor" (ātappaṃ)...
Energy (*vīriya*). That very same [energy] is "exertion" (*padhāna*) because it must be exerted; it is "application" (*anuyoga*) because it must be pursued.

"Diligence" (*appamāda*) means non-separation from mindfulness. "Right attention" (*sammāmanasikāra*) means the strategic attention that proceeds by way of [contemplating] the impermanent as impermanent, and so forth.

"Concentration of mind" (*cetosamādhi*) means the concentration of the first jhāna. "This is the first attainment of seeing" means this [attainment] regarding the thirty-two parts [of the body] as repulsive.
The attainment of the first jhāna produced by attending to [the body] through the contemplation of repulsiveness is called the "first attainment of vision.
However, if one becomes a stream-enterer (sotāpanna) by making that jhāna the basis, this is the "first attainment of vision" in the primary sense.
"And having transcended" means having passed beyond. "Skin, flesh, and blood" refers to the skin, the flesh, and the blood. "Bone" [refers to the bone].

"He reviews" means he reviews it as "bone, bone. Having reviewed it as "bone, bone," the attainment of jhāna based on the divine eye, which has bone as its object and is produced by that review, is called the second attainment of vision.
However, if one takes that jhāna as a basis and produces the path of a once-returner (*sakadāgāmimagga*), this is the second [attainment] in the literal sense.
The attainment of vision (*dassanasamāpatti*). However, the Elder Sumati of Kāḷavallī said, "It is appropriate up to the third path.
"The stream of consciousness" (*viññāṇasota*) means consciousness itself. "Uninterrupted on both sides" means not cut off by either of the two parts.
"Established here in this world" means established in this world through desire and lust (*chandarāga*). The same applies to the second phrase as well.

This is the method. Alternatively, karma that is approaching from its own nature is said to be "established in this world. Karma that is drawing forth existence (kammabhava) is said to be "established in the other world.
What is expressed by this? The knowledge of others' minds (cetopariyañāṇa) of those in training (sekkha) and worldlings (puthujjana) is expressed.
For the knowledge of others' minds of those in training and worldlings is indeed called the third attainment of vision (dassanasamāpatti).
"Not established in this world" means that because of the absence of desire and lust, it is not established in this world.

The same method applies to the second phrase as well. Alternatively, karma that does not approach from the perspective of karma is called "not established in this world"; that which does not drag one toward existence through karma (*kammabhava*) is called "not established in the other world.
What is expressed by this? It is the knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*) of one whose taints are destroyed.
It has been explained. For one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), the knowledge of others' minds (cetopariyañāṇa) is called the fourth attainment of vision (dassanasamāpatti).

Furthermore, insight (vipassanā) undertaken regarding the thirty-two aspects (dvattiṃsākāra) is the first attainment of vision; insight undertaken regarding the meditation object of a skeleton (aṭṭhi-ārammaṇa) is the second attainment of vision.

The knowledge of others' minds belonging to those in training (sekkha) and worldlings (puthujjana) is [the third], while the knowledge of others' minds belonging to one whose taints are destroyed is the fourth.
These two terms are indeed fixed. According to another method: the first jhāna is the first attainment of vision;
the second jhāna is the second; the third jhāna is the third; and the fourth jhāna is the fourth attainment of vision.
Likewise, the first path is the first attainment of vision; the second path is the second; and the third path is the third.
"The fourth path is the fourth attainment of vision. The rest here should be construed in the same manner as previously explained.
Commentary on the Designation of Persons (Puggalapaṇṇatti):
Regarding the phrase "in the Designations of Persons," it refers to those things that are designated according to worldly convention as "a being, a person, a man, an individual."

Regarding "among the designations of the world": for the Buddhas, there are two types of discourse—discourse on conventional designation (*sammuti-kathā*) and discourse on ultimate reality (*paramattha-kathā*)—as explained in detail in the *Poṭṭhapāda Sutta*.
Among these, "among the designations of persons" (*puggala-pannattīsu*) refers to this discourse on conventional designation.

Now, demonstrating those persons whom the Blessed One is unsurpassed in designating when he designates them, he says: "Venerable sir, there are these seven persons," beginning with "one liberated both ways" (*ubhatobhāga-vimutto*).

In this context, "one liberated in both ways" (ubhatobhāgavimutta) means one who is liberated by way of two parts: liberated from the form-body (rūpakāya) through the formless attainments (arūpasamāpatti), and liberated from the name-body (nāmakāya) through the Path.
This is fivefold: by way of those who have attained Arahantship after emerging from each of the four formless attainments and contemplating formations (saṅkhāra);
and by way of Non-returners who have attained Arahantship after emerging from the attainment of cessation (nirodha).
The Pāli text here, however, comes down as referring to one who has attained the eight liberations: "And what kind of person is one liberated both ways?
Here, a certain person dwells having personally realized the eight liberations with the body, and having seen [reality] with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed.
One who is liberated by wisdom is a "wisdom-liberated" (paññāvimutta) one. He is either a dry-insight practitioner (sukkhavipassaka) or one who [has attained] the four jhānas.
It is fivefold by way of these four who, having emerged [from the attainment], attained *arahantship*, and the one who has already emerged.
However, the text here is presented specifically by way of the negation of the eight liberations (*aṭṭhavimokkha*). As it is said:
"He does not dwell having touched the eight liberations with his body; but having seen with wisdom, his taints (*āsava*) are utterly destroyed. This is called..."
"A person liberated by wisdom.
One who realizes the limit of what has been touched is a "body-witness" (kāyasakkhi). He first touches the contact of meditative absorption (jhānaphassa) and subsequently realizes cessation, Nibbāna.
Starting from the stage of the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpattiphala), he proceeds up to the stage of the path of arahantship.
It should be understood that there are six kinds. For this very reason it was said: "In this case, a certain person dwells having personally realized the eight liberations with the body;
and having seen with wisdom, some of his taints are utterly destroyed. This person is called a 'body-witness' (kāyasakkhī).
One who has reached the view is a "view-attainer" (diṭṭhippatto). Herein, this is the brief definition: conditioned phenomena are suffering, [nibbāna] is bliss...
"Cessation" is known, seen, understood, realized, and perceived by means of wisdom; thus one is "attained to vision.
In detail, however, this person also has six types, just like the body-witness (kāyasakkhi). Therefore it was said: "Here, a certain person understands as it really is:
'This is suffering'... [and so on] ... 'This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.'"
He understands; the Dhammas proclaimed by the Tathāgata have been clearly seen and pursued by his wisdom, and having seen them with wisdom, some of his taints (āsava) are completely destroyed.
This person is called one who has attained vision (diṭṭhippatto).
One liberated through faith (saddhāvimutto) is one liberated by faith. He too is of six kinds according to the method already stated. Therefore it was said: "In this case, someone..."
A person understands as it really is: "This is suffering"; understands as it really is: "This is the origin of suffering"; understands as it really is:
"This is the cessation of suffering"; and understands as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
Furthermore, the teachings proclaimed by the Tathāgata have been clearly seen and investigated by his wisdom. By means of wisdom...

Upon seeing this, some of his taints (*āsava*) are completely exhausted, though not as they are for one who has attained through vision (*diṭṭhippatto*). This person is called "one liberated by faith" (*saddhāvimutto*).

For in the case of the one liberated by faith, at the moment of the preliminary path, the destruction of the defilements occurs as if he were placing his faith, as if he were settling his mind, and as if he were resolving with confidence. In the case of the one who has attained through vision...
At the moment of the preliminary path, the knowledge that severs the defilements proceeds being unclouded, sharp, and keen. Therefore,
just as when one cuts a plantain tree with a sword that is not very sharp,
the cut surface is not smooth, the sword does not move swiftly, a sound is heard, and a greater effort must be exerted— such is the case here.

This is the development of the preliminary path for one liberated by faith. However, the development of the preliminary path for one liberated by wisdom should be understood as being like this: when a plantain tree is cut with an extremely sharp sword, the place where it is cut is smooth, the sword glides swiftly, no sound is heard, and there is no need for great exertion of effort.
One who recollects the Dhamma is a *dhammānusārī*. "Dhamma" here means wisdom (*paññā*); the meaning is that one develops the path preceded by wisdom.
The same method applies to the *saddhānusārī* as well; both of these are situated precisely on the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*). And this has been said:
"In the case of a person practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, if the faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*) is predominant..."
He possesses wisdom; he develops the Noble Path with wisdom as its vehicle and wisdom as its precursor. This person is called a "follower by Dhamma" (dhammānusārī).

Likewise: "In the case of a person who has entered upon the practice for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, if the faculty of faith is predominant, and he develops the Noble Path with faith as its vehicle and faith as its precursor, this person is called a 'follower by faith' (saddhānusārī)."

This is the summary here; however, this detailed discussion on those liberated in both ways and so forth is set forth in the *Visuddhimagga* in the section on the development of wisdom (*paññābhāvanā*).
Therefore, it should be understood according to the method explained therein. The remainder here also should be applied in the same manner as before.

What is wisdom? For one who, with difficulty and through exertion, arouses concentration and slowly masters that state, the wisdom that is understanding...
[as before] ...non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view—this is called wisdom of difficult progress and slow direct knowledge.
In this context, what is wisdom of difficult progress and quick direct knowledge? [For one who,] with difficulty and through exertion...

The wisdom, understanding, and so forth, up to right view, of one who arouses concentration and quickly realizes that state—this is called the wisdom of the painful practice with quick direct knowledge.
In this context, what is the wisdom of the pleasant practice with sluggish direct knowledge?
It is the wisdom of one who arouses concentration without difficulty or exertion, but who sluggishly realizes that state.
That wisdom which is understanding... [as before] ...right view: this is called the wisdom of the pleasant way with sluggish direct knowledge.

In that regard, what is the wisdom of the pleasant way with swift direct knowledge? For one who, without difficulty and without exertion, arouses concentration and swiftly realizes that state, that wisdom which is understanding...
[as before] ...right view: this is called [the wisdom of the pleasant way with swift direct knowledge].
"The easy way with quick direct knowledge is wisdom. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation, however, is stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.
The rest should also be applied here in the same manner as before.
[End of] the commentary on the conduct of speech and so forth.

153. "Nor connected with false speech": even while engaged in the practice of conversation, some monk here speaks without interrupting the course of discourse, yet he does not speak what is connected with false speech.

Having avoided the eight types of ignoble speech, he speaks only that which is endowed with the eight types of noble speech. "Nor sowing dissension": even while engaged in the practice of conversation...
He does not utter speech that causes division. Nor does he speak slander; this is indeed a synonym for that very same thing.
For divisive speech is called "slander" (*pesuṇiya*) because it makes empty the state of being dear. "This is its very name," said the Elder Mahāsīva.
And he does not utter speech born of contentiousness; that is, he does not speak such words as, "You are immoral."

When it is said, "You are immoral; your teacher is immoral," or when it is said, "You have committed an offense," he does not utter words of external distraction—such as, "I went to Pāṭaliputta after wandering for alms"—nor does he speak words of counter-argument.
"Seeking victory" means being intent on victory, just as Hatthaka the Sakyan was toward the sectarians.
"By name, whether by means of what is Dhamma or what is not Dhamma, one may be defeated"—this refers to speaking anything that is true or false.
The meaning is that one does not speak while desiring victory or having victory as one's primary aim. "With wisdom (*mantā*), one speaks words with wisdom":

here, "wisdom" (*mantā*) is said to be *paññā* (understanding); thus, "with wisdom" means with *paññā*. Again, "with wisdom" means having investigated. This is what is meant: regarding the proper conduct of speech...
Remaining steady even while speaking for a portion of the day, he speaks only appropriate discourse after having investigated with wisdom.
"Like a treasure" means it is worthy of being deposited even within the heart. "At the proper time" means at the appropriate and opportune moment.
For speech spoken in this way is indeed not false, not divisive, not harsh, not deceitful, and not frivolous.

And such speech as this is said to be based on the Four Noble Truths, based on the Three Trainings, based on the ten bases of discourse, based on the thirteen ascetic practices (dhutaṅgas), based on the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and based on the Path.
Therefore it was said: "Venerable sir, this is unsurpassed in the practice of conversation"; this should be connected in the same manner as before.
"Sacco cassa saddho ca": A bhikkhu established in virtue and conduct should be truthful—that is, one who speaks the truth—and faithful—that is, one endowed with faith.
One might ask: "Has truth not already been mentioned below? Why is it stated again here? Truth was mentioned below in reference to verbal truth;
however, a bhikkhu established in virtue and conduct must avoid false speech even in a joke.
This was stated here to show that he does not do [these things]. Now, in order to show that he maintains his life by means of the Dhamma and in accordance with justice, it is said:
"and he is not a deceiver," and so forth. In this context, terms such as "deceiver" (kuhaka) and the rest have been explained in detail in the *Brahmajāla Sutta*.
"Guarded in the sense-faculties" and "moderate in eating" mean that he is one who guards the doors of the six sense-faculties and is also one who knows the proper measure in food.
“Samakārī” means one who acts with equanimity; the meaning is that, having abandoned bodily crookedness and so forth through body, speech, and mind, he conducts himself with evenness.

“Devoted to the practice of wakefulness” means that, having divided the day and night into six periods, he dwells diligently engaged in the practice of wakefulness according to the method stated as: “During the day, by means of walking and sitting. “Untiring” means free from sloth.
Free from physical sloth: he is one who has initiated energy both physically and mentally.
Having dispelled the company of crowds, he dwells alone in the four postures by way of the eight bases for exertion.
He is also one who has initiated mental energy; having abandoned and dispelled the company of defilements, he dwells alone by way of the eight meditative attainments.
Moreover, by warding off the arising of defilements in whatever way possible, he is one who has initiated energy through mental vigor (*cetasika-vīriya*).

He is a meditator (*jhāyī*) in the sense of meditating upon both the object and its characteristics. He is mindful (*satimā*), being endowed with mindfulness capable of recollecting what was done long ago and so forth.
He possesses beautiful eloquence (*kalyāṇa-paṭibhāna*), meaning he is both perfected in speech and perfected in inspired presence. His inspired presence is appropriate (*yutta-paṭibhāna*).

Furthermore, he is not one whose eloquence is loose. For a bhikkhu established in the practice of virtue is not one whose eloquence is loose, but rather one whose eloquence is disciplined, like the Elder Vaṅgīsa.
"Possessed of intelligence" means endowed with wisdom capable of proceeding. "Possessed of steadfastness" means endowed with wisdom capable of maintaining. Regarding "possessed of discernment": here—
"Thought" (*mati*) is merely a name for wisdom (*paññā*); therefore, the meaning is "one who possesses wisdom. Thus, by these three terms as well, wisdom alone is described.
In that regard, the energy of performing the duties of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*) was explained below; here, it is the energy of grasping the Buddha’s word.
Likewise, insight-wisdom (*vipassanā-paññā*) was explained below; here, it is the wisdom of grasping the Buddha’s word. And not in sensual pleasures...
"Free from greed" means free from greed for both sensual pleasures as objects (*vatthukāma*) and sensual pleasures as defilements (*kilesakāma*).

"Mindful and discerning" means that he conducts himself endowed with both mindfulness and wisdom in the seven instances, such as when going forward and returning; this is the meaning. "Discerning" (*nepakka*) is wisdom;
because he is endowed with that, he is called "discerning. The remainder here should also be construed in the same manner as before.
Commentary on the Chapter on the Method of Instruction (Anusāsanavidhādivaṇṇanā) 154.
“By means of personal and systematic attention” means by means of one’s own skillful mental attention (*upāyamanasikāra*).
“Practicing in accordance with what has been instructed” means practicing in the same way that the instruction was given by me. Of the three...
"Of the complete destruction of the fetters," and so forth, has already been explained. The remainder here also should be construed in the same manner as before. 155.

"Knowledge of the liberation of other persons" refers to the knowledge of the liberation from defilements by means of their respective paths for other persons, such as stream-enterers and others. The remainder here also should be construed in the same manner as before.
156. "In such-and-such a place I was, with such-and-such a name": one who recollects a previous existence thus grasps at name and clan.
He proceeds. One recollects only the pure aggregates (*khandha*), while another is able to do so and another is not.
In this regard, without taking the case of the one who is able as the standard, it is taken according to the one who is unable. What does the one who is unable do?
Recollecting only the pure aggregates, he goes back until he stands at the limit of many hundreds of thousands of births.
He descends [into the discussion] by grasping at name and clan. Showing this, he said, "one of such a name," and so forth.
"He spoke thus" means that this holder of a speculative view spoke thus. In that regard, although he says "eternal," his statement that "those beings transmigrate" is internally contradictory;
however, because he is a holder of a speculative view, he does not perceive this. Of the holder of a speculative view...
Indeed, there is no fixed position or rule here; it has been explained in detail in the *Brahmajāla Sutta* that "having grasped this, one lets go of that, and having let go of this, one grasps that.
This is the third eternalist doctrine; thus the Elder spoke of three eternalist doctrines by way of those who gain their views through acquisition alone.
However, the Blessed One, including even the proponents of reasoning (*takkīvāda*), [spoke of] four in the *Brahmajāla*.
Thus it was said. Furthermore, the detailed exposition of these three doctrines should be understood according to the method already set forth in the *Brahmajāla Sutta*.
The remainder here also should be expanded upon in the same manner as before.

157. "By way of counting" means by way of collective counting (*piṇḍagaṇanā*). "By way of calculation" means by way of mental counting (*manogaṇanā*) using the unbroken sequence (*acchiddaka*). In both cases:
This demonstrates the mere calculation of the total sum. What is meant is this:

even by grouping them into hundreds of years, thousands of years, hundreds of thousands of years, or tens of millions of years, it is impossible to calculate them as "this many hundreds of years" or "this many tens of millions of years.
However, because you have fulfilled the ten perfections (pāramīs), [you possess] the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa).
Because you have well-penetrated [the Dhamma], unobstructed knowledge carries you like a hero.

Therefore, having placed skill in the knowledge of teaching foremost, he demonstrates that one could show "this much" even by setting a limit according to the number of years, or by defining it according to the number of eons.
As for the meaning of the text here, it is exactly as stated in the method already given. The rest should also be construed here in the same manner as before.
158. “This is unsurpassed, venerable sir, regarding the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings.
Venerable sir, this teaching on the knowledge of beings by way of their death and rebirth-linking is unsurpassed for you alone. The Buddhas of the past taught it in just this way;
the Buddhas of the future will teach it in just this way. You have indeed conformed to the knowledge of those Buddhas of the past and the future.
He declared: “For this reason also, venerable sir, I am thus confident in the Blessed One. Thus he explains.
The meaning of the text here has already been explained in detail.
159. “With taints, with acquisitions” means with fault, with censure. “It is not called noble” means it is not noble supernormal power (*ariya-iddhi*).
It is said: "Taintless and without substrate" means free from fault and free from reproach. "Called noble" means it is called noble psychic power (*ariyiddhi*).
"He dwells there perceiving the unrepulsive": how does he dwell there perceiving the unrepulsive?
He radiates loving-kindness toward repulsive beings and applies the perception of elements to conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*). As it is said: "How..."
How does one dwell perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive? Toward an undesirable object, one either pervades it with loving-kindness or analyzes it by way of its elements.

"One dwells there perceiving the repulsive" means that toward beings who are not repulsive, one pervades them with the perception of foulness (asubhasaññā), and toward conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra), one applies the perception of impermanence (aniccasaññā). As it is said: "How does one perceive the repulsive in the unrepulsive?"
"How does he dwell? Toward a desirable object, he pervades it with the perception of foulness, or he contemplates it as impermanent.
The meaning should be understood in the same way for the remaining phrases as well.
"He dwells there equanimous" means that toward the desirable he feels no lust, and toward the undesirable he feels no hatred, unlike others who dwell without such equanimity.
They give rise to delusion; by not giving rise to it in this way, one dwells equanimous toward the six objects through the sixfold equanimity.
"This is unsurpassed, venerable sir, regarding the various kinds of psychic power"—venerable sir, this teaching concerning these two types of psychic power is unsurpassed.
"The Blessed One knows that"—the Blessed One fully and completely understands that teaching. That...
"By the Blessed One" means that he has fully and completely known that teaching. "There is nothing further to be directly known" means there is nothing further to be directly realized.
There is no such thing—neither another Dhamma nor another person—that the Blessed One does not know;
this does not exist. "Whatever another ascetic or brahmin might directly know" refers to whatever you yourselves have not yet directly known.

"There is no other ascetic or brahmin who, through direct knowledge, could surpass the Blessed One, nor one who would possess superior wisdom—namely, in the various modes of psychic power (*iddhividhā*).
Here, *yadidaṃ* is a mere particle. There is no one superior to the Blessed One in the various modes of psychic power.
For even the Buddhas of the past taught these two types of psychic power, and those of the future will likewise teach them.

"You too, having compared them with your own knowledge, taught these very same things. Thus, demonstrating that the Blessed One is unsurpassed in the various modes of psychic power (*iddhividhā*), he explains:
"For this reason also, venerable sir, I am thus confident in the Blessed One.
Up to this point, those very qualities which the General of the Dhamma, while seated in his daytime quarters, contemplated as the sixteen successive states are shown.
160. Now, demonstrating the qualities of the Blessed One by another way, he said, "Venerable sir, that which... and so forth.
Therein, "by a clansman endowed with faith" refers to those called clansmen endowed with faith, namely the Bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present. Therefore...
This is what is meant by "that which is to be attained by an omniscient Bodhisatta. But what is it that he must attain? It is the nine supramundane states (*lokuttara-dhamma*).

Regarding the phrases "with energy aroused" and so forth, all terms such as "energy" (*vīriya*), "fortitude" (*thāma*), and others are synonyms for energy. Therein, "with energy aroused" means with energy exerted.
"Possessing fortitude" means endowed with fortitude, that is, possessing firm energy. "With manly fortitude" [means...]
"By that steadfast one"—this means by one who possesses the human strength that ought to be attained. The same method applies to the two following phrases as well.
"By a great man capable of bearing the foremost burden of men" (*purisadhorayha*) refers to the great person capable of carrying that burden which must be borne by Buddhas of incomparable power.
"That has been reached by the Blessed One" means that all of this, which is to be reached by the Buddhas of the past and the future, has been attained by the Blessed One.
This shows that everything has been attained; there is not even a single quality lacking in the Blessed One.

"Devotion to the pleasure of sensual desires among sensual pleasures" means devotion to the pleasure of sensual desires regarding objective sensual objects (*vatthukāma*). Just as other recluses and brahmins, such as Keṇiya the matted-hair ascetic and others, [thought]:
"Who knows about the next world? Pleasant is the touch of this female wanderer’s soft, hairy arm."
He shows that [others] are devoted to sensual pleasure, enjoying whatever forms and other objects they encounter while sporting with female wanderers adorned with hair-tufts;
he shows that he is not so devoted. "Low" means base.
"Village" means the practice of those living in villages. "Ordinary" means that which is practiced by worldlings (*puthujjana*).
"Un-Aryan" means not faultless, or not to be practiced by the Noble Ones (*ariya*). "Connected with what is unbeneficial" means joined with what is harmful.
"Devotion to self-mortification" means devotion to the tormenting and afflicting of oneself. "Suffering" means connected with suffering, or consisting of suffering;
for example, as some ascetics and brahmins, thinking, "We shall avoid devotion to the pursuit of sensual pleasure," engage in bodily mortification.
They run after it, thinking, "Then we shall release it," and thus they pursue sensual pleasure; the Blessed One does not do so.
Rather, having avoided both these extremes, the Blessed One has practiced that very right practice which was described as:
"There is, monks, this Middle Way discovered by the Tathāgata, which produces vision. Therefore, he said: "And not devotion to self-mortification," and so forth.

"Of those pertaining to higher consciousness" (*ābhicetasika*) means of those belonging to higher consciousness; the meaning is that they exist having transcended the states of mind belonging to the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*).
"Of pleasant dwellings in this very life" (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra*) means of pleasant dwellings within this very personal existence (*attabhāva*).

For in the *Poṭṭhapāda Sutta*, the fruition attainment (*phalasamāpatti*) of the second jhāna accompanied by rapture (*sappītika*) is spoken of. In the *Pāsādika Sutta*, the jhāna that serves as the basis for insight (*vipassanāpādaka-jhāna*) together with the Path (*magga*) is spoken of.
In the *Dasuttara Sutta*, there is the attainment of the fruit of the fourth jhāna. In this *Sampasādanīya Sutta*, the jhānas as pleasant dwellings in the present life are explained.
"Obtaining at will" means obtaining according to one's desire. "Obtaining without difficulty" means obtaining without hardship. "Obtaining without trouble" means obtaining in abundance.
This concludes the commentary on the manner of giving instruction.
161. "In one world-system" means in a ten-thousandfold world-system (*dasasahassilokadhātu*). There are indeed three fields:
the field of birth (*jātikhetta*), the field of authority (*āṇākhetta*), and the field of range (*visayakhetta*). Among these, the "field of birth" refers to the ten-thousandfold world-system.

For at the time of the Tathāgata’s descent into his mother’s womb, at the time of his emergence [from it], at the time of his full enlightenment, at the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, and at the relinquishing of the life-force—[it is this field that is affected].
And at the time of his final *parinibbāna*, it trembles. However, the field of authority (*āṇākhetta*) consists of one hundred thousand million world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*).
For within this, the authority of the *Āṭānāṭiya*, *Moraparitta*, *Dhajaggaparitta*, *Ratanaparitta*, and so forth, prevails. But there is no limit to the field of the domain (*visayakhettassa*);
for the Buddhas, "as far as their knowledge extends, so far extends the knowable; as far as the knowable extends, so far extends their knowledge. The knowable is bounded by knowledge."*
Because of the statement, "Knowledge has the limit of what is to be known," there is nothing that is not its object.
However, regarding these three fields, there is no sutta stating that Buddhas arise in another world-system apart from this one;
rather, there is [a sutta] stating that they do not so arise. The three Piṭakas are the Vinaya Piṭaka and the Sutta Piṭaka.
The Abhidhamma Piṭaka. There have been three councils: the council of the Elder Mahākassapa, the council of the Elder Yasa, and the council of the Elder Moggaliputtatissa.

In the word of the Buddha contained within the Tipiṭaka as established by these three councils, there is no sutta stating that "Buddhas arise elsewhere besides this Cakkavāḷa," whereas there is one stating that they do not so arise.
"Neither before nor after" means that they do not arise simultaneously; rather, it is said that they arise either before or after.

In this context, "before" should not be understood as the period from the time the Bodhisatta sat at the seat of enlightenment with the resolve, "I shall not rise until I have attained awakening," up until his taking of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) in the mother's womb. For the Bodhisatta...
Indeed, at the moment of taking rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), the demarcation of his field was established by the very shaking of ten thousand world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*).
The arising of another Buddha is thereby prevented. Furthermore, it should not be understood that [the field] ceases after the final Nibbāna;
for as long as even relics the size of a mustard seed remain, so long do the Buddhas remain. Indeed, while the relics persist, the Buddhas themselves persist.
Therefore, the arising of another Buddha within this interval is indeed precluded;
however, once the Parinibbāna of the relics has occurred, the arising of another Buddha is not precluded.
This concludes the discussion on the disappearance of the Tipiṭaka.
There are three kinds of disappearance: the disappearance of the scriptures (*pariyatti*), the disappearance of realization (*paṭivedha*), and the disappearance of practice (*paṭipatti*).
In this context, "scriptures" refers to the Three Baskets (*piṭaka*). "Realization" refers to the realization of the Truths. "Practice" refers to the path.
Among these, both realization and practice may exist or they may not exist. For at one time, there are monks who bring about realization...
When there are many [who have attained realization], this monk is a worldling (puthujjana), and he must be pointed out by extending one's finger.
In this very island, at one time, there was not even a single monk who was a worldling. Those who fulfill the practice (paṭipatti) are also sometimes many and sometimes few.
Thus, both penetration (paṭivedha) and practice may exist or may not exist. However, as for the endurance of the Dispensation (sāsana):
The scriptures are the authority. For a wise person, having heard the Tipiṭaka, fulfills both [theoretical and practical knowledge].

Just as our Bodhisatta, after producing the five higher knowledges and the seven meditative attainments in the presence of Āḷāra, asked him for the preliminary exercise for the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he replied, "I do not know it. Then, [he went] to Udaka...
Having approached him and communicated the distinction he had attained, he asked about the preliminary practice for the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
the teacher explained it, and immediately upon hearing his words, the Great Being accomplished that jhāna.
In the same way, a wise bhikkhu fulfills both [requirements] by hearing the scriptures (pariyatti). Therefore, when the scriptures are preserved, the Dispensation (sāsana) endures.
It remains. But when that [Abhidhamma Piṭaka] disappears, then first the Abhidhamma Piṭaka is lost.
Among its parts, the *Paṭṭhāna* disappears first of all. Gradually, later on, the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* disappears;
when that has disappeared, even though the other two Piṭakas remain, the Dispensation (Sāsana) truly remains.
Therein, as the Sutta Piṭaka is disappearing, first the Aṅguttara Nikāya disappears, starting from the Elevens down to the Ones.
Immediately after that, the Saṃyutta Nikāya disappears, starting from the Cakkapeyyāla down to the Oghataraṇa.
Immediately after that, the Majjhima Nikāya disappears, starting from the Indriyabhāvanā...
The *Mūlapariyāya* disappears. Immediately thereafter, the *Dīghanikāya* disappears from the *Dasuttara* up to the *Brahmajāla*.
Even the inquiry of a single verse or two passes away; it is unable to sustain the teaching, just like the inquiries of Sabhiya and Āḷavaka.
These, it is said, belong to the interval of the time of Kassapa Buddha.
They were unable to preserve the Dispensation.
Even when two of the Piṭakas had disappeared, as long as the Vinaya Piṭaka remained, the Dispensation continued to endure.

When the Parivāra and the Khandhakas had disappeared, as long as the Ubhatovibhaṅga remained, it indeed persisted. When the Ubhatovibhaṅga had disappeared, [the Dispensation endured] even as long as the Mātikā remained.

When it is established, it remains established. When the *mātikā* (the summary of rules) has disappeared, but the *pātimokkha*, *pabbajjā*, and *upasampadā* remain, the Dispensation (*sāsana*) persists;
the outward sign (*liṅga*) continues for a long duration. However, the lineage of white-robed ascetics was unable to sustain the Dispensation from the time of Buddha Kassapa onwards.
It endured for a thousand years through those who had attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), and through those possessed of the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*).

It remained for a thousand years with those possessing the threefold knowledge (*tevijja*). It remained for a thousand years with those practicing dry-insight (*sukkhavipassaka*). It remained for a thousand years with those observing the *pātimokkha*.

However, from the moment of the final penetration of the Truths and from the moment of the final breach of morality, the Dispensation (*sāsana*) is said to have declined. From that point onward, the arising of another Buddha is no longer precluded.
The Explanation of the Periods Without the Dispensation:
There are three kinds of *parinibbāna*, namely, the *parinibbāna* of the defilements (*kilesa*), the *parinibbāna* of the aggregates (*khandha*), and the *parinibbāna* of the relics (*dhātu*).
Among these, the *parinibbāna* of the defilements occurred at the seat of enlightenment (*bodhipallaṅka*). The *parinibbāna* of the aggregates occurred at Kusinārā. The *parinibbāna* of the relics...
"In the future, it will come to pass. Indeed, at the time of the decline of the Dispensation, the relics in this island of Tambapaṇṇi shall assemble and proceed to the Mahācetiya.
From the Mahācetiya they shall go to the Rājāyatana-cetiya on Nāgadīpa. Thence they shall proceed to the Mahābodhipallaṅka.
Even from the abode of the Nāgas, from the world of the gods, and from the Brahma-world, the relics shall go to the Mahābodhipallaṅka alone."
They will go. Not even a single relic the size of a mustard seed shall perish along the way.
All the relics, gathered together upon the Great Enlightenment Seat (Mahābodhipallaṅka), becoming a single solid mass like a lump of gold, will emit six-colored rays of light.
These rays will pervade the ten-thousandfold world system (dasasahassilokadhātu), and then the deities of the ten-thousandfold universe (dasasahassacakkavāḷa) will assemble.

"Today the Teacher attains final Nibbāna; today the Dispensation declines; this is now our last sight of him"—thinking thus, they will feel a grief even greater than that on the day the One of Ten Powers passed away.

Except for those who have reached the stage of non-returning and whose taints are destroyed, the rest will not be able to maintain their composure. From among the relics, the fire element will arise and...
It will rise as far as the Brahma-world. As long as there is even a mustard-seed’s worth of relics remaining, it will continue as a single flame.
When the relics have been completely consumed, it will be extinguished. Having displayed such great majesty, once the relics have vanished, the Dispensation is said to have vanished.

As long as it does not thus disappear, so long it is called "not-lattermost. Thus, that they might arise neither first nor last—that situation is impossible. But why do they not arise neither first nor last?
Because of their non-extraordinary nature. For Buddhas are extraordinary persons. As it is said: "Bhikkhus, one person, when arising in the world, arises [as such]."
