“A marvelous person! Who is that one person? It is the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
For if two, four, eight, or sixteen were to arise together, they would not be marvelous.
Indeed, even in a single monastery, there is no magnificent gain or honor for two cetiyas; likewise, monks do not become marvelous simply by being numerous.
If they were to arise, Buddhas would likewise arise; therefore, they do not arise. Furthermore, because there would be no distinction in their teaching:
for whatever Dhamma—such as the divisions of the foundations of mindfulness—one [Buddha] teaches, that same teaching would have to be taught by another who had arisen [at the same time];
thus, it would not be marvelous. However, when one [Buddha] alone teaches the Dhamma, the teaching itself becomes marvelous, owing to the absence of dispute.

Furthermore, if many Buddhas were to arise, they might dispute with one another like the disciples of various teachers, saying, "Our Buddha is handsome," or "Our Buddha has a sweet voice," or "He is a recipient of gains and is meritorious. For this reason as well, they do not arise simultaneously.
Moreover, this very reason was explained in detail by the Elder Nāgasena when he was questioned by King Milinda. For it is said there:
"Venerable Nāgasena, this was indeed spoken by the Blessed One:
'It is impossible, monks, it is out of the question, that two Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, should arise simultaneously and at the same time in a single world-system;
such a thing is not possible. Yet, Venerable Nāgasena, all the Tathāgatas, while teaching, [spoke of] thirty-seven..."
They teach the factors conducive to enlightenment; in their discourse they speak of the Four Noble Truths;
in their instruction they train in the three trainings; and in their guidance they direct toward the practice of heedfulness.
If, venerable Nāgasena, the teaching of all Tathāgatas is one, their discourse is one, their training is one, and their guidance is one—
For what reason do two Tathāgatas not arise simultaneously? First of all, by the arising of even a single Buddha, this world becomes filled with light;
if there were a second Buddha, this world would become even more intensely illuminated by the radiance of both.
Furthermore, when two Tathāgatas were giving instruction, they would instruct easily, and when exhorting, they would exhort [with ease].
“May they instruct me happily; tell me the reason for this, so that I may become free from doubt.
“Great King, this ten-thousandfold world system is the single retainer of a Buddha; it sustains the qualities of only one Tathāgata.
If a second Buddha were to arise, this ten-thousandfold world system would not be able to sustain them; it would tremble.”
It would shake, it would bend, it would incline, it would lean, it would scatter, it would be dispersed, it would fall apart, and it would not remain in its place.
Great King, just as if there were a boat that could support only one person, and with one person having boarded it, that boat were balanced;
then a second person were to come who was similar in lifespan, complexion, age, stature, and whether thin or stout—
"Suppose, Great King, a man with all his limbs and members were to board that boat; would that boat, Great King, be able to carry both of them?
"Certainly not, Bhante; it would move, shake, lean, incline, bend, scatter, disperse, fall apart, and fail to remain steady;
it would sink into the water. "In the same way, Great King..."
This ten-thousandfold world system is the single domain of one Buddha’s sustaining power; it sustains the virtues of only one Tathāgata.
If a second Buddha were to arise, this ten-thousandfold world system would not be able to sustain him... [and so on] ...it would not even find a place to stand.
Or again, Great King, it is as if a man were to eat food until his fill, filling himself completely up to his throat.

If that person, having eaten his fill until his stomach was full, rounded, without gaps, and made rigid—so that his spine could no longer bend—were to eat that same amount of food once again, would that man, O Great King, be happy? "Certainly not, Venerable Sir;
he would die from eating it all at once. "In the very same way, O Great King, this ten-thousandfold world system is the single vessel for a Buddha."
...pe... "it would not find a place [to rest].
"Venerable Nāgasena, does the earth tremble because of the excessive weight of the Dhamma? "In this case, Great King, suppose there were two carts filled with jewels up to their very openings;
having taken jewels from one cart and placed them in the other..."
"Suppose they were to pour [the jewels] into a cart; would that cart, Great King, be able to bear the weight of the jewels from two carts?
"No, venerable sir. Its nave would burst, its spokes would break, its rim would give way, and its axle would snap.
"But why, Great King, would the cart break under the excessive weight of the jewels?"
“Yes, venerable sir,” he replied. “In the same way, Great King, the earth trembles because of the excessive burden of the Dhamma.
Furthermore, Great King, this reason has been set forth to illustrate the power of the Buddha;
now hear another appropriate reason for why two Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas do not arise simultaneously. If, Great King...”
If two Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas were to arise simultaneously, a dispute would arise among their assemblies, saying, "He is your Buddha;

he is our Buddha," and they would become divided into two factions. Great King, it is just as if a dispute were to arise among the retinues of two powerful ministers, saying, "He is your minister; he is our minister," and they would become divided into two factions.

It happens thus: likewise, Great King, if two Perfectly Enlightened Ones were to arise at the same moment, a dispute would arise within their assemblies, saying, "The Buddha belongs to you" and "The Buddha belongs to us," and they would become divided into two factions.
This, Great King, is one reason why two Perfectly Enlightened Ones do not arise at the same moment.
Furthermore, Great King, hear another further reason why two Perfectly Enlightened Ones do not arise simultaneously.
If, Great King, two Perfectly Enlightened Ones were to arise at one and the same moment, then the statement, "The Buddha is supreme," would be false;
likewise, the statements, "The Buddha is the eldest," "The Buddha is the best," and "The Buddha is the most distinguished," would be false.

The statement that "the Buddha is supreme," "the Buddha is preeminent," "the Buddha is peerless," "the Buddha is equal to the unequaled," "the Buddha is matchless," "the Buddha is without counterpart," and "the Buddha is without rival" would be false.
Great King, you should also accept this reason according to its meaning: for what reason could there be two perfectly enlightened Buddhas?
They do not arise simultaneously.
Furthermore, Great King, it is the natural disposition of the Blessed Buddhas that only one Buddha arises in the world at a time.
For what reason? Because of the greatness of the qualities of an omniscient Buddha; for this reason, Great King, even another...
Whatever is great, that is indeed one. The earth, Great King, is great, yet it is only one. The ocean is great, yet it is only one.
Sineru, the king of mountains, is great, yet it is only one. Space is great, yet it is only one.
Sakka is great, yet he is only one. Māra is great, yet he is only one. Mahābrahmā is great, yet he is only one.
"The Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is great; he alone is in the world. Wherever they arise, there is no room for others.
Therefore, Great King, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, arises in the world as one alone.
"Well explained, venerable Nāgasena, is this question by means of similes and reasons."

"In accordance with the Dhamma" means the preliminary practice that is in conformity with the ninefold supramundane Dhamma. "One who speaks in accordance with the Dhamma" means one who speaks with reason.
"Discussion and counter-discussion" means discussion itself.
162. Regarding "the venerable Udāyī": there are three elders named Udāyī—Lāḷudāyī, Kāḷudāyī, and Mahāudāyī. Here...
Mahā-Udāyī is intended here. It is said that as he listened to this sutta from beginning to end, five-colored rapture arose within him;
it would travel from the soles of his feet up to the crown of his head, and from the crown of his head back down to the soles of his feet;
it would descend from both ends into the middle, and from the middle out to both ends.
He went. With his body suffused by uninterrupted rapture and with powerful gladness, he spoke these words beginning with, “It is wonderful, venerable sir!

regarding the virtues of the One Possessed of the Ten Powers. “Fewness of wishes” (*appicchatā*) means freedom from craving. “Contentment” (*santuṭṭhitā*) means satisfaction in four requisites in three ways.
“Effacement” (*sallekhatā*) means the state of having worn away all defilements. “In that he indeed... (*yatra hi nāma*)... [etc.]
"Who indeed"—meaning he will not reveal himself; "he will not manifest his own virtues.
"They would carry a banner"—meaning they would wander about Nālandā holding up banners, saying, "Who is there who is equal to us?
"Behold, Udāyin, the fewness of desires in the Tathāgata"—behold, Udāyin, such as is the Tathāgata’s...
He spoke thus, accepting the elder’s statement regarding fewness of desires (*appicchatā*). If it is asked: "Does the Blessed One neither reveal himself nor speak of his own virtues?"—the answer is:
No, he does not fail to speak. He speaks by way of fewness of desires and so forth, but he does not speak for the sake of robes and the like.
For this very reason, he said: "Behold, Udāyin, the fewness of desires in the Tathāgata," and so on. [This refers to] a being capable of awakening.
However, having come [to this realization], he speaks according to the needs of those to be trained (veneyya). As it is said:
"I have no teacher, and no one equal to me is found;
in the world with its devas, there is no rival to me."
In this way, many verses and discourses illustrating the virtues of the Tathāgata should also be recited in detail.
(163) "You should speak constantly" means you should speak again and again. Do not think, "He spoke to me in the morning," and thus fail to speak at midday or other times;
nor do you think, "He spoke to me today," and thus fail to speak on subsequent days.
The meaning [is as follows]. "He proclaimed" means he spoke. This discourse is called a "veyyākaraṇa" because it is devoid of verses (niggāthaka).
"Adhivacana" means a name. However, this phrase beginning with "Thus indeed" was established by the compilers of the collection (saṅgītikāra).
The rest is entirely clear in meaning throughout.
The commentary on the Sampasādanīya Sutta of the Dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathā, titled Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, is completed. 6.
The commentary on the Pāsādika Sutta.
The Explanation of the Passing of Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta:
164. Thus have I heard: this is the Pāsādika Sutta. Herein, this is the commentary on the words not [already] explained:
“The Sakyans called Vedhañña” means that certain Sakyans who were trained in archery were named Vedhañña. “In their mango grove, in a palace” refers to theirs.
There was a long palace built for the purpose of learning a craft in the Mango Grove, and he dwelt there.

"Has recently passed away" means he has just now passed away. "Divided into two parts" means split into two, having become two factions. Regarding "quarrels and so forth": a quarrel is a preliminary dispute;
that which has increased through the taking up of sticks and the like, and through the transgression of the formal rules (paṇṇatti), is a "strife."
“Dispute” (*vivāda*) is contradictory speech in the manner of saying, “You do not understand this Dhamma and Vinaya,” and so forth.
“Piercing” (*vitudanta*) means wounding. “My word is beneficial” (*sahitaṃ me*) means my speech is connected with the welfare [of others].

“What you have long practiced has been overturned” (*adhiciṇṇaṃ te viparāvattaṃ*) means that which you have long practiced and mastered through habitual cultivation has turned back upon encountering my argument.
"An accusation has been leveled against you" means: "I have brought a charge of fault against you. "Go for the sake of clearing the accusation" means:
"Take a bowl of alms-food and wander about, approaching various people and seeking further [support] for the purpose of clearing the accusation.
"Or refute it" means: "Alternatively, free yourself from the charge I have brought against you. "If you are able" means: "If you can. "It will surely be your execution" means: [if you fail].
"Only death. Regarding "among the followers of Nātaputta": among the disciples of Nātaputta. "Disgusted with form" means those whose nature is one of weariness;

they do not even perform such acts as salutation. "Detached from form" means those whose affection has vanished. "Averse to form" means those whose nature is to turn away from performing their duties with proper care.
"Just as" (yathā tan ti): just as [they are] by way of being disgusted, detached, and averse toward a Dhamma and Discipline that is ill-proclaimed and of such a nature.
It must have come to be; likewise, it has arisen—this is the meaning. "Ill-spoken" means badly recited. "Ill-expounded" means poorly made known.
"Not conducive to tranquility" means incapable of effecting the pacification of lust and the other defilements. "With its stupa broken" means with its foundation destroyed.
For here, Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta himself is the "stupa" in the sense of being their foundation; he, however, is broken and dead. Therefore it was said.
“*Bhinnathūpe*”: in one who is without a refuge, meaning devoid of a refuge due to the very absence of such a one.
But surely this son of Nāṭa was a resident of Nāḷandā; why then did he pass away in Pāvā?
It is said that after hearing the qualities of the Buddha spoken in ten verses by the householder Upāli, who had penetrated the Truths, his blood turned hot...
He abandoned him. Then, taking him while he was still unwell, they went to Pāvā. There he passed away. As he was passing away, he thought:
"My doctrine is not leading to liberation and is devoid of essence; we ourselves are lost, but let not the rest of the people become fillers of the states of woe.
However, if I say, 'My teaching does not lead to liberation,' they will not believe me."
“What if I were to have these two people learn [the texts] not by a single recitation? After my passing, they will quarrel with one another;
the Teacher, on account of that dispute, will deliver a discourse on the Dhamma, and through that they will come to know the greatness of the Dispensation.
Then, one pupil approached him and said, “Venerable sir, you are frail; even for me, in this—”
“Teach the essence of the Dhamma; the Teacher is our authority. “Friend, after my passing, you should hold to eternalism,” he said to one.
Another approached him, and he caused that one to grasp annihilationism.

Thus, instead of making these two people hold the same view, he had many grasp various positions through different methods and then passed away. After they had performed his funeral rites, they gathered together.
They asked one another, "Friends, what did your teacher declare to be the essence? One stood up and said, "He declared mine.
"What did he declare? "Eternalism. Another contradicted him and said, "He declared mine to be the essence.
In this way, they all increased their mutual dispute, each saying, "He declared mine to be the essence; I am the senior," and they began to revile one another.
Having reviled him and struck him with their hands and feet, they departed in different directions by way of the same path. 165.
Now, as for "Cunda the novice," this was the Elder who was the younger brother of the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta).
During his time as one not yet fully ordained, the monks addressed him as "Cunda the novice," and even during his time as an elder, they continued to address him in that same manner.
They practiced [these things]. Therefore it was said: “The novice Cunda.
As for the passage, “Having spent the rains retreat at Pāvā, he approached Sāmagāma, where the Venerable Ānanda was,” why did he approach him?
It is said that after Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta had passed away, people throughout Jambudīpa were discussing this here and there: “The Nigaṇṭha...”
"Nāṭaputta was known as a teacher who was alone; with his passing away, such a dispute arose among his disciples.
But the ascetic Gotama is as well-known throughout Jambudīpa as the moon or the sun, and his disciples are likewise well-known.
What kind of dispute will there be among the disciples when the ascetic Gotama has attained final nibbāna?"
Having heard that talk, the Elder thought: "I shall take this matter and report it to the One of Ten Powers;
the Teacher, taking this as the occasion for instruction, will deliver a discourse. He then departed and went to Sāmagāma, where the Venerable Ānanda was staying.

"Sāmagāma" is the name of that village because of the abundance of *sāmāka* grass there. "Where the Venerable Ānanda was": instead of going directly to the presence of the Blessed One, he approached where his preceptor, the Venerable Ānanda, was.
It is said that during the time of the Buddha, the Elder Sāriputta and the Elder Ānanda looked after one another.
The Elder Sāriputta looked after the Elder Ānanda, thinking, "He is performing the service of attending upon the Teacher. The Elder Ānanda [thought], "The Blessed One..."

“the foremost of disciples,” he claimed the Elder Sāriputta as his own. Having ordained the young sons of noble families, he caused them to receive the formal acceptance (upajjhāya) from the Elder Sāriputta. The Elder Sāriputta did exactly the same.
In this way, by each one giving his own bowl and robes, ordaining them, and causing them to receive the formal acceptance, there came to be five hundred bhikkhus for each of them.
The Venerable Ānanda, having obtained excellent robes and other requisites, gave them to the Elder.
Regarding the worship of the Jewel of the Dhamma:
It is said that a certain brahmin thought, "Worship of the Buddha-jewel and the Saṅgha-jewel is well known, but [the worship of the Dhamma-jewel is not]."
“How indeed is the jewel of the Dhamma honored? Thus he approached the Blessed One and asked about this matter.
The Blessed One said: “If you, brahmin, desire to honor the jewel of the Dhamma, honor one who is learned.
“Venerable sir, point out such a learned person. “Ask the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. He [then] asked the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Having approached him, he said, "Venerable sir, please point out one who is very learned. The Elder Ānanda replied, "The brahmin.
The brahmin honored the Elder with a set of three robes worth a thousand pieces of gold. The Elder took them and went into the presence of the Blessed One.
The Blessed One asked, "Ānanda, where did you get these? "They were given by a certain brahmin, venerable sir."
"But I wish to give this to the Venerable Sāriputta. "Give it, Ānanda. "He has set out on a journey, venerable sir.
"Give it when he returns, venerable sir; the training rule has been laid down. "But when will Sāriputta return?
"In about ten days, venerable sir. [The Buddha said: "I allow you, Ānanda, to store an extra robe for a maximum of ten days."
He laid down a training rule.
The Elder Sāriputta likewise gave whatever pleasing thing he obtained to the Elder Ānanda.
He, in turn, gave even this younger brother of his to the Elder as his co-resident. Therefore it was said: "Whatever [he received]..."
“He approached the venerable Ānanda as his preceptor. It was because he thought: “My preceptor is of great wisdom;
he will report this matter to the Teacher, and then the Teacher will teach the Dhamma accordingly.
*Kathāpābhataṃ* means the source of the discourse. For the root (*mūla*) is called *pābhata*. As it has been said:
“Even with a small load, the wise and discerning person raises themselves up, like a tiny fire that is fanned into a blaze.
[The phrase] “to see the Blessed One” means for the purpose of seeing the Blessed One. But had the Blessed One not been seen by him before?
He had never been seen before. For this venerable one goes to wait upon [the Teacher] eighteen times in a single day—nine times by day and nine times by night.
Although he wishes to go a hundred or even a thousand times a day, he does not go without a reason;
he goes only after taking up a specific question. On that day...
Desiring to depart because of that conversation, he spoke thus.
[Commentary on the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Fully Enlightened One] 166.
"For it is so, Cunda," said the Blessed One, even though the Elder Ānanda had announced this; for the Elder Ānanda—
The owner of this discourse is the Elder Cunda; he is the one who knows its beginning, middle, and end.
Therefore, when the Blessed One was speaking with him, he said, "It is indeed so, Cunda," and so forth. The meaning of this is:
Cunda, it is indeed so that in a Dhamma and Vinaya of such a poorly proclaimed nature, the disciples become divided and engage in quarrels and the like.
They dwell piercing [others] with their word-arrows.

Now, because the teaching that leads to liberation becomes evident only by contrast with the teaching that does not lead to liberation, he first shows the teaching that does not lead to liberation, saying:
"In this case, Cunda, there is a teacher who is not a Fully Enlightened One," and so forth. Therein, having departed from that...
"Dhammas proceed" means they do not proceed continuously; the meaning is that they proceed by descending repeatedly, with intervals between them.
"These are gains for you, friend" means these qualities, such as practice in accordance with the Dhamma, are gains for you.
"Well-gotten" means even your human state is well-gotten. "Let him practice thus" means let him practice in this way. As...
"The Dhamma has been taught by the Teacher" refers to the manner in which the Dhamma was spoken by the Teacher.
"And he who exhorts" refers to the teacher who exhorts. "And that which he exhorts" refers to the pupil whom he exhorts.
"And he who is exhorted" refers to the pupil who, having been exhorted in this way, practices for the sake of that goal exactly as he was exhorted by the teacher.

"All those three" means all three of them. For here, the teacher generates demerit because he has incited [others to it]; the student who has accepted [the task] generates demerit because he has accepted it;
and the one who is practicing generates demerit because he is practicing. Therefore it was said: "All those generate much demerit.
By this same method, the meaning should be understood in all the sections.
167. Furthermore, "practicing the method" (*ñāyappaṭipanna*) here means practicing the cause. "He will accomplish the method" means he will bring the cause to fruition.
"He exerts energy" means he performs an energy that produces suffering for himself. For this has been said:
"Monks, in a poorly proclaimed Dhamma and Discipline, he who exerts energy dwells in suffering; he who is indolent dwells in happiness."
168. Having thus shown the teaching that does not lead to liberation, he now, showing the teaching that does lead to liberation, said:

"But here, Cunda, there is a teacher who is a perfectly enlightened Buddha," and so forth. In this context, "leading" (*niyyānika*) means it leads for the sake of the path and for the sake of the fruit.
169. "He arouses energy" means he arouses the energy that produces his own happiness. For this has been said:
"Monks, in this well-expounded Dhamma and Vinaya, he who is indolent dwells in suffering; he who has aroused energy dwells in happiness. 170.
Thus the Blessed One, having shown praise for the clansman who practices rightly within the liberating teaching, [spoke as follows].
Again, expanding the teaching, he said here: "In this world, Cunda, the Teacher arose," and so forth. In that context, *aviññāpitatthā* means "whose meaning has not been made known" (*abodhitatthā*).
Regarding *sabbasaṅgāhapadakaṃ*: it is "made by means of words that include everything"; the meaning is that it is not something made by including everything.
There is also a reading, *sabbasaṅgāhapadagataṃ*; [this means] it has not entered into all the words that include everything.

The meaning is: "not born of a single bond. "Possessing wonders" (*sappāṭihīraka*) means leading to liberation (*niyyānika*). "As far as gods and humans" means well-proclaimed from the world of the gods down to the world of humans.
"It becomes a cause for regret" means it produces remorse. The phrase "and our Teacher in the world" is stated for the purpose of showing the way in which that regret arises for them.
"It does not become a cause for regret" refers to [the state] of the disciples having approached the Teacher.
Because one has attained what ought to be attained, it causes no remorse. 172.

"Thera" means firm, being endowed with the qualities that constitute seniority. The terms such as "rattaññū" (long-standing) have already had their meaning explained. "Etehi ce pi" means by these aforementioned [qualities]. 173. "Attained security from bondage":
because it is secure from the four bonds, Arahantship is here called "security from bondage" (*yogakkhema*); that—
The meaning is "attained. "Able to fully explain the True Dhamma" means they are capable of correctly proclaiming his True Dhamma because it was received in his very presence. 174.

"Practitioners of the holy life" refers to noble disciples living the life of celibacy (*brahmacariya*). "Those who enjoy sensual pleasures" refers to lay followers who have attained the stage of stream-entry (*sotāpanna*).

“*Iddhañceva*,” and so forth, have already been explained in detail in the *Mahāparinibbāna Sutta*. “Attained the pinnacle of gain and the pinnacle of fame” means having reached both the highest point of material gain and the highest point of renown.
“Furthermore, Cunda, I now have elder bhikkhu disciples,” refers to the elders such as Sāriputta, Moggallāna, and others.
“Bhikkhunīs” refers to the elder bhikkhunīs such as Khemā and Uppalavaṇṇā. “Lay disciple followers” refers to householders dressed in white garments.

"Practitioners of the holy life (*brahmacārin*)" refers to Citta, Gahapati Hatthaka, Āḷavaka, and others. "Enjoyers of sensual pleasures (*kāmabhogin*)" refers to Cūḷa-Anāthapiṇḍika, Mahā-Anāthapiṇḍika, and others.
"Practitionesses of the holy life (*brahmacārinī*)" refers to Nandamātā and others. "Enjoyers of sensual pleasures (*kāmabhoginī*)" refers to Khujjuttarā and others.
(176) "Endowed with all aspects (*sabbākārasampanna*)" means endowed with all causes. "This very thing" means this very holy life (*brahmacariya*).
One who speaks of this very Dhamma correctly by way of cause and method might say thus: "Udakāssudanti" means "Udaka indeed.
"Passaṃ na passatīti" means "one who sees does not see. It is said that he asked this question of the great multitude.
When they replied, "We do not know, Teacher; please tell us," he said: "This question is profound regarding the suitability of nutriment..."

“Having reflected for a short while, it is possible to explain. Then, after they had performed great honors for four months, as he was explaining that question, he said, beginning with, “And what does one not see? In this context, *sādhunisitassa* means well-sharpened or keen;
for it is said that the surface of a well-sharpened razor is perceived, but its edge is not perceived—this is the meaning here.
Commentary on the Dhamma to be Chanted Together (Saṅgāyitabbadhammādivaṇṇanā) 177.
*Saṅgamma samāgammā* means having come together, having assembled. *Atthena atthaṃ, byañjanena byañjanaṃ* means by comparing meaning with meaning and phrasing with phrasing;
the sense is: "by those who are harmonizing the meaning along with the meaning, and the phrasing along with the phrasing. *Saṅgāyitabbaṃ* means that which is to be chanted together.
It should be recited and studied. "In this very holy life" means: in this entirety of the holy life of the Dispensation (*sāsana-brahmacariya*).
"In that regard": in the midst of the Saṅgha, or regarding what has been spoken by him.

"He grasps the meaning wrongly and misrepresents the phrasing" refers to [the case where one understands] "the four foundations of mindfulness" (*cattāro satipaṭṭhānā*) as "the foundation of mindfulness" (*satipaṭṭhāna*) [merely] as the object (*ārammaṇa*).
He grasps the meaning. He applies the phrasing: “The foundations of mindfulness. Regarding this meaning, friend, he considers:
“Is ‘mindfulness itself is the foundation of mindfulness’ the correct sense? Regarding the meaning “the four foundations of mindfulness,” he considers:
“Are these the phrases, or are they ‘the four foundations of mindfulness’? Which of these phrases is more appropriate? This is for the sake of this [meaning].
Which of these two sets of phrasing—“the four foundations of mindfulness” or “mindfulness itself is the foundation of mindfulness”—is more appropriate and more closely connected to the meaning?

Is the meaning of this phrase “the four foundations of mindfulness” that “mindfulness itself is the foundation of mindfulness,” or is the meaning rather that “the object is the foundation of mindfulness”?
Regarding this meaning, friend, [it is] “the object...”
Regarding the meaning of "establishment of mindfulness" (*satipaṭṭhāna*): "And those which" refers to those very things spoken by me;
"and this which" refers to this very thing spoken by me. "It is neither to be exalted" means that you should first abide correctly in both the meaning and the phrasing.
Furthermore, it is neither to be exalted nor to be disparaged; rather, it is to be made understood.
It should be made known. "And of that meaning" refers to the meaning: "Mindfulness itself is the foundation of mindfulness.
"And of those expressions" refers to the expression: "foundations of mindfulness. "For the purpose of pondering" means for the purpose of reflecting upon and retaining [the teaching].
In this manner, the meaning should be understood in all sections.
"181. 'Tādisan' means one such as you. 'Atthūpetan' means endowed with meaning; that is, one who understands the meaning.
'Byañjanūpetan' means endowed with phrasing; that is, one who understands the phrasing. In this way, praise this bhikkhu.
For this bhikkhu is not merely called your disciple, Cunda; he is called a Buddha. Thus the Blessed One [praised] the bhikkhu who was well-versed in the scriptures."
He established [him] in his own place.
182. Now, expanding upon the teaching even further than that, he said, "Cunda, I have not [said... and so forth. Therein:
"Corruptions pertaining to the present life" (*diṭṭhadhammikā āsavā*) are those corruptions that arise in this world due to the cause of requisites.

"Corruptions pertaining to the future life" (*samparāyikā āsavā*) are those corruptions that arise in the next world due to the cause of quarrels. "For restraint" (*saṃvarāya*) means for the purpose of closing [the doors] so that they do not enter.
"For warding off" (*paṭighātāya*) means for the purpose of repelling them by striking at their root. "It is enough for you, as far as cold is concerned..."
"For the warding off" means it is capable of warding off cold for you. This is what is meant:
that robe which has been permitted by me to you was not permitted so that you might wear it while indulging in vanity or pride;
rather, having worn it and having performed the warding off of cold and other such functions, one should practice the ascetic life (samaṇadhamma) properly for the sake of happiness.

"You shall apply your attention" is what was permitted. And just as it is with the robe, so it is with almsfood and the rest. Furthermore, the word-by-word commentary here should be understood according to the method already stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.
This concludes the commentary on the pursuit of pleasure and so forth.

183. *Sukhallikānuyogo* means devotion to the pursuit of pleasure; the meaning is "inclination toward the enjoyment of pleasure. *Sukheti* means "it makes one happy. *Pīṇeti* means "it makes one plump or nourished. 186.
*Aṭṭhitadhammā* means those whose intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) has perished. "We have no tongue" means that whatever they wish for, they say;
sometimes they speak of the Path, sometimes of the Fruit, and sometimes of Nibbāna—this is the intention. *Jānatā* means "by one who knows."
"By one who knows with the knowledge of omniscience. "Sees" means by one who sees with the five eyes.
"Deep-rooted" means having entered deep into the ground. "Well-planted" means firmly planted.
"In the same way, friends," means that one whose taints are exhausted is incapable of transgressing nine points. His non-transgression therein is unshakable and unshaking.
In this regard, even stream-enterers and those beyond are incapable of intentionally depriving a living being of life and so forth.
"To enjoy sensual pleasures by means of hoarding" means to enjoy them after having made a hoard of both material objects (*vatthu-kāma*) and defilements (*kilesa-kāma*).
"Just as formerly when he was a householder" means that he is incapable of enjoying them in the same manner as he did previously when he was a layman.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Questions (Pañhabyākaraṇa-vaṇṇanā) 187.
For stream-enterers and others dwelling in the midst of a household remain with the outward marks of a householder for as long as life lasts.

However, one whose taints are exhausted, having attained Arahantship, passes away into final Nibbāna while still a human being or goes forth into homelessness. Among the gods of the Four Great Kings and the other realms...
He does not remain even for a moment among the gods of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*). Why? Because of the absence of any place of seclusion (*viveka*).
However, while remaining in the state of a terrestrial deity (*bhummadeva*), he remains even after attaining *arahantship*. It is by way of this [state] that this question has arisen.
Furthermore, his status as a monk (*bhikkhu*) should be understood because his faults have been destroyed. "Atīraṃ" means boundless, unlimited, and vast. And yet...

Regarding the phrase "the future": they might say this thinking that the ascetic Gotama does not declare [anything] concerning the future period in such a way; rather, it seems he knows only the past, not the future.

For while his recollection of five hundred and fifty Jātakas in the past is well known, no such extensive recollection regarding the future is observed. It is with this thought in mind that they would speak thus.
What is that "how"? It is the non-demonstration [of the future]. What indeed is this non-demonstration? How indeed?
By what cause does one who does not know fail to recollect the future? Is it because of a lack of desire to recollect that he does not recollect? [The answer is:

by means of a knowledge and vision directed elsewhere—that is, by means of a knowledge that has become "vision" through its capacity to see as if it were direct perception, being directed toward something other [than the future].
They imagine that knowledge and vision occurring with reference to one thing while directed toward another should be included and defined as "acting otherwise.
For they imagine that such knowledge and vision is present at all times and continuously, whether walking or standing, asleep or awake; yet no such knowledge exists.
Therefore, it should be understood that fools and the incompetent imagine things in this very way.
"One who follows after beings" refers to [the knowledge] associated with the recollection of past lives. "As much as he desires" means:
thinking "I shall know as much as I wish to know," he directs his knowledge. Then, for him, it was like an arrow shot into a fragile leaf-cup.
Knowledge proceeds unimpeded and unobstructed as if it were a physical object; therefore, he recollects as much as he desires.
"Born at the foot of the Bodhi tree" means born at the root of the Bodhi tree. "Knowledge arises" means the knowledge of the four paths arises.
"This is the last birth" means that because the root of birth has been abandoned by that knowledge, this is the final birth. "There is no more renewed existence now."
Furthermore, another kind of knowledge arises. "Not connected with the goal" means it is not based on the welfare of this world or the welfare of the next world.
"The Tathāgata does not declare that" means the Tathāgata does not speak such non-leading talk as, for example, the story of the Battle of the Bhārata or the abduction of Sītā.
"Real, true, but not connected with the goal" refers to base talk such as talk about kings and so forth.
“The Tathāgata knows the right time” means he knows the proper occasion. Having established the basis and the cause, he speaks only at the appropriate and fitting time.
“Therefore he is called the Tathāgata”: because he speaks exactly as it ought to be spoken, changing the letter *da* to *ta*, he is called the Tathāgata;
this is the meaning. “Seen” refers to the sense-sphere of visible forms (*rūpāyatana*). “HearD” refers to the sense-sphere of sounds (*saddāyatana*).
The sense-sphere of odors, the sense-sphere of tastes, and the sense-sphere of tangibles are so called because they are to be smelled, tasted, and touched after having been sensed and reached.

"Apprehended" (*viññāta*) refers to the sense-sphere of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*), such as pleasure, pain, and so forth. "Attained" (*patta*) means attained either by seeking or without seeking.

"Sought" (*pariyesita*) means sought, whether it was attained or not attained. "Mentally explored" (*anuvicaritaṃ manasā*) means mentally traversed by the mind. [Thus it has been said: "By the Tathāgata..."

By the phrase "fully awakened," this is shown: for whatever objective form— blue, yellow, and so forth— enters the range of the eye-door within these immeasurable world-systems of this world including its devas,
[the Buddha knows] that "this being, at this very moment, having seen such an objective form, has become glad, dejected, or neutral."
All that has been thus fully awakened to by the Tathāgata.
Likewise, whatever sound-object—such as the sound of a kettle-drum or the sound of a drum—arises at the ear-door from these immeasurable world-systems of this world with its devas;
whatever odor-object—such as the scent of roots or the scent of bark—arises at the nose-door; and whatever taste-object—such as the taste of roots or the taste of stems—arises [at the tongue-door].

An object of taste comes into the range of the tongue-door. An object of touch—divided into the earth element, fire element, and air element, such as hard, soft, and so forth—comes into the range of the body-door.
[The mind-door consciousness knows] all this, thinking: "At this very moment, having touched such an object of touch, this being has become glad, dejected, or neutral."

Thus has it been perfectly awakened to by the Tathāgata. Likewise, whatever object of a phenomenon—such as pleasure, pain, and so forth—arises within the range of the mind-door from among the infinite world-systems of this world with its devas, [the Tathāgata knows]:
"At this very moment, having cognized such an object of a phenomenon, this being is happy, or unhappy, or neutral."
"All this has been thus fully awakened to by the Tathāgata.
For, Cunda, among these beings, there is nothing seen, heard, sensed, or cognized that has not been seen, heard, sensed, or cognized by the Tathāgata.
Even regarding what this great multitude has sought and obtained—

There is that which exists even though it has not been sought; there is that which exists even though it has been sought but not attained; there is that which exists even though it has neither been sought nor attained.
For the Tathāgata, there is nothing among all these that is called "unattained" or "not realized through knowledge.
Therefore, he is called the "Tathāgata. He is called the "Tathāgata" because he has gone exactly as the world has gone.
It is so called. In the Pāḷi, however, it is stated as "abhisambuddha" (fully awakened), which has the same meaning as the word "gata.

In this manner, the meaning of the conclusion "Tathāgata" should be understood in all sections; its logical justification has already been explained in the detailed exposition of the term "Tathāgata" in the Brahmajāla Sutta.
This concludes the commentary on the points left undeclared (*abyākataṭṭhāna-vaṇṇanā*).

189. Having thus declared his own incomparability, unsurpassedness, omniscience, and status as the King of Dhamma, he now uttered this lion’s roar, saying, "Cunda, it is possible that among the views held by the many recluses and brahmins, there is nothing unknown or unseen by me; everything revolves within the scope of my knowledge," and so forth.
In this context, "Tathāgata" refers to a being. "This is not conducive to welfare, friends" means it is not conducive to welfare in this world or the next world.
"And not conducive to the Dhamma" means it is not dependent upon the nine supramundane states (navalokuttaradhamma).
"Not pertaining to the fundamentals of the holy life" means it does not constitute the foundation for the entire holy life of the Dispensation as comprised within the three trainings.
190. Regarding the passage beginning with "This is suffering," with the exception of craving (*taṇhā*), all remaining phenomena belonging to the three planes are declared to be "this is suffering.
Craving, which brings about and generates that very suffering, is declared to be "the origin of suffering.

The non-occurrence of both is declared to be "the cessation of suffering. [The path] consists in the full understanding of suffering, the abandoning of its origin, and the realization of its cessation.
It has been declared that "the Noble Path is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering. In such passages as, "For this, friend, is beneficial," etc., the meaning is as follows:

this [Path] is based on the welfare of this world and the world beyond, it is based on the nine supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma), and it is the beginning, the primary, and the forerunner of the entire holy life (brahmacariya) of the Dispensation.
Commentary on the View Based on the Past (Pubbantasaṅhagatadiṭṭhinissaya-vaṇṇanā) 191.
Now, do not think that I did not explain that which I did not explain because I was ignorant of it.
On the contrary, knowing it fully, I did not explain it thinking, "Even if this were explained, there would be no purpose in it. As for how...
Roaring the lion’s roar, “That which was to be declared has indeed been declared by me,” he spoke again the words beginning with, “And those, Cunda...

Herein, *diṭṭhiyo* (views) means the very same as *diṭṭhinissayā* (bases of views), *diṭṭhinissitakā* (those dependent on views), or *diṭṭhigatikā* (those who have gone to views); this is the meaning.
“This alone is the truth” means that this very vision is the truth. “The rest is vain” means that the speech of others is vain. “Not self-made” means not made by oneself.
192. "In that regard" (*tatra*) means among those recluses and brahmins. "Is this, friends, as it is said?"—the meaning is:
"Friends, is that which you say—that 'the self and the world are eternal'—actually so, or is it not so?
It is in this way that I question you. And "but what they have said thus": but when they say, "This alone is the truth, all else is false."
They say this, but I do not grant them that. "By way of designation" means by way of the designation of views.

"Equal and the same" means equal with respect to equal knowledge. "That is to say, by way of higher designation" refers to what is called the higher designation (*adhipaññatti*). In this regard, I alone am superior and more excellent;
there is no one equal to me. In that context, it is said: "by way of designation" and "by way of higher designation."
These two are one in meaning. As for their distinction, there are two: *paññatti* (concept) and *adhipaññatti* (higher concept). Therein, *paññatti* refers to the concept of views (*diṭṭhipaññatti*).

*Adhipaññatti* refers to the six concepts mentioned thus: the concept of aggregates (*khandhapaññatti*), the concept of elements (*dhātupaññatti*), the concept of bases (*āyatanapaññatti*), the concept of faculties (*indriyapaññatti*), the concept of truths (*saccapaññatti*), and the concept of persons (*puggalapaññatti*). However, here...

Regarding the term "by way of description" (*paññattiya*), both "description" (*paññatti*) and "superior description" (*adhipaññatti*) are intended here; so too regarding the term "superior description.
For the Blessed One is unsurpassed by way of description, and he is also unsurpassed by way of superior description. Therefore he said:
"I alone am superior therein, namely, by way of superior description."
196. *Pahānāya* means for the purpose of abandoning. *Samatikkamāya* is a synonym for that same term. *Desitā* means taught. *Paññattā* means established.
For, through the development of the foundations of mindfulness, when all phenomena have been analyzed apart from their density and seen as they truly are, one arrives at the certainty:
"This is merely a heap of formations; no being is to be found here."
"There is the abandoning of all bases for views. Therefore it was said:
"For the abandoning and transcending of the bases for views, these four foundations of mindfulness have been taught and established by me in this way. The remainder is everywhere of obvious meaning.
Thus ends the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, the commentary on the *Dīghanikāya*.
The commentary on the Pāsādika Sutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Lakkhaṇa Sutta:
Explanation of the Thirty-two Marks of a Great Man.
199. *Evaṃ me sutaṃ* (Thus have I heard) is the *Lakkhaṇa Sutta*.
Herein, this is the commentary on the words not [already] explained. *Dvattiṃs’imānīti* means "these thirty-two.

*Mahāpurisalakkhaṇānīti* means the characteristics of a Great Man, the marks of a Great Man, the signs of a Great Man—the causes for recognizing that "this is a Great Man. The passage beginning with "Of the Great Man who is endowed with these" and so forth is found in the *Mahāpadāna Sutta*.
This should be understood according to the method already explained in detail.
Why did he say, "Even the outside seers preserve [this tradition], yet they do not know that 'by the performance of this action one acquires this mark'?
It was because it was appropriate to the occasion (aṭṭhuppatti). For this sutta is one accompanied by an occasion.
But where did the origin of this [discourse] arise? It arose among the people within the village.
At that time, it seems, the inhabitants of Sāvatthī, sitting in their own homes, at their doorways, and in assembly halls and such places, raised this discussion:
"The Blessed One has eighty minor marks, a fathom-wide aura, and the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, by which..."

The Blessed One’s body shines exceedingly, like the *pāricchattaka* tree in full bloom, like a forest of lotuses in full blossom, like a golden archway variegated with various jewels, or like the vault of the sky radiant with the rays of stars;
emitting six-colored rays that dart and quiver hither and thither. And by this very deed, this mark [arose] for the Blessed One.
"It has not been stated that they are produced [without cause];

rather, the Blessed One has said that even a mere ladleful of rice or a bowl of conjey arises in this way solely due to conditions provided in the past. What deed, then, did the Teacher perform by which these marks were produced?"
Then the Venerable Ānanda, while walking about within the village, heard this conversation.

Having finished his meal and returned to the monastery, he performed the duties toward the Teacher, paid homage, and stood before him, saying, "Venerable Sir, I heard a certain conversation within the village.
When the Blessed One asked, "What did you hear, Ānanda? he reported everything. The Teacher [then spoke] to the Elder.
Having heard these words, and having addressed the monks who were seated surrounding him,
he said this in order to show which kamma had produced each mark, after first enumerating the thirty-two marks of a Great Man: "Monks, there are these thirty-two marks of a Great Man."
Commentary on the Characteristic of Well-Placed Feet (Suppatiṭṭhitapādatā): 201.

Regarding the phrases "previous birth" (*purimaṃ jātiṃ*) and so forth, the aggregates (*khandhā*) previously inhabited are called "birth" (*jāti*) by way of having been born. Likewise, they are called "existence" (*bhava*) by way of being;
or they are called "abode" (*niketa*) in the sense of a dwelling place (*ālaya*) by way of having been inhabited. This applies to all three terms.
The meaning is: "abiding in the continuity of the aggregates (khandhasantāna) in which he previously resided.

Now, since that continuity of aggregates also persists in the heavenly worlds and so forth, yet wholesome karma capable of producing [specific] characteristics is not easily performed there—it is only easy for one who has become a human—therefore, showing what kind of karma was performed by him while he was such as he was, [the text says]: "previously, being a human being..."
He said: "Or rather, this is not the reason. Even when he was born as an elephant, horse, deer, lion, monkey, or other such beings, the Great Man fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs).

However, because it is not easy to illustrate the deeds performed while established in such forms of existence, whereas the deeds performed while established in human form can be easily illustrated, he therefore said, 'Formerly, being a human being...'"

"Of firm undertaking" means having a steadfast grasp. "Regarding wholesome states" refers to the ten courses of wholesome action. "Of unshakable undertaking" means having an unwavering grasp and an irreversible grasp.
For the mind of a Great Being recoils like a hen’s feather when it encounters unwholesome karma, as if it has met fire;
yet when it encounters the wholesome, it expands like a canopy. Therefore, he is one of firm undertaking.
He is one whose undertaking is steadfast. No ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, or Brahmā is able to make him relinquish his wholesome undertaking.
In this regard, there are these instances: formerly, it is said, the Great Man was reborn in the womb of a squirrel. Then, when the rains had fallen...

A flood came, seized the nest, and carried it right into the ocean. The Great Being, thinking, "I will bring out my two little sons," repeatedly moistened his tail and splashed the water out from the ocean.
On the seventh day, Sakka, having reflected, arrived there and asked, "What are you doing? He explained it to him. Sakka [drew] the water from the great ocean...
He spoke of the state of being difficult to extricate. The Bodhisatta said, "It is not even fitting to converse with such a lazy person;
do not stay here," and sent him away. Sakka, thinking, "The grasp taken by such an extraordinary man cannot be made to let go," was pleased and brought his two sons to give them to him.
Even in the time of Mahājanaka, while crossing the great ocean, he asked, "Why..."
When asked by the deity, "Are you crossing the great ocean? he replied, "I am crossing it in order to reach the other shore, take over the kingdom in my family's ancestral realm, and give gifts.
Then, when the deity said, "This great ocean is both deep and wide; when will you cross it?
he replied, "This ocean of yours is like that, but as for my own inner aspiration..."
"Having returned, it will appear like the Minor Schedule (Khuddakamātikā).
You yourself shall see me after I have crossed the ocean, brought back wealth from the far shore, and taken over the kingdom inherited by my family while bestowing gifts.
The deity, thinking, "It is impossible to make this extraordinary man relinquish what he has grasped," embraced the Bodhisatta, carried him off, and laid him down in the pleasure garden.
Thus, having raised the parasol and made a daily renunciation of five hundred thousand [pieces of gold], he later went forth into homelessness.
In this way, no ascetic... nor even a Brahmā could cause the Great Being to relinquish his undertaking of wholesome qualities.
Therefore it is said: "He was firm in his undertaking of wholesome states; his undertaking was steadfast."
Now, in order to show those wholesome states (*kusala-dhamma*) in which his undertaking was firmly established, he said, "In bodily good conduct," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "in giving and sharing" (*dāna-saṃvibhāge*): here, "giving" (*dāna*) is so called by way of the act of giving itself, while "sharing" (*saṃvibhāga*) is so called by way of the act of distributing.

Regarding "in the undertaking of virtue" (*sīla-samādāne*): this refers to the time of fulfilling the five precepts, the ten precepts, and the fourfold purity of virtue (*catupārisuddhi-sīla*). Regarding "in observing the Uposatha": this refers to the various types [of Uposatha] beginning with the fourteenth day.
At the time of observing the Uposatha. *Matteyyatāya* means in the duty to be performed toward one’s mother. The same method applies to the remaining terms as well.
*Aññataraññataresu* means “and in other such [cases] as these. Regarding *adhikusalesu*: here there are wholesome states (*kusalā*) and there are super-wholesome states (*adhikusalā*).
All wholesome states of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*) are called simply “wholesome,” while those of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) are “super-wholesome. Both...

Those are called wholesome; those pertaining to the formless realm are superior wholesome. All of those are called wholesome; those wholesome states that serve as conditions for the attainment of the perfections of a disciple are called superior wholesome.
Those also are called wholesome; those wholesome states that serve as conditions for the attainment of private enlightenment (paccekabodhi) are superior wholesome.
Furthermore, those wholesome states that serve as conditions for the attainment of omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa) are here termed "superior wholesome."
These are intended. Among those superior wholesome states, he was one who took them up firmly and maintained them steadfastly.

Regarding the phrases "because it has been performed" and "because it has been accumulated": here, what has been done even once is indeed "performed," but through repeated performance, it becomes "accumulated.
Regarding "because it has been heaped up": karma that has been massed together and gathered into a heap is called "heaped up. Therefore, [it is said] "because it has been heaped up."
By saying that the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*) is too narrow for the deed performed by him and the peak of existence (*bhavagga*) is too low, he shows: "Thus great is my deed.
"Vipulattā" means because of its immeasurability. By this, he shows: "The deed performed by me is infinite and boundless. "Adhiggaṇhāti" means he overcomes;
the meaning is that he obtains more than other deities. "Paṭilabhati" means he attains.
"With all the soles of his feet" is an elaboration of the statement, "He places his foot evenly on the ground.

In this context, "with all" means with every part; he does not touch [the ground] first with one part and later with another, but touches it evenly with all the soles of his feet, and lifts them up evenly. For even when the Tathāgata...
Thinking, "I shall step upon a hell many hundreds of fathoms deep," he extends his foot.
At that very moment, the sunken place rises up like a blacksmith's bellows filled with air until it becomes level with the earth; even the elevated places sink down.
For one who extends his foot thinking, "I shall step far away," even a mountain the size of Sineru becomes like a well-planted vetta-sprout.

It bends down as if bowing and approaches near his feet. For instance, when he performed the Twin Miracle and extended his foot with the thought, "I shall step upon Mount Yugandhara," the mountain bent down and came near his foot. He too, having stepped upon it, stepped with his second foot onto the Tāvatiṃsa realm.
Indeed, there is no place where one should stand that is not already marked by the wheel-sign (cakralakṣaṇa).
It is unable to become uneven. Stumps, thorns, gravel, potsherds, or excrement, urine, saliva, mucus, and so forth, either move away beforehand, or they sink right there into the earth.
For by the power of the Tathāgata’s virtue, the power of his merit, the power of the Dhamma, and the majesty of the ten perfections, this great earth—
It is properly strewn with soft flowers. 202.
"Bounded by the ocean" means having the ocean as its limit. For one exercising sovereignty over that [earth], there is no intervening tree, mountain, or river as a boundary;
the great ocean itself is the boundary. Therefore it is said, "bounded by the ocean."
It is "entire" (*akhila*), meaning it is free from thorns (*akaṇṭaka*) and devoid of robbers (*niccora*).

For thieves are called "thorns" (*khila*) in the sense of having a harsh touch; they are called "causes" (*nimitta*) in the sense of being the basis for calamity; and they are called "thorns" (*kaṇṭaka*) in the sense of piercing. It is "prosperous" (*iddha*), meaning well-flourishing. It is "thriving" (*phīta*), meaning blossoming with all forms of excellence.

It is "secure" (*khema*), meaning fearless. It is "peaceful" (*siva*), meaning free from affliction. It is "without mire" (*nirabbuda*), meaning devoid of the *abbuda* hell, where beings are massed together in dense clusters.
The meaning is: "having been left by wandering bandits who have fled. "Unshakable" (*akkhambhiyo*) means not to be obstructed; no one is able to move it from its place.
"By an adversary" (*paccatthikena*) means by one who desires opposition. "By an enemy" (*paccāmittenā*) means by a hostile foe.
Both of these are synonyms for an enemy (*sapatta*). "By internal [factors]" (*abbhantarehi*) means by lust and so forth that have arisen within.
"By outsiders" means by ascetics and others. For even though outsiders—Devadatta, Kokālika, and others who were ascetics;
Soṇadaṇḍa, Kūṭadaṇḍa, and others who were brahmins; deities equal to Sakka; Māra, who followed him for seven years;
and Brahmās such as Baka—were unable to suppress him.

To this extent, the Blessed One has explained the deed (*kamma*), that which is similar to the deed (*kammasarikkhaka*), the characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*), and the benefit of the characteristic (*lakkhaṇānisaṃsa*).
"Deed" refers to the deed performed with firm energy throughout four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand aeons.
"That which is similar to the deed" means: "May the world, including the devas, know that this was performed with firmness."
The mark of a Great Man with well-placed feet. "Mark" means the state of having well-placed feet.
"Benefit of the mark" means the state of being unassailable by adversaries. 203.
Regarding the phrase "herein this is said": when those various classifications such as karma have been stated, this further [verse] is also spoken, arranged in metrical stanzas (*gāthābandha*).

This was said with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*). However, the ancient elders (*porāṇakattherā*), having stated that "these verses were established as explanatory verses (*vaṇṇanāgāthā*) by the Elder Ānanda," passed them on.
At a later time, the elders said, "They are a single-word extraction of the meaning (*atthuddhāra*).
In this context: *sacce* refers to truth in speech; *dhamme* refers to the dhamma of the ten paths of wholesome action; *dame* refers to the taming of the sense faculties.

"Saṃyameti" refers to restraint through virtue (*sīla-saṃyama*). Regarding the phrase "in purity, virtue, abiding, and the observance (*uposatha*)," there is threefold purity beginning with bodily purity (*kāya-soceyya*).

Virtue itself, being the foundation (*ālaya*), is called "the abiding in virtue" (*sīlālaya*). The act of the observance is the "observance" (*uposatha*). "In non-harming" means in non-violence (*avihiṃsā*).
"He practiced fully" means he practiced it in its entirety.

*Anvabhīti* means experiencing. *Veyyañjanikā* refers to those who recite the marks (*lakkhaṇapāṭhakā*). *Parābhibhū* means one capable of overcoming others. *Sattubhī* means he is unshakable by enemies.

"He never goes to being obstructed" means that this Supreme Person (*aggapuggala*) does not, in any way whatsoever, go to a state of being suppressed. "For this is his nature" means that for him, this is the natural law (*dhammatā*), this is his inherent character (*sabhāva*).
The Description of the Mark of the Wheel on the Soles of the Feet.

204. *Ubbegauttāsabhayaṃ* means both the fear of agitation (*ubbega*) and the fear of terror (*uttāsa*). Therein, the fear based on plundering, binding, and so forth, arising from thieves, kings, or enemies, is called agitation;
the fear that causes the hair to stand on end at that very moment, depending on such things as fierce elephants and horses, or snakes and yakṣas, is the fear of terror.
[This is] the name. All that has been dispelled and pacified. "Provided" means made ready. How does he provide it?
Having caused alms-halls to be built in the forest at dangerous places, he causes people who have arrived there to eat, gives them provisions, and escorts them through.
To those unable to enter that place, he sends men and causes them to enter. In cities and other such places as well, in various [locations]...
He established guards at strategic points; thus he made his arrangements. And he gave a gift together with its retinue:
"food and drink" refers to the ten bases of giving.
Therein, "food" means rice gruel and cooked rice. When giving that, he did not give it by placing it at the gate, but rather within the residence.
Having smeared the ground with green clay, scattered parched grain and flowers, prepared a seat, and hung a canopy, he paid honor with perfumes, incense, and other offerings.
He had the community of monks sit down and gave them rice gruel. While giving the gruel, he provided it with various condiments.
At the conclusion of the gruel-drinking, having washed their feet and anointed them with oil, he offered various kinds of...
Having given endless snacks, at the conclusion he gave excellent food consisting of many soups and many side dishes.
When giving drinks, he gave the eight kinds of drinks beginning with mango juice, and that too after providing rice and gruel. When giving clothing, he did not give merely plain cloth;
rather, having given enough for single-layered and double-layered garments and so forth, he also gave the dye and the thread.

He gave thread, had it spun, provided seats for the bhikkhus at the place where needlework was done, and gave rice-gruel, food, foot-ointment, back-ointment, dye, a dry leaf, a dye-vat, and even a robe-dyer and a kappiya-kāraka (one who prepares things made allowable).
"Vehicles" refers to sandals. When giving those, one may also give a sandal-bag, a sandal-stick, ointment-oil, and—below—
And having made food and the other items his very retinue, he gave them. Even when giving garlands, he did not give mere pure garlands;
rather, having mixed them with perfumes, he gave those [perfumes] as the retinue for the first four [requisites].
He gave perfume both for the purpose of worshipping the Bodhi-tree, the shrine, the throne, the books, and so forth, and for the purpose of fumigating the shrine-hall.
Even when giving fragrant scents, he did not give only the pure scent itself;
rather, he gave it together with the containers for the scent-pastes and the vessels for mixing them, making these five items its accompaniments.

Likewise, even when giving ointments such as yellow orpiment, realgar, and Chinese flour for the purpose of worshipping shrines and the like, he did not give only the pure ointment itself, but [gave it] along with the ointment-vessels.
Together with the six items mentioned below, he gave them as his retinue. "A bed" means a couch and chair. When giving that, he did not give it merely in its bare state;

rather, together with a woolen coverlet, a blanket, a bedspread, supports for the couch, and even a stick for cleaning the fingernails, and including the seven items mentioned below, he gave them as his retinue. "A dwelling place" (āvasathaṃ).

He did not give merely the house itself; rather, having had it decorated with flower-garlands and creepers, furnished with well-arranged couches and seats, and provided with eight lower attendants, he gave it to him. "Lamps" means lamp-oil.
When giving that, [one gives it] at the shrine courtyard, the Bodhi-tree courtyard, at the head of the Dhamma-preaching assembly, in one's own residence, or at the place where books are read.

"Light this lamp," he said; thus he did not give mere pure oil, but gave it together with the wick, the vessel, the oil-container, and so forth—giving these nine items below as its accessories. "Well-apportioned intervals" means having well-apportioned spaces between them.
"Kings" refers to those who have been consecrated. "Landholders" refers to lords or governors. "Princes" refers to royal princes. Here, "work" includes its accessories.
Generosity. The mark of the wheel (cakralakṣaṇa) arises for this reason: "May the world, including the devas, know by this cause that I gave gifts together with their requisites.
This very mark of the wheel is what is called a "mark" (lakkhaṇa). The benefit (ānisamsa) is having a large retinue. 205.
Regarding the phrase "herein this is said," these verses are spoken to elucidate that meaning. For there are two kinds of verses.
There are two [types of] exposition: the exposition of the meaning [of the words] themselves (*tad-attha-paridīpanā*) and the exposition of the specific meaning (*visesa-attha-paridīpanā*).

Therein, the exposition of the meaning that has actually entered into the text is called the exposition of the meaning itself; the exposition of what has not entered into the text is called the exposition of the specific meaning.
These, however, are the expositions of the meaning itself. Therein, "pure" means previously; "purattha" is a synonym for that same word.
"In former births" (*purimāsu jātīsu*) is an indication that [the Buddha] rejects the notion that these marks were produced by karma performed in previous lives other than this one.
"Dispelling the fear of agitation and terror" (*ubbegauttāsabhayāpanūdana*) means the remover of both the fear of agitation and the fear of terror. "Zealous" (*ussuka*) means intent upon it.
"The hundredfold merit-signs" (*satapuññalakkhaṇa*) refers to each individual mark being produced by a hundred thousand meritorious deeds. Thus...
They did not approve of the idea that "anyone whatsoever might become a Buddha. Rather, they approved of this meaning:
"In infinite world-systems, if all beings were each to perform a single deed a hundred times, the Bodhisatta alone was reborn having performed each of those deeds a hundredfold.
Therefore, they accepted the expression "possessing the marks of a hundred merits."
"Human, asura, sakka, and rakkhasa" means humans, asuras, sakkas, and rakkhasas.
206. Regarding the description of the twenty characteristics beginning with long heels:
"In between" means in the interval between rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) and death-consciousness (cuti). Here, "kamma" refers to abstaining from the taking of life.

Regarding "resembling their actions": when committing the taking of life, out of fear of being heard by the sound of footsteps, they walk by treading with the very tips of their toes and cause others to fall.

Then, for this reason—so that people may know of their deed—they become those with inwardly curved feet, or outwardly curved feet, or crouching feet, or those with pointed heels, or those with broad heels. [They do so] with the tips of their feet.
Furthermore, so that the world with its devas may know by this reason that the Tathāgata has not caused another to be killed, the Great Man’s mark of long heels is produced.
Likewise, those who kill another walk with their bodies held high so that others might see them;
therefore, they walk in a stooped manner when killing another. Then, thinking, "In this way these people went and had another killed," [the mark arises].
Thinking, "May others know this deed of theirs by this sign," they become hunchbacked, dwarfish, or cripples who crawl on chairs.

But for the Tathāgata, thinking, "May the world with its devas know that he has gone thus without having harmed others by this sign," the mark of a Great Man consisting of straightness like a Brahmā (brahmujugatta) is produced. Likewise, those who harm others [use] weapons...
Or, taking up a club, they kill another with their fists clenched.
They have short fingers or short hands, or crooked fingers, or hands like a serpent’s hood, so that people may know by this reason the fact of their having killed another.
But for the Tathāgata, the world together with its devas knows by this reason the fact of his not having killed others.
Thinking, "May he know," the Great Man’s mark of long fingers is produced. This is the correspondence of action (*kamma-sarikkhaka*) here.
These three marks are what is called "marks" (*lakkhaṇa*). Longevity is the benefit of the marks (*lakkhaṇānisaṃsa*).
207. Regarding the phrase "fear of being killed and slain": here, killing consisting of death is "death-killing" (*maraṇavadha*); from that death-killing...
"Fear" refers to the fear of death and execution; having recognized that for himself, he "abstained from killing others.
Just as I have fear of death and my own life is dear to me, so too it is for others—knowing this, he abstained from killing others.
"By good conduct" means by what was well-practiced. "He went to heaven" means he went to the celestial realm.

"Having fallen away and come here again" (*caviya punaridhāgato*) means having passed away and returned here once more. "Long-toed" (*dīghapāsaṇhiko*) means having long toes. "Like Brahmā, straight" (*brahmāva sujū*) means as straight as Brahmā.

"With beautiful arms" (*subhujo*) means having handsome arms. "With a fine complexion" (*susū*) means even in old age, he has the appearance of a youth. "Well-proportioned" (*susaṇṭhito*) means endowed with excellent proportions.

"Whose fingers are soft and tender" (*mudutalunaṅguliyassa*) means his fingers are both soft and delicate. "By three" (*tīhi*) means by three. "By the marks of the foremost among men" (*purisavaraggalakkhaṇehi*).

By means of the auspicious marks of the Supreme Man. "For long-term sustenance" (*cirayapanāya*) means for the purpose of sustaining [the body] for a long time, that is, for the sake of possessing a long life-span.

"He sustains for a long time" (*ciraṃ yapeti*) means he sustains it for a long duration. "If he goes forth even longer than that" (*cirataraṃ pabbajati yadi tato*) means if he goes forth, he sustains it for an even longer period than that; such is the meaning. "And he sustains by means of the cultivation of mastery and supernormal powers" (*yāpayati ca vasiddhibhāvanāya*) means that, having attained mastery (*vasippatto*), he sustains himself through the cultivation of supernormal powers (*iddhi*).
The Description of the Marks of the Seven Protuberances (*sattussadatā-lakkhaṇa-vaṇṇanā*).
208. *Rasitānaṃ* means of those things endowed with flavor. Regarding the terms "edibles" (*khādanīya*) and so forth: "edibles" refers to flour-based snacks and the like;
"foodstuffs" (*bhojanīya*) refers to the five types of cooked food; "tastings" (*sāyanīya*) refers to things to be tasted, such as ghee and fresh butter;
"lickables" (*lehanīya*) refers to things to be licked, such as flour-porridge; and "drinks" (*pāna*) refers to the eight types of beverages.
In this context, "kamma" refers to the gift of excellent food given during the four incalculable eons plus a hundred thousand aeons.
"Kammasarikkhaka" (the correspondence to the kamma) means that when coarse food has entered the stomach, the blood dries up and the flesh withers.
Therefore, [the donor thinks]: "By this means, let people know that these beings have been given coarse food."
They become like human *petas*, with little flesh and little blood, finding food and drink difficult to obtain.
However, when excellent food has entered the womb, the flesh and blood increase; they become full-bodied, gracious, and beautiful to behold.
Therefore, let the world together with its devas know that the Tathāgata’s state of being a giver of excellent food for a long time is due to this very reason.
The mark of a Great Man characterized by being surrounded by beings is produced. By "mark" is meant specifically the mark of being surrounded by beings.
The benefit is the attainment of refined things.

209. "Eatable, drinkable, lickable, and tastable" means that which is to be chewed, that which is to be eaten, that which is to be licked, and that which is to be tasted. "A giver of the finest, most excellent flavors" means a giver of the highest, most excellent flavors, or a giver of the finest, most excellent tastes among the best.

*Satta cussadeti* means the seven protuberances (*ussada*). *Tadatthajotakanti* means that which indicates those things—namely, that which indicates the various kinds of food such as hard food (*khajja*) and soft food (*bhojja*);

the meaning is: "conducive to the acquisition of those. *Pabbajampi cāti* means "even while going forth" (*pabbajamāno*). *Tadādhigacchatīti* means "he attains that" (*taṃ adhigacchati*). *Lābhiruttamanti* means "one who obtains the supreme" (*lābhi uttamaṃ*).
[End of] The Description of the Characteristics of the Hands, Feet, and Other Limbs.

210. Regarding the phrase "by giving" (*dānena*) and so forth: some person is to be won over by giving alone; he wins him over by giving. He gave requisites for renunciants to those who have gone forth, and requisites for householders to those who are householders.
Regarding "by kind speech" (*peyyavajjena*): some person might say, "This man gives what ought to be given, but with a single word he spoils everything and destroys it;
what is the use of his gift? Another person might say, "Although this man does not give gifts, when he speaks..."
Rather, he anoints [the person] as if with oil. Whether or not this person gives, his mere words are worth a thousand;
such a person does not expect a gift, but expects only pleasant speech.
He won him over with pleasant speech.
"By way of beneficial conduct" means by way of discourse that increases welfare. For some person does not expect either a gift or pleasant speech;
they expect only talk concerning their own benefit and talk concerning their growth. To such a person one should say: "This should be done by you; this should not be done by you.
Such a person should be associated with; such a person should not be associated with. Thus...
He gathered them through beneficial conduct.
"By way of equality" means by way of sharing in the same pleasure and pain. For some person does not expect even a single [return] for gifts and so forth;
rather, he shares in the same pleasure and pain by sitting on the same seat, lying on the same bed, or eating together.
He expects [reciprocity]. In that regard, one who is inferior by birth but superior in wealth is difficult to associate with. For it is not possible to share enjoyments with him as equals;
and if one does not do so, he becomes angry. Likewise, one who is inferior in wealth but superior by birth is also difficult to associate with.
For he thinks, "I am of noble birth," and [thus refuses] to share enjoyments with one who is endowed with wealth.
If he does not desire [to share], he becomes angry when that is not done. But one who is inferior in both respects is easy to manage;
for he does not desire common enjoyment with the other, nor does he become angry when it is not done. One who is equal in both respects is likewise easy to manage.
However, among monks, one who is immoral is difficult to manage; for it is not possible to have common enjoyment with him.
[He is] prone to anger when [something] is not done for him; likewise, he becomes angry when it is not being done. One who possesses virtue (*sīlavā*) is easy to associate with.
For one who possesses virtue does not become angry even when things are not being given or not being done.

He does not look upon another with an evil mind even if that person does not share enjoyments with him. Furthermore, sharing enjoyments with such a person is easy to accomplish. Therefore, regarding such a person, in this way—
He gathered them through impartiality.
"They are well-gathered by him" means they are well-gathered by him. Whether he gives or does not give, whether he acts or does not act, they remain well-gathered;
they do not break apart. "When it is time for him to give, then he gives. Now..."
They think: "We suppose he has nothing, which is why he does not give. Are we only to attend upon him when he is giving? We shall not attend upon him when he is not giving and not acting.
Here, "kamma" refers to the work of gathering others through giving and so forth performed over a long period. "Kammasarikkhaka" (resembling that kamma) refers to...

Thus he is one who does not hold [others] together; thinking, "May people know his state of not holding others together for this reason," he has stiff hands and feet and the characteristic of having unevenly placed limbs.

However, because the world with its devas thinks, "May they know the Tathāgata’s state of long-term holding [others] together for this reason," these two characteristics are produced. This is the characteristic.
This very thing is the twofold characteristic. The benefit is having one's retinue well-restrained.

211. *Kariyā* means having done; *cariyā* means having practiced. *Anavamatenā* means not being treated with contempt. There is also a reading *anapamodenā*, which does not mean "without negligence," but rather "not dejected" and "not haughty"—this is the meaning.
*Caviyā* means having passed away. *Atirucira-suvaggu-dassaneyyaṃ* means both exceedingly beautiful and very pleasing, as well as charming and worthy of being seen. *Susu-kumāro* means very delicate.
"Obedient to his retinue" means his retinue is obedient and follows his word. "To be commanded" means he may be directed according to his will in matters of what should and should not be done.
"The earth" refers to this very earth. "Seeking to win their affection and welfare" means being pleasant in speech while seeking their benefit and happiness.
"Those who are well-disposed toward one who carries out his word" means those who are faithful to him because he acts upon their instructions.
They were full of confidence. "In accordance with the Dhamma" means both the Dhamma and what is in conformity with the Dhamma.
212. Regarding the description of the characteristics such as the raised foot and so forth:
"connected with the goal" means dependent on the welfare of this world and the next; "connected with the Dhamma" means dependent on the ten courses of wholesome action.
“He pointed it out to many people” means he spoke a discourse that serves as an illustration for many people. “Of living beings” means of sentient beings (*sattā*).
