All terms beginning with “the foremost” are synonyms for one another. Here, “kamma” refers to speech that has been practiced for a long time, which leads upward and is connected with the goal.
One who does not speak such exalted speech is said to have a quality corresponding to that kamma.
For this reason, so that people might know his speech was not uttered in a haughty manner, he has feet with the ankles turned downward and body hair growing downward.
However, because the world with its devas knows that for a long time the Tathāgata has spoken such lofty speech,
the characteristic of having high-ankled feet and the characteristic of having upward-pointing body hair are produced.

The "characteristic" (*lakkhaṇa*) refers to these two characteristics themselves. The "benefit" (*ānisaṃsa*) is the state of excellence. 213. Saying "they cause to move" (*erayanti*), he means they speak.
"He showed it to many people" (*bahujanaṃ nidaṃsayī*) means he demonstrated what is beneficial for many people. "The chariot of the Dhamma" (*dhammayāga*) is the sacrifice of the gift of the Dhamma.
"With hair standing erect" (*ubbhamuppatitalomavā*) means that he has hair on his body that stands upright. "Possessing ankle-bones" (*pādagaṇṭhirahū*) refers to the ankles of the feet.
They were. "Well-established" means perfectly established. "Covered with flesh and blood" means filled with both flesh and blood.
"Enveloped in skin" means covered and concealed by skin. "It moves" means it goes. "Of extraordinary stride" means one who dwells extraordinarily, one who dwells in the supreme state.
Commentary on the Characteristic of the Antelope-Legged Thigh (Eṇijaṅghalakkhaṇa) 214.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Or a craft," etc.: "craft" refers to two types of crafts—the inferior craft and the superior craft.
The inferior craft consists of the craft of the reed-worker, the potter's craft, the weaver's craft, and the barber's craft.
"Craft" (sippa) refers to writing, finger-calculation, and arithmetic. "Science" (vijjā) refers to various kinds such as snake-charms and the like.

"Conduct" (caraṇa) refers to the five precepts, the ten precepts, and the morality of restraint according to the Pātimokkha. "Action" (kamma) refers to the wisdom that understands the ownership of one's own actions.
"They would suffer" (kilisseyyuṃ) means they would become exhausted. He thought: "The duties of a resident pupil (antevāsika-vatta) are indeed difficult; may they not endure this for long."

"Fit for a king" (*rājārahāni*) refers to elephants, horses, and so forth, which are suitable for a king; because they constitute parts of the king's army, they are called "royal factors" (*rājāṅgāni*).
"Royal enjoyments" (*rājūpabhogāni*) refers to the articles of use and enjoyment belonging to a king, as well as the seven treasures (*sattaratanāni*).
"Worthy of a king" (*rājānucchavikāni*) means things appropriate for a king; this term includes all of those aforementioned items. "Fit for a recluse" (*samaṇārahāni*)...
"Suitable for recluses" refers to robes and so forth appropriate for them. "Recluse-constituents" (*samaṇaṅga*) means the four assemblies that constitute the components of the recluses.
"Recluse-enjoyments" (*samaṇūpabhoga*) means the requisites for the use of recluses. "Conducive to recluses" (*samaṇānucchavika*) is a synonym for those very same things.
In this context, however, "work" (*kamma*) refers to the careful and long-term study of crafts and so forth. "Resembling work" (*kammasarikkhaka*) means:
When one who teaches a craft with such diligence tires his pupils by making them sit in the squatting posture,
sending them on errands, and so forth, the flesh of his calves becomes as if scraped away. However,
because the world with its devas may know by this reason that the Tathāgata taught with such diligence, the characteristic of eni-like calves— rounded and tapering upwards— is produced.
This very thing is what is called a "mark" (*lakkhaṇa*). The benefit is the attainment of what is suitable. 215.
"That which does not cause harm" means that craft which does not result in injury to anyone. "He will be defiled" means he will become weary.
"Covered with fine skin" means enveloped by delicate skin. But how could one mark arise from a different kamma?
Does it arise? It does not arise. However, that which does arise is a secondary characteristic (anubyañjana); therefore, it is mentioned here. 216.
Commentary on the Characteristic of Fine Skin:
"Or an ascetic" (samaṇaṃ vā) means an ascetic in the sense of having stilled evil. "Or a brahmin" (brāhmaṇaṃ vā) means a brahmin in the sense of having banished evil.

In such phrases as "of great wisdom" (*mahāpañño*), the meaning is that one is endowed with great wisdom and so forth. Herein, this is the distinction between great wisdom and the others. In this context, what is great wisdom? It is called great wisdom because it comprehends the great aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*);

it is called great wisdom because it comprehends the great aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation.

She is called "of great wisdom" (mahāpaññā) because she comprehends the great points and non-points, the great attainments of meditation (vihārasamāpatti), the great Noble Truths, the great foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna),
right efforts (sammappadhāna), bases of psychic power (iddhipāda), the great faculties (indriya), powers (bala),
the great factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), the great Noble Path, the great fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala), the great direct knowledges (abhiññā), and the great ultimate goal, Nibbāna.
What is wide wisdom (*puthupaññā*)? Wisdom that operates upon various and diverse aggregates is wide wisdom.

It is [wisdom] regarding various and diverse elements (*dhātu*), various and diverse bases (*āyatana*), various and diverse dependent originations (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), various and diverse emptinesses and non-apprehensions, various and diverse meanings, phenomena (*dhamma*), etymologies, and inspired eloquences;
and regarding various and diverse aggregates of virtue (*sīla*), and various and diverse aggregates of concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the vision of the knowledge of liberation.
Wisdom that proceeds by transcending various and diverse states, various and diverse dwellings and attainments, various and diverse noble truths,

various and diverse foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, bases of power, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, various and diverse noble paths, fruits of recluseship, and direct knowledges—
transcending all phenomena shared with worldlings and proceeding toward the ultimate truth of Nibbāna— is called "vast wisdom" (puthupaññā).
What is wisdom accompanied by joy? Here, someone who abounds in joy, abounds in rapture, abounds in contentment, and abounds in gladness fulfills virtuous conduct;

he fulfills restraint of the sense faculties; he fulfills moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness, the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation. This is wisdom accompanied by joy.
Wisdom of laughter (*hāsapaññā*). One who abounds in laughter... [and so on] ...one who abounds in gladness penetrates what is possible and what is impossible;

thus it is wisdom of laughter. One who abounds in laughter fulfills the meditative attainments (*vihārasamāpatti*); thus it is wisdom of laughter. One who abounds in laughter penetrates the Noble Truths; thus it is wisdom of laughter.
[It likewise penetrates] the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the Noble Path.
It is called "wisdom of joy" because one develops it. It is called "wisdom of joy" because one who abounds in joy realizes the fruits of recluseship.

It is called "wisdom of joy" because one penetrates the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*). It is called "wisdom of joy" because one who abounds in joy, who abounds in rapture, contentment, and gladness, realizes the ultimate goal, Nibbāna.
What is impulsive wisdom (*javanapaññā*)? Whatever form there is—past, future, or present; far or near—all that form it impulsively cognizes as impermanent:
this is impulsive wisdom. It impulsively cognizes it as suffering and as non-self: this is impulsive wisdom. Whatever feeling there is...
[and so on] ...whatever consciousness there is—past, future, or present—[it impulsively cognizes all that as impermanent, suffering, and non-self: this is impulsive wisdom].
All that consciousness swiftly impels [the mind] by way of impermanence, suffering, and non-self; thus it is "impelling wisdom" (*javanapaññā*). The eye...
[and so on] ...aging-and-death, whether past, future, or present, swiftly impels [the mind] by way of impermanence, suffering, and non-self; thus it is "impelling wisdom.
Form, whether past, future, or present, is impermanent in the sense of destruction, suffering in the sense of terror, and non-self in the sense of corelessness.
Having weighed, scrutinized, analyzed, and made manifest [the nature of] form, one swiftly speeds toward its cessation, Nibbāna; thus it is "swift wisdom" (javanapaññā).

Having likewise made manifest feeling, perception, volitional formations, consciousness, the eye... [and so on] ...down to aging-and-death—whether past, future, or present—as impermanent in the sense of destruction...
[and so on] ...one swiftly speeds toward their cessation, Nibbāna; thus it is swift wisdom.

Swift wisdom (*javanapaññā*). Having weighed, scrutinized, clarified, and made manifest that form—past, future, and present—and that the eye … [and so on] … down to aging-and-death is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation;
having done so, one swiftly courses toward the cessation of aging-and-death, which is Nibbāna: this is swift wisdom.
What is sharp wisdom (*tikkhapaññā*)? It is called sharp wisdom because it swiftly cuts off the defilements (*kilesa*).
One does not tolerate a thought of sensual desire that has arisen, nor a thought of ill will that has arisen, nor a thought of cruelty that has arisen;
one does not tolerate whatever evil, unwholesome states have arisen, such as lust, hatred, delusion, anger, enmity, contempt, domineering, envy, and avarice.

She does not tolerate, abandons, dispels, eliminates, and brings to non-existence deceit, guile, stubbornness, resentment, conceit, arrogance, intoxication, negligence, all defilements, all misconduct, all volitional formations, and all kamma leading to existence;
thus she is one of sharp wisdom. In a single sitting, she realizes the four noble paths and the four fruits of recluseship.
One possesses sharp wisdom when the four analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) and the six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) have been attained, realized, and touched by means of wisdom.

What is penetrative wisdom? Here, a certain person is full of agitation regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), full of terror, full of weariness, full of dissatisfaction, and full of lack of delight;
he does not find pleasure in all conditioned phenomena, as his face is turned outward.
It is "penetrative wisdom" (nibbedhikapaññā) because it penetrates and shatters the mass of greed (lobhakkhandha) never before penetrated or shattered;
it is penetrative wisdom because it penetrates and shatters the mass of hatred, the mass of delusion, anger, resentment...
[and so on]... all kamma leading to existence, which have never before been penetrated or shattered.
217. "He waited upon the one gone forth" means that he approached and attended upon a wise person who had gone forth.

"Internal meaning" (*atthantara*): just as some who seek out flaws listen with a mind intent on finding fault, making a defect their internal focus, so too—without such listening—he made the meaning his internal focus and listened to and reflected upon the discourse endowed with meaning.

"Having gone for the sake of attainment" means having gone for the purpose of obtaining [the fruit]. "Skilled in the sign of arising" means expert in both the process of arising and the signs thereof. "He will see by piercing insight" means he will see after having known.

"In the instructions on the goal and in the acquisitions" means: the meaning is, in those acquisitions which are the knowledges that discern what is beneficial and what is not beneficial among the instructions on the goal.
*Suvaṇṇavaṇṇalakkhaṇavaṇṇanā* (The Description of the Characteristics of the Golden Hue)
218. "Not given to anger" means that because anger has been abandoned by the path of the Non-returner (*anāgāmimagga*), he is not subject to anger;
rather, it means that even if anger should arise in him, he would quickly dispel it—thus, he is not under the sway of anger.

"He does not become resentful" means that he does not cling [to the object], like a crooked thorn that pierces a vital spot here and there. In the phrases "he does not become angry" and "he does not harbor ill will," the former refers to the initial arising [of the emotion].
Anger; more powerful than that is ill-will (*vyāpāda*); more powerful than that is resentment (*paṭigha*).
Not doing any of those, he did not become angry, he did not harbor ill-will, and he did not resent. "Indignation" (*appaccaya*) means dejection (*domanassa*).
"He did not manifest it" means he did not make it evident through a bodily gesture or a verbal expression.
In this context, "kamma" refers both to long-term freedom from anger and to the giving of fine rugs and other such gifts.

"Correspondence to the kamma" (kammasarikkhaka) means that for one who is angry, the complexion of the skin becomes turbid, the face is unpleasant to look upon, and there is no ornamentation resembling fine clothing and coverings.
Therefore, he who is both prone to anger and a non-giver of clothing and coverings [suffers] because of this reason.
One becomes ugly and misshapen so that people may know one’s state of being prone to anger and the like.
However, the face of one who is free from anger shines, and the complexion of the skin becomes serene. Indeed, beings become pleasing through four causes:
by the giving of food, or the giving of clothing, or by sweeping [the ground], or by freedom from anger. These four causes have been practiced for a long time.

These were indeed performed by the Tathāgata. Therefore, so that the world with its devas might know through this reason that these have been performed by him, the mark of a Great Man characterized by a golden complexion is produced.
This very mark is what is called a "mark" (*lakkhaṇa*). The benefit is the acquisition of fine carpets and such.
219. *Abhivissajjī* means he bestowed. Just as a god rains upon the great earth—where "god" (*sura*) refers to a deity—he was like a god raining upon the great earth.
"Like the excellent Soma of the gods": *indoti* means like the most excellent Soma among the gods. "Desiring non-renunciation":
they desire non-renunciation, that is, the state of a householder. "In the great earth": in the vast earth. "Of coverings, clothes, and fine mantles":
of coverings, clothes, and the finest upper garments. "Destruction" (*panāsa*) means loss.
Commentary on the Characteristic of the Male Organ Being Concealed by a Sheath (Kosohitavatthaguyha-lakkhaṇa): 220.
"He was one who brought even his mother into harmony with his son"—this deed could only be accomplished by one established in sovereignty.
Therefore, while the Bodhisatta was exercising kingship, within the city—at the crossroads and so forth, and at the four city gates—
He stationed men in the four directions outside the city, instructing them: "Perform this task.
When they saw his mother lamenting, "Where is my son? I do not see my son," and searching for him, they said to her, "Come, mother, you shall see your son.
Taking her with them, they led her away, bathed her, fed her, and after searching for her son, they brought him back to her. This same method was applied in every case.

Herein, "kamma" means that which brings about the companionship of relatives for a long time. "Kammasarikkhaka" (similarity to kamma) means that relatives who have become companions conceal each other's faults.
Even though they may engage in quarreling at times of conflict, when a fault arises in one, they do not wish to let another know it, thinking, "This is indeed his fault."
When this was said, everyone rose up and exclaimed, "Who has seen it? Who has heard it? Among our kinsmen, there is no one who would do such a thing!
And so, while the Tathāgata was performing that act of gathering his kinsmen, he had for a long time been committing this act known as the concealment of a fault.
Then the world, including the devas, [perceived] the fact that he had performed such an act for this reason.
Thinking, "May he know," the characteristic of the male organ being concealed by a sheath (*kosohitavatthaguyha*) is produced. This very thing is what is called the "characteristic.
Having many sons is the benefit. 221.
*Vatthachāditaṃ* means that which is to be covered by a cloth, namely, the private parts.
*Amittatāpanā* means the tormenting of enemies. *Gihissa pītiṃ jananā* means generating joy for one who has become a householder.
222. Regarding the description of the characteristics such as being well-proportioned (*parimaṇḍala*):
"He knows what is equal" means that he knows, "This one is equal to Tārukkha; this one is equal to Pokkharasāti," thus [knowing] them as equal in their respective ways.
He knows. "He knows by himself" means he knows for himself. "He knows the person" means he knows the person [thinking], "This one is considered the best.
"He knows the distinction between persons" means that, rather than treating a mung bean as equal to a bean, he knows the distinction of one who is distinguished by virtue.
"This one is worthy of this" means this person is worthy of such-and-such an offering and honor. It is the maker of distinctions between persons.
Having recognized the distinction between individuals, he acted as a benefactor. He gave each person exactly what they deserved.
For he who gives half a coin to one who deserves a full kahāpaṇa destroys the other's half; and he who gives two coins to one who deserves only one destroys his own coin.
Therefore, doing neither of these, he gave each person precisely what they deserved.
In passages such as "the wealth of faith" (*saddhādhanam*), the status of faith and the other qualities as "wealth" should be understood in the sense of being the attainment of excellence.
Here, "action" (*kamma*) refers to an act of impartial gathering performed after recognizing a particular individual over a long period.

"That which corresponds to the action" (*kammasarikkhaka*) refers to the two characteristics that arise so that the world, including the devas, may know this person by means of that action: "Let the world know him for this reason."
"Lakkhaṇa" (the marks) refers to these two marks themselves. "Dhanasampatti" (wealth and prosperity) is the benefit.
223. "Tuliyā" means having weighed; "paṭivicayā" means having investigated thoroughly. "Mahājanasaṅgāhakaṃ" means the gathering of the great multitude.
"Samekkhamāno" means looking with equanimity. "Atinipuṇā manujā" means highly skilled people—human beings possessing subtle wisdom who are readers of the marks.
“Many and various things worthy of householders”: he receives many and various things suitable for householders.
“A young, tender boy”—they prophesied, “this young boy shall receive [these gifts] from the lord of the earth,” that is, from the king.
[This concludes] the description of the characteristics such as the lion-like upper body and so forth.
224. "Desirous of security from bondage" means desirous of safety from the bonds [of defilement].

"By means of wisdom" means by means of the wisdom that one's own actions are one's own property (*kammassakatapaññā*). Here, "action" refers to the desire for the welfare of the great masses of people. "That which corresponds to action" means:

"May the world together with its devas know, by this very reason, that because of this desire for the welfare of the great masses of people, he expects nothing but their prosperity"—thus these [qualities] are completely fulfilled on all sides.
The three characteristics arise unimpaired. This very triad of characteristics is what is called "characteristic.
The benefit consists in the non-decline of wealth and so forth, as well as of faith and so forth.
225. "By faith" means by the faith of conviction (*okappana-saddhā*) and the faith of serene confidence (*pasāda-saddhā*). "By virtue" means by the five precepts and the ten precepts.
"By learning" means by hearing the scriptures (*pariyatti*). "By their intelligence" means:
he thought, "How might they increase through these?"—this is the meaning. "By means of dhamma" means by worldly dhamma. "By many virtues" means by other many supreme qualities.
"The state of having an undiminishing nature" means a nature that does not decline.
Commentary on the Characteristic of Reaching the Tip of the Tongue (Rasaggasaggitālakkhaṇa) 226.
"Flowing evenly" means that they flow having become equalized, such that even a quantity the size of a sesame seed placed on the tip of the tongue pervades everywhere.
Here, "action" (kamma) refers to non-injurious action. "Similarity to action" (kammasarikkhaka) means...
When one receives blows from hands and other such means, blood coagulates here and there;

forming knots upon knots, it draws pus within, and thus the internal organs break apart—thus he becomes one of many diseases. But by the Tathāgata, this work of producing health has been performed for a long time.
"Let the world, including the devas, know this by this reason"—thus it is called "producing health."
The characteristic of being the supreme among the supreme flavors is produced. This is indeed what is meant by "characteristic. Freedom from illness is the benefit. 227.
"By execution and killing" means by execution and killing as commanded thus: "Kill this one! Strike this one down! "By oppression" means by being cast into prison.
[End of] the commentary on the characteristics of the deep-blue eyes and so forth.
228. He did not stare wide-eyed like a crab, nor did he gaze with anger by drawing back his eyes.
Nor was he "squinting," meaning he did not look with the corners of his eyes turned askance. Furthermore, he was not one who "looks after deliberation";
for one who looks after deliberation is so called when, having become angry, they close their eyes and do not look at another whenever that person gazes upon them, and then [only] later...
He does not look at one who is walking with anger; such was not his way. There is also a reading, *vineyyapekkhitā*, which has the same meaning.
Regarding *ujumano tathā pasaṭamuju-mano*: having become straight-minded, he looks straight;
and just as he looks straight, so too he looks wide, expansive, and broad. *Piyadassano* means one who is to be looked upon with affection by those who love him.
In this context, "action" refers to the act of looking upon the great multitude with eyes of affection for a long time. Regarding what is called "correspondence to action":
when one looks while angry, one becomes like one-eyed or like a crow-eyed person; moreover, the eyes become crooked and turbid.
However, for one who looks with a serene mind, the fivefold clarity of the eyes is manifest. Thus it was with the Tathāgata.

And he looked [at her] in such a way. Then, so that the world with its devas might know by this reason his state of having been looked upon with a beloved eye for a long time, these two marks of a Great Man, which produce perfection of the eyes, were manifested.
This very pair of marks is what is called "the mark. The benefit is being lovely to behold. "Those who apply themselves" means those engaged in the science of marks (*lakkhaṇa-śāstra*).
Commentary on the Characteristic of the Uṣṇīṣa Head:
230. "He was a leader of the many" means he was a leader of the many people, the eldest of the group.
Others followed his example in view. Here, "action" (kamma) refers to leadership. That which corresponds to action is as follows:

He who, having become a leader, performs wholesome deeds such as giving, wanders about without embarrassment, with his head held high and his mind filled with rapture and gladness; he becomes a Great Man (mahāpurisa). The Tathāgata acted in this manner.
And so that the world, including the devas, might know by this reason that "this is the deed of leadership," there appeared the mark of the turbaned head (uṇhīsasīsalakkhaṇaṃ).
It is produced. This very thing is what is called a "characteristic" (*lakkhaṇa*).
The benefit is the conformity with the majority of people. 231. "It will belong to many people" means it will come to be for the multitude.
"Those who provide service" means attendants; the meaning is that there will be many attendants for him. "They bring it then" means even in his childhood, at that very time, thus...
They explain it. "Messenger" (*paṭihāraka*) means the state of being a servant. "One who has practiced mastery" (*visavī*) means one who has attained proficiency.
232. Regarding the description of the characteristics such as having a single hair per pore:
"It follows along" (*upavattati*) means it conforms to the underlying intention; here, "kamma" refers to speaking the truth over a long period of time.

The mark called *kammasarikkhaka* (correspondence with deeds) arises as both the single-hair mark (*ekekaloma-lakkhaṇa*) and the woolly-hair mark (*uṇṇā-lakkhaṇa*), so that the world with its devas may know by this reason his state of having spoken for a long time with undivided and pure speech.
These two marks together constitute what is called "the mark. It is the quality of conforming to the inclinations of the great masses of people.
The benefit. "With limbs covered by hair growing one by one" means a body whose every pore is filled with a single hair.
234. Regarding the description of the forty [major] marks and so forth:
"An unbreakable assembly" means an assembly that cannot be divided. Here, "kamma" refers to abstaining from malicious speech for a long time.

Regarding the explanation: "Kammasarikkhaka" (correspondence with past deeds) means that, it is said, because one who speaks maliciously breaks the harmony of others, his teeth become both incomplete and sparse.

However, for the Tathāgata, this pair of marks arises so that the world, including the devas, may know by this reason his long-standing abstention from malicious speech. This indeed is what is called a "mark."
Two characteristics. The benefit is having an unbreakable assembly. "Four tens" means four times ten, which is forty. 236.
Description of the characteristics such as the broad tongue:
"He has speech that is acceptable" means he has speech that should be accepted. Here, "kamma" refers to speaking gently for a long time.

Regarding "those whose actions correspond": those who are harsh-speakers have their tongues bound, hidden, forked, or rendered indistinct, so that by this means people may know the fact that they spoke harsh words after repeatedly turning their tongues over.
Furthermore, those who [turn their tongues over] to speak harsh words...
They do not speak; they are not those with bound tongues, hidden tongues, or forked tongues. Their tongues are supple and the color of red woolen cloth.

Therefore, the world together with its devas, thinking, "May the world know by this reason that for a long time the Tathāgata has not uttered harsh speech after having turned back his tongue," produces the mark of the broad tongue. [This is the mark resulting from] avoiding harsh speech.

And as they speak, their voices break. Having broken their voices, they become hoarse, or have a cracked voice, or a crow-like voice, so that people may know they have spoken harsh words with the intent of making their speech heard.
But those who do not speak harsh words that cause the breaking of the voice, their speech remains sweet and lovely. Therefore, for the Tathāgata...

The characteristic of the Brahma-voice arises with the thought: "May the world, including the devas, know by this reason that for a long time I have not spoken harsh words which cause the breaking of harmony.
This is indeed the pair of characteristics. The benefit is the quality of having speech that is persuasive and acceptable.
237. *Ubbādhikaṃ* means causing affliction because it is associated with abuse. *Bahujanappamaddanaṃ* means crushing many people.
Regarding the phrase *so na bhaṇi pharusaṃ giraṃ*, the negative particle *a-* here should be construed with the word *bhaṇi* that follows.
*Bāḷhaṃ* means powerful or excessively harsh. "He did not utter harsh speech" (*bāḷhaṃ giraṃ so na abhaṇī*)—this is the meaning here. *Susaṃhitaṃ* means well-composed.
*Pemasañhitaṃ*: connected with affection. *Sakhilaṃ*: gentle. *Vācā*: words (plural). *Kaṇṇasukhā*: pleasing to the ear (plural). There is also the reading *kaṇṇasukhaṃ*;
the meaning is that it causes pleasure to the ears in this way. *Vedayatha*: you have caused to be known.
*Brahmassarattaṃ*: the state of having a Brahma-like voice. *Bahuno bahuṃ*: much for many people. There is also the reading *bahūnaṃ bahuṃ*.
*Pāṭho*: the meaning is that it is "much" for many people.
238. *Sīhahanulakkhaṇavaṇṇanā*:
"He is indestructible" means he cannot be destroyed or displaced, either in terms of his qualities or his position. Here...
"Kamma" means not engaging in idle chatter. "Kammasarikkhaka" (resembling kamma) refers to those who do engage in such talk;

because of this, their jaws become inward-turned, crooked, or protruding, so that people may know by this reason that they have been speaking in idle chatter. But the Tathāgata, however, was not thus.

He did not speak. Therefore, so that the world together with its devas might know by this reason that he had not engaged in idle chatter for a long time by constantly moving his jaw, the mark of the lion’s jaw is produced.
This very mark is what is called a "mark" (*lakkhaṇa*). Its benefit is invincibility.
239. *Avikiṇṇavacanabyappatho* means that his path of speech (*vacanapatha*) was like that of previous Bodhisattvas whose words were not scattered;
thus he is one whose path of speech is unscattered. *Dvidugamavaratarahanuttamalatthā* means:
"going by twos" (*dvidugama*) refers to going with two at a time—that is, four [at once]. He attained the state of the jaw (*hanu*) of a lion, which is the most excellent among quadrupeds.
Meaning: "Lord of men" means the ruler of human beings. "Suchness" means having such a nature. 240.
Regarding the description of the characteristics of even teeth and so forth:
"Pure retinue" means a completely purified retinue. Here, "action" refers to right livelihood. It is similar to action.
Indeed, for one who maintains life by an uneven and defiled livelihood, even their teeth become uneven and their fangs become defiled.
However, so that the world with its devas may know, by this very reason, that the Tathāgata maintains life by an even and pure livelihood,
the characteristic of even teeth and the characteristic of perfectly white fangs are produced.
This very pair of characteristics is what is called "the characteristic. Having a pure retinue is the benefit. 241. *Avassaji* means he abandoned.
*Tidivapuravarasamo* means equal to Sakka, the foremost of the city of the Thirty-three (*tidivapura*).

*Lapanajaṃ* means produced from the mouth; the meaning is "teeth. *Dijasamasukkasucisobhanadanto*: because they were born twice, they are called "twice-born" (*diya*); [thus] his teeth are as white, pure, and beautiful as those of the twice-born.
He has teeth that are white, clean, and beautiful; thus he is "one whose teeth are as white, clean, and beautiful as those of a bird" (*dijasamasukkasucisobhanadanta*).
And there is no piercing by the country: for that country which is bounded by his world-system (*cakkavāḷa*), there is no piercing, oppression, or affliction by another.
Furthermore, they practice what is beneficial and bring happiness to many people; that is, the many people, having come to share in the same joys and sorrows, [abide] in that country.
They practice for each other’s benefit and happiness. *Vipāpa* means free from evil. *Vigatadarathakilamatha* means free from physical distress and fatigue.

*Malakhilakalikilese panudehi* means: "Drive away the stains (*mala*), the barrenness (*khila*), the strife (*kali*), and the defilements (*kilesa*)," that is, drive away all defilements such as the stains of lust and so forth, the barrenness of lust and so forth, and the strife of hatred. The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
The commentary on the Lakkhaṇa Sutta in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya, is completed. 8.
Commentary on the Siṅgāla Sutta.
Nidāna-vaṇṇanā 242.
“Thus have I heard” refers to the Siṅgāla-sutta. Herein, this is the commentary on the words not [already] explained: “In the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
“Bamboo Grove” (Veḷuvana) is the name of that park. It is said that it was surrounded by bamboos eighteen cubits [in height].
It was surrounded by a wall, equipped with gate-towers and watchtowers, blue in luster, and delightful; therefore it is called Veḷuvana.
Furthermore, they provided fodder for the squirrels there, and thus it is called Kalandakanivāpa.
It is said that formerly a certain king, having come there for the purpose of a pleasure excursion in the park, fell asleep during the day, intoxicated by liquor.
He fell asleep. His attendants, thinking "the king is asleep," departed here and there, enticed by flowers, fruits, and other offerings.
Then, drawn by the smell of the liquor, a black snake emerged from a hollow tree and came toward the king.
Seeing this, a tree deity, saying "I give life to the king," approached in the guise of a crow and [stood] at the root of his ear.

He made a sound. The king woke up. The black snake retreated. Seeing it, he thought, "My life has been given back to me by this black one," and he established a supply of fodder there for the black ones and caused the proclamation of safety to be sounded.
Therefore, from that time forth, it came to be known as "Kalandakanivāpa. For "Kalandaka" is a name for black ones.

Now at that time: at the time when the Blessed One, having made Rājagaha his alms-resort village, was dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place; at that time. Siṅgālaka the householder’s son:
“Siṅgālaka” is his name. “Householder’s son”: the son of a householder is a householder’s son. It is said that his father was a wealthy householder.
Having deposited them, there were forty crores of wealth stored in his house.
He was a lay follower who had reached certainty under the Blessed One and was a stream-enterer; his wife was likewise a stream-enterer. But his son was faithless and lacked conviction.
Then his parents constantly exhorted him thus: "Dear son, approach the Teacher; [approach] the General of the Dhamma..."
"Go to Mahāmoggallāna, Mahākassapa, and the eighty great disciples. He replied:
"I have no business going to you ascetics; rather, it is I who should go to the presence of the ascetics and pay them homage.
When bowing down to pay homage, my back aches and my knees become sore; one must sit upon the ground."
"When one stays there, one's robes become soiled and worn out; from the moment one sits nearby, conversation and discourse begin;
when that occurs, trust arises; and once that exists, one must accept invitations and provide robes, alms-food, and other requisites.
This being the case, my purpose is frustrated; I have no need to approach you ascetics."
Thus, although his parents exhorted him throughout his life, they were unable to lead him into the Teaching.
Then, as his father lay upon his deathbed, he thought, "It is right that I give my son some instruction," and further reflected:
"I shall give him this advice: 'My dear son, pay homage to the quarters,' for he does not understand the true meaning."
He will pay homage to the directions; then, when the Teacher or his disciples see him, they will ask, "What are you doing?
He will reply, "My father instructed me, 'Pay homage to the directions.
Then they will teach him the Dhamma, saying, "Your father did not cause you to pay homage to these directions; rather, he caused you to pay homage to those directions."
Thus, having recognized the excellence of the Buddha’s teaching, [the father thought], "He will perform meritorious deeds.

Then, having summoned him, he said, "Dear son, rising early in the morning, you should pay homage to the six directions. For a discourse given to one lying on his deathbed is something to be remembered for as long as life lasts.
Therefore, that householder’s son, recollecting those words of his father, acted accordingly.
Therefore, it was said: “Having risen early and departed from Rājagaha,” and so forth.
243. “In various directions” means in many directions. Now, showing those, he said: “The eastern direction,” and so on.
“He entered”: he had not yet actually entered; however, because he had set out with the intention, “I shall enter,” he is described in this way even while still on the road.
The Blessed One saw him, but it was not only now that he saw him;

for at dawn time, while surveying the world with his Buddha-eye, he had seen this man paying homage to the direction and thought: "Today I shall preach the Sigālaka Sutta, the householder’s discipline, to the householder’s son Sigālaka.
This discourse will be fruitful for the great multitude; I must go there. Therefore...
Having set out early in the morning, he entered Rājagaha for alms; and as he was entering, he saw him exactly as before. Therefore it is said:
“The Blessed One saw. He said this: it is said that even though the Teacher was standing not far away, he did not see him, but continued to pay homage to the directions.
Then the Blessed One [addressed him], like a lotus blooming upon contact with the rays of the sun.
Opening his mouth like a great lotus, he spoke these words, beginning with, "What is it, householder’s son?
244. Regarding the description of the six directions:
"In what way, venerable sir? it is said that upon hearing those words of the Blessed One, he thought: "That which..."
"It seems my father said that these six directions should be honored," she thought; "but it seems these are not the ones meant.

It seems there are other six directions that should be honored by a noble disciple (ariyasāvaka). Well then, let me ask about those very directions to be honored by a noble disciple and then honor them.
Thus, inquiring about them, he said, "But how, venerable sir? and so forth. In this context, *yathā* is merely a particle.
"But how?"—this is the very phrase of the question. "Defilements of action" (*kammakilesa*): beings are defiled by those actions;
therefore, they are called "defilements of action. "By means of bases" (*ṭhānehi*): by means of causes. "Ways to ruin" (*apāyamukhāni*): ways to destruction. "He":
that noble disciple who has entered the stream (*sotāpanna*). "Free from fourteen evils": free from these fourteen evil and blameworthy things.
"Covering the six directions" means covering the six quarters. "For the conquest of both worlds" means for the purpose of conquering both this world and the world beyond.
"This very world becomes undertaken" means that for one such as this, the five enmities do not exist in this world;
therefore, this very world becomes undertaken, satisfied, and brought to fulfillment. In the world beyond as well—
The five enmities do not exist; therefore, he has accomplished the next world. Consequently, with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world. 245.
Thus the Blessed One, having established the summary outline, now elaborates upon it: for whom [do] the four...
He said, "Kamma-kilesa," and so forth. "Kamma-kilesa" means both that which is kamma and that which is a defilement (*kilesa*) because it is associated with defilements;
thus, it is "kamma-defilement. For only one who possesses defilements kills a living being; one free from defilements does not kill. Therefore, the destruction of life is called a "kamma-defilement.
The same principle applies to taking what is not given and the other [unwholesome actions]. Then, "another" means yet another [passage] that elucidates this very same point.
The meaning is that he spoke in the form of verses.
246. Regarding the commentary on the four bases and so forth:
"He performs evil karma"—the Blessed One said this because when the agent is shown, the non-agent becomes evident. Therefore...
Having established the heading, “he does not commit an evil deed,” he spoke thus, showing first of all the perpetrator out of skill in teaching.
Therein, “one who goes by way of favoritism” means one who goes astray through desire—that is, through affection—and performs what should not be done.
The same method applies to the subsequent terms as well. Therein, “this person is my friend, or a close associate, or one seen in person…” [and so forth].
Or if, thinking "a relative or someone giving me a bribe is doing this," one makes that which has no owner have an owner through the influence of desire (*chandavasena*),
this is called committing an evil deed while falling into the perversion of desire (*chandāgati*). Or if,

thinking "this person is my enemy," one makes that which has an owner ownerless through the influence of an existing enmity or through anger arising at that very moment, this is committing an evil deed while falling into the perversion of hatred (*dosāgati*).

He indeed commits [an offense]. However, one who, out of dullness or delusion, or having said this or that, makes someone who has no owner into an owner, commits an evil deed while following the course of delusion (*mohāgati*). But one who, being afraid—thinking, "This person is a royal favorite or dependent on a corrupt official;
he might even do me harm"—makes someone who has no owner into an owner, follows the course of fear (*bhayāgati*).
This is what is called performing an evil deed. However, when one distributes anything and gives more out of affection, thinking,
"This person is my close friend or a relative," or gives less out of hatred, thinking, "This person is my enemy," or— out of sheer delusion—
gives more to some and less to others without knowing what has been given or not given, [thinking], "If this person is not given [this]..."
Fearing that someone might even do him harm, he gives an extra portion;
yet, though he is of fourfold type, by proceeding in due order through favoritism and the rest, he is said to perform evil karma.

But the noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*), even if he were to face the destruction of his life, does not succumb to favoritism and the rest. Therefore it is said: "By these four grounds, he does not perform evil karma."
"His fame diminishes": for one who goes along a wrong path, both his reputation and his honor diminish and decline.
Commentary on the Six Gates to the Downfall (Chaapāyamukha): 247.
"Devotion to the use of fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants that cause negligence": herein, "fermented liquor" (*surā*) refers to flour-liquor, cake-liquor, and rice-liquor.
"Kinnapakkhittā sambhārasaṃyuttā" refers to the five types of *surā* (fermented liquor). "Meraya" refers to the five types of *āsava* (distilled spirits):

flower-liquor, fruit-liquor, honey-liquor, molasses-liquor, and that which is prepared from various ingredients. All of these are *majja* (intoxicant) by virtue of their capacity to cause intoxication.
"Pramādaṭṭhāna" means a cause of negligence; it is a designation for the volition (*cetanā*) by which one drinks that intoxicant. "Anuyoga" means...
The pursuit of that basis for negligence consisting of fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants is their repeated practice.
Because, for one devoted to this, existing wealth declines and unarisen wealth does not arise, it is therefore called "a door to the loss of wealth.
"Devotion to wandering through streets at improper times" means being intent on wandering through streets at the wrong time.
"Attending festivals" means going to public spectacles by way of watching dancing and so forth. "Devotion to indolence" means being occupied with and intent upon physical laziness. 248.
Having thus established the matrix for the six doors of demerit, he now analyzes them, saying: "Six indeed, for me..."
He spoke the words beginning with “householder’s son, [it is] a danger. Therein, *sandiṭṭhikā* means that which is to be seen for oneself;

it pertains to this world. *Dhanajānī* means the loss of wealth. *Kalahappavaḍḍhanī* means that which increases quarrels of speech as well as physical quarrels such as the seizing of hands and so forth.
*Rogānaṃ āyatanaṃ* means the field for various diseases, such as eye-diseases and the like. *Akittisañjananī* means that which produces ill-repute.
For having drunk liquor, they strike even their mother and their father; they say much that should not be said and do what should not be done.
Because of that, they incur reproach, punishment, and even the amputation of hands, feet, and other limbs; they incur ill-repute both in this world and in the world beyond.
Thus, for them, that liquor is called "the producer of ill-repute. It is "that which reveals one's private parts."
For when a private part is exposed, it arouses and destroys modesty (*hiri*); therefore, it is called "the shameful" (*kopīna*).

Furthermore, those intoxicated by the madness of liquor wander about exposing various parts of their bodies; thus, because that liquor points out the shameful, it is called "that which points out the shameful" (*kopīnanidaṃsanī*).
"That which weakens wisdom" means that it weakens the wisdom of one's own actions as a master of karma, as in the case of the Elder Sāgata.
It weakens wisdom; therefore, it is called "that which weakens wisdom. However, it cannot weaken the wisdom of the Path (magga-paññā).
For those who have already attained the Path, this [ignorance] does not even enter their inner mouth. The sixth term means the sixth cause. 249.
"His own self is unguarded and unprotected" means that, wandering at improper times, he indeed treads upon stumps, thorns, and the like.
Knowing that he encounters even snakes and yakkhas and goes to such-and-such places, even his enemies lie in wait for him to seize or kill him.
Thus, his own self is neither guarded nor protected.
Even his children and wife think, "Our father, our master, wanders about at night; how much more so must we?"—and thus his sons, daughters, and wife [also become unprotected].
Having made plans outside and wandering about at night, they meet with ruin and disaster.
In this way, even his wife and children remain unprotected and unguarded. Regarding "property":
knowing that his wife, children, and attendants wander about at night, thieves enter the empty house and carry off whatever they desire. In this way, even his property—
It is unguarded and unprotected. "He is suspected" means that even regarding evil deeds committed by others, he is suspected, thinking, "This must have been done by him.

Whatever house door he passes through, whatever theft or adultery has been committed by another, when it is said, "This was done by him," that suspicion takes root in him even though it is untrue and non-existent.
It is established. Regarding the phrase "of many states of suffering": it is impossible to say that there is only this much suffering or only this much mental distress;
rather, in the absence of any other person, all [the burden] must be borne by one who wanders at improper times.
Thus, he stands at the forefront of many states of suffering, being their leader.
250. Regarding "Where do they dance?": having asked, "In what place is there dancing such as that of actors and performers?", one must go to whichever village or town it exists in.

For one who prepares clothes, perfumes, garlands, and so forth today, thinking, "Tomorrow I will go to see the dance," there is an interruption of work for the entire day; by means of seeing the dance—

He remains in that very place for one day, two days, or even three days. Then, although he obtains favorable rains and other such conditions, because he does not perform the sowing and other necessary tasks at the proper time for sowing and so forth, wealth that has not yet arisen does not arise for him.

Knowing that he has gone abroad, thieves do as they please in his unguarded house; thus, even the wealth that has already arisen perishes for him. This applies also to the verses beginning with "Where is the song? and so forth.
The method is exactly the same. Their distinction has already been stated in the *Brahmajāla Sutta*.
251. "Victory is enmity": thinking "I have won," one seizes another's cloak or turban in the midst of an assembly.
The other person thinks, "You are insulting me in the midst of this assembly; very well, I shall teach you a lesson," and thus he binds enmity there.

Thus, by conquering, he himself engenders enmity. "He conquers" means that when one has been defeated by another, he grieves over whatever binding, garment, or other wealth such as gold and bullion was taken from him, thinking, "Alas, it was mine!
Alas, that is no longer mine! On account of that, he sorrows. In this way, the victor sorrows for his lost wealth. This is the case for one who belongs to the assembly.
"His word does not hold" means that when he is questioned as a witness in a legal dispute, his word does not prevail or stand firm;
people will say of him, "This man is a gambler and a maker of bets; do not accept his word. He is despised by friends and companions;
for his friends and companions speak thus: "Good sir, even you, being a son of good family, are a maker of bets!"
“Having become cut and shattered, you wander about; this is not worthy of your birth or lineage. From now on, do not act in this way.
Although he was told this, he did not follow their advice. Consequently, they did not stand or sit together with him.
Because of him, even when questioned as witnesses, they would not speak. Thus, he was treated with contempt by his friends and companions.
"Those who come for marriage and those who go for marriage": "those who come for marriage" are those who wish to take a girl from his house;
"those who go for marriage" are those who wish to give a girl to his house. "He is unchosen" means he is undesired.
"Not capable of supporting a wife" means he is not competent to support a wife. Even if a girl is given to his house or even if she comes from his house, [she is not ours].
It must indeed be established in this way. 252.
Commentary on the Six Dangers of Bad Friendship:
"Gamblers" refers to those who gamble with dice. "Addicts" refers to those addicted to women, those addicted to food, those addicted to cakes, and those addicted to radishes.
"Pipāsā" means a craving for drink. "Nekatikā" means those who deceive by means of a counterfeit. "Vañcanikā" means those who deceive through face-to-face trickery.
"Sāhasikā" refers to those who commit acts of violence, such as breaking into a single house. "Tyāssa mittā hontī" means they become his friends.
He does not delight in the company of other true persons (sappurisā), nor does he take pleasure in adorning himself with perfumes, garlands, and the like, or in using excellent beds.
Like a pig that has been led to a pit of dung, he approaches only those who are evil friends. Therefore, he meets with much misfortune both in this present life and in the future. 253.
"It is too cold" and thus one does not perform work—this refers to people who, having risen early from their beds, [say]: "Come, sir, let us go to work."
When told, "Let us go," he replied, "It is still too cold; my bones seem to be breaking. You go first; I shall know later.
Thus, warming himself by the fire, he sat down. They went and performed their work, while his own work fell behind.
The same principle applies to the cases of "too hot" and so forth.
"He is called a drinking companion": some person becomes a friend only in the place of drinking, that is, with regard to liquor and fermented spirits.

There is also the reading "a leaf-companion" (*pannasakhā*), which has the same meaning. "A companion in private" (*sammiyasammiyo*): one who speaks thus, saying "Agreed, agreed," is a friend only in one's presence;
in one's absence, he is like an enemy and seeks only an opportunity [to harm]. "When matters have arisen": when such duties or tasks have come into being.

"Abounding in enmity" (*verappasava*) means being full of enmity. "Causing harm" (*anatthatā*) means acting for the sake of harm. "Excessive miserliness" (*sukadariyatā*) means being thoroughly stingy, a state of stubborn avarice.
"He sinks into debt like a stone into water" means that, like a stone sinking into water, he sinks into debt.
"One who shows no rising by night" means one whose nature is to not rise during the night. "This has become too late" means this [debt] has become overdue.
Those who, having spoken thus, do not perform their work—thus, "with neglected tasks" means having abandoned their duties.
"Opportunities pass by, O youth," means that for such persons, opportunities elapse; they do not remain with them.
"More than grass" means even more than grass. "He does not lose his happiness" means that person does not abandon his well-being.
He becomes as if possessed of happiness. By this line of discourse, he shows this meaning:
"While being a householder, one should not perform such actions; for one who does so, there is no growth. In this world and the next, one meets only with reproach.
*Commentary on the "Counterfeit Friends" and so forth.*
254. Now, whatever harm arises for one who acts in this way, or whatever other fears, calamities, or misfortunes there may be—all these arise depending upon the fool.

Therefore, in order to show that such fools are not to be associated with, and to demonstrate that fools are enemies in the guise of friends, he said: "Householder’s son, there are these four kinds of enemies," and so forth.
In this context, "one who takes for other purposes" (aññadatthuhara) is one who comes with empty hands and invariably takes whatever he can.
"One whose excellence lies in speech" (vacīparama) is one whose excellence is merely verbal; by speech alone, he acts as if he were a donor or a benefactor.
"One who speaks agreeably" (anuppiyabhāṇī) speaks what is pleasing. "A companion in misfortune" (apāyasahāya) is one who becomes a companion during the loss of wealth.
255. Having thus shown the four kinds of enemies, he speaks the passage beginning with "But by four things, householder's son," further analyzing each one there by means of four reasons.
In that context, "he is one who takes for his own ends" means he is exclusively a taker.
Having returned from his friend’s house empty-handed, he praises the color of the clothes and other items his friend is wearing; thinking, "He is truly..."
“You, friend, are praising him,” saying this, he puts on another [robe] and gives it to him.
“Seeking much with little” means that having given anything whatsoever in small measure, he seeks much from that person’s presence.
“He performs services out of fear” means that when fear arises for himself, he acts like a slave and performs various services; however, he does not do so at all times.
He acts when fear has arisen, not out of affection; thus he is called a "non-friend. He serves for the sake of his own interest:
he does not serve by way of friendship, but serves while expecting only his own benefit.
256. He greets with reference to the past: when a companion arrives, [he says], "You did not come yesterday or the day before; for us..."

"In this previous year the crop was extremely abundant; we sat looking along the road after setting aside many seeds of rice, barley, and so forth, but today it is all exhausted"—in this way, one takes hold of the past. As for "by the future":
"In this coming year our crop will be pleasing; the rice and other grains will be heavy with fruit"—thus one takes hold of the harvest through the future.
"Once it is finished, we shall be able to provide for you"—in this way, one favors another with the future.
"In vain" means that, sitting on the back of an elephant or the pelt of a horse, one sees a companion and says, "Come, sir, sit here.
Or, having put on a pleasing garment, one thinks, "This is indeed suitable for my companion; but I have no other."
He speaks thus; this is what is called "winning over by means of what is useless. He points out misfortune regarding present duties:
when it is said, "I have need of a cart," he says things such as, "Its wheel is broken" or "Its axle is snapped.
257. He also sanctions his evil deeds: when it is said, "Let us do whatever [is necessary] among the acts of killing living beings and so forth," he says, "Excellent, my friend!"
“I shall do so,” he consents. The same method applies to wholesome things as well. He is a companion: when told, “They are drinking liquor at such-and-such a place;
come, let us go there,” he goes saying, “Very well. This method applies everywhere.
“Thus having understood” means having recognized that “these are counterfeit friends.”
**Commentary on the Friend who is Kind (Suhadamitta):

260.** Having thus shown those evil friends who should not be associated with, [the Buddha] now, showing those virtuous friends who should be associated with, spoke again the passage beginning, "These four, O householder’s son... Herein, *suhada* means those with beautiful hearts.
**261.** "He protects one who is heedless" means: [one who has] fallen asleep in the middle of a village, at the village gate, or on the road after drinking liquor.
Seeing this, [he thinks], "Someone might even steal the lower and upper garments of one lying in such a manner," so he sits nearby and takes them when the person wakes up and departs.

Regarding "the property of one who is negligent": while a friend has gone outside or is intoxicated from drinking liquor, [the thief], thinking "someone might steal anything at all" from the unprotected house, enters the house and [takes] that person's wealth.

He protects. Regarding "of one who is afraid": when some kind of fear has arisen, he becomes a refuge by removing that fear, saying, "Do not be afraid; while a companion such as I stands by you, why should you fear? Regarding "twice the wealth":
when some duty or task arises and he sees his companion come into his presence, he asks, "Why have you come? [The answer is: "There is work at the royal court..."
"It exists. "What is required to obtain it? "One kahāpaṇa. "Work in the city cannot be accomplished for the price of a single kahāpaṇa;
take two. Whatever he says, he gives him double that amount. 262.
"He reveals his secret" means that, without telling another person a matter suitable to be kept secret by himself, [he reveals it].
He reveals that very thing to him. "He conceals his secret" means he protects the secret told by him in such a way that no one else knows it.
"He does not abandon him in times of distress" means he does not forsake him when danger has arisen.
"Even his own life for his sake" means even his own life is surrendered for the sake of that companion; even disregarding his own life—
He indeed performs that action. 263.
"He restrains from evil" means: while we are looking on and looking on, he restrains him, saying, "You may not do such a thing;
do not commit the five enmities or the ten courses of unwholesome action. "He establishes in what is good" means: in wholesome action.

He encourages them toward what is wholesome by saying: "Abide in the three refuges, the five precepts, and the ten courses of wholesome action; give gifts, perform meritorious deeds, and listen to the Dhamma.
He makes known what has not been heard before: he explains subtle and profound reasons that were previously unheard. He points out the path to heaven:
he declares the way to heaven by saying, "Having performed this deed, one is reborn in heaven."

264. "He does not rejoice at non-becoming" means that he does not rejoice upon seeing or hearing of such loss—whether of his children and wife or of his retinue—due to their non-becoming or lack of growth; rather, he becomes displeased.
"At becoming" means that he rejoices upon seeing or hearing of such prosperity or the attainment of power due to their growth.

He becomes pleased. "He restrains one who speaks dispraise" means that when someone says, "So-and-so is ugly, unattractive, ill-born, and immoral," he restrains that person by saying such things as, "Do not speak thus;
he is handsome, attractive, well-born, and endowed with virtue. [He likewise restrains] one who speaks praise...

"He praises" means that when someone says, "So-and-so is handsome, attractive, well-born, and endowed with virtue," one praises that person who is speaking the praise of another to one's own friend, saying, "Oh, you speak well! What you have said is eloquent; it is exactly so: this man is handsome, attractive, well-born, and endowed with virtue."
265. "He shines like a flame in the water": he radiates like a fire burning on the peak of a mountain at night.
"While gathering wealth": while accumulating wealth through righteous and equitable means, without oppressing either himself or others, and making it into a heap.
"Moving like a bee": just as a bee moves without crushing the color or fragrance of the flowers.
Having brought in nectar with its mouth and its wings, it gradually builds a honeycomb the size of a wheel;
thus, as it gradually creates a great mass of wealth, its riches go to accumulation. How?
Like an anthill being built up little by little by termites. Therefore he said:
“‘It is built up like an anthill’: the meaning is that they proceed toward accumulation just as an anthill is built up.
‘Having gathered together’ means having collected. ‘Able-bodied’ means one who possesses the necessary nature or capacity, being fit to establish a household life.
Now, advising how the household life should be established, he says: ‘One should divide wealth into four parts,’ and so forth.”
In that context, "he indeed binds friends" means that by dividing [his wealth] in this way, he truly binds his friends, establishing them as inseparable.
For only one who possesses wealth is able to establish friends, not another.
"One part he should enjoy for himself" means he should enjoy the wealth with one portion. "With two parts he should engage in work."
One should employ two portions for work such as agriculture and trade. "And one should set aside the fourth" means that having set aside the fourth portion, one should store it away.
"It will be for times of distress" means that the affairs of families do not remain the same at all times;
sometimes distresses arise due to kings and other causes. Therefore, [one should think]: "When such distresses have arisen..."
He said, “One portion should be set aside as a store. But among these four portions, which portion should be taken to perform wholesome deeds?

The portion stated as “one should enjoy the wealth. Having taken from that, it should be given to the monks, to the poor, travelers, and others, and wages should be paid to weavers, barbers, and so forth.
Commentary on the Section on Covering the Six Directions (Chaddisāpaṭicchādanakaṇḍa) 266.
Thus, by this line of discourse, the Blessed One showed how a noble disciple, having abandoned unwholesome states through four reasons,
having avoided the six doors of loss for wealth through six reasons, and cultivating sixteen kinds of friends, [attains his goal].
Having established a household and supporting a wife, he lives by a righteous livelihood and shines like a mass of fire among gods and humans.
Having thus given advice for the purpose of avoiding qualities that should be shunned and for the purpose of cultivating qualities that should be practiced,
[the Blessed One] now spoke the passage beginning with "And how, householder’s son," showing the six directions that are to be honored.

In this context, "one who covers the six directions" refers to one who dwells in such a way that no fear comes from the six directions, and thus remains secure and fearless; such a person is called "one who covers the six directions.

Regarding the passage beginning with "The eastern direction should be understood as mother and father," mother and father are to be understood as the eastern direction because of their prior service. [The same applies to] teachers.
The south is the direction because of being worthy of offerings (*dakṣiṇīyatā*). The west is the direction because of following behind one's wife and children.
The north is the direction because, since he overcomes various specific sufferings by relying on friends and colleagues, they are his support.
The slaves and laborers are the lower direction because they stand at the base of one's feet. The ascetics and brahmins [are the upper direction] by virtue of their qualities...
The upper direction is to be understood as such by virtue of its being situated above. 267.

"I shall support those who supported me": I was suckled at the breast by my mother and father; they raised my hands and feet, removed the mucus from my mouth with their own mouths, bathed me, and adorned me.
Thus, having been supported, nourished, and cared for by them, I am now [confronted by] those two aged ones.
"I shall support them by washing their feet, bathing them, and giving them rice gruel and food;
I shall perform their duties. Setting aside his own work, he will go and attend to whatever business arises for his parents in the royal court and other such places.
"I shall maintain the family lineage"—thinking thus, he will look after the fields, lands, silver, gold, and so forth belonging to his parents.
Even one who protects [the lineage] without letting it perish is said to "establish the family lineage.

One who removes parents from an unrighteous lineage and establishes them in a righteous lineage is also said to "establish the family lineage," as is one who maintains without interruption the distribution of *salākabhatta* and other offerings that have come down through the family lineage.
It is with reference to this that it was said: "I shall establish the family lineage."

Regarding the phrase "I shall attend to my inheritance": when parents, having brought a child who does not abide by their instruction and has practiced wrongly before the court of law, disinherit him, he is not worthy of the inheritance. However, when he abides by their instruction, they make him the master of the family property.
It is with the intention, "I shall conduct myself in this way," that it is said, "I shall attend to my inheritance."
"Thinking, 'I shall bestow a gift,' they make a transfer of merit for them [the parents], [saying]: 'Starting from the third day, I shall bestow gifts.

They restrain them from evil means that, having explained the danger of killing living beings and so forth—both in this present life and in future lives—they restrain them, saying, 'Dear one, do not do such a thing,' and they censure even what has already been done. They establish them in the good means that Anāthapiṇḍika..."
Even by giving bribes as it were, they establish them in the undertaking of virtue, concentration, and so forth.

"They teach them a craft" means that, having recognized their adherence to their own instructions, they teach them the crafts inherited through their lineage, such as finger-calculation (*muddā*) and arithmetic. "In a fitting manner" means in accordance with their family, character, physical appearance, and so on.
"At the proper time, they hand over the inheritance" means they give the wealth at the right time. In this context, "the constant time" and "the timely occasion" refer to [the appropriate moments].
There are two kinds of giving. Giving at all times means giving by saying, "Rising up again and again, take this;
let this be your provision for travel; perform wholesome deeds with this. Giving at specific times means giving on occasions such as the tying of the topknot, marriages, and so forth.
Furthermore, it includes giving at the final time to one lying on the deathbed, saying, "Perform wholesome deeds with this."
They are called "giving at the proper time. "It is concealed" means that it is covered so that whatever danger might come from the eastern direction does not come;

for if children have gone astray, yet their parents have acted rightly by caring for them since they were small, [the thought arises]: "These children are unworthy of their parents"—this is the danger.
Fear might come. Sons who practice rightly while parents practice wrongly—this fear that "the parents are not worthy of their sons" might come.
When both have practiced wrongly, both kinds of fear arise. When both have practiced rightly, none of it occurs.
Therefore it is said: "It is concealed, secure, and free from fear."
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One said this to Siṅgālaka: “Householder’s son, it is not that your father had you pay homage to the eastern direction as recognized by the world.
Rather, he had you pay homage to your mother and father, treating them as equivalent to the eastern direction.
For this is the eastern direction taught to you by your father, and no other.”

268. "By rising" means by rising from one's seat. For when a pupil sees his teacher approaching even from afar, he should rise from his seat, go forward to meet him, take his belongings from his hand, prepare a seat for him, and having seated him, perform fanning, washing the feet, and anointing the feet.
It is with reference to this that it is said, "by rising. "By attendance" means...
By going to attend upon [the teacher] three times a day. However, at the time of learning a craft, one must certainly go.
"With a desire to hear" means by listening with faith; for one who listens without faith does not attain distinction.
"With service" means with the remaining minor services. For a pupil, having risen early in the morning before the teacher...
Having given water for the mouth and tooth-sticks, even at the time of the meal, one should take drinking water, perform services such as attending to him, and after paying homage, depart.
Soiled garments and the like must be washed, and bathing water must be provided in the evening. One should attend to him during times of illness.
Even by one who has gone forth, the entire duty toward a pupil (antevāsika-vatta) must be performed. It is with reference to this that [the following was said].
It is said: “Through service. Regarding “carefully receiving the craft”:
careful reception means that after receiving a small amount, one should recite it many times; even a single word must be grasped with complete purity.
“They train those who are well-trained” means: “In this way you should sit, in this way you should stand, in this way you should eat...”
“They should eat; evil friends should be avoided; virtuous friends should be cultivated”—thus they train and discipline them in proper conduct.

“They cause them to grasp what is well-grasped”: they cause them to grasp it in such a way that it is well-grasped, having clarified both the meaning and the phrasing and having demonstrated the practical application.
“They provide for their friends and companions”: ‘This is our resident pupil...’”
“‘He is learned and possesses great knowledge, equal to me; you should recognize him as such’—having thus described his virtues, they establish him among their friends and kinsmen.
‘They provide protection in all directions’ means that by teaching him a craft, they provide him with security in every direction.
For once he has mastered a craft, wherever he goes and displays that craft, gain and honor arise for him there.”

Thus it is said to be "done by the teacher"; when the great multitude speaks of his virtue, they first speak of the teacher's own virtue, thinking, "Ah, this is indeed a resident pupil who has washed the teacher's feet and lived [under him].
Even the gain arising for him, vast as the Brahma-world, belongs to the teacher alone.
Furthermore, having recited the spell (*vijjā*) over him, the robbers in the forest do not [attack] him as he goes along.
Non-human beings, such as the Dīghajāti spirits and others, do not harass him; even those teaching him act as a protective charm for him in all directions.
Or, having developed doubts about whichever direction he has gone to, people who come into his presence say:
"In this direction our pupil lives; and between him and me there is a difference in this craft."
"There is none; go and ask him himself"—thus, even by supporting a pupil in this way, they provide protection for the arising of gain and honor for him there;
the meaning is that they establish a foundation for him.
The rest here should be construed in the same manner as before.
269. In the third section on the directions, "by honoring" means by speaking with respectful discourse, such as "O Queen Mother, O Tissāmātā.
"By not disparaging" means by not speaking in a way that insults or treats one with contempt, as servants, laborers, and the like might do after beating or harassing them.
"By not transgressing" means not going beyond that [wife] to engage with another woman outside [the marriage].
One who serves her is said to "transgress" by not doing so; likewise, by not acting [as required]. Regarding the phrase "by relinquishing authority":
for women, even after receiving ornaments like those of great ladies, become angry if they are not permitted to manage the food;
thus, when the authority over the kitchen is relinquished by saying, "Place the ladle in your hand and do as you please," all authority has been surrendered.
The meaning is: "by means of such an action. "By the bestowing of ornaments" means by the giving of ornaments according to one's own wealth.
"With well-ordered work" means with work that is properly managed by performing each respective task thoroughly, without missing the proper times for cooking rice-gruel, meals, and so forth.
"With a retinue held in affection" means [held together] by means of honor and the like, as well as by the sending of gifts and messages.
And she has her retinue well-gathered. Here, "retinue" refers to the relatives of both the husband and herself.

"Not transgressing" means that, apart from her husband, she does not desire anyone else even in her mind. "Accumulated wealth" refers to the riches brought in by performing such tasks as farming and trade.
"She is skillful" means she is clever and proficient in preparing rice-gruel, meals, and so forth. "Diligent" means she is free from laziness.
Just as other lazy people remain seated when they should be sitting and remain standing when they should be standing, he does not act thus;
rather, with an expanded mind, he accomplishes all his duties. The rest here should also be construed in the same manner as before.
270. In the fourth section on the directions, "by way of non-deception" means that whatever name he takes up, he does not deceive that person.
"This too is in our house; this too is there—take it and go. By giving in this way, without deceiving them, [he fulfills his duty].
And "his other offspring honor him" means: the children of a friend are called *pajā* (offspring);
their children and grandchildren are called *aparapajā* (other offspring). They honor him, cherish him, and treat him as their own during auspicious occasions and the like.
They perform auspicious rites and so forth for them. The rest here should also be understood in the same manner as before.
271. "By arranging work according to one's strength" means: what should be done by the young should not be assigned to the elderly, nor what should be done by the elderly to the young;
what should be done by women should not be assigned to men, nor what should be done by men to women—without such [inappropriate] assignments.
By means of arranging their work according to each individual’s strength;

by the provision of food and wages—meaning, having observed what is appropriate for each, such as "this one is a junior monk" or "this one lives alone," providing them with both meals and travel expenses;
and by nursing the sick—meaning, not assigning work when they are unwell, but attending to them by giving suitable medicines and so forth.
"By sharing wonderful flavors" means that having obtained wonderful, sweet flavors, one does not eat them oneself but shares them with others from that supply.
"By relinquishing at the proper time" means by relinquishing both at the regular time and at the appropriate time.
Regarding the relinquishment at the regular time: those who perform their work throughout the entire day become exhausted.
Therefore, knowing the proper time so that they do not become weary, there is the granting of leave.
"Relinquishment at the proper time" means giving away ornaments, goods, food, drink, and so forth on occasions such as festivals and lunar celebrations.
"Those who take what is given" means those who, having not taken anything by theft, take only what has been given by the owners. "Performers of good deeds" means: "What of this..."
Thinking, "We receive nothing for the work we have done," they do not brood over it, but with contented hearts perform their tasks as well as can be done.
They are "bearers of fame and praise" because when a conversation arises in the midst of the assembly, people say:
"Who is there equal to our masters? We do not even know our own state as slaves, yet they [know] even our status as masters."
"We do not know; thus they show us compassion"—thus they are "carriers of talk on virtues. The rest here should also be construed according to the previous method.

Regarding the phrases beginning with "with loving bodily action": bodily actions and so forth performed after having established a mind of loving-kindness (*mettacitta*) are called "loving" (*mettā*).
Among these, going to the monastery thinking, "I shall invite the monks," and the making of water-vessels (*dhamakaraṇa*), [are examples].
Taking up a water-strainer and performing services such as massaging the back and feet is called loving bodily action (*metta-kāyakamma*).
Seeing monks who have entered for alms, saying things such as "Give the rice-gruel respectfully! Give the meal!
and likewise applauding, listening to the Dhamma attentively, and performing hospitable greetings are loving verbal action (*metta-vacīkamma*).
“May our preceptors (kulūpaka-theras) be free from enmity and free from ill will”—thinking thus is what is called loving-kindness as mental action (mettā-manokamma).

Regarding “the state of having doors unbarred”: this means the state of not having the doors closed. In that regard, even if one has opened all the doors, one who does not give to or do favors for those possessing virtue is indeed one whose doors are closed.
Conversely, even if one has closed all the doors, one who gives to and does favors for them [is one whose doors are open].
"Only with the door open. Thus, when virtuous people arrive at the door of one's house, one should give without saying "there is nothing," even if there actually is;
