this is what is called "having the door unbarred. Regarding "by the provision of material goods":
"material goods" refers to food that is to be consumed before the midday meal; therefore, [one should provide] for the virtuous...
The meaning is: by the providing of rice-gruel and alms-food. "Compassionating with a virtuous mind" means by extending benevolence in this way:
"May all beings be happy, free from enmity, free from affliction, and free from distress.
Furthermore, even when entering the houses of attendants together with other virtuous fellow-celibates, they are said to be "compassionating with a virtuous heart. This was heard.
"Clarifying" means that having explained the meaning of whatever has been heard by them by nature, they dispel their doubt, or cause them to practice for the sake of suchness.
The rest here should also be construed according to the previous method.
"Able" means capable of maintaining a household after providing for wife and children. "Wise" means [one who is proficient] in the place of honoring the quarters.
"Being wise" (*paṇḍito*): "Gentle" (*saṇho*) means being gentle either by perceiving subtle meanings or by speaking with gentle words.
"Eloquent" (*paṭibhānavā*): being eloquent in the sense of reflecting upon the directions [of discourse]. "Humble in conduct" (*nivātavuttī*): one whose behavior is lowly [in its modesty].

"Free from stubbornness" (*atthaddho*): devoid of rigidity. "One who exerts himself" (*uṭṭhānavā*): endowed with the energy of exertion. "Diligent" (*analaso*): free from indolence. "Of uninterrupted conduct" (*acchinnavuttī*): by way of acting continuously.
"Of unbroken conduct. "Wise" means endowed with the wisdom that arises from situational understanding (*ṭhānuppatti-paññā*).
"A gatherer" means one who gathers [people] by means of the four bases of sympathy (*saṅgahavatthu*).

"One who makes friends" means one who seeks out friends. "Generous" means one who recognizes the words of those who have previously done him a service. When he has gone to his friend's house, [he thinks]: "To my friend..."

The meaning is that he prepares for his friend who has come to his house as much as was promised—or even more—when he recalled the words spoken [by his wife]: “Give him a turban, give him a garment, give the food and wages for the men.
Furthermore, it refers to one who, having gone to a friend’s house with the thought, “I will take such-and-such,” feels shame when it comes to taking it from a friend who has arrived.
One who, knowing that another has come for a certain purpose, speaks so as to accomplish that aim—even if the other is unable to ask or does not wish to speak—is called "munificent" (*vadaññū*).
Alternatively, one who observes what his friend lacks and gives that very thing to him is also munificent.
One who leads by showing various matters through wisdom is a "leader" (*netā*). One who leads by demonstrating various reasons is a "guide" (*vinetā*).
"One who leads again and again" is an inducer (*anunetā*).
"In this or that" means toward this or that person. "Like the linchpin of a chariot":

just as a chariot moves only when the linchpin is present and does not move when it is absent, so too the world proceeds only when these means of integration (*saṅgaha*) are present and does not proceed when they are absent.
Therefore it was said: “These indeed are the means of integration in the world, like the linchpin of a moving chariot.
“Not for the sake of her son does a mother [fail to act]”: if a mother were not to employ these means of integration toward her son, she would not receive honor or worship on account of her son.

*Saṅgahā ete*: here *ete* (these) is used in the accusative case. Alternatively, the reading is *saṅgahe ete* (in these means of integration). *Sammapekkhantī* means they look upon [him] rightly. *Pāsaṃsā ca bhavantī* means they become worthy of praise.
274. Thus, O householder’s son, regarding those directions with which your father spoke when he said, "You should pay homage to the directions," these are those six directions.

Showing that if you would follow your father’s word, you should pay homage to these directions, the Blessed One brought his teaching to its conclusion while standing upon Sigālaka’s question, and then entered Rājagaha for alms. Sigālaka, too, [took refuge] in the refuges...
Having established himself and distributed forty million pieces of wealth for the sake of the Buddha’s teaching, he performed meritorious deeds and became destined for heaven.
Furthermore, in this sutta, there is no duty to be performed by householders that has not been mentioned; this discourse is indeed the "Vinaya for Householders.
Therefore, for one who hears this and practices according to the instructions, there is only progress.
"It is to be expected, not a decline.
Thus ends the commentary on the Siṅgāla Sutta in the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, the commentary on the *Dīghanikāya*.
9. Commentary on the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta:
Commentary on the First Recitation Section 275.
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta. Herein, this is the commentary on the words not previously explained: "protection in the four directions."
"Having stationed," means having established a guard for Sakka, Lord of the Devas, in the four directions for the purpose of warding off the army of the asuras.
"Having stationed a troop," means having stationed a military force. "Having stationed a protection," means having stationed guards in the four directions.
Thus, having made the protection of Sakka, Lord of the Devas, well-arranged, [he dwelt] in the city of Āṭānāṭa.
Having sat down and composed this protective chant (*paritta*) concerning the seven Buddhas,
and having made a proclamation saying, "To those who do not obey the Teacher’s command of the Dhamma and our royal command,

we shall do such-and-such to them," she arranged for her own protection in the four directions by means of four armies, beginning with a great army of *yakkhas*, and then departed at the time of dawn.
During the night... [as before] ...they sat down to one side.
Regarding the phrase "when the night had advanced" (*abhikkantāya rattiyā*), the word *abhikkanta* is seen in the senses of "waning," "beautiful," "handsome," "excellent," "rejoicing," and so forth.
In this context: "Venerable sir, the night has advanced; the first watch has passed; the community of monks has been seated for a long time."
In such passages as, "Venerable sir, let the Blessed One recite the Pātimokkha to the bhikkhus," it is seen in the sense of destruction (*khaya*).
In such passages as, "This one is more excellent and more sublime than these four persons," it is seen in the sense of beautiful (*sundara*).
"Who is worshipping my feet, shining with the glory of supernormal power? [In this case, it means "shining"].
"In ‘With surpassing beauty, illuminating all directions,’ it refers to one who is handsome.
In ‘Excellent, Master Gotama! and similar phrases, it refers to approval. But here, it refers to the passing away. By that, it means ‘at the end of the night,’ or ‘when the night has been exhausted.

In the phrase ‘of surpassing beauty’ (*abhikkantavaṇṇa*), the word *abhikkanta* here refers to being handsome; the word *vaṇṇa*, however, [refers] to skin, praise, clan, group, cause, shape, measure, the sense-sphere of form, and so forth."
It is seen. In that regard, in such passages as “The Blessed One is golden-hued,” it refers to the skin.
In such passages as “But when, householder, were these praises of the ascetic Gotama uttered by you? it refers to praise.
In such passages as “There are these four castes, Master Gotama,” it refers to the class of families. In such passages as “Now, by what characteristic is one called a ‘scent-thief’? it refers to...
In the sense of a cause: as in “having manifested the form of a great king elephant,” and so forth; in the sense of shape: as in “three shapes of a bowl,” and so forth;
in the sense of measurement: as in “the three measurements of a bowl,” and so forth; in the sense of the sense-sphere of visible form: as in “color, odor, taste, and nutritive essence,” and so forth.
Here, however, it should be understood as the skin. Thus, by this [term], what is meant is “possessing a surpassing color and a beautiful skin.”
Regarding the term *kevalakappa*: here the word *kevala* has many meanings, such as "without remainder," "for the most part," "unmixed," "excessive," "firm," "disjunction," and so forth.
For instance, in passages such as "the holy life (*brahmacariya*) that is complete (*kevala*) and perfect and pure," its meaning is "without remainder. Likewise, in the passage:
"And the entire region of Aṅga and Magadha, having taken abundant hard food and soft food, desired to set out... [the meaning is "entire"].
In such passages as "there are," it refers to the majority; in such passages as "the origin of this entire mass of suffering," it refers to non-mixture;
in such passages as "surely this venerable one has only mere faith," it refers to non-excess; and [in the passage]:
"Venerable sir, the venerable Anuruddha’s co-resident named Bāhika has stood for the schism of the entire Saṅgha."

In such instances as these, it has the sense of firmness (*daḷhattha*). In such instances as “He is called a perfected one (*kevalī*), one who has lived the holy life, a supreme person,” it signifies dissociation (*visaṃyoga*).
But here, its sense of being without remainder (*anavasesattha*) is intended.

Furthermore, this word *kappa* has many meanings, including: conviction (*abhisaddahana*), conventional usage (*vohāra*), time (*kāla*), designation (*paññatti*), cutting off (*chedana*), alternative (*vikappa*), a trace (*leśa*), and all-encompassing state (*samantabhāva*).
For instance, in such passages as, "This is indeed credible for Master Gotama, just as it is for an Arahant, a Fully Enlightened One," its meaning is "firm conviction.
In such passages as, "I allow you, monks, to consume fruit according to the five ascetic conventions," its meaning is "convention" (usage).
And in such passages as, "By which, indeed, I always abide according to convention," [its meaning is "habitual practice"].
*Kāla* (time). In such passages as “Thus spoke the Venerable Kappa,” it means designation (*paññatti*). In such passages as “adorned, with hair and beard trimmed,” it means cutting (*chedana*).
In such passages as “the two-finger-breadth allowance is permitted” (*kappati dvaṅgulakappo*), it means an arrangement (*vikappa*).
In such passages as “there is time to lie down,” it means a slight amount (*leso*). In such passages as “having illuminated the entire Veḷuvana grove,” it means all-aroundness (*samantabhāvo*). Here—
However, the meaning intended here is "entirety. Therefore, in the phrase "the entire Vulture Peak," the meaning should be understood as "the Vulture Peak in its entirety, on all sides.
"Illuminating" means pervading with the radiance issuing from his robes, garlands, ornaments, and body, like the moon or the sun.
"And as if making a single radiance and a single light" is the meaning. "They sat to one side": for the devatās, there is no such thing as a place to sit near the One of Ten Powers;
however, in this sutta, they sat down out of respect for the protection (paritta).
276. As for Vessavaṇa: although the four Great Kings had arrived, Vessavaṇa was the one who inspired confidence in the One of Ten Powers.
Being skilled and well-trained in the delivery of discourse, the Great King Vessavaṇa said this to the Blessed One.

"Exalted" means endowed with great power and majesty. Regarding "abstention from taking life": having shown the danger of taking life both in this present life and in future lives, he teaches the Dhamma on abstaining from it.
The same method applies to the remaining [precepts] as well. In that regard, there exist...
"Exalted *yakkhas* dwell there" means that in those lodgings there are exalted *yakkhas* who reside permanently.
"Āṭānāṭiya" is its name because it was composed in the city of Āṭānāṭa. But does the Blessed One have any doctrine that is not directly perceived by him?
No, he does not. Then why did Vessavaṇa say, "Venerable sir, let the Blessed One learn [this]," and so forth? It was for the purpose of making way [for the teaching].
For he spoke thus while requesting an opportunity to recite this protective charm (*paritta*) to the Blessed One.

He also said, "When spoken by the Teacher, this protective charm will become weighty. "For the sake of dwelling in comfort" means for the sake of dwelling happily in the four postures (*iriyāpatha*), such as walking, standing, and so forth.
277. "Of the Visionary One": it is not only Vipassī who is the Visionary One; all seven Buddhas are Visionary Ones. Therefore...
Each Buddha has these seven names. All Buddhas are possessed of vision;
all are compassionate toward all beings; all are "bathed" because they have washed away the defilements (*kilesa*); all are crushers of Māra’s army;
all are those who have lived the holy life (*vusitavant*); all are liberated; and all are *Aṅgīrasas* because rays of light issued from their limbs. And not only this...
It is said that these seven names of the Buddhas are indeed their incalculable names according to their qualities as Great Seers (*mahesi*).
However, Vessavaṇa spoke thus by way of his own well-known name. Here, "those people" refers to those whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*).
"Be free from backbiting" is merely a heading for the teaching; the meaning is: "be truthful, free from backbiting, gentle, and speakers of measured speech. "Greatness" means...
They have attained greatness. There is also the reading *mahantā*, which has the same meaning as *mahantā* (great). *Vītasāradā* means free from fear and devoid of horripilation.
*Hitam* means beneficial through the pervasion of loving-kindness (*mettā*). In the phrase *yaṃ namassanti*, *yaṃ* is merely a particle.
*Mahattam* means greatness. Or rather, this is the reading itself; thus it is said: "And those in the world who are extinguished by the extinction of defilements..."

"They who have seen things as they truly are, and who, endowed with the qualities of true knowledge and so forth, pay homage to Gotama—who is beneficial to gods and humans—those people are free from backbiting; may homage be paid to them as well.
However, in the commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), it says, "Those people are free from backbiting" means "those Buddhas are free from backbiting";
thus, in this way, the praise of the Buddhas alone is expressed in the first verse. Therefore, the first verse [is dedicated] to the seven...
[The names] are spoken by way of the Buddhas. In the second verse, "Gotama" is merely the opening of the teaching.
It should be understood that this too is spoken by way of the seven [Buddhas]. This is the meaning here:
"I pay homage to Gotama, whom the wise among gods and men in the world revere, and to those Buddhas who preceded him."
278. “From where it rises” means from which place it emerges. “The sun” (*ādicca*) is the son of Aditi; or this is merely a synonym for the word *sūriya*.
“Possessing a great orb” means having a large disk (*maṇḍala*). “And when it is rising” means while it is emerging.
“Even the darkness ceases” means the night disappears. “And when it has risen” means once it has emerged.
*Ahrada* means a water-lake. *Tattha* (there) means in that place from which the sun rises.
*Samuddo* (the ocean): that which was called a lake is not something else; rather, it is the ocean. *Saritodako*:
one whose water has spread out, or "having waters flowing in" (*saritodako*), meaning various kinds of rivers have entered its waters. Thus they know it there.
They know that lake right there in this way. How do they know it? They know it as "the ocean, the water of the rivers.
*Ita* means from Sineru or from the place where they are sitting. *Jana* refers to this great multitude. *Ekanāmā* means having a single name;
by the name of Indra, they all have one and the same name. Indeed, it is said that they gave them all the very same name as Sakka, the king of the gods. Eighty ten... [one hundred].
“Eko ca” means ninety-one people. “Indanāmā” means those whose name is indeed “Inda.

“Buddhaṃ ādiccabandhunaṃ” means he is a Buddha because he has departed from the sleep of the defilements (kilesa), and he is the kinsman of the Sun (Ādiccabandhu) because his lineage is the same as that of the Sun.

“Kusalena samekkhasī” means he gazed upon the great multitude with faultless and subtle omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa). “Amanussāpi taṃ vandanti” means even non-human beings (amanussa) pay homage to him.
Having said, "He surveyed the great multitude with his omniscient knowledge," they pay homage.

"We have heard this often"—this is what we have heard repeatedly. When asked by us, "Pay homage to the Victor Gotama! Pay homage to the Victor Gotama!", they reply, "We pay homage to the Victor Gotama."
279. "By whom they are called *petas*": those who have passed away are called *petas*; they are told by which direction they should be carried out.
"Backbiters, eaters of back-flesh": those who speak maliciously and, like those eating the flesh of another's back, criticize others behind their backs.
They are told by which [direction] they should be carried out; all of these are to be carried out through the southern gate.
"Let them burn, or be cut, or be slain to the south of the city"—thus they are addressed.
"From here, that is the southern direction"—by which direction those *petas* and the slanderers and so forth are told to be led out;
"from here" means from Sineru or from the place where they are sitting. "Of the *kumbhaṇḍas*"—
It is said that those gods have large bellies, and their private parts are as large as a jar;
therefore, they are called Kumbhaṇḍas.
280. "Where the sun sets" means in whichever direction the sun goes to its setting.
281. *Yena*: by which direction or region. *Mahāneru*: the great Sineru, the king of mountains. *Sudassano*:

"beautiful to behold" because it is made of gold. For the eastern face of Sineru is made of silver, the southern face of jewels, the western face of crystal, and the northern face of gold; thus, it is lovely to behold.
Therefore, the meaning here is that Sineru is called Sudassana in that particular direction.
"Humans are born there" means that humans are born there in Uttarakuru. "Without 'mine'" means they are devoid of possessiveness even regarding clothing, ornaments, drink, food, and so forth.
"Without property" means they have no property in the form of wives; for it is said that they have no sense of possessiveness such as, "This woman is my wife."
When they see their mother or sister, no sensual desire arises.
Nor are ploughs led there; even the ploughs are not taken to the field with the thought, "We shall do the work of ploughing.
It is "grown on unploughed ground," meaning it grows spontaneously in the forest on land that has not been tilled. It is "rice-grain fruit," meaning its fruit consists of nothing but rice grains.
"Having cooked in a *tuṇḍikīra*," means having poured [the food] into a pan and cooked it with smokeless embers.
It is said that there are so-called "fire-stone" (*jotikapāsāṇa*) stones there. Having placed those three stones, they set the pan upon them.
Heat is generated from the stones and cooks the food; then they eat the meal from that pan.
They eat only the food; there is no other soup or curry. As they eat, the flavor is exactly to their liking.
They give this very place to those who arrive there, for they have no thought of stinginess.
Even Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and others of great psychic power go there and receive almsfood.

"Having made the cow one-hoofed" means: having taken the cow and made it a one-hoofed vehicle, the *yakkhas* who are attendants of Vessavaṇa mount it and follow along, wandering from region to region—that is, they travel in various directions. "Having made the beast one-hoofed" means:
setting aside the cow, they take the remaining species of four-footed beasts and make them one-hoofed vehicles, and thus they follow along from region to region.
"Making a woman a vehicle" means having made a pregnant woman—a woman who is mostly pregnant—a vehicle.
They travel sitting upon her back; it is said that her back is able to bear the bending [of the load]. But other women they yoke to the vehicles.
"Making a man a vehicle" means taking men and yoking them to the vehicles. And when they take them, they do not take those who possess right view.
They were unable [to do so]. For the most part, they took those living as outcaste border-dwellers.
It is said that a certain countryman, having sat down near a certain elder, fell asleep; the elder asked, "Lay follower, you are sleeping very deeply.
He replied, "Venerable sir, today we have been exhausted all night long by the servants of Vessavaṇa."
"Making a maiden their vehicle" means that they take maidens, make them into vehicles with single hooves, and yoke them to chariots.
The same method applies to "the vehicle of a youth. "The attendants of that king" refers to the king’s female attendants.

"Elephant-vehicle, horse-vehicle" means that they do not travel by means of ox-carts and the like alone; they also travel about having mounted elephant-vehicles, horse-vehicles, and so forth. "A divine vehicle" means...
Furthermore, many kinds of divine vehicles were indeed present for them; these, first of all, were their convenient means of transport.
Yet they moved about even while reclining on excellent couches in palaces, or while seated on chairs, litters, and so forth. Therefore it is said:
“Palaces and litters. Of the illustrious Great King—thus [it refers to one] endowed with such power and renown.
"These vehicles are produced for the Great King.
And "his cities were well-constructed in the sky" means that for that king, these cities beginning with Āṭānāṭā were well-constructed in the atmosphere;
they existed as cities. For one of his cities was named Āṭānāṭā, and another...
One is called Kusināṭā, one is called Parakusināṭā, one is called Nāṭasūriyā, and one is called Parakusiṭanāṭā.
"To the north of Kasivanta" means that standing there, another city named Kasivanta lies directly in the northern direction.
"And beyond Janogha" means that after this [city], there is another city named Janogha. "Ninety-nine... [etc.]
There is also another city named Navanavatiyo; another is named Ambaraambaravatiyo;
and there is yet another royal capital named Āḷakamandā.
Regarding this Kuvera Mahārāja, it is said that before the Buddha had appeared, he was a brahmin named Kuvera who [planted] a sugarcane field...

Having had seven machines constructed, he joined them together. He performed meritorious deeds by giving away the income produced from one machine hall to the great multitude of people who came and went.
A much greater income arose right there from the remaining halls;
pleased by this, he took what was produced from the remaining halls as well and gave alms for twenty thousand years. He passed away...
Having done so, he was reborn among the Cātumahārājika gods as a son of the gods named Kuvera.
Later on, he ruled over the royal capital of Visāṇā; from that time forth, he is called Vessavaṇa.
"Paṭiesantā" means those who investigate, individually examining the meanings and instructing others.
Twelve yakṣa-bones proclaim [the message]. It is said that those yakṣa-bones, having received the message, announce it to twelve yakṣa gatekeepers.
The yakṣa gatekeepers then announce that message to the Great King.
Now, pointing out the names of those yakṣa-bones, he says "tatolā," and so forth. Among them, one is named Tatolā.
One was named Tattala, one was named Tatotala, one was named Ojasi, one was named Tejasi, and one was named Tatojasi.
Regarding Sūra and Rāja: one was named Sūra, one was named Rāja, and one was named Sūrorāja. Regarding Ariṭṭha and Nemi:
one was named Ariṭṭha, one was named Nemi, and one was named Ariṭṭhanemi.
"Even the lake there is called Dharaṇī": this means that there is a certain lake of water there named Dharaṇī;
it is said that there is a great lotus pond fifty *yojanas* in extent. "From which the clouds rain":
from which lotus pond the clouds take water and then rain. "From which the rains descend": from which the showers of rain spread forth.
They enter [the lake]. It is said that when clouds arise, the old water from that lotus pond dries up.
A cloud rising above fills that lotus pond with fresh water. The old water, having moved downward, flows out.
When the lotus pond is full, the clouds disperse. "Sabhā" means an assembly hall. Regarding that lotus pond...
On the bank there is a jeweled pavilion twelve *yojanas* in extent, surrounded by a creeper named Sālavatī; it is with reference to this that it was said.

"They attend upon" means they sit down. "Trees always bearing fruit" indicates that in that place, surrounding that pavilion, there are trees such as mangoes and rose-apples which are perpetually in fruit, as well as *campaka*, *māla*, and other trees which are always in bloom. "Filled with flocks of various birds."
It was crowded with various flocks of birds; it resounded with the songs of peacocks and *koñca* cranes—that is, it was filled with the singing of peacocks and *koñca* birds.

There was also the sound of *jīvañjīvaka* birds here—meaning there was the cry of *jīvañjīvaka* birds crying out, "Live! Live! There were also *uṭṭhavacittaka* birds, which warble, "Arise, Citta! Arise, Citta!"
There they roam about. *Kukkuṭaka* means wild jungle fowl. *Kuḷīraka* means golden crabs.
*Vana* means in the lotus grove. *Pokkharasātaka* refers to birds called *pokkharasātaka*.
*Sukasāḷikasaddettha* means the sound of parrots and mynas is there. *Daṇḍamāṇavakāni ca* means human-faced birds.
It is said that they walk about holding golden staffs with both hands, stepping upon one lotus leaf and placing the golden staff upon the next lotus leaf.
That lotus pond, Sāti, is beautiful at all times; it is beautiful at all times.
"Kuveranaḷinī" means Kuvera’s lotus-pond, which has become a lotus lake; its name is Dharaṇī.
The lotus pond shines constantly and without interruption.
(282) “Yassa kassaci” (of whomever): this was said by Vessavaṇa after he had completed the Āṭānāṭiya protection, in order to show the preliminary practice for it.
Therein, “well-learned” means learned thoroughly after having purified both the meaning and the phrasing.
"Mastered and learned thoroughly" means they have been acquired in their entirety without omitting any words or phrases.
For if one recites while contradicting either the meaning or the text, or if one has not mastered it at all, the protective charm (*paritta*) lacks power;
however, for one who recites having mastered it completely, it possesses power. This is also true for one who recites after learning it for the sake of gain.
It shows that it does not accomplish one's welfare; rather, for one who stands on the side of renunciation and speaks with loving-kindness as the precursor, it leads only to their own welfare.
"A follower of the *yakkhas*" means one who serves the *yakkhas*. "A site" means a house-site. "A dwelling" means a permanent residence there. "An assembly" means a gathering.
"Anāvāhya" means not fit for marriage alliance. "Avivāhya" means not fit for matrimonial alliance. The meaning is that one should not enter into marriage or matrimonial alliance with them.

"Even with their own perfect [forms]" means they would revile one with insults that have complete phonetic components, having attributed to these beings such personal forms as "Kaḷārakkhi" (Black-Eyed One) or "Kaḷāradantā" (Black-Toothed One); these are what are called "yakṣa-reviling."
"They shall revile" is the meaning. "Even an empty bowl for him" means it is a metal bowl just like those of the monks;
that [bowl] is turned upside down over his head until it reaches his throat. Then they strike it in the middle with an iron bolt.
"Fierce" means wrathful. "Obstructed" means hostile. "Impetuous" means acting with excessive violence. "They do not even heed the great kings" means...
They do not heed his words; they do not carry out his commands. "Of the great kings' men" refers to the twenty-eight generals of the *yakṣas*.
"Of the men" refers to those among the *yakṣa* generals who are obedient to their will. "Known as 'obstructors'" means enemies and adversaries.
"It should be censured" means that by one who, having recited a protective charm (*paritta*), is unable to make the non-human beings retreat, [the fault] of these *yakṣas* [should be pointed out].
The meaning is that one should cause [the listener] to be made aware of these things.
Regarding the discourse on the preliminary rites for the *paritta*:
standing here, the preliminary rite for the *paritta* should be explained. For first of all, the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta...
One should not speak [of this]. These—namely, the *Mettasutta*, the *Dhajaggasutta*, and the *Ratanasutta*—should be recited for seven days.
If he is released, that is well. If he is not released, the *Āṭānāṭiyasutta* should be recited.
While reciting it, the monk must not eat flour or meat, nor should he dwell in a cemetery. Why? Because of non-human beings (*amanussa*).
They obtain the opportunity. Having had the place for the recitation of the *paritta* smeared with green cow dung, one should sit there after arranging a pure seat.
The monk who performs the *paritta* should be led from the monastery to the house surrounded by shield-bearers and swordsmen.

One should not speak while sitting in the open air; rather, one should speak while sitting with the doors and windows closed, surrounded by those holding weapons, having preceded the act with a mind of loving-kindness (*mettā*).
Having first caused them to take up the training rules (*sikkhāpada*), the protective chant (*paritta*) should be performed for one who is established in virtue (*sīla*).
If even by this means one is unable to release them, they should be brought to the monastery and [placed] on the courtyard of the shrine (*cetiyangaṇa*).
Having had [the image] laid down, having performed the worship of the seat, having lit the lamps, and having swept the courtyard of the shrine, auspicious words should be spoken.
A proclamation for the entire assembly should be made. There is a tree known as the "eldest" in the monastery grove;
there, it should be sent word that the Saṅgha of bhikkhus is awaiting your arrival. At the place where the entire assembly gathers...
It is impossible for one who has not come to be [there]. Therefore, the one possessed by a non-human being should be asked, "What is your name?
Once the name has been stated, he should be addressed by that very name: "O [Name], you have a share in garlands, scents, and so forth;
you have a share in the seat-offering; you have a share in the alms-food; the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus has recited the Mahāmaṅgala Sutta for your benefit as a gift; in the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus..."
He should be released with the words, "Release him out of respect. If he does not release him, one should inform the deities:
"You know; this non-human being does not follow our word, but we shall carry out the Buddha’s command," and a protective recitation (*paritta*) should be performed.
This, first of all, is the preliminary procedure for laypeople. But if a monk has been seized by a non-human being:
Having washed the seats and caused the entire assembly to be summoned, and having given alms-food for perfumes, garlands, and so forth, the *paritta* should be recited.
This is the service for the monks.
Regarding "they should wail": having caused the entire assembly to be summoned, the twenty-eight commanders of the *yakkhas* should be made to wail.
"Viravitabbaṃ" means that one should converse with them by saying things such as, "This yakkha is seizing [me]," and so forth.
In this context, "gaṇhāti" (seizes) means it becomes obsessively attached to the body. "Āvisati" (enters) is a synonym for that same term; alternatively, it means it clings and does not depart.
"Heṭheti" (harms) means it afflicts by increasing the disease that has arisen. "Viheṭheti" is a synonym for that very same thing.
This is a synonym. "He harms" means that by making one's flesh and blood thin, he causes suffering. "He injures" is a synonym for that same thing.
"He does not release" means that, being seized by negligence, he does not wish to let go; thus should they cry out against these [beings]. 283.
Now, in order to show those against whom they should cry out in this way, he says: "Of which yakkhas... and so forth. Therein:
“Indo,” “Soma,” and so forth are their names. Among them, Vessāmitta is a certain *yakkha* who dwells on Mount Vessāmitta.
Yugandhara likewise dwells on Mount Yugandhara. Hiri, Netti, and Mandiya are Hiri, Netti, and Mandiya.
Maṇi, Māṇi, Vara, and Dīgha are Maṇi, Māṇi, Vara, and Dīgha. And Serīsaka.
Together with them was another named Serīsaka. [One should report to those generals of the yakṣas: “‘These yakṣas...
‘This yakṣa harasses, torments, and does not release [this person]; thus it should be reported to these yakṣa generals.
Then the Saṅgha of bhikkhus exercises its own authority of the Dhamma, thinking: ‘We too shall exercise our authority as yakṣa kings.’”
“They will exert themselves. Thus, showing that there will be no opportunity for non-human beings and that there will be a comfortable dwelling for the disciples of the Buddha, he said:
‘This, dear sir, is the Āṭānāṭiya protection,’ and so forth. All of that, as well as what follows, has a plain meaning.”
The commentary on the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya, is completed. 10.
Commentary on the Saṅgīti Sutta.

296. *Evaṃ me sutaṃ* (Thus have I heard) is the Saṅgīti Sutta. Herein, this is the commentary on the words not previously explained: "While wandering on a journey" means while wandering on a regular, fixed tour.

At that time, it is said, the Teacher, having spread the net of his knowledge throughout the ten thousand world-systems and surveying the world, saw the Malla kings residing in the city of Pāvā and [thought]: "These kings are within the net of my omniscient knowledge..."
As he reflected, "What indeed is this that is being announced from within?", he thought: "The kings have had a council hall built;

when I arrive, they will have me recite auspicious verses. After I have spoken the blessing for them and dismissed them, I shall say to Sāriputta, 'Give a discourse on the Dhamma to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Then Sāriputta, having mastered the three Piṭakas, [will speak] with fourteen additional questions..."
Having adorned it with a thousand questions, he will preach the Saṅgītisutta to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus;
and by reflecting upon that discourse, five hundred bhikkhus will simultaneously attain arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
Seeing this purpose, he set out on his wandering journey. Therefore it was said: "Wandering on tour among the Mallas."
297. Commentary on the Ubbhaṭaka and Navasandhāgāra:
"Ubbhaṭaka" is its name; or it is so called because of its height. "Sandhāgāra" refers to a council hall situated in the center of the city.
Regarding the phrase "by a recluse": here, at the very time of acquiring the site for the house, the deity [already]...
They take up their residence. Therefore, instead of saying "by a deva," it is said, "by a recluse, or a brahmin, or by anyone who has become human.
"They approached the Blessed One" means that having heard of the Blessed One's arrival, they thought:
"The Blessed One was not brought here by us going ourselves, nor was he summoned by sending a messenger; rather, he came of his own accord."
Thinking, “The Great Community of Bhikkhus, accompanied by a vast retinue, has arrived at our dwelling place;
we have had a council hall constructed here, and we shall bring the One of Ten Powers there and have him recite auspicious verses,” they approached.
“They approached where the council hall was” means that on that day, it is said, there was fresco work being done in the council hall.
When the builders had finished their work and were merely waiting for the word, the Buddhas, it is said, have a disposition for the forest and delight in the forest;
they might either dwell within the village or not. Therefore, thinking, "We shall attend to the Blessed One only after ascertaining his mind," they approached the Blessed One.
But now, having gained his consent and desiring to attend to him, they went to the assembly hall.
"Sabbasanthariṃ" means so that it was entirely strewn. "They approached the Blessed One" refers here to those Malla kings who,
having repaired the assembly hall and had the city streets swept, raised banners,
and placed full water-jars and plantain trees at the doors of their houses, illuminated the entire city with garlands of lamps and other lights.
Having made it like a scattered constellation of stars, let the milk-drinking infants be given their milk; let the young children be fed very quickly and put to bed;
do not make a loud noise. "Today the Teacher will dwell within the village for one night;
Buddhas, indeed, desire little noise. Having thus caused the drum to be beaten, he himself took up a torch.
Taking [the bowl], they approached the Blessed One.
"Placing the Blessed One at their head" means having placed the Blessed One in front.
There, seated in the midst of both the monks and the lay followers, the Blessed One shone exceedingly; he was pleasing on all sides, golden-hued, and handsome.
It is beautiful to behold. From the front part of the body, a golden-colored ray rises up and occupies a space of eighty cubits.
From the back of the body, from the right hand, and from the left hand, a golden-colored ray rises up and occupies a space of eighty cubits.
Starting from the hairline at the top, from all the curls of the hair, a ray the color of a peacock’s neck rises up.
In the vault of the sky, it occupies a space of eighty cubits. From the soles of his feet below, rays the color of coral arise and occupy a space of eighty cubits within the solid earth.
Thus, for a distance of eighty cubits all around, the six-colored rays of the Buddha shine, quiver, and radiate. All the quarters of space are filled with golden campaka flowers.
They shone forth as if being scattered, as if being sprinkled by streams of molten gold flowing from golden jars, as if enveloped in spread-out golden cloths,

and as if strewn with the pollen of *kiṃsuka* and *kaṇikāra* flowers stirred up by the *verambha* winds. And the Blessed One’s body, radiant with the eighty minor marks, the fathom-wide aura, and the thirty-two excellent major marks, appeared like the risen stars.
It shone as if it were the vault of heaven, like a forest of lotuses in full bloom, or like a hundred-yojana *pāricchattaka* tree in its entirety;
it gleamed as if overwhelming with its own splendor the majesty of thirty-two moons, thirty-two suns, thirty-two universal monarchs (*cakkavattirāja*),
thirty-two divine kings, and thirty-two great Brahmās, all arranged in succession.
All the monks sitting around him were likewise few in desires, contented, secluded, unattached, energetic, eloquent, patient with correction,
reprovers of evil, endowed with virtue, endowed with concentration, and endowed with wisdom, liberation,
and the knowledge and vision of liberation. Surrounded by them, the Blessed One appeared like one encircled by red woolen blankets.
It shone like a mass of gold, like a golden ship situated in the midst of a grove of red lotuses, or like a golden palace surrounded by a coral railing.
The eighty great elders also, having donned that cloud-colored refuse-rag robe, appeared like great elephants clad in jeweled armor.
They surrounded him—those who had cast off passion, shattered the defilements, disentangled their tangles, severed their bonds, and were unattached to either family or faction.

Thus the Blessed One himself, free from passion, was surrounded by those free from passion; free from hatred, by those free from hatred; free from delusion, by those free from delusion; free from craving, by those free from craving;
free from defilement, by those free from defilement; he himself, the Awakened One, was surrounded by those awakened through great learning.
Like filaments surrounded by petals, like the pericarp surrounded by filaments;
like the six-tusked elephant king surrounded by eight thousand elephants, like the swan king Dhatarattha surrounded by ninety thousand swans,
like a universal monarch surrounded by his military divisions, like Sakka, the king of the gods, surrounded by hosts of Maruts, [and] like [Brahmā] surrounded by hosts of Brahmās.
Like the Great Brahmā Hārita, seated in that assembly in the peerless garb of a Buddha and with the immeasurable grace of a Buddha,
he instructed the Mallas of Pāvā for much of the night with a discourse on the Dhamma and then dismissed them. And here,
"discourse on the Dhamma" should be understood as an incidental talk connected with the expression of appreciation for the assembly hall.
At that time, as if causing the celestial Ganges to descend, as if drawing up the essence of the earth,
as if grasping a great rose-apple fruit by its crown and shaking it, and as if pressing a yojana-long mass of honey-juice with the wheel of his chariot and drinking the honey-drink,
the Blessed One delivered a miscellaneous discourse bringing welfare and happiness to the Mallas of Pāvā.
300. "Silent, silent"—in whichever direction he looked, there he saw only silence.
"Having looked around" means having looked here and there with two eyes: the fleshly eye and the divine eye.
For with the fleshly eye he observed their external deportment; therein, not even of a single bhikkhu...
There was no fidgeting with the hands, nor fidgeting with the feet; no one raised their head, no one spoke, and no one sat dozing.
All of them, trained in the three trainings, sat as motionless as the flame of a lamp in a windless place.
Thus, he scrutinized their deportment with his fleshly eye. Then, increasing his vision—
Having seen the heart-form with his divine eye, he looked into the virtue residing within it.
He saw their virtue—leading to Arahantship—as a lamp burning inside a pot among many hundreds of bhikkhus. For those bhikkhus were practitioners of insight;
thus, seeing their virtue, [he thought]: "These bhikkhus are also worthy of me, and I too am worthy of them."
“Appropriate,” he said. Having fixed his attention on the surface of the eyes and looked upon the community of monks, he addressed the Venerable Sāriputta: “My back is aching. Why was it aching?
For during the six years that the Blessed One exerted himself in the Great Struggle, there was great physical suffering for him. Later, in his old age, a wind arose in his back.
"Having spread out his outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*)," it is said, those kings arranged a proper couch on one side of the assembly hall, thinking,

"Perhaps the Teacher might lie down. The Teacher, thinking, "It will be of great fruit for these men that they have made use of this through the four postures," spread out his outer robe there and lay down.
Commentary on the Story of the Split Nigaṇṭhas (301).
Regarding the passage beginning with "Upon his passing away," everything that needs to be said has already been stated above.
(302). He addressed [them]: wishing to teach the well-expounded Dhamma which brings about the pacification of quarrels and the like, he addressed them.
The Explanation of the Single [Dharma] (Ekakavaṇṇanā). 303. "Therein" means in that Dhamma. "Should be chanted together" means it should be chanted by those who are in harmony;

it should be recited with uniform words and non-contradictory expressions. "Should not be disputed" means no dispute should be raised regarding either the meaning or the phrasing. "A single Dhamma" means...
Desiring to demonstrate the flavor of harmony in many ways—by way of single, dual, triple, and so forth—he first said, "One dhamma.

"All beings" means all beings in every state of existence, whether in the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava) and so on, in the fine-material existence (saññābhava) and so on, or in the one-aggregate existence (ekavokārabhava) and so on.
"Sustained by nutriment" means those whose stability is due to nutriment; thus, for all beings...
He demonstrates: "Friends, it is shown that there is one phenomenon called 'stability,' which is a cause and a nutriment, known as it truly is and rightly proclaimed by our Teacher.
Now, if this is so, does it not contradict the statement: "The non-percipient beings are without cause, without nutriment, and without contact," and so forth?
It does not contradict it; for in their case, jhāna serves as the nutriment. Even so, [the definition holds].
“Bhikkhus, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have come to be, or for the assistance of those seeking rebirth.
What are the four? Edible nutriment, whether gross or subtle; second, contact; third, mental volition;
fourth, consciousness. This too is contradictory, yet this too is not contradictory. For in this regard:

In the Sutta, in the non-figurative sense (*nippariyāya*), only those phenomena characterized by nutriment are called "nutriments. Here, however, in the figurative sense (*pariyāya*), a condition is called "nutriment.

For a condition is required for all phenomena; and whatever fruit it produces, it is said to "bring" (*āharati*) that very fruit, and therefore it is called "nutriment" (*āhāra*). It is for this reason that he said: "Bhikkhus, even ignorance, I say, has a nutriment..."
“I say, monks, that ignorance has nutriment; it is not without nutriment. And what, monks, is the nutriment for ignorance?
It should be said: ‘The five hindrances. Monks, I say that the five hindrances have nutriment; they are not without nutriment.
And what, monks, is the nutriment for the five hindrances? It should be said: ‘Inappropriate attention. This is what is intended here.”
For when this nutriment of conditions (*paccayāhāra*) is taken, both the figurative nutriment (*pariyāyāhāra*) and the non-figurative nutriment (*nippariyāyāhāra*) are entirely included.

Among these, the nutriment of conditions is found in the state of non-percipient beings (*asaññabhava*). Indeed, when a Buddha has not yet appeared, those who have gone forth in a heretical order perform preliminary work on the wind-kasiṇa, attain the fourth jhāna, and emerging from that, [think]: "Alas, mind!"...

One should strive for this mind; indeed, the non-existence of the mind itself is good, for it is precisely by depending on the mind that suffering with its conditions—such as killing, imprisonment, and so forth—arises.

Having developed patience and preference through the realization that "when the mind is absent, these do not exist," they pass away without falling away from their meditative absorption (*jhāna*) and are reborn in the non-percipient realm (*asañña-bhava*).
Whatever posture was adopted by each individual while in the human world, [that remains their mode of being].
Having been reborn with that mode of conduct (*īryāpatha*), he remains for five hundred eons either standing, sitting, or lying down.
Even for such beings, nutriment as a condition is obtainable; for whatever jhāna they have developed and by which they were reborn, that very state becomes their condition.
Just as an arrow shot by the force of a bowstring remains [in flight] for as long as the force of the bowstring lasts, so too...
They go; thus they remain as long as the condition for meditative absorption (jhāna) exists.

When that has ceased, they fall like an arrow whose momentum is exhausted. But as for those hell-beings described as neither subsisting on the fruit of emergence nor subsisting on the fruit of merit—what is their nutriment?
For them, karma itself is the nutriment. If it is asked, "Are there five nutriments?"—yes, there are five.
"It is not to be said that there are not five [nutriments]. Has it not been stated that nutriment is a condition?
Therefore, the very same kamma by which they were reborn in hell becomes their nutriment by way of being a condition for their continued existence. It is with reference to this that it was said:
"And one does not die so long as that evil kamma has not been exhausted."
No dispute should be raised here concerning edible food (*kabaḷīkāra-āhāra*). For even the saliva produced in the mouth performs the function of nutriment for them.
Indeed, saliva becomes a condition that is experienced as suffering in hell, and as happiness in heaven.

Thus, in the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*), there are four nutriments in the direct sense. In the fine-material and immaterial existences (*rūpārūpabhava*), with the exception of non-percipient beings (*asañña*), for the rest—

Regarding the three [nutriments]: by means of this nutriment—namely, the nutriment of physical food for those who are non-percipient and for the rest—he answered the second question, "All beings subsist on nutriment," without providing the formal handover with "This, friend," nor repeating the extraction with "There is, friend.
Instead, he answered the second question: "All beings subsist on volitional formations."
But why did he not cause it to be taken out or extracted?
Because even when being taken out or extracted from here and there, it was difficult to master or recite; therefore, he released it by joining two [parts] together as one.
In this release as well, the conditions mentioned below are called "formations" (saṅkhāra) because they construct their own fruit. Thus...
Below, the nutriment condition was explained; here, it is the formations condition—this is the distinction between the two.

"The direct (nippariyāya) nutriment was taken below, whereas here the figurative (pariyāya) nutriment is intended; had this been taken [in the same way], the distinction would have become clear," said the Elder Mahāsīva.
For [the nutriment condition applies] to both that which is bound to the faculties and that which is not bound to the faculties.
It is necessary to obtain conditions; indeed, there is no such thing as a phenomenon (dhamma) without a condition.
In this regard, for grass, trees, creepers, and so forth—which are not bound by sense-faculties—the essence of earth (pathavī-rasa) and the essence of water (āpo-rasa) serve as conditions.
For when it does not rain, the grass and other plants wither, but when it rains, they become green. Thus, the essence of earth and the essence of water are their conditions.
It exists. For that which is bound by the faculties, ignorance, craving, karma, nutriment, and so forth, are the conditions;
thus, what was previously described as "nutriment" in terms of being a condition is here called "volitional formations. This alone is the distinction here.
"This, friends," [the Blessed One said], meaning that our Teacher, having sat at the seat of Great Enlightenment, by means of his own omniscient knowledge—

Having realized it, this one thing has been taught. Regarding that one thing, you all must recite it together and not dispute it, so that this holy life (*brahmacariya*) of yours may endure as you recite it together.
For by one monk [it was said]: "Friends, there is indeed one thing well-expounded."
"What is the one thing? All beings subsist on nutriment; all beings subsist on volitional formations.
When this has been said, another will hear his statement and speak further; and another will hear that person's statement as well.

In this way, through the sequence of successive discourse, this holy life (brahmacariya), enduring for a long time, will be for the welfare and benefit of the world with its devas. Thus, it is by way of the "single" [teaching].
The Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, demonstrated the flavor of concord.
Thus ends the commentary on the single [verse]. Now begins the commentary on the pair [of verses].
304. Having thus shown the essence of harmony by way of single factors, he now began the teaching again to show it by way of dyads.
Therein, regarding the dyad of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*): "name" (*nāma*) refers to the four immaterial aggregates (*arūpakkhandha*) and Nibbāna.

Among these, the four aggregates are "name" in the sense of naming (*nāmana*). "In the sense of naming" means in the sense of making names. For just as [they are so called] because they are agreed upon by the great multitude...

The name of Mahā-Sammata was "Mahā-Sammata" (the Great Elect). Just as parents give their son a name based on his reputation, saying, "Let him be named Tissa," or "Let him be named Phussa," or just as a name arises from one's qualities, such as "Dhamma-preacher" or "Master of the Vinaya," it is not so with feeling and the other aggregates.
For feeling and the others are like the great earth and so forth.
They arise while making their own names for themselves. When they have arisen, their names are already established.

For no one says to the arisen feeling, "You shall be named 'feeling,'" nor does it have any need for its name to be taken by anyone, just as when the earth has arisen, no one says, "You shall be named 'earth.'"

There is no need for the act of assigning a name; when the world-system, Mount Sineru, the moon, the sun, and the constellations arise, there is no need for the act of assigning names such as "you shall be named the world-system" or "you shall be named a constellation"—the name simply arises, and the designation of spontaneous birth (opapātika) falls into place.
In the same way, when feeling arises, [there is no need to think] "you shall be named feeling."
There is no need for the act of naming; as soon as that feeling has arisen, it is already "feeling" by name.
The same principle applies to perception and the other aggregates: in the past, feeling was simply feeling; perception, mental formations, and consciousness were simply consciousness.
So too in the future and in the present. But Nibbāna is always Nibbāna. It is called "name" (nāma) in the sense of naming, and also in the sense of bending (namana).
And herein, the four aggregates are called "name" (nāma), for they bend toward their object. In the sense of bending, all [five] aggregates are "name.
For the four aggregates bend toward one another with respect to the object, and Nibbāna bends the blameless states within itself by way of being the object-predominance condition.

“Form” (*rūpa*) refers to the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements; all of that is “form” in the sense of being subject to transformation (*ruppana*). Its detailed exposition should be understood according to the method set forth in the *Visuddhimagga*. “Ignorance” (*avijjā*) is non-knowing regarding suffering and so forth.

This too has been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*. “Craving for existence” (*bhavataṇhā*) is the longing for existence. As it is said: “In this context, what is craving for existence? It is the desire for existence among states of existence,” and so forth.
"Bhava-diṭṭhi" (the view of existence): "bhava" is said to mean eternalism; it is the view that arises by way of eternalism.
This is elaborated upon in the Abhidhamma in such passages as: "Therein, what is the view of existence? 'The self and the world will exist'—such a view, such a resort to views," and so forth.
"Vibhava-diṭṭhi" (the view of non-existence): "vibhava" is said to mean annihilationism; it is by way of annihilationism...

The view that arises. This too is explained in detail in that very same place by way of such passages as: "Therein, what is the view of non-becoming (*vibhavadiṭṭhi*)? 'Neither self nor world shall come to be. Any such view, any resort to views," and so forth.

Shamelessness (*ahirika*) is the state of being without shame, explained in detail as: "that which does not feel shame where one ought to feel shame. Fearlessness of wrongdoing (*anottappa*) is the mode of being without dread, explained in detail as: "that which does not feel dread where one ought to feel dread."

“Moral shame (hirī) and moral dread (ottappa)” refers to the moral shame and moral dread explained in detail as: “that by which one feels shame at what should be shunned, and that by which one feels dread at what should be dreaded.
Furthermore, herein, moral shame originates from within oneself, while moral dread originates from without.
Moral shame has oneself as its governing influence, whereas moral dread has the world as its governing influence. Moral shame is established in the nature of modesty.
Moral dread (*ottappa*) is established by way of fear. A detailed exposition on this point has been stated in its entirety in the *Visuddhimagga*.

As for "obstinate speech" (*dovacassatā*): because painful speech exists in this person who is a receiver of opposition, one who is contrary, disagreeable, and disrespectful, he is called "difficult to speak to" (*dubbaca*).
His action is "obstinacy in speech" (*dovacassa*), and the state of that is "obstinate speech" (*dovacassatā*). In detail, however, this is [explained] as follows: "Therein..."
What is stubbornness (*dovacassatā*)? It is recorded in the Abhidhamma as: "Stubbornness when one is being spoken to according to the Dhamma.

In terms of its meaning, it is the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*). They say: "This is a designation for the four aggregates when they occur in this manner. As for "evil friendship" (*pāpamittatā*):
those persons who are evil—such as those lacking faith and so forth—are his friends, thus he is an evil friend; of such a person...
The state [of this hindrance] is association with evil friends. In detail, however, it is defined as follows: "In this context, what is association with evil friends?
Those persons who are faithless, immoral, unlearned, stingy, and lacking wisdom.

Whatever association, frequenting, close following, intimacy, thorough intimacy, devotion, thorough devotion, and conformity with them—that is [association with evil friends]. This too, in its essential meaning, should be understood as being like difficult-to-speak-to-ness (*dovacassatā*).

Being easy to correct and having virtuous friends should be understood by way of the opposites of what has been stated. Both of these, moreover, are spoken of here as a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane.

Skill in offenses is the state of skill regarding offenses, as it is said: "The five classes of offenses are offenses; the seven classes of offenses are offenses. Skill in those offenses is wisdom, understanding. This is the nature of skill in offenses.

Skill in emerging from offenses (*āpattivuṭṭhānakusalatā*) is the wisdom described as "the skill in emerging from those offenses, which is understanding and comprehension," namely, the wisdom that knows the limits of emerging from offenses together with the formal ritual procedure (*kammavācā*). Skill in attainments (*samāpattikusalatā*) is the wisdom described as:
"There is an attainment with applied thought and sustained thought; there is an attainment without applied thought and with only sustained thought;
there is an attainment without applied thought and without sustained thought. That which is skill in these attainments is wisdom."
"Understanding"—this refers to the wisdom that knows the delimitation of absorption (appanā) together with its preliminary work (parikamma).
"Skill in emerging from attainment" refers to the wisdom described as "the understanding and knowledge that is skill in emerging from those attainments";

it is the wisdom capable of emerging from attainment according to the very time-limit previously determined, such as the wisdom that delimits the time of emergence by thinking, "I shall emerge when the sun has reached this point."
Skill in the elements (*dhātukusalatā*) is the wisdom that discerns the intrinsic nature of the eighteen elements—the eye element, and so forth, up to the mind-consciousness element—as it is said:
"The skill in those elements is wisdom, understanding. It is the wisdom of hearing, retaining, reflecting upon, and penetrating [the truth] regarding these eighteen elements.
Skill in attention (*manasikārakusalatā*) is the skill in attending to those elements... [and so on].
"Wisdom is understanding"—thus it is said; this refers to the wisdom of comprehension, penetration, and reflection regarding those very same elements (*dhātu*).
"Skillfulness in the sense bases" refers to the learning, attention, and understanding of the twelve sense bases—namely, the eye base... [and so on] ...the mental-object base—as it is said:
"The skillfulness in the sense bases regarding those sense bases is wisdom, understanding. This refers to the understanding through the learning and attention directed toward the twelve sense bases.
Wisdom (*paññā*). Furthermore, skill in the elements (*dhātu-kusalatā*) applies to learning, attention, hearing, comprehension, penetration, and reviewing;

so too do skill in attention (*manasikāra-kusalatā*) and skill in the sense bases (*āyatana-kusalatā*). However, this is the distinction here: learning, comprehension, and reviewing are mundane (*lokiya*);
penetration is supramundane (*lokuttara*); and comprehension and attention are mixed, being both mundane and supramundane. Skill in dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda-kusalatā*)...

“Wisdom regarding ‘with ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise]…pe… there is an arising’” refers to the wisdom that functions by way of learning and so forth concerning the twelve modes of conditions.
Skill in the causal basis (*ṭhānakusalatā*) means: “Whatever states are the cause-condition for the arising of whatever states, those [states]...”

"Place" (*ṭhāna*) is the wisdom and understanding regarding that which has been stated thus: "The eye and visible form are both the place and the cause for the arising of eye-consciousness, having made the eye its basis and visible form its object. Thus, it is the wisdom capable of delimiting the place.
Skill in non-places (*aṭṭhānakusalatā*) is [the knowledge of] those various phenomena which are not the causes or conditions for the arising of those various phenomena.

"Regarding that specific 'impossible case' (*aṭṭhāna*), the wisdom (*paññā*) and understanding (*pajānanā*) spoken of as follows—namely, 'taking the eye as the basis (*vatthu*) and visible form as the object (*ārammaṇa*), ear-consciousness and the rest do not arise;

therefore, for those [consciousnesses], the eye and visible form are neither the locus (*ṭhāna*) nor the cause (*kāraṇa*)'"—such is the wisdom capable of delimiting what is impossible. Furthermore, in this dyad, "to what extent... [the text continues].
"But, Bhante, it is fitting to say that a bhikkhu is skilled in what is possible and what is impossible. "In this case, Ānanda, a bhikkhu understands:
'It is impossible, it is out of the question, that a person endowed with right view should regard any conditioned phenomenon as permanent—such a case does not exist.
And yet, there is the possibility that an ordinary person might regard some conditioned phenomenon [as permanent]."
The meaning should also be understood from this sutta: “...one might approach [it] as permanent.
Regarding honesty (*ajjava*): there are three types of dishonesty (*anajjava*), namely, crookedness like cow’s urine, crookedness like the moon, and crookedness like the tip of a plough.
For a certain monk, in his first stage of life, wanders among the twenty-one improper searches and the six improper resorts; in his middle and final stages of life, [he continues likewise].
One who is modest, scrupulous, and desirous of training—this is called "crookedness like cow's urine.

One who fulfills the fourfold pure virtue (catupārisuddhisīla) in both the first and the last stages of life, being modest, scrupulous, and desirous of training, while being similar to the former in the middle stage—this is called "crookedness like the moon.
One who fulfills the fourfold pure virtue in both the first and the middle stages of life...
One who is modest, conscientious, and desirous of training—remaining the same in the later stage of life as he was in the earlier—is said to have "the crookedness of a plough-tip.
Another, having abandoned all such crookedness, is pleasant, modest, conscientious, and desirous of training throughout all three stages of life.
That which is his state of rectitude is called "straightforwardness" (*ajjava*). It is also stated in the Abhidhamma: "In this regard, what is..."
"Uprightness (*ajjava*): That which is uprightness, straightness, lack of crookedness, and lack of deviousness—this is called uprightness.

Regarding "shamefulness" (*lajjava*): "In this context, what is shamefulness? It is that which feels shame where one ought to feel shame; it is feeling shame at the attainment of evil, unwholesome states.
This is called shamefulness"—thus it refers to the state of being shameful as it has been described.

"Patience" (*khanti*) refers to patience as endurance, which is described thus: "In this context, what is patience? That which is patience, the state of being patient, forbearance, absence of ferocity, absence of irritation, and composure of mind.
"Gentleness" (*soracca*) refers to gentleness as non-transgression, which is described thus: "In this context, what is gentleness?
Non-transgression by body, non-transgression by speech, and non-transgression by both body and speech. This is called..."
Gentleness (*soracca*) is the state of being well-disposed (*suratabhāva*), as it is said: "The entire restraint of virtue (*sīlasaṃvara*) is gentleness.
Regarding amiability (*sākhalya*): "In this context, what is amiability?

That speech which is harsh, rough, bitter to others, offensive to others, bordering on anger, and not conducive to concentration—having abandoned such speech, that speech which is gentle, pleasant to the ear..."
"Speech that is endearing, heart-moving, urbane, pleasing to many people, and agreeable to many people—such speech he utters.
That which therein is softness of speech, kindly speech, and gentleness of speech: this is called *sākhalya* (courtesy).
Thus is described the state of being friendly and gentle. "Hospitality (*paṭisanthāro*)" refers to this worldly coexistence through material gifts and through the Dhamma.
It has two openings; just as those openings are not visible, so too is there a welcoming reception (*paṭisantharaṇa*) by means of both material goods and the Dhamma, like a rug covering a seat.
It is also said in the Abhidhamma: "In this context, what is welcoming reception? Welcoming reception by means of material goods and welcoming reception by means of the Dhamma.
Herein, someone is a welcome host by means of welcoming reception through material goods..."
or by a welcome of the Dhamma. This is called a welcome. Herein, “welcome with material things” means a gathering together through material gifts.
When performing this, it is permissible—even without selecting the foremost among parents, those who serve as monks, royal servants, or thieves—to give [to them].
For if one gives after having touched [the recipient], kings and thieves...
They even do what is harmful and bring about the loss of life; yet, they are delighted when gifts are given without being touched [by greed].
Stories such as those concerning the thieves and the nāgas (*coranāgavatthu*) should be told here; these are detailed in the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya.

Giving recitations with care, providing explanations of the scriptures (*pāḷivaṇṇanā*), and delivering discourses on the Dhamma—this is called gathering through the Dhamma and welcoming with the Dhamma.
Non-cruelty (*avihiṃsā*) refers both to compassion (*karuṇā*) and to the preliminary stage of compassion. For this has been said: "In this context, what is non-cruelty?
That which is compassion toward sentient beings, the state of being compassionate, the state of having become compassionate, and the liberation of mind through compassion—this is called non-cruelty.
Purity (*soceyya*) refers to the state of being pure by way of loving-kindness (*mettā*) and the preliminary stage of loving-kindness. And this has also been said: "In this context..."
What is purity? That which is loving-kindness toward beings, the state of being friendly, the state of having been friendly, and the liberation of mind through loving-kindness—this is called purity.
As for "forgetfulness" (*muṭṭhassacca*): it is the loss of mindfulness; as it is said: "In this context, what is forgetfulness? It is that which is non-mindfulness, lack of recollection..."
“Lack of mindfulness, lack of refuge, lack of support, failure of memory, and forgetfulness—this is called *muṭṭhassacca* (confusion of mindfulness).

Regarding *asampajañña* (lack of clear comprehension): “In this context, what is *asampajañña*? It is that which is ignorance (*aññāṇa*), non-seeing (*adassana*), the shackle of ignorance (*avijjālaṅgī*), delusion (*moha*), and the root of unwholesomeness (*akusalamūla*)”—thus it is precisely ignorance (*avijjā*) that is so described.
Mindfulness (*sati*) is simply mindfulness itself. Clear comprehension (*sampajañña*) is knowledge (*ñāṇa*).

“Not guarding the doors of the sense faculties” refers to the breach of restraint regarding the sense faculties, which is explained in detail by way of the following passage: “In this regard, what is the non-guarding of the doors of the sense faculties?
Here, someone, having seen a form with the eye, grasps at its signs,” and so forth. “Lack of moderation in eating” refers to the lack of moderation in food, which is explained as follows:
“In this regard, what is lack of moderation in eating? Here, someone, without reflecting and without proper attention...”

One consumes food for the sake of pleasure, intoxication, beautification, and adornment. "Lack of contentment therein, lack of moderation, and lack of reflection regarding food"—thus is the state of being immoderate in eating described.
The subsequent pair of two should be understood by way of the opposite of what has been stated. As for the power of reflection:
"In this context, what is the power of reflection? It is that which is wisdom, understanding... thus it is described.

The knowledge of imperturbability is explained in detail as that which does not waver due to lack of reflection. "Power of development" (*bhāvanābala*) is the power arisen in one who is developing [the path].
In terms of meaning, there are seven factors of enlightenment under the heading of the energy factor of enlightenment (*vīriyasambojjhaṅga*). And this has also been said:
"In this context, what is the power of development? That which is the cultivation, development, and frequent practice of wholesome states—this is called..."
The power of development (*bhāvanābala*). "The seven factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) are the power of development.

Regarding the power of mindfulness (*satibala*): it is mindfulness itself by way of its unshakability through forgetfulness. Regarding the power of concentration (*samādhibala*): it is concentration itself by way of its unshakability through restlessness (*uddhacca*).
Tranquility (*samatha*) is concentration; insight (*vipassanā*) is wisdom (*paññā*). It is tranquility itself that, having grasped that mode [of object], again...
The "sign of serenity" (*samathanimitta*) is so called by way of the sign of the serenity that is to be practiced; the same method applies to the "sign of exertion.
Exertion is energy (*vīriya*); non-distraction is one-pointedness (*ekaggatā*).

Furthermore, by means of these—mindfulness (*sati*), clear comprehension (*sampajañña*), the power of reflection (*paṭisaṅkhānabala*), the power of development (*bhāvanābala*), the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration (*samādhibala*), serenity, insight (*vipassanā*), and the sign of serenity—[the path is established].

The six dyads—namely, the sign of exertion, exertion itself, and non-distraction—and subsequently the dyad of the perfection of virtue and view, explain the phenomena (dhammas) that are a mixture of mundane and supramundane.
Regarding "failure in virtue" (*sīlavipatti*): "In this context, what is failure in virtue? It is bodily transgression... [and so on] ...all unvirtuous conduct."

"Failure in virtue" refers to non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), which is the destroyer of virtue as stated thus. "Failure in view" refers to wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*) that destroys right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*), as it is recorded thus:
"In this context, what is failure in view? There is no giving, there is no sacrifice.
"Perfection in virtue" refers to that very same gentleness (*soracca*) previously mentioned, as it is stated thus: "In this context, what is perfection in virtue? It is bodily non-transgression."

It is called "perfection of virtue" (*sīlasampadā*) because of the accomplishment and fulfillment of virtue. And here, the statement "all restraint of virtue is perfection of virtue" is said for the purpose of including the mental [aspects].
As for "perfection of view" (*diṭṭhisampadā*): "In this regard, what is perfection of view?
There is the given, there is the offered... [and so on]... they declare having realized it for themselves"—such is [the perfection of view].
“Wisdom is understanding”—thus it is the knowledge that has become the fulfillment of right view as it appears in the texts.
Regarding “purity of virtue,” this refers to virtue capable of bringing about purification. Furthermore, in the Abhidhamma it is said: “In this context, what is purity of virtue?
It is bodily non-transgression, verbal non-transgression, and both bodily and verbal non-transgression. This is [the definition].
"purity of virtue" is thus analyzed. "Purity of view" refers to a vision capable of bringing about purification.

In the Abhidhamma, however, this is stated as follows: "In this context, what is purity of view? It is the knowledge of the ownership of kamma, the knowledge in conformity with the Truths, the knowledge of one possessing the Path, and the knowledge of one possessing the Fruit. And herein, there are three kinds of misconduct.
Even that which is done by oneself or by another is not called "one’s own" because it destroys one's welfare;
whereas good conduct is called "one’s own" because it generates welfare—knowing thus is what is called the knowledge of the ownership of kamma.

Standing upon that, having accumulated much kamma leading to the round of existence, those who attained Arahantship with ease after ease are beyond counting. This is insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*).
However, because it conforms to the truth of speech and does not contradict the ultimate truth, it is called "knowledge conforming to the truth" (*saccānulomika-ñāṇa*).

Regarding the statement, "Purification of view and the striving of one who has seen according to the view," here "purification of view" refers to knowledge and vision (*ñāṇadassana*), while "the striving of one who has seen according to the view" refers to the energy (*vīriya*) associated with that very [knowledge]. Furthermore, by the first phrase...
The knowledge of the four paths; by the final phrase, the energy associated with that is indicated. In the Abhidhamma, however, this dyad is analyzed as follows:
"Now, purification of view is that wisdom which is understanding, non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, and right view;
and the striving of one who has seen thus is that mental arousal of energy which is right effort. Thus is this dyad explained.

Regarding the phrase, “A sense of urgency (*saṃvega*) toward things that inspire urgency,” here “a sense of urgency” refers to the knowledge that views birth and so forth as fearsome—namely, the fear of birth, the fear of aging, the fear of illness, and the fear of death. A “thing that inspires urgency” refers to birth, aging, illness, and death;
for these four are indeed suffering: birth is suffering, aging is suffering, illness is suffering, and death is suffering. Thus...
They are called "places that cause agitation" because they are the causes for the arising of agitation.
And "appropriate striving for one who is agitated" refers to the striving by means of a skillful method for one in whom agitation has arisen.
This is a designation for the energy described as follows: "Here, a bhikkhu generates desire for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states."
"And non-contentment with wholesome states" means the desire for more in the cultivation of wholesome states by one who is not contented.
Indeed, a person endowed with this, having fulfilled virtue, arouses meditative absorption (*jhāna*).
Having attained absorption, he begins insight (*vipassanā*). One who has begun insight, without grasping at *arahantship*, does not stop midway.
He does not fall away. And regarding "unwaveringness in exertion," this refers to what is stated thus:

"For the development of wholesome states, it is diligent performance, constant performance, steadfast performance, non-slackening conduct, non-abandonment of desire, non-abandonment of the burden, cultivation, development, and frequent practice"—this being by way of devotion to wakefulness after dividing the day and night into six parts.
It is the state of not turning back until one has attained Arahantship while striving in the exertion undertaken.
"Vijjā" (clear knowledge) refers to the three clear knowledges. "Vimutti" (liberation) refers to two kinds of liberation: the liberation of the mind (*adhimutti*) and Nibbāna.
In this context, the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) are called "liberation of the mind" because they are well-liberated from the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and other defilements. Nibbāna...
It should be understood as "liberation" (vimutti) because it is released from all that is conditioned (saṅkhata).

"Knowledge of destruction" (khaye ñāṇa) is knowledge regarding the noble path (ariyamagga) which brings about the destruction of the defilements (kilesa). "Knowledge of non-arising" (anuppāde ñāṇa) is [knowledge] regarding the noble fruit (ariyaphala) which has arisen either at the conclusion of the non-arising—by way of rebirth-linking—of the respective defilements to be abandoned by each path, or at the end of their non-arising.
"Knowledge. For this very reason it was said: "Knowledge of destruction is the knowledge of one possessing the path; knowledge of non-arising is the knowledge of one possessing the fruit.
"These, friends," and so forth, should be applied according to the method already stated for the single [factors].
Thus, by means of thirty-five pairs, the Elder demonstrated the essence of harmony.
The commentary on the dyads is finished. Regarding the commentary on the triads (305):
Having thus demonstrated the essence of harmony by way of dyads, he now began again to demonstrate it by way of triads.
In this context, "one is greedy" is *lobha* (greed). It is both unwholesome and a root, or it is the root of unwholesome states;

thus it is an "unwholesome root" (*akusalamūla*). "One hates" is *dosa* (hatred). "One is deluded" is *moha* (delusion). Their opposites, beginning with non-greed (*alobha*), should be understood accordingly.
They are "bad conduct" because they are badly practiced, or because they are deformed practices; thus they are "misconduct" (*duccarita*). Misconduct by way of the body, or from the body...
