"Misconduct" (*duccarita*) refers to bodily misconduct (*kāyaduccarita*). The same method applies to the remaining [two] as well.

They are called "good conduct" (*sucarita*) because they are well-practiced or beautiful practices. Both of these triads should be explained either by way of their formal designation (*paññatti*) or by way of the courses of action (*kamma-patha*).
First, by way of designation: transgression of the training rule prescribed for the door of the body is bodily misconduct; non-transgression is...
Good bodily conduct. Transgression of a training rule prescribed for the door of speech is bad verbal conduct; non-transgression is good verbal conduct.
Transgression of a training rule prescribed for both doors is bad mental conduct; non-transgression is good mental conduct. This is the discourse on the formulated rules (*paṇṇatti-kathā*).
However, the three volitions beginning with the taking of life occur at both the door of the body and the door of speech.

The volitions that arise when abstaining from bodily misconduct constitute bodily good conduct (*kāyasucarita*). The four volitions associated with abstaining from false speech and so forth constitute verbal misconduct (*vācīduccarita*).
The three mental factors associated with volition—namely, covetousness, ill will, and wrong view—constitute mental misconduct (*manoduccarita*).

Furthermore, for one who abstains from killing living beings and so forth, the three volitions and the three abstinences (*virati*) that arise constitute bodily good conduct. For one who abstains from false speech and so forth, the four [volitions]...

Volition and the abstentions constitute verbal good conduct (*vācīsucarita*). The three factors associated with volition—non-covetousness, non-ill will, and right view—constitute mental good conduct (*manosucarita*).
This is the discourse on the courses of action (*kammapatha*).
Thought associated with sensual desire is sensual thought (*kāma-vitakka*). Thought associated with ill will is ill-will thought (*byāpāda-vitakka*).
Thought associated with cruelty is "cruelty-thought" (*vihiṃsā-vitakka*). Among these, two arise with respect to both sentient beings and formations (*saṅkhāra*).
For sensual-desire thought arises when one thinks of dear and pleasing sentient beings or formations;
ill-will thought arises from the moment one begins to look upon an unpleasant and disagreeable sentient being or formation with anger, until its destruction.
It arises. Cruel thought does not arise with respect to formations (*saṅkhāra*), for there is no such thing as a formation that can be made to suffer.
However, it arises with respect to sentient beings at the time of thinking, "May these beings be slain, cut off, destroyed, or may they cease to exist.
Thought associated with renunciation is renunciation-thought (*nekkhamma-vitakka*). That, prior to the stage of the foul (*asubha*), belongs to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*).

In the meditation on the foul (*asubha-jjhāna*), it belongs to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*). When that meditation is made the basis (*pādaka*) at the time of the arising of the path and its fruition, it is supramundane (*lokuttara*).
Thought associated with non-ill-will (*abyāpāda*) is "thought of non-ill-will. Prior to the development of loving-kindness (*mettā*), it belongs to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*).
In the meditation on loving-kindness, it belongs to the fine-material sphere. When that meditation is made the basis at the time of the arising of the path and its fruition, it is supramundane.
Thought associated with non-cruelty is "thought of non-cruelty. This is of the sense-sphere level (*kāmāvacara*) prior to compassion;

it is of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) during the jhāna of compassion; and it is supramundane (*lokuttara*) at the time of the arising of the path and fruit when that jhāna has been made the basis.
When non-greed is the primary factor, the other two [non-hatred and non-delusion] follow along with it. When loving-kindness (*mettā*) is the primary factor, the others...
Two [other thoughts] follow upon that. When compassion is the head, the other two follow upon it.

Thoughts of sensual desire and so forth should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. For this is merely a difference in teaching; in terms of actual meaning, however, there is no distinction between thoughts of sensual desire (*kāma-vitakka*) and intentions of sensual desire (*kāma-saṅkappa*).
Perception associated with sensual desire is perception of sensual desire. Perception associated with ill will is perception of ill will.

Perception associated with cruelty is perception of cruelty. The manner of their arising should be understood as being like that of sensual thought and the others, for these are indeed associated with them.
Likewise, perception of renunciation and the others are also associated only with thoughts of renunciation and so forth; therefore, they should be understood in exactly the same way.
The state of belonging to the sense-sphere and so forth should be understood.

Regarding the sense-sphere element (*kāmadhātu*) and the others: "Thought (*takka*), applied thought (*vitakka*), and wrong intention (*micchāsaṅkappa*) associated with sensual desire—this is called the sense-sphere element.
All unwholesome states (*akusaladhamma*) are also the sense-sphere element. This is the sense-sphere element. [Furthermore: "Thought and applied thought associated with ill-will..."

“Wrong intention—this is called the element of ill will (*byāpādadhātu*). It is the resentment, the hostility, and the displeasure of the mind toward the ten grounds for resentment. This is the element of ill will.
“Thought, applied thought, and wrong intention associated with cruelty—this is called the element of cruelty (*vihiṃsādhātu*). Here, someone [strikes] with the hand or with a clod of earth...”
"Whether with a staff, or a weapon, or a rope, or by some other means, one harms living beings"—this is the element of cruelty (*vihiṃsā-dhātu*).
In this regard, there are two ways of speaking: the inclusive and the undifferentiated. Therein, when the element of sensual desire (*kāmadhātu*) is grasped, the other two are already grasped;
yet, having extracted them from that, he shows: "This is the element of ill will (*byāpāda-dhātu*)," and "This is the element of cruelty."

This is called the "comprehensive discourse. However, when the Blessed One speaks of the sense-sphere element (*kāmadhātu*), he sets aside the ill-will element (*byāpādadhātu*) in the place of the ill-will element, and the cruelty element (*vihiṃsādhātu*) in the place of the cruelty element, and teaches that what remains is called the sense-sphere element;
this is called the "unmixed discourse."
Regarding the element of renunciation (*nekkhammadhātu*) and the others: “Thought, applied thought, and right intention associated with renunciation—this is called the element of renunciation.
All wholesome states (*kusala-dhamma*) are also the element of renunciation. This is the element of renunciation. “Thought...

[as before] ...associated with non-ill will—this is called the element of non-ill will. That which is loving-kindness toward beings... [as before] ...the liberation of mind through loving-kindness (*mettā-cetovimutti*): this is [the element of non-ill will]. This is [the element of non-ill will].
The element of non-ill will (*abyāpādadhātu*). “Thought associated with non-cruelty… [as above] …this is called the element of non-cruelty (*avihiṃsādhātu*).

That which is compassion toward beings… [as above] …the liberation of mind through compassion (*karuṇācetovimutti*)”—this is the element of non-cruelty. Here too, two expositions should be understood according to the method already stated.

Furthermore, regarding “another three elements”: there are yet another three elements in the sense of emptiness (*suññatā*). Among them: “In this context, what is the element of sensual desire (*kāmadhātu*)?”
The sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*), described in detail as "having the Avīci hell as its lower limit," is called the sense-sphere element (*kāmadhātu*).

The fine-material and immaterial existences (*rūpārūpabhava*), described in detail as "having the Brahma-world as its lower limit" and "having the gods who have reached the base of infinite space as their upper limit," are the other two elements.
For in the context where the term "element" (*dhātu*) occurs, it refers to existence (*bhava*).
They are to be delimited. In the context of "the arrival at existence" (*bhava*), they are to be delimited by way of the element (*dhātu*);

here, however, the delimitation is explained by way of existence. Among the form element and so forth, the form and formless elements are simply the form and formless existences. By the "element of cessation," Nibbāna is meant.

Among the inferior and so forth, the "inferior element" refers to the twelve unwholesome types of consciousness. The remaining phenomena of the three planes are the "middling element. The nine supramundane phenomena are the "exalted element."

“Craving for sense-pleasures” (*kāmataṇhā*) is lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure. Lust for the fine-material and immaterial realms, accompanied by attachment to meditative absorption (*jhāna-nikanti*) and the view of eternalism (*sassatadiṭṭhi*), is craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*) as a longing for becoming.
Lust accompanied by the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*) is craving for non-existence (*vibhavataṇhā*).
Furthermore, with the exception of the latter two types of craving, all remaining craving is called craving for sense-pleasures. As it is said: “In this context, what is craving for existence?”
“Lust accompanied by the view of existence (*bhava-diṭṭhi*), infatuation, infatuation of the mind—this is called craving for existence (*bhava-taṇhā*).

In that regard, what is craving for non-existence (*vibhava-taṇhā*)? Lust accompanied by the view of annihilation (*uccheda-diṭṭhi*), infatuation, infatuation of the mind—this is called craving for non-existence.

All remaining craving is craving for sensual pleasure (*kāma-taṇhā*). Furthermore, among these, craving for sensual pleasure is lust directed toward the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*).
Craving for sense pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*). Craving for existence in the fine-material and immaterial realms is the other two types of craving.
In the Abhidhamma, however, these are explained in detail as: "connected with the sense-sphere element... connected with the immaterial-sphere element. What does this section show?

It shows that all phenomena belonging to the three planes, insofar as they are objects of passion, constitute the bases for craving; thus, all cravings are subsumed under craving for sense pleasures and then extracted from there.
The other two [cravings] show the two types of *taṇhā*. Among *rūpataṇhā* and the rest: desire and lust for the existence of form (*rūpabhava*) is *rūpataṇhā*;
desire and lust for the formless existence (*arūpabhava*) is *arūpataṇhā*; lust accompanied by the annihilationist view (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*) is craving for cessation (*nirodhataṇhā*).
Regarding the triad of fetters (*saṃyojana*): they are called fetters because they fetter and bind one to the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*). When there is a body distinguished by form and so forth...

View (*diṭṭhi*) that exists regarding the body is the "personality view" (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*). Because one who investigates with this is distressed and unable to reach a definitive conclusion, it is called "perplexity" (*vicikicchā*).
Because one clings to rules and observances, it is called "clinging to rules and observances" (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*).
In terms of its actual meaning, however, it is the twenty-based view (*vīsativatthukā diṭṭhi*) as it occurs in the method beginning with, "One regards form as self."
“Personality-belief” (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) is so called. “Doubt” (vicikicchā) is the eightfold indecision that has come down in the manner beginning with “he is doubtful about the Teacher.

“Misapprehension by rules and observances” (sīlabbataparāmāsa) is as follows: “In this case, someone misapprehends purification through virtue, purification through vows, or purification through both virtue and vows;
whatever view there is of such a kind, that is a ‘proclivity of views’,” and so forth.
The adherence to rites and rituals (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*) is, by way of its method, the grasping of a perversion.

Regarding the phrase "the three taints" (*āsavā*): here, they are called taints either in the sense of having been stored up for a long time or in the sense of flowing out (*āsavana*). In this regard, it is said:
"Bhikkhus, no prior limit of ignorance is known; it cannot be discerned that before this ignorance did not exist, and that afterwards it came into being."
“Bhikkhus, no prior limit is discerned for craving for existence and the view of existence; it is not that before this there was no view of existence, and only afterwards did it come to be.
Thus, first of all, the taints (āsava) are to be understood by way of their long-standing persistence.
From the eye, they flow, leak, stream out, and proceed toward forms. From the ear, toward sounds. From the nose, toward odors. From the tongue...

They flow (*savanti*), leak out (*āsavanti*), pour forth, and proceed toward tastes; toward tangible objects through the body; and toward mental phenomena through the mind. Thus, they should be understood as "outflows" (*āsava*) in the sense of flowing out.
In the scriptures, however, in some places two outflows are mentioned: "outflows pertaining to the present life and outflows pertaining to future lives.

In other places, three are mentioned: "Monks, there are these three outflows: the outflow of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*), the outflow of existence (*bhavāsava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avijjāsava*). [This is stated] in the Abhidhamma.
These same four, together with the taint of views, make five. In the *Nibbedhika-pariyāya*: "Bhikkhus, there are taints leading to hell;
there are taints leading to the animal womb; there are taints leading to the realm of hungry ghosts;
there are taints leading to the human world; there are taints leading to the world of the devas"—thus there are five. In the *Chakkanipāta*...
In the *Āhuneyyasutta*, within the exposition on all taints (*sabba-āsava-pariyāya*), it is said: "Monks, there are taints to be abandoned by restraint;
there are taints to be abandoned by avoidance; there are taints to be abandoned by endurance;
there are taints to be abandoned by removal; there are taints to be abandoned by cultivation. Thus, there are six.
These same [defilements], together with those to be abandoned by vision, make seven. However, in this Saṅgīti Sutta, there are three.

Therein, that which is called "lust for sensual pleasures" (*kāmacchanda*) refers to passion (*rāga*) directed toward the five strands of sensual pleasure; this is known as the *āsava* of sensuality (*kāmāsava*).

That which is called "lust for existence" (*bhavacchanda*) refers to passion accompanied by the view of eternalism (*sassatadiṭṭhi*), or the aspiration for existence; this is the *āsava* of existence (*bhavāsava*).

It is called "ignorance" (*avijjā*). Ignorance that has come down in the manner described by the passage beginning with "ignorance regarding suffering" (*dukkhe aññāṇa*) is what is known as the "taint of ignorance" (*avijjāsava*).

The [terms] "sensual existence" (*kāmabhava*) and so forth are stated precisely according to the [realms of] "the sensual element" (*kāmadhātu*) and so on. Regarding the "searches for sensual pleasure" (*kāmesanā*) and so forth: "In this context, what is the search for sensual pleasure? Whatever desire for sensual pleasures and clinging to sensual pleasures there is—this is called..."

“Search for sensual pleasures”: thus it is said; the lust that seeks after sensual pleasures is called the search for sensual pleasures (*kāmesanā*). “In this context, what is the search for existence?

Whatever desire for existence, whatever clinging to existence regarding states of existence—this is called the search for existence (*bhavesanā*)”; thus it is said; the lust that seeks after existence is called the search for existence.
“In this context, what is the search for the holy life? ‘The world is eternal’... [or] ‘it neither exists nor does not exist’... [and so forth].
“The view, the state of views, the perverted grasp, such as ‘the Tathāgata does not exist after death’—this is called the search for the holy life (*brahmacariyesanā*).
Thus, the view that seeks the holy life as it is conventionally recognized by those who hold such views is what is meant by the “search for the holy life.
And this includes not only views rooted in craving for existence (*bhavarāga*), but also those associated with them.
Kamma, too, is indeed a search. For this has been said: "In this context, what is the search for sense-pleasures (*kāmesanā*)?

Lust for sense-pleasures and the unwholesome bodily, verbal, and mental actions associated with it—this is called the search for sense-pleasures. In this context, what is the search for existence (*bhavesanā*)?
Lust for existence and the unwholesome bodily, verbal, and mental actions associated with it—this is called the search for existence."

In this context, what is the search for the holy life (*brahmacariyesanā*)? It is the view of grasping at extremes (*antaggāhikā diṭṭhi*), along with the unwholesome bodily action, verbal action, and mental action associated therewith; this is called the search for the holy life.
Regarding the various modes (*vidhāsu*): [it is used] in such expressions as "In what manner do they say one possesses virtue? In what manner do they say one possesses wisdom? and so forth.
*Vidhā* means shape or configuration (*ākāra-santhāna*). In such passages as “knowledge-basis by way of one kind, knowledge-basis by way of two kinds,” it means a constituent part (*koṭṭhāsa*).
In such passages as “the conceit ‘I am better’ is a *vidhā*,” it refers to pride (*māna*). Here, that [latter sense] is intended.

For pride is called *vidhā* because it discriminates (*vidahana*) by way of being superior and so forth. By the phrase “I am better,” three types of pride are indicated, according to whether one is superior, equal, or inferior.
Thus it has been said. This same method applies to those who are equal and those who are inferior.

For this so-called conceit (*māna*) is ninefold: threefold regarding one who is superior, threefold regarding one who is equal, and threefold regarding one who is inferior. Among these, the conceit "I am superior to one who is superior" arises in kings and in renunciants.
For a king, by virtue of his kingdom or his wealth and vehicles, thinks, "Who is there equal to me? and thus gives rise to this conceit.
Even one who has gone forth may harbor the conceit, "Who is there equal to me? by virtue of his moral discipline (*sīla*), ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), and so forth.

The conceit, "I am equal to those who are superior," also arises in relation to these very things. For instance, a king might harbor such conceit as, "What difference is there between me and other kings in terms of my kingdom or my wealth and vehicles?
Even one who has gone forth may likewise harbor such conceit on account of his moral discipline, ascetic practices, and so forth.
He conceives this conceit: "What difference is there between me and another bhikkhu? The conceit, "I am inferior to one who is superior," also arises among these very people.
For instance, a king whose kingdom or wealth, vehicles, and so forth are not very abundant, conceives this conceit:
"The mere title 'king' belongs to me; what kind of king am I? He thus puffs himself up with pride.
Even though he has gone forth, one who has little gain and honor thinks, "I am a preacher of the Dhamma, learned, and a great elder"—this is mere talk.
He conceives this pride, thinking: "What kind of Dhamma-preacher am I? What kind of learned man? What kind of great elder am I, for whom there is no gain or honor?
The pride "I am superior to my equal" and so forth arise in ministers and others. For instance, a minister or a provincial official [might think thus].
Or he conceives such pride as: "What other royal official is equal to me in terms of enjoyments, vehicles, mounts, and so forth?
or "What distinction is there between me and others? or "I have the mere title of 'minister,' yet I do not even have enough food and clothing;
what kind of minister am I? Thus he harbors these forms of conceit.
“‘I am better than one who is inferior’—such conceit and other defilements arise even in slaves and the like. For a slave might think:
‘Whether by my mother’s side or my father’s, what other slave is there equal to me? Others became slaves because they were unable to support themselves due to their physical frailty;

but I am superior because I have come down through an unbroken lineage,’ or because of his status in that lineage, or because he is a slave of pure descent on both sides, compared to such-and-such a slave.”
He conceives these two types of pride: either thinking, "What difference is there between my name and his? or, "I have entered into servitude by way of my low birth;
however, on account of my mother and father, there is no status of a slave for me—why then am I called a slave?
Just as with a slave, so too do Pukkusas, Caṇḍālas, and others likewise conceive such pride.

And herein, these three types of conceit—namely, "I am superior" in relation to one who is superior, "I am equal" in relation to one who is equal, and "I am inferior" in relation to one who is inferior—are called conceits that accord with reality (*yāthāvamāna*);
they are to be abandoned by the path of Arahantship. The remaining six types of conceit are called conceits that do not accord with reality (*ayāthāvamāna*);
they are to be abandoned by the first path.
"Three periods" means three times. Regarding "the past period," and so forth, there are two methods: the method of the Suttantas and the method of the Abhidhamma.
According to the method of the Suttantas, that which is prior to rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) is called the past period; that which follows death (cuti) is called the future period;
and that which is between death and rebirth-linking is called the present period. According to the method of the Abhidhamma...
The period subsequent to the moment of dissolution (*bhaṅga*) is called the past time (*addhā*). The period prior to arising (*uppāda*) is called the future time.
The three moments [of arising, presence, and dissolution] are called the present time. This distinction of past and so forth belongs to phenomena (*dhamma*), not to time itself.

However, it should be understood that although time does not exist here in an ultimate sense (*paramattha*), it is spoken of by that very conventional designation (*vohāra*) in dependence upon phenomena distinguished as past and so forth.
“Three ends” means three sections. For in such passages as “It rots inside the waistband,” *anta* refers simply to the interior.
In such passages as “This indeed is the end of suffering,” *anta* refers to the further limit. In “This, monks, is the lowest form of livelihood,” *anta* refers to the state of being base.
In such passages as “Personal existence, friend, is the first end,” *anta* refers to a section. Here, it refers to a section.
This is what is intended. "Personal existence" (sakkāya) refers to the five aggregates of clinging. "The origin of personal existence" is the prior craving that produces them.
"The cessation of personal existence" is Nibbāna, which is the non-occurrence of both.
As for the Path, because it is the means for attaining cessation, it should be understood as being included when cessation is grasped.

"Suffering as suffering" (*dukkhadukkhatā*) means the state of suffering that is itself suffering; this is the name for painful feeling (*dukkhavedanā*). "Suffering inherent in formations" (*saṅkhāradukkhatā*) means the state of suffering by virtue of being conditioned (*saṅkhāra*);
this is the name for neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*adukkhamasukhā vedanā*). For that [feeling], because it is conditioned, is oppressed by arising, aging, and dissolution;
therefore, since it lacks the nature of other types of suffering, it is called "suffering inherent in formations. "Suffering due to change" (*vipariṇāmadukkhatā*) refers to change...
“Suffering-ness” (dukkhatā) is a name for pleasant feeling. For when pleasure undergoes change, suffering arises; therefore, pleasure is said to be the suffering of change.

Furthermore, with the exception of painful feeling and pleasant feeling, all phenomena belonging to the three planes should be understood as the suffering of formations (saṅkhāradukkhatā), according to the statement: “All formations are suffering.”
"Fixed in the wrong way" (*micchattaniyata*) means being fixed by having a wrong nature. This is the name for those who possess both fixed wrong view and an immediate (*ānantariya*) kamma.
"Fixed in the right way" (*sammattaniyata*) means being fixed in the right nature; this is the name for the four noble paths.
"Not fixed" (*aniyata*) means not fixed; this is the name for all remaining phenomena.
“Tayo tamā” means that ignorance (*avijjā*) is called “darkness” (*tamo*), according to the statement: “Darkness is delusion, confusion, the flood of ignorance, a great terror.
Here, however, doubt (*vicikicchā*) is expressed by way of its synonym, ignorance. “Ārabbha” means having approached. “Kaṅkhati” means he gives rise to doubt.
“Vicikicchati” means that while investigating, he falls into difficulty; he is unable to reach a definitive conclusion. “Nādhimucchatī” means...
In that regard, he is unable to become infatuated. "He does not find confidence" means he is unable to establish a state of serene trust directed toward that [object].
"Things not to be guarded" means they are not to be protected. He demonstrates that there is no need for individual guarding at each of the three doors;
rather, all are guarded by mindfulness alone. "There is nothing for the Tathāgata" means: "This or that has arisen in me suddenly."
“Bodily misconduct—this I guard and conceal so that others do not know of it.
There is no such bodily misconduct for the Tathāgata to be guarded against. The same method applies to the other [forms of misconduct] as well.
But are the physical conduct and so forth of other arahants whose taints are destroyed impure? They are not impure; yet they are not as pure as those of the Tathāgata.

For one who has heard little and whose taints are destroyed, although he does not commit any offense that is blameworthy by nature in the world, yet because he is unskilled in the formal rules (paṇṇatti),
he commits such offenses through the door of the body as the construction of a large dwelling, the construction of a small hut, building together with others, and sleeping together.
He commits such offenses through the door of speech as acting as a go-between, reciting the Dhamma word-for-word, speaking more than five or six words, and reporting what has actually occurred.
One incurs the offense of accepting money at the mind-door by way of consenting to what has been placed nearby;
for even in one whose taints are destroyed and who resembles the General of the Dhamma, mental misconduct certainly arises at the mind-door through the presence of censure.
This was the case when Sāriputta and Moggallāna were dismissed along with five hundred bhikkhus during the four matters at Cātumā.
When the Sakyans of Cātumā had asked the Blessed One for forgiveness on their behalf, the Elder was questioned by the Blessed One:
“Sāriputta, what was your thought when I dismissed the Saṅgha of bhikkhus? He replied: “I was dismissed by the Teacher because of the incompetence of that assembly.
From this day forward, I shall not exhort others; having formed this resolve, he said: ‘Thus…’”
“Venerable sir, it occurred to me: ‘The Bhagavā has dismissed the Saṅgha of bhikkhus;
now the Bhagavā will dwell at ease, devoted to a pleasant abiding in this very life, and we too shall now dwell at ease, devoted to a pleasant abiding in this very life.
Then the Teacher, bringing a rebuke against that mental misconduct of his, said: “Wait a moment, Sāriputta!”
"Sāriputta, you must not let such a thought arise in you again. Even the mere thought, "I will not advise or instruct another thus," became what is called a mental misconduct for the Elder;
however, the Blessed One does not possess even this much, and this is no wonder. For one who has attained omniscience, there can be no misconduct.
Even while he was established on the Bodhisattva stages and engaged in ascetic exertion for six years, there was no [result].
When his skin clung to his backbone because of his emaciation, a doubt arose among the deities that "the ascetic Gotama has passed away.
[Then they said: "Siddhattha, why do you weary yourself? It is possible both to enjoy wealth and to perform meritorious deeds."
Even when addressed by Māra the Evil One, not even a mere thought occurred to him, "I shall enjoy wealth.
Then Māra followed him for six years during the time of his Bodhisatta practice and for one year during the time of his Buddhahood;
finding no fault whatsoever, he departed after saying this:
“For seven years I followed the Blessed One step by step;
yet I could find no flaw in the mindful Sambuddha.
Moreover, the absence of misconduct in the Blessed One is to be understood by way of the eighteen qualities of a Buddha.
The eighteen qualities of a Buddha are as follows: there is no misconduct of body for the Tathāgata, no misconduct of speech, and no misconduct of mind;
the Buddha’s knowledge regarding the past is unimpeded, his knowledge regarding the future is unimpeded, and his knowledge regarding the present is unimpeded;
all bodily action of the Buddha, the Blessed One, proceeds in accordance with knowledge, and all vocal action [proceeds in accordance with knowledge].
All mental action of the Buddha, the Blessed One, follows after his knowledge;
there is no decline in his zeal, no decline in his energy, no decline in his mindfulness;
there is no frivolity, no clamor, no wavering, no impulsiveness, no unengaged mind, and no unwholesome state of consciousness.
"Kiñcana" means impediments. "Lust is a kiñcana": when lust arises, it binds and fetters beings; therefore, it is called a *kiñcana*.
The same method applies to the other two as well. "Fires" (*aggi*) is so called in the sense of burning. "The fire of lust": when lust arises, it burns and consumes beings;
therefore, it is called a fire. The same method applies to the others as well. In this regard, there is a story concerning a young bhikkhunī at the Cittalapabbata Monastery.
Having gone to the Uposatha hall, she stood looking at the statue of the gatekeeper. Then, lust arose within her. Having meditated upon that very [object], she passed away.
As the bhikkhunīs were departing, they said, "This young woman is standing there; call her!
One of them went and took her by the hand, asking, "Why are you standing here? As soon as she was grasped, she turned over [and died].

It fell down. This, first of all, is the basis for the non-consumption of lust. As for the non-consumption of hatred, the Manopadosika devas (the "mind-corrupted" devas) are to be seen as the example.
As for the non-consumption of delusion, the Khiḍḍāpadosika devas (the "corrupted-by-play" devas) are to be seen. For it is through delusion that they experience a lapse of mindfulness;
therefore, by means of their play, they pass beyond the time for taking food and die.

In the passage beginning with "the fire worthy of offerings" (*āhuneyyaggi*), "offering" (*āhuna*) refers to honor. Those who are worthy of such an offering are "those worthy of offerings" (*āhuneyyā*).
For parents are worthy of honor from their children because of the great assistance they provide. Indeed, children who act wrongly toward them are reborn in the hells and other lower realms.
Therefore, although parents do not themselves burn [in hell], they become the conditions for that burning.
Thus, in the sense of being a place where offerings are burned, they are called the "fire to which offerings are due. This matter should be illustrated by the story of Mittavindaka:
Mittavindaka, having been told by his mother, "Dear son, today observe the Uposatha and listen to the preaching of the Dhamma in the monastery all night;
I will give you a thousand [pieces of money]," accepted the Uposatha out of greed for wealth and went to the monastery.
Perceiving that this place was free from fear from any quarter, he lay down beneath the Dhamma-seat and, having slept through the entire night, went home.
Early in the morning, his mother prepared and offered him rice-gruel; he drank it all while still holding the thousand pieces of gold.
Then the thought occurred to him: "I shall gather wealth. He then desired to set out upon the ocean by ship.
Then his mother said to him, "Dear son, there is forty million pieces of wealth in this family; enough of going," and she tried to stop him.
Disregarding her words, he continued on his way. His mother stood before him;
then, becoming angry and thinking, "She is standing in front of me," he struck her with his foot, and having stepped over her as she fell, he went on.
His mother rose up and said, "My son, you who have committed such an act against a mother like me—do you truly imagine that there will be happiness for you in the place where you are going?
As he boarded the ship and traveled on, on the seventh day the ship came to a halt. Then those men said, "Surely there is a wicked man here; cast lots!"
They said, "As the voting sticks were being distributed, they fell to him alone three times. They gave him a raft and cast him into the ocean.

He went to an island and, while enjoying prosperity together with *vimāna*-petīs, was told by them, "Do not go further and further ahead," even as he beheld prosperity twice and then twice again that amount.
Gradually, he saw a man carrying a razor-wheel. To him, that wheel appeared like a lotus flower.
He said to him, "Sir, give me that lotus you are wearing. "This is not a lotus, master;
it is a razor-wheel," he replied. "You are deceiving me! Have you never seen a lotus before?"
Having said this, he spoke thus: "Having anointed yourself with red sandalwood and wearing your ornaments, you do not wish to give me a lotus flower.
He thought, "This man too, having performed an action similar to what I have done, wishes to experience its fruit.
Then, saying to him, "Come now, you! he threw a discus at his head. Thus it was said:
“From four he attained eight, and from eight, sixteen;
from sixteen, thirty-two—thus the wheel of insatiable desire rolled forward.
For the person overcome by craving, the wheel spins upon his head.”
The term *gahapati*, moreover, refers to the master of the house. He is of great benefit to his wife by providing her with bedding, clothing, ornaments, and so forth.

When she transgresses against him, the woman is reborn in the hells and other realms of suffering; therefore, he too is called the "householder-fire" (*gahapataggi*) in the sense that he burns [her], according to the same principle as before.
In that regard, the story is as follows: During the time of Buddha Kassapa, there was a female lay follower (upāsikā) who was a stream-enterer (sotāpanna). Her wife was unfaithful.
Having seen her with his own eyes, he asked, "Why do you act in this way?
She replied, "If I act in such a manner, let this dog of mine tear her apart and devour her! Having said this, she died and was reborn as a *vemānika* peta in the Kaṇṇamuṇḍaka cremation ground.
Having sacrificed, she was reborn there. By day she experienced prosperity, but by night she experienced suffering.
At that time, the King of Bārāṇasī, while out hunting, entered the forest and eventually arrived at Kaṇṇamuṇḍaka Lake;
he enjoyed prosperity with her. She deceived him, and he experienced suffering during the night. Having realized this, he wondered, "Where indeed does she go?"
Following closely behind and standing not far away, she saw a dog that had emerged from the Kaṇṇamuṇḍaka ditch and was gnawing at him with a "paṭapaṭa" sound;
she cut it in two with her sword. There were two. When she cut again, there were four.
When she cut again, there were eight. When she cut again, there were sixteen. She said, "What are you doing, Master? He replied, "What..."
He said, "It is so. She replied, "Without doing that, spit a lump of phlegm on the ground and crush it with your foot.
He did exactly that. The dogs vanished. On that day, her karma was exhausted.
The king, feeling remorseful, began to depart. She said, "My lord, my karma is exhausted; do not go. But the king went on without even hearing her.

Regarding the phrase "the fire of those worthy of offerings" (*dakkhiṇeyyaggi*): here, "offering" (*dakkhiṇā*) refers to the four requisites, and the "Community of Bhikkhus" is the one worthy of offerings.

This community is of great benefit to householders by enjoining them toward wholesome qualities such as the three refuges, the five precepts, the ten precepts, the service of mother and father, and the service of righteous recluses and brahmins. Householders who have practiced wrongly toward that [community]...

Having reviled and abused [others], they are reborn in the hells and other realms; therefore, that fire is also called "the fire of those worthy of offerings" (*dakkhiṇeyyaggi*) in the sense of burning [them] in the same manner as previously described.
To clarify this point, the story of Revatī from the *Vimānavatthu* should be cited in detail.
Regarding the phrase "the grouping of form is threefold," "threefold" means by way of three divisions. "Grouping" (*saṅgaha*) is according to genus, kind, action, and enumeration.

There are four kinds of grouping (*saṅgaha*). Among these: "Let all the kṣatriyas come" and so forth is a grouping by birth (*jāti-saṅgaha*). "All the Kosalans" and so forth is a grouping by lineage (*sañjāti-saṅgaha*).
"All the elephant-riders" and so forth is a grouping by activity (*kiriyā-saṅgaha*). [Question: To which aggregate-counting does the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*) belong? [Answer:
The eye-base belongs to the counting of the form-aggregate (*rūpakkhandha*). [Objection: If the eye-base [belongs] to the form-aggregate...
"Comprehended" (*saṅgahita*) refers here to "comprehension by enumeration" (*gaṇanasaṅgaha*); that is what is intended in this context.
Therefore, "the threefold comprehension of matter" means the enumeration of matter according to three categories.
Regarding "with visibility," etc.: it is "with visibility" because it occurs together with what is called visual consciousness, which functions with reference to itself.

It is "with demonstration" (*sanidassana*). It is "with resistance" (*sappaṭigha*) because it is capable of striking against the eye; in its actual meaning, this is simply the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*).
That which is called eye-consciousness has no demonstration, thus it is "without demonstration" (*anidassana*). It is "with resistance" because it is capable of striking against the ear and so forth;
in its actual meaning, these are the nine sense-spheres beginning with the eye-sphere (*cakkhāyatana*). As previously described...
It is "non-demonstrable" (*anidassana*) because it has no demonstration. It is "non-reactive" (*appaṭigha*) because it has no resistance.
Excluding that [space] in terms of meaning, the remainder is subtle form (*sukhumarūpa*), consisting of the ten bases.

The three formations (*saṅkhārā*): they are called "formations" because they form (*saṅkharonti*) co-nascent phenomena and future resultant phenomena, making them into a heap. That which forms thoroughly is "volitional formation" (*abhisaṅkhāra*). A meritorious volitional formation is a "meritorious volitional formation" (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*).
“In this context, what is the formation of merit? It is wholesome volition pertaining to the sense sphere and the fine-material sphere, consisting of giving, virtue, and meditation.
This is a designation for the eight types of wholesome great-citta volition of the sense sphere and the five types of wholesome volition of the fine-material sphere mentioned here.
And herein, there are exactly eight volitions consisting of giving and virtue.

They are [of three kinds]. Thirteen are also made of development (*bhāvanāmaya*). For just as one who is reciting a well-mastered text may not know the connection even after going through one or two [sections], but later knows it when reflecting upon it, in the same way, for one performing the preliminary work of the *kasiṇa* while reviewing familiar jhāna, there is development even though it is dissociated from knowledge (*ñāṇavippayutta*).
Therefore it is said: "Thirteen are also made of development."

In that context, regarding the [meritorious formations] consisting in giving and so forth: "The volition, the act of intending, the state of having intended, which arises with reference to giving, having made giving its object—this is called the meritorious formation consisting in giving.

The volition, the act of intending, the state of having intended, which arises with reference to virtue, with reference to development, having made development its object—this is called the meritorious formation consisting in development."
This is the brief explanation. Furthermore,
regarding the four requisites such as robes, the six objects of sense such as visible forms,

or the ten bases of giving such as food and so forth— when one gives each of these, starting from the time of their production in the preliminary stage, through the time of relinquishment, [the merit increases].

The volition that occurs at three times— namely, at the time of giving, at the time of reflecting with a joyful mind afterwards, and at the time of recollecting— is called "consisting of giving" (*dānamaya*).
Furthermore, for one who goes to a monastery thinking, "I shall go forth to fulfill my virtue," for one who is going forth,

for one who reflects, "It is well, it is well, I have gone forth, having brought my aspiration to its fulfillment," and for one who restrains himself according to the *pātimokkha*— [the volition occurring at these times is likewise so called].

The volition that arises when one reflects upon the requisites such as robes, when one restrains the doors of the eye and so forth regarding forms and other objects that have come into range, and when one purifies one’s livelihood, is called "consisting of virtue" (*sīlamaya*).
Furthermore, according to the path of insight (*vipassanā-magga*) described in the *Paṭisambhidā*: "For one who develops the eye as impermanent, suffering, and non-self... [and so on]."
The mind; visible forms; mental phenomena; eye-consciousness... pe ...mind-consciousness; eye-contact... pe ...mind-contact;
feeling born of eye-contact... pe ...feeling born of mind-contact; perception of visible forms;
and for one who develops aging-and-death as impermanent, suffering, and non-self—the volition that arises is called "consisting in development. This is the detailed explanation.
That which is both non-meritorious (*apuñña*) and a volitional formation (*abhisankhāra*) is a non-meritorious volitional formation (*apuññābhisankhāra*).
This is a designation for the volitions associated with the twelve unwholesome types of consciousness. As it has been said: "In this context, what is the non-meritorious volitional formation?

It is unwholesome volition pertaining to the sense-sphere; this is called the non-meritorious volitional formation. "Imperturbable" (*āneñja*) means motionless, peaceful, and consisting of fruition (*vipāka*).

It is called the "imperturbable volitional formation" (*āneñjābhisaṅkhāra*) because it constructs only the formless (*arūpa*). This is a designation for the four types of wholesome volition belonging to the formless realm (*arūpāvacara*).
As it is said: "In this context, what is the imperturbable volitional formation? Wholesome volition belonging to the formless realm—this is called the imperturbable volitional formation."
In the *Puggalattika* (Treatise on Persons), there are seven types of persons. One who trains in the three trainings is a *sekha* (trainee).

One whose taints are destroyed is an *asekha* (non-trainee) because, having completed the training, he will not train further. An ordinary person (*puthujjana*) is neither a trainee nor a non-trainee because he is excluded from the trainings.
In the triad on elders, a householder who is advanced by birth is called an elder by birth. “Bhikkhus, there are these four qualities that make one an elder.

Here, bhikkhus, an elder is virtuous; he is learned; he is an attainer of the four jhānas; and through the destruction of the taints, he has realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom.
[He is] learned, an attainer of the four jhānas, and through the destruction of the taints...
“He dwells having himself, in this very life, realized through direct knowledge and attained the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom.

These, monks, are the four qualities that make one an elder. When these qualities have been thus stated, one who is endowed with one or more of them is called a *dhammatthera* (an elder by way of the Dhamma).
Another monk, however, is known simply as an *aññataratthera* (an elder by name).

Likewise, one who is called "Thera" by name, or whom novices and others address as "Thera, Thera" upon seeing that he has gone forth at an advanced age—this is what is known as a conventional Thera (*sammuti-thera*).
Among the bases for the performance of merit, giving alone is "consisting of giving. And that performance of merit [is the cause] of those various benefits.
“Basis” (*vatthu*) means a basis for the performance of merit (*puññakiriyavatthu*). The same method applies to the other two as well.

In terms of meaning, however, these three bases for the performance of merit should be understood together with the volition consisting in giving and so forth mentioned previously, along with the volitions belonging to the preliminary and subsequent stages.
Furthermore, in each case, for one who performs the action starting from the preliminary stage by means of the body, it constitutes bodily action (*kāyakamma*). For that purpose—
When one utters speech, it is verbal action (*vacīkamma*). When one thinks with the mind without moving the limbs of the body or the members of speech, it is mental action (*manokamma*).

For one giving food and so forth, at the time of giving, there is the basis for performing meritorious deeds consisting of giving (*dānamaya-puññakiriyavatthu*), whether by saying "I give food and so forth" or by reflecting upon the perfection of giving (*dānapāramī*).

For one who gives while standing at the head of their duties, it is that consisting of virtue (*sīlamaya*). The contemplation of things through their destruction and vanishing is [the basis for performing meritorious deeds consisting of meditation].
Having established [the mind], for one who gives, there is the basis of meritorious action consisting in mental development (*bhāvanāmaya*).

There are also seven other bases of meritorious action: the basis of meritorious action accompanied by reverence (*apacitisahagata*), that accompanied by service (*veyyāvaccasahagata*), the presentation of what has been received (*pattānuppadāna*), the rejoicing in what has been received (*pattabbhanumodana*), that consisting in teaching (*desanāmaya*), that consisting in hearing (*savanāmaya*), and the basis of meritorious action consisting in rectitude of view (*diṭṭhijugata*).
In this regard, it should be understood as being accompanied by reverence through such acts as going out to meet an elder,
receiving his bowl and robes, saluting him, and providing him with a path. It is also accomplished by performing duties toward those who are senior,
and by taking the bowl of a monk who has entered a village for alms, and after having him collect alms in the village, bringing them back to him.

Having heard, "Go and bring the monks' alms-bowls," one should understand the *pattāharaṇa* (bringing of bowls) as being accompanied by service (*veyyāvaccasahagata*) through the act of going quickly and bringing the bowls.
The *pattānuppadāna* (offering of bowls) should be understood as the act of offering the four requisites with the thought, "May there be merit for all beings.
The *pattabbhanumodana* (rejoicing in the offering of bowls) is the act of rejoicing in the bowl offered by others, saying, "Excellent! Very well!"
It should be understood as follows: One person teaches while standing on the desire, "May they know me thus as a 'Dhamma-preacher,'" being heavy with gain;
that [teaching] is not of great fruit. Another teaches others without expecting anything for himself regarding the Dhamma he is proficient in;
this is called the basis of meritorious action consisting in teaching. Another, while listening, thinks, "Thus I am 'faithful'..."
If one hears [the Dhamma] thinking, "They will know [it]," that is not of great fruit.

However, when one hears the Dhamma with a mind softened by the radiation of goodwill, thinking, "In this way it will be of great fruit for me," this is the basis of meritorious action consisting in hearing.
But being free from dogmatic views is the defining characteristic of all [merit]. For whatever merit one performs, it becomes of great fruit only through the straightness of one's view.
Thus, the inclusion of these seven bases for meritorious action should be understood as occurring through the first three alone.
For herein, reverence and service are included in that consisting of virtue; the transfer of merit, the rejoicing in merit, and the dedication of merit are included in that consisting of generosity;
teaching and listening are included in that consisting of meditation; and the rectification of views pertains to all three.
"Bases for censure" means grounds for censure. "By what is seen" means that one censures after having seen a transgression either with the fleshly eye or with the divine eye.
"By what is heard" means that one censures after having heard another's voice through either the ordinary ear or the divine ear.
"Or by suspicion" means by suspicion based on what has been seen, or suspicion based on what has been heard, or suspicion based on what has been sensed.
He urges [them]. This is the summary here; the detailed exposition, however, should be understood according to the method stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*.

"Arising in the sense-sphere" (*kāmūpapatti*) means either the pursuit of sensual pleasures or the acquisition of sensual pleasures. "Those with established sensual pleasures" (*paccupaṭṭhitakāmā*) means those whose sensual pleasures are fixed, whose objects are fixed.
"Just as humans" (*seyyathāpi manussā*): for humans [have their desires] toward a fixed object.
They exercise control over them. Wherever their hearts are bound, they will bring a woman even after giving a hundred or a thousand [coins], and enjoy her as their exclusive possession.
Some are called "gods," namely those who dwell in the four divine worlds; they too exercise control over women in fixed locations.
Some are called "those in the states of loss" (*vinipātika*); setting aside those in the hells, this includes the rest, such as fish, turtles, and so forth.
For they exercise control only over those things that have already been determined. A fish [controls] its own mate, and a tortoise its own mate.

"Having fashioned, having fashioned" means: having fashioned their respective forms in whatever way they desire—whether blue, yellow, or otherwise—just like the deities with beautiful bodies in the presence of the Venerable Anuruddha. Thus, they are called "Delighting in Creations" (Nimmānaratī).

Thus, those who find delight (*rati*) in the various things created by themselves are called *Nimmānarati* (Delighters in Creation). "Those whose sensual pleasures are created by others" (*paranimmitakāmā*) means their sensual pleasures are created by others.
For, having known their minds, others create objects of sensual enjoyment according to their desire, and they exercise mastery over them.
How do they know the mind of another? By way of habitual association. Just as one skilled [in a craft...]

Just as a cook, while the king is eating, knows whatever he takes in large quantities is to his liking, and having thus recognized the object that is naturally pleasing to him, creates exactly such a form;
they dwell there under his control and engage in sexual intercourse. However, some elders [hold that it occurs] merely by smiling, merely by looking, or merely by embracing.
And they say that their sensual purpose is accomplished; however, this is rejected in the Commentary with the words, "But this is not so.

For a tangible object does not accomplish a sensual purpose for one who does not touch it with the body. Indeed, for all six [classes of beings] belonging to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), sensual pleasures remain exactly as they are. And this has also been said:
“Regarding these six [devas] of the sense-sphere, who have all their desires fulfilled:
how much is the lifespan reckoned for them all?
“Happy rebirths” means the attainment of happiness. Having produced [happiness] again and again, they dwell in happiness—thus it was said below.
The meaning is that, having produced the bliss of the first jhāna, one experiences the bliss of the subsequent resultant jhānas.
"Saturated with bliss" means moistened by the bliss of the second jhāna. "Completely saturated" means moistened all over. "Filled" means full. "Pervaded" is a synonym for the same.
This too is said with reference specifically to the bliss of the resultant jhāna. It was bliss.
"Ah, what happiness!"—it is said that a great craving for existence arises in them; therefore, from time to time, they utter such an inspired exclamation (*udāna*).
"Only peace" means only the sublime. "Contented" means being satisfied because they do not aspire to any happiness beyond that.
"Experiencing happiness" means they experience the bliss of the third *jhāna*.

“Wisdom of those in training” (sekkhā paññā) refers to the seven types of noble wisdom. The wisdom of an Arahant is “beyond training” (asekkhā). All remaining wisdom is “neither of training nor beyond training” (nevasekkhānāsekkhā).
Regarding the wisdom consisting in reflection (cintāmayā paññā) and the others, the detailed exposition is as follows: “In this context, what is wisdom consisting in reflection?

It is the wisdom that arises from one’s own reflection upon the spheres of work established by application, or the spheres of craft established by application, or the branches of science established by application; or it is the wisdom concerning the ownership of one’s actions (kammassakatā), or that which conforms to the truths.”

Or whether it be that one acquires, without having heard it from another, such a conformable acceptance (*khanti*), view (*diṭṭhi*), preference (*ruci*), liberation (*mutti*), perspective (*pekkhā*), and acceptance through contemplation of the Dhamma (*dhammanijjhānakkhanti*)—namely, that "form is impermanent," and so on, up to "consciousness is impermanent"—this is called wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayā paññā*).
In this regard, what is wisdom born of hearing (*sutamayā paññā*)? It is [the wisdom] regarding the spheres of action prescribed by yoga, and so on.
Having heard from another, one acquires the acceptance that arises from reflecting on the Dhamma; this is called wisdom born of hearing. (In this context, what is wisdom born of cultivation?
All wisdom of one who has attained meditative absorption is wisdom born of cultivation.
“The weapon of learning”: learning itself is the weapon. In terms of its actual content, that is the word of the Buddha contained in the Three Piṭakas. For it is by depending upon that...
Relying on the weapon of wisdom, the bhikkhu, like a brave warrior, crosses over the wilderness of saṃsāra—just as one would cross a great desert—unshaken and without being distressed.
Therefore it was said: “Bhikkhus, an Ariyan disciple armed with learning abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome;
he abandons what is blameworthy and develops what is blameless; he preserves himself in purity.”
“Seclusion as a weapon”: this threefold seclusion—namely, seclusion of body, seclusion of mind, and seclusion from acquisitions—is itself the weapon. Its differentiation is as follows:
seclusion of body belongs to those who dwell in seclusion and delight in renunciation;
seclusion of mind belongs to those whose minds are purified and have attained supreme clarity; and seclusion from acquisitions belongs to persons who are free from acquisitions.
For one who delights in these three kinds of seclusion does not fear anything from any quarter. Therefore, this too is called a "weapon" in the sense of being a refuge.
Only mundane and supramundane wisdom is the weapon; thus it is "the weapon of wisdom.
He who possesses it does not fear anything from any quarter, nor does anyone fear him. Therefore, that too is called a "weapon" precisely in the sense of being a refuge.

The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anaññātaññassāmītindriya*) is the faculty that has arisen in one who is practicing with the thought, "I shall know the Dhamma not yet known or understood.

This is a designation for the knowledge of the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga-ñāṇa*). The faculty of "final knowledge" (*aññindriya*) is the faculty that has become final knowledge, that has become thorough understanding.
This is a designation for the knowledge [of the four paths] starting from the fruit of stream-entry through the six stages.

The faculty of one who has already known (*aññātāvindriya*) is the faculty regarding those states in which the function of knowing has reached its consummation for those who have already known; this is a designation for the knowledge of the fruit of arahantship.
The fleshly eye (*maṃsacakkhu*) is the sensitivity of the eye. The divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*) is knowledge dependent on light.

The wisdom-eye (*paññācakkhu*) is mundane and supramundane wisdom. Regarding the trainings in higher virtue and so forth: it is both "higher virtue" (*adhisīla*) and a "training" (*sikkhā*) because it is to be trained in, thus it is the "training in higher virtue. In the other [cases]...
This same method applies to both as well. In this context, the distinction should be understood as follows: virtue is *adhisīla*, the mind is *adhicitta*, and wisdom is *adhipaññā*.
"Virtue" refers to the five precepts and the ten precepts; the restraint of the *pātimokkha* is called *adhisīla*. The eight attainments [are *adhicitta*].

The mind (*citta*) is the jhāna that serves as the basis for insight (*vipassanā*); thus, it is "higher mind" (*adhicitta*). Knowledge of the ownership of kamma (*kammassakatañāṇa*) is wisdom (*paññā*);

thus, it is "higher wisdom" (*adhipaññā*). Even when there is no appearance of a Buddha, the five precepts and the ten precepts continue to exist; therefore, they are simply "virtue" (*sīla*). However, the virtue of restraint by the Pātimokkha exists only when there is an appearance of a Buddha;
therefore, it is "higher virtue" (*adhisīla*). The same principle applies to the mind and wisdom as well. Furthermore, Nibbāna...

The five precepts or the ten precepts undertaken by one aspiring [for higher states] are indeed *adhisīla* (higher virtue). Even the eight attainments (*samāpatti*) entered into are indeed *adhicitta* (higher consciousness).
Alternatively, all mundane virtue is simply *sīla*, while supramundane virtue is *adhisīla*. The same principle applies to consciousness and wisdom as well.

Among the meditative developments (*bhāvanā*), for one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), the body associated with the five doors is called "development of the body" (*kāyabhāvanā*). The eight attainments are "development of consciousness" (*cittabhāvanā*).

This is what is meant by "name. The wisdom of the fruit of arahantship is called the "development of wisdom. For one whose taints are destroyed, the body associated with the five doors is cultivated in an absolute sense. Moreover, his eight attainments are not weak as they are for others;
it is precisely for him that wisdom is said to be "developed" through the attainment of the fullness of wisdom. Therefore, it was said thus.
Among the unsurpassables, insight is the unsurpassable vision; the path is the unsurpassable practice. The fruit is the unsurpassable liberation.
Alternatively, the fruit is the unsurpassable vision, and the path is the unsurpassable practice. Nibbāna is the unsurpassable liberation.
Alternatively, Nibbāna is the unsurpassable vision, for there is nothing further beyond it that can be seen. The path is the unsurpassable practice.
The fruit is the unsurpassed liberation. "Unsurpassed" (*anuttariya*) means supreme or pre-eminent.

Among the concentrations, the concentration of the first jhāna possesses both applied thought (*savitakka*) and sustained thought (*savicāra*). According to the fivefold method, the concentration of the second jhāna is without applied thought but with sustained thought alone (*avitakkavicāramatta*). The remainder is without both applied and sustained thought (*avitakka-avicāra*).

Regarding emptiness and the other [two doors], there is a threefold exposition: by way of arrival (*āgamana*), by way of qualities (*saguṇa*), and by way of object (*ārammaṇa*). By way of arrival, for instance, a certain bhikkhu...
Having resolved upon it as non-self, having seen it as non-self, he emerges from it as non-self; his insight is then called "emptiness" (*suññatā*). Why?
Because of the absence of the defilements that create the state of non-emptiness.

Through the arrival of insight, path-concentration is called "empty. Through the arrival of the path, fruition-concentration is called "empty. Another [practitioner], having resolved upon it as impermanent...
Having seen [the object] as impermanent, he emerges from it as impermanent. His insight is called "signless" (*animittā*). Why? Because of the absence of the defilements that create signs.
Through the arrival of insight, path-concentration is called "signless. Through the arrival of the path, the fruit is called "signless.
Another person, having focused upon [the object] as suffering, sees it as suffering and emerges from it as suffering; his insight...
It is called "wishless" (*appaṇihita*). Why? Because of the absence of the defilements that produce wishing. Through the arrival of insight, path-concentration is called wishless;
through the arrival of the path, the fruit is called wishless. This is the discourse from the perspective of arrival.

Furthermore, path-concentration is called "empty" (*suññata*) because it is empty of lust and the rest; it is "signless" (*animitta*) because of the absence of the signs of lust and so forth; [and it is wishless] because of the absence of the wishing for lust and so forth.

"Non-existence" and "wishless"—this is the discourse by way of its qualities. Because Nibbāna is empty of lust and so forth, and because of the absence of the longing for the signs of lust and so forth, it is both emptiness, signless, and wishless.
The path-concentration that has that as its object is likewise emptiness, signless, and wishless.
This is the discourse by way of its object.

“Purities” (*soceyyāni*) refers to those states that produce purity and constitute the practice of purity. Their detailed exposition should be understood by way of the three types of good conduct (*sucarita*), as stated in this manner: “In this context, what is bodily purity? It is abstaining from the destruction of life,” and so forth.

“Sagehoods” (*moneyyāni*) refers to those states that produce the state of a sage (*muni*) and constitute the practice of sagehood. Their detailed exposition is as follows: “In this context, what is bodily sagehood?
The abandoning of the threefold misconduct of body is bodily sagehood; the threefold good conduct of body [is also bodily sagehood].”
Bodily integrity (*kāyamoneyya*): knowledge regarding the body as an object is bodily integrity; full understanding of the body is bodily integrity;
the path accompanied by the full understanding of the body is bodily integrity; the abandoning of desire and lust for the body is bodily integrity;

the attainment of the fourth jhāna through the cessation of bodily formations is bodily integrity. In this context, what is verbal integrity (*vacīmoneyya*)? [It is] of the fourfold verbal misconduct...

The abandoning of verbal misconduct is verbal integrity (*vācīmoneyya*); the fourfold good conduct of speech is verbal integrity; knowledge regarding the object of speech is verbal integrity; full understanding of speech is verbal integrity;
the path accompanied by full understanding is verbal integrity; the abandoning of desire and lust for speech is verbal integrity;

and the attainment of the second *jhāna* through the cessation of verbal formations is verbal integrity. In this context, what is mental integrity (*manomoneyya*)? It is the [abandoning] of the threefold mental misconduct...
“Abandoning is mental purity; the threefold good conduct of mind is mental purity; knowledge regarding the object of the mind is mental purity;

full understanding of the mind is mental purity. The path accompanied by full understanding, the abandoning of desire and lust for the mind, and the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling through the cessation of mental formations—this is mental purity.”

"In the Kosala country" means increase; "decrease" means non-increase. The means for each of these is the "method" (*upāya*). Skillfulness regarding them is "expertise" (*kosalla*). The detailed explanation, however, has already been stated in the *Vibhaṅga*.
For it is said there: "In this regard, what is skillfulness in increase?
When one attends to these states, unarisen unwholesome states do not arise, and arisen unwholesome states cease. Or else, for me..."
When attending to the Dhamma, unarisen wholesome states arise, and arisen wholesome states lead to increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment. The wisdom, understanding, and so forth...
right view therein—this is called skill in acquisition (*āyakosalla*). In this regard, what is skill in avoidance (*apāyakosalla*)? When attending to these [unwholesome] states...
"Unarisen wholesome states do not arise, and arisen wholesome states cease.

Or else, when I attend to these states, unarisen unwholesome states arise, and arisen unwholesome states lead to their increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment. This [is the first kind of dissatisfaction].
In this context, wisdom is understanding... [as detailed] ...right view. This is called skill in the non-perishing.

Furthermore, all wisdom regarding the means to that end is "skill in means. This, however, should be understood as knowing the causes for acting immediately upon the occasion, in order to remedy a matter that has arisen urgently or in the face of danger.
It occurs by way of the mode of immersing oneself in conceit. Among those, it functions as the making of pride thus: "I have been free from illness for sixty or seventy years;
I have never before eaten even a fragment of myrobalan.
Yet these others wander about saying, 'Such-and-such a place hurts me, I am taking medicine'; who else is so free from illness as I?"

The intoxication of health (*ārogyamada*). The intoxication of youth (*yobbanamada*) is the pride of remaining in one's youth, thinking: "We shall perform meritorious deeds when we are old; let us wait for now while we are young.
The intoxication of life (*jīvitamada*) is the pride of thinking: "I have lived long, I am living long, I will live long; I have lived happily, I am living happily, I will live happily."

That which has come down from the dominant influence is "dominant" (*ādhipateyya*). Making oneself the dominant or the foremost by thinking, "I am thus limited in virtue, concentration, wisdom, and liberation;
this is not fitting for me," and thereby refraining from evil, is called "dominance over self" (*attādhipateyya*).
Refraining from evil by making the world the dominant influence is called "dominance over the world" (*lokādhipateyya*).
Making the supramundane state (*lokuttaradhamma*) the dominant influence (*adhipati*), its non-performance is called "dominance by the Dhamma" (*dhammādhipateyya*).
"Bases for discussion" (*kathāvatthūni*) means grounds for discussion. "The past time" (*atītaṃ vā addhānaṃ*) means the past phenomenon;
the meaning is "the past aggregate. Furthermore: "Monks, whatever form is past, ceased, and changed, [regarding that] it is said: 'It was.'"
The designation for it is ‘was’; its conventional term is ‘was. It does not have the designation ‘is,’ nor does it have the designation ‘will be.
Herein, the meaning should be illustrated by the *Niruttipatha-sutta* as it has come down:
“Knowledge” (*vijjā*) is so called in the sense of piercing through darkness. It is also knowledge in the sense of making known. For the knowledge of recollecting past lives...
It is called *vijjā* (clear vision) because, as it arises, it pierces the darkness that conceals past lives and makes those past lives known.
It is called *vijjā* because the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth (*cutūpapāta-ñāṇa*) pierces the darkness that conceals death and rebirth-linking (*cuti-patisandhi*) and makes that known.

It is called *vijjā* because the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa*) pierces the darkness that conceals the Four Noble Truths and [makes] the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths known.
It is called *vijjā* because it makes [the truth] known.

Among the dwellings (*vihāra*), the eight attainments (*samāpatti*) are the divine dwelling; the four immeasurables (*appamaññā*) are the Brahma-dwelling; and the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) is the noble dwelling.
The miracles (*pāṭihāriya*) have already been explained in detail in the Kevaṭṭa Sutta.

“In these cases, friends,” and so forth, should be applied according to the method already stated. Thus, by way of sixty sets of three (tīkā), the Elder, while explaining one hundred and eighty questions, demonstrated the essence of harmony.
The commentary on the sets of three is finished.
The commentary on the sets of four.

306. Having thus shown the flavor of concord by way of triads, he now began the teaching again in order to show it by way of tetrads. Therein, the "tetrad of the foundations of mindfulness" has already been explained in detail.
Regarding the "tetrad of right exertion": "He generates desire" means he generates that "desire, longing, the wish to act, which is wholesome and a desire for the Dhamma," as it has been stated.
"He exerts himself" means he makes effort. "He arouses energy" means energy...
It generates. "He exerts the mind" means he supports the mind. This is the summary here;
the detailed exposition, however, is found in the *Sammappadhāna-vibhaṅga*.
Among the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*), concentration that proceeds by depending on desire is "concentration of desire. The formations that constitute the exertion are...

The "exertion-activities" (*padhāna-saṅkhārā*). "Endowed with" means possessed of those qualities. "A basis for success" (*iddhi-pāda*) means a foot that is success itself, or a foot that has become success;
thus, it is called a "basis of success. The same method applies to the remaining [bases] as well. This is the summary here;

the detailed exposition, however, is found in the *Iddhipādavibhaṅga*. Its meaning is elucidated in the *Visuddhimagga*. The discussion on meditation (*jhāna*) is also explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*.

"For the sake of dwelling in happiness in this very life" means for the purpose of dwelling in happiness within this very personal existence (*attabhāva*). Here, the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) and the absorptions produced later on by one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) are spoken of.
"He attends to the perception of light" means that whether by day or by night, he attends to the light of the sun, moon, lamps, gems, and so forth, as "light.
"He resolves upon the perception of day" means that having thus attended to it, he establishes the perception of "daytime."
"As by day, so by night": just as the light was seen by day, in that very same way he brings it to mind at night.
"As by night, so by day": just as the light was seen at night, in exactly that same way he brings it to mind by day.
Thus, "with a mind opened" means with a mind that is not shut off; "uncovered" means not enveloped on all sides.
"Shining with radiance" means possessing light. "For the attainment of knowledge and vision" means for the purpose of attaining knowledge and vision.
What is expressed by this? The light that dispels drowsiness, or the preparatory light, is expressed. What is indicated by this?

It is the divine-eye knowledge (*dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa*) of one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*). Whether that [knowledge] has arisen or not yet arisen, it is simply the attainment of the foundational jhāna.
With this in mind, it is said: "He develops a radiant mind.
"For the sake of mindfulness and clear comprehension" means for the purpose of the mindfulness and clear comprehension consisting of the seven bases.

In such passages as "feelings arise known," the basis is known, the object is known, and both the basis and the object are known by one whose taints are destroyed. This is due to the state of the basis and object being known.
In this way feelings arise, in this way they persist, and in this way they cease. Not only feelings are mentioned here, but also perception and the rest;
and even those not explicitly mentioned, such as volition and so forth, are known to arise, persist, and cease.
Moreover, the arising of feeling is known, its presence is known. From the origination of ignorance...
The arising of feeling is from the arising of craving; the arising of feeling is from the arising of contact.
Even one who sees the characteristic of production sees the arising of the aggregate of feeling. In this way, the arising of feeling is known.
How is the manifestation of feeling known? For one who attends to it as impermanent, its manifestation as exhaustion is known.

It becomes so. When one attends to it as suffering, its appearance as terror becomes known. When one attends to it as non-self, its appearance as emptiness becomes known. Thus the appearance of feeling becomes known; one knows it as exhaustion, as terror, and as emptiness. How does the subsiding of feeling become known? Through the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of feeling... [and so on] ...up to... the cessation of birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. This is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. In this way, the subsiding of feeling becomes known. Thus, through the appearance of feeling, the subsiding of feeling becomes known. Through the subsiding of feeling, the appearance of feeling becomes known. Through the appearance and the subsiding of feeling, both the appearance and the subsiding of feeling become known. One who knows the appearance and the subsiding of feeling is called a "knower of the appearance and the subsiding of feelings. It is for this reason that this was said. Furthermore, how is the appearance of perception known? Through the appearance of form, the appearance of perception is known. Through the subsiding of form, the appearance of perception is known. Through the appearance and the subsiding of form, the appearance and the subsiding of perception are known. How is the subsiding of perception known? Through the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of perception... [and so on] ...up to... the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. In this way, the subsiding of perception is known. Thus, through the appearance of perception, the subsiding of perception is known. Through the subsiding of perception, the appearance of perception is known. Through the appearance and the subsiding of perception, both the appearance and the subsiding of perception are known. One who knows the appearance and the subsiding of perception is called a "knower of the appearance and the subsiding of perceptions. It is for this reason that this was said. Furthermore, how is the appearance of volitional formations known? Through the appearance of ignorance, the appearance of volitional formations is known. Through the subsiding of ignorance, the appearance of volitional formations is known. Through the appearance and the subsiding of ignorance, the appearance and the subsiding of volitional formations are known. How is the subsiding of volitional formations known? Through the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations... [and so on] ...up to... the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. In this way, the subsiding of volitional formations is known. Thus, through the appearance of volitional formations, the subsiding of volitional formations is known. Through the subsiding of volitional formations, the appearance of volitional formations is known. Through the appearance and the subsiding of volitional formations, both the appearance and the subsiding of volitional formations are known. One who knows the appearance and the subsiding of volitional formations is called a "knower of the appearance and the subsiding of volitional formations. It is for this reason that this was said. Furthermore, how is the appearance of consciousness known? Through the appearance of name-and-form, the appearance of consciousness is known. Through the subsiding of name-and-form, the appearance of consciousness is known. Through the appearance and the subsiding of name-and-form, the appearance and the subsiding of consciousness are known. How is the subsiding of consciousness known? Through the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of consciousness... [and so on] ...up to... the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. In this way, the subsiding of consciousness is known. Thus, through the appearance of consciousness, the subsiding of consciousness is known. Through the subsiding of consciousness, the appearance of consciousness is known. Through the appearance and the subsiding of consciousness, both the appearance and the subsiding of consciousness are known. One who knows the appearance and the subsiding of consciousness is called a "knower of the appearance and the subsiding of consciousness. It is for this reason that this was said. Furthermore, how is the appearance of contact known? Through the appearance of the sixfold sense base, the appearance of contact is known. Through the subsiding of the sixfold sense base, the appearance of contact is known. Through the appearance and the subsiding of the sixfold sense base, the appearance and the subsiding of contact are known. How is the subsiding of contact known?
