Through the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of contact... [and so on] ...up to... the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. In this way, the subsiding of contact is known. Thus, through the appearance of contact, the subsiding of contact is known. Through the subsiding of contact, the appearance of contact is known. Through the appearance and the subsiding of contact, both the appearance and the subsiding of contact are known. One who knows the appearance and the subsiding of contact is called a "knower of the appearance and the subsiding of contacts. It is for this reason that this was said. Furthermore, how is the appearance of feeling known? Through the appearance of contact, the appearance of feeling is known. Through the subsiding of contact, the appearance of feeling is known. Through the appearance and the subsiding of contact, the appearance and the subsiding of feeling are known. How is the subsiding of feeling known? Through the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of feeling... [and so on] ...up to... the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. In this way, the subsiding of feeling is known. Thus, through the appearance of feeling, the subsiding of feeling is known. Through the subsiding of feeling, the appearance of feeling is known. Through the appearance and the subsiding of feeling, both the appearance and the subsiding of feeling are known. One who knows the appearance and the subsiding of feeling is called a "knower of the appearance and the subsiding of feelings. It is for this reason that this was said. Furthermore, how is the appearance of craving known? Through the appearance of feeling, the appearance of craving is known. Through the subsiding of feeling, the appearance of craving is known. Through the appearance and the subsiding of feeling, the appearance and the subsiding of craving are known. How is the subsiding of craving known? Through the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of craving... [and so on] ...up to... the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. In this way, the subsiding of craving is known. Thus, through the appearance of craving, the subsiding of craving is known. Through the subsiding of craving, the appearance of craving is known. Through the appearance and the subsiding of craving, both the appearance and the subsiding of craving are known. One who knows the appearance and the subsiding of craving is called a "knower of the appearance and the subsiding of cravings. It is for this reason that this was said. Furthermore, how is the appearance of clinging known? Through the appearance of craving, the appearance of clinging is known. Through the subsiding of craving, the appearance of clinging is known. Through the appearance and the subsiding of craving, the appearance and the subsiding of clinging are known. How is the subsiding of clinging known? Through the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of clinging... [and so on] ...up to... the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. In this way, the subsiding of clinging is known. Thus, through the appearance of clinging, the subsiding of clinging is known. Through the subsiding of clinging, the appearance of clinging is known. Through the appearance and the subsiding of clinging, both the appearance and the subsiding of clinging are known. One who knows the appearance and the subsiding of clinging is called a "knower of the appearance and the subsiding of clingings. It is for this reason that this was said. Furthermore, how is the appearance of existence known? Through the appearance of clinging, the appearance of existence is known. Through the subsiding of clinging, the appearance of existence is known. Through the appearance and the subsiding of clinging, the appearance and the subsiding of existence are known. How is the subsiding of existence known? Through the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of existence... [and so on] ...up to... the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. In this way, the subsiding of existence is known. Thus, through the appearance of existence, the subsiding of existence is known. Through the subsiding of existence, the appearance of existence is known. Through the appearance and the subsiding of existence, both the appearance and the subsiding of existence are known. One who knows the appearance and the subsiding of existence is called a "knower of the appearance and the subsiding of existences. It is for this reason that this was said. Furthermore, how is the appearance of birth known? Through the appearance of existence, the appearance of birth is known. Through the subsiding of existence, the appearance of birth is known. Through the appearance and the subsiding of existence, the appearance and the subsiding of birth are known. How is the subsiding of birth known? Through the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of birth... [and so on] ...up to... the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. In this way, the subsiding of birth is known. Thus, through the appearance of birth, the subsiding of birth is known. Through the subsiding of birth, the appearance of birth is known. Through the appearance and the subsiding of birth, both the appearance and the subsiding of birth are known. One who knows the appearance and the subsiding of birth is called a "knower of the appearance and
In this way, the subsiding of feeling is known. The meaning here should be understood by this same method.

"Thus, form," and so forth, is exactly as previously stated. "This, friend, is the development of concentration" refers to the development of the jhāna-concentration that serves as the foundation for the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsava*).
308. "The immeasurables" (*appamaññā*): they are called "immeasurables" because they pervade everything without exception, without taking any measure. [End of] the word-by-word commentary.

Furthermore, the method for developing these forms of concentration has already been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*. The discussion on the formless attainments (*arūpa*) has likewise been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*.

"Supports" (*apassenāni*) means supports. "Having reflected" (*saṅkhāya*) means having known through wisdom. "He uses" (*paṭisevati*) means that having known through wisdom, he uses only what is fit to be used.
And the detailed explanation of this follows the method beginning with: "He uses his robe after wise reflection," and so forth.
It is to be understood thus: "Having reflected, he endures one thing" means that having known through wisdom, he endures only that which is fit to be endured.
The detailed explanation here should be understood according to the method beginning with, "Through wise reflection, he is patient with cold," and so forth.
"He avoids" means that having known through wisdom, he avoids only that which is fit to be avoided. Its detailed explanation [is as follows]: "Through wise reflection..."
It should be understood according to the method beginning with: "One wisely avoids a fierce elephant.
"He dispels" means that having known it through wisdom, he dispels only that which is to be dispelled; he pushes it away, removes it, and does not allow it to enter within.
Its detailed explanation should be understood according to the method beginning with: "He does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensual desire."
Commentary on the Four Noble Lineages (Ariyavaṃsacatukka): 309. "Noble lineages" (ariyavaṃsa) means the lineages of the noble ones (ariya).

Just as there is a lineage of kshatriyas, a lineage of brahmins, a lineage of vaiśyas, a lineage of śūdras, a lineage of ascetics, a lineage of clans, and a lineage of kings, so too is this eighth one, the noble lineage, a noble tradition.

There is what is called the noble lineage (*ariyapaveṇī*). Furthermore, among these lineages, this noble lineage is declared to be supreme, just as the fragrance of black sandalwood is supreme among fragrances such as root-fragrance. But who are those noble ones (*ariya*) whose lineages these are?
"Noble ones" refers to Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples of the Tathāgata; the lineages of these noble ones are the "noble lineages."
For prior to this, at the conclusion of four incalculable eons plus one hundred thousand eons, four Buddhas appeared: Taṇhaṅkara, Medhaṅkara, Saraṇaṅkara, and Dīpaṅkara.
They were noble ones (ariya), and their lineages are thus called the "Noble Lineages" (ariyavaṃsa). After the final Nibbāna of those Buddhas, once an incalculable eon had passed...
The Buddha named Koṇḍañña appeared... [and so on] ...in this eon, four Buddhas have appeared: Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, Kassapa, and our Blessed One Gotama.
The "lineages of the Noble Ones" (ariyavaṃsa) refers to the lineages of those Noble Ones.
Furthermore, it refers to the lineages of all the Noble Ones—the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples—of the past, future, and present.
These are the noble lineages. Furthermore, they are to be known as the foremost, as the highest. They are to be known as ancient, having been practiced for a long time.
They are to be known as lineages, as traditions. They are old, not newly arisen.
They are unmixed, unadulterated, and not discarded. They have never been mixed even by past Buddhas.
They have not been mixed with [other doctrines] before. "What is the use of these?"—they have not been discarded before. "They are not being mixed" means they are not being discarded even now.
"They will not be mixed" means they will not be discarded even by future Buddhas. They are uncondemned by those in the world who are wise recluses and brahmins;
they are not censured or reviled by wise recluses and brahmins.

"He is content" means he is content by way of contentment with the requisites (*paccaya-santosā*). "With whatever kind of robe" means with any one among those that are coarse, fine, rough, excellent, firm, or worn-out; the meaning is that he is content with whatever he happens to obtain.
For regarding robes, there are three kinds of contentment: contentment with what is obtained, contentment with what is suitable to one's strength, and contentment with what is appropriate.
The same method applies to alms-food and the other requisites as well. Their detailed exposition should be understood according to the method already stated in the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta*.
With reference to these three kinds of contentment, it is said: "He is content; he is content with whatever robe he obtains, and so forth."
And here, the robe must be understood; the field for robes must be understood; the rag-robe must be understood;
contentment with robes must be understood; and the ascetic practices connected with robes must be understood.

Therein, "the robe must be understood" means that the six types of robes beginning with linen and the six corresponding types of robes beginning with *dukūla* cloth must be understood. These are twelve.

Permissible robes (*kappiyacīvara*) are as follows: a robe of *kuśa* grass, a robe of flax, a robe of bark, a blanket of hair, a blanket of animal fur, a felt robe, leather, an owl’s wing, a tree-bark cloth, a vine-cloth, an *eraka*-grass cloth, a plantain-leaf cloth, a bamboo-leaf cloth, and so forth.
However, impermissible robes (*akappiyacīvara*) include these and others. Regarding the "robe-field" (*cīvarakkhetta*): [it refers to] from the Saṅgha, or from a group, or from relatives...

One should understand that there are six sources [of robes] based on their arising—namely, from a friend, from oneself, through wealth, or as a rag from a dust heap—and eight sources based on the eight headings (*mātikā*). As for "rag from a dust heap" (*paṃsukūla*), it refers to:

one from a charnel ground, one from a shop, one from a street, one from a rubbish heap, one from a weaver’s workshop, one from a bathing place, one from a ford, one from what has been left behind and picked up again, one burnt by fire, and one gnawed by cattle.
The twenty-three kinds of refuse rags (*paṃsukūla*) should be understood as follows: one gnawed by termites, one gnawed by rats, one cut at the edge,

one with frayed hems, one brought down from a flagstaff, one from a stupa, one belonging to a monk, one from the sea, one used for royal consecration, one from a traveler’s path, one blown down by the wind, one produced by supernormal power (*iddhimaya*), and one given by a deity.

And here, "midwifery" refers to the removal of the impurities of the womb. "That which has been gone to and returned from" refers to a robe brought back after having been wrapped around a corpse and taken to the cemetery.
"Brought by flag" refers to what is brought after raising a flag. "Stūpa" refers to a robe worshipped at an anthill.
"Ocean-born" refers to what has been cast onto dry land by the waves of the ocean. "Traveler's" refers to [what is obtained] by those going on a journey.
Having been crushed with stones out of fear of thieves, his robe was torn away. "Produced by psychic power" refers to the robe of one who comes as a monk (*ehibhikkhu*). The rest is self-evident.

Regarding contentment with robes: there are twenty forms of contentment with robes—contentment with thoughts, contentment with going [for alms], contentment with seeking, contentment with acquisition, contentment with receiving a moderate amount, contentment with avoiding greediness, and contentment with whatever is obtained.
Contentment according to one’s strength, contentment according to what is suitable, contentment with water, contentment with washing,
contentment with making [the robe], contentment with size, contentment with thread, contentment with sewing, contentment with dyeing, contentment with allowable [robes],
contentment with use, contentment by avoiding hoarding, and contentment by relinquishing.
In this regard, it is permissible for the bhikkhu who is striving for attainment to dwell in a fixed residence for three months and engage in reflection for about one month.
For he makes his robe during the robe-making month after the Pavāraṇā ceremony; a paṃsukūlika, however, makes it in just half a month.
Thus, reflecting for only a month or half a month is "contentment with reflection. And by a bhikkhu who is satisfied with contentment through reflection—
One should become like the Elder Paṃsukūlika who dwelt in the Eastern Khandarājī.
It is said that the Elder came to the Cetiyapabbata monastery thinking, "I shall pay homage to the Cetiya. Having paid homage to the Cetiya, he thought, "My robe is worn out;
I shall obtain one in a place where many people dwell. He then went to the Mahāvihāra.
Having seen the senior elder (saṅghatthera), he asked for a place to stay and resided there. On the following day, taking his robe, he returned and paid homage to the elder.
"What is it, friend? the elder asked. "Venerable sir, I am going to the village gate," he replied. "I too shall go, friend," said the elder.
"Very well, venerable sir," he said, and as they were walking, he stood at the gateway of the Great Bodhi tree and [praised] those possessed of merit.
Thinking, "I shall obtain what is pleasing at the dwelling place," he turned back from that very spot, reflecting, "My thought is not pure.
On the following day, he turned back from near the courtyard of the mango grove; on the next day, from the northern gate of the Great Cetiya;
and likewise turning back each time, on the fourth day he went into the presence of the Elder. The Elder [perceived]: "The thought of this bhikkhu is not pure."
Thinking, "It will be so," he took a robe and entered the village together with him, asking questions along the way.
That night, a certain man, obstructed by the urge to defecate, voided his excrement right onto his own garment and discarded it in a rubbish heap.
When the Elder Paṃsukūlika saw that it was swarming with blue flies, he raised his hands in reverential salutation. The Great Elder—
“Friend, why do you raise your joined palms toward a rubbish heap? “Venerable sir, I am not raising my joined palms toward a rubbish heap;
I am raising them toward my father, the One of Ten Powers.

It was a difficult task performed by me when I took from the cemetery a rag-robe discarded after being used to wrap the body of Puṇṇā the slave-girl, having shaken off the insects as large as a water-jar.”
“Venerable Sir,” he said. The Great Elder thought, “The thought of this wearer of rag-robes is pure.
The Elder Paṃsukūlika, remaining in that very spot, developed insight and attained the three fruits;
taking that cloth, making it into a robe, and putting it on, he went to the Eastern Khandarājī and attained the supreme fruit of Arahantship.
Furthermore, for one going for the sake of robe-cloth, not thinking, "Where shall I get it? but going with the meditation subject as the primary focus, is called "contentment in going.
For one searching, however, not searching with just anyone, but taking a modest and virtuous bhikkhu along to do the searching, is called "contentment in searching.
While searching in this way, seeing the robe-cloth being brought from a distance, [thinking], "This will be pleasing; this..."
"Disagreeable"—not thinking thus, but being content with whatever is obtained among coarse or fine items, is called "contentment with what is acquired.

For one who accepts what has been obtained, being content with just enough for one's own needs—thinking, "This much will be for my double-layered robe; this much for my single-layered robe"—is called "contentment in accepting a moderate amount.
Furthermore, for one seeking a robe, walking from door to door in sequence without thinking, "I shall obtain something agreeable at such-and-such a house," is called "contentment in avoiding greed."

For one who is able to subsist on any kind of coarse or refined food whatsoever, maintaining oneself with exactly what has been obtained is called "contentment with whatever is received" (*yathālābha-santuṭṭhi*).
Knowing one’s own strength and maintaining oneself with whatever one is capable of sustaining oneself with is called "contentment according to one's capacity" (*yathābala-santuṭṭhi*).
Giving what is pleasing to another and maintaining oneself with whatever [is left] is called "contentment with what is suitable" (*yathāsāruppa-santuṭṭhi*).
“Contentment with water” means washing with whatever water is available for washing, without discriminating, “Where is the pleasant water?
Where is the unpleasant? However, it is permissible to avoid waters that are turbid with yellow clay, red ochre, or the juice of rotting leaves.

“Contentment with washing” means washing by squeezing with the hands after rubbing them with the fist or similar implements, rather than scrubbing with sticks and such. Likewise, if it does not become clean in this way, it is permissible to wash it using water that has been heated by adding leaves.
Having washed it in this way, making it without discriminating between "this is thick" and "this is thin," but rather making it with whatever amount is sufficient, is called "contentment in making.
Making it merely to cover the three circles is called "contentment in measure.

Furthermore, without reflecting, "I shall seek out pleasing thread for the purpose of making the robe," but instead taking any kind of thread whatsoever—whether brought from the streets and such, or from a shrine, or even that placed at one's own feet—and making the robe with it, is called "contentment in thread."
However, when sewing the border, it should not be pierced more than seven times at the distance of a single finger-breadth;
for one who does so, there is no breach of the rule even if he has no companion. But when piercing at the distance of three finger-breadths, it must be done seven times;
for one who does so, he must indeed have a companion traveling along the path. If he has none—
There is a breach of his rule of conduct; this is what is called "contentment with sewing.
However, one who dyes robes must not seek out black antelope skins and the like for dyeing. One should dye using whatever is obtained from *soma*, bark, and so forth.
But if these are not available, one may take discarded dye from humans in the forest.
Or, having had it boiled by the bhikkhus, one should dye it using discarded dregs; this is called contentment with dyeing (*rajanasantosa*).

Taking any of the blue, mud-colored, black, or dark-grey [dyes], such that it becomes a visible garment when sitting on the back of an elephant, is called contentment with what is allowable (*kappasantosa*).
Using it merely for the purpose of covering the private parts is called contentment with use (*paribhogasantosa*).
However, having obtained cloth, it is permissible for one who cannot obtain thread, needle, or a maker to set it aside; but for one who can obtain them, it is not permissible.
Even if he has finished [the robe], if he wishes to give it to his pupils or others, and they are not present, it is permissible to set it aside until their arrival.
As soon as they have arrived, it must be given. If he is unable to give it, he must make a formal determination (adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ) over it.
When another robe-cloth is available, it is permissible to determine even a rug as one’s own;

for that which is not determined becomes an accumulation, whereas that which is determined does not. Thus said the Elder Mahāsīva. This is called “contentment consisting in the avoidance of accumulation.

Furthermore, when distributing [robes], one should not give by looking at the face; rather, they should be distributed while abiding in the qualities conducive to harmony (*sāraṇīya-dhamma*). This is called “contentment consisting in distribution.”
The ascetic practices connected with robes are the refuse-rag-wearer’s practice and the three-robe-wearer’s practice.
A detailed explanation of these should be understood from the *Visuddhimagga*.

Thus, fulfilling the Great Noble Lineage of Contentment with Robes, a bhikkhu maintains these two ascetic practices. By maintaining them, he is content through the Great Noble Lineage of Contentment with Robes.
"One who speaks in praise" means: one person is contented but does not speak in praise of contentment;
another is not contented but speaks in praise of contentment; another is neither contented nor speaks in praise of contentment;
and another is both contented and speaks in praise of contentment. To demonstrate this, [the text says]: "In regard to contentment with whatever robe..."
And it is said: "one who speaks in praise [of such things].
"Improper search" (*anesana*) refers to various kinds of improper search, such as engaging in the practice of acting as a messenger or carrying messages. "Unsuitable" (*appatirūpa*) means improper.
"Without having obtained" (*aladdhā ca*) means not having acquired [the robe]; for example, as someone thinks: "How indeed shall I obtain a robe?"
Being together with meritorious bhikkhus, he acts with hypocrisy and is afraid and apprehensive;
but a contented bhikkhu, not having obtained a robe, is not thus apprehensive. "Having obtained" means having acquired it through lawful and righteous means.
"Unattached" means free from greed and longing. "Uninfatuated" means not having fallen into a swoon of excessive craving.
"Uninfatuated" means not overwhelmed or enveloped by craving. "Seeing the danger" means perceiving the peril in improper search and in the enjoyment of what has been acquired through greed.
"Possessing the wisdom of escape" means understanding precisely that escape which has been described as: "only for the warding off of cold."
"Contentment with whatever robe" means contentment with any kind of robe whatsoever. "Does not exalt himself" means he does not engage in self-exaltation by thinking, "I am a wearer of rag-robes;
I took up the practice of wearing rag-robes at the very moment of my full ordination; who is there equal to me?
"Does not disparage others" means [he does not think], "But these other monks are not wearers of rag-robes."
Or, one does not disparage another by saying, "They do not possess even the mere practice of wearing rag-robes.
For "one who is skillful" (*dakko*) therein means one who is clever, proficient, and competent in that contentment with robes, or in praising them, and so forth.

"Diligent" (*analaso*) means free from laziness through constant application. "Clearly comprehending and mindful" (*sampajāno paṭissato*) means [endowed] with both clear comprehension-wisdom and mindfulness.
And he is devoted. "Established in the noble lineages" means firmly grounded in the noble lineages.
"With whatever almsfood" means with any kind of almsfood whatsoever. Here too, the almsfood must be understood; the field for almsfood must be understood;
contentment with almsfood must be understood; and the ascetic practice connected with almsfood must be understood.

Therein, "almsfood" (*piṇḍapāta*) refers to the sixteen types of almsfood: boiled rice, sour gruel, flour, fish, meat, milk, curd, ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, molasses, rice-gruel, solid food, and soft food.
"The field for almsfood" (*piṇḍapātakkhetta*) refers to: meals provided for the Saṅgha, designated meals, invitations, tickets for meals, and fortnightly meals.

The fifteen fields for alms-food are: that on the Uposatha day, that on the first of the month (Pāṭipada), food for newcomers, food for those departing, food for the sick, food for those attending the sick, food for those on duty, food for those in charge of a hut, food by rotation, and food for the monastery.
Contentment with alms-food consists of contentment with thoughts regarding alms-food, contentment with the journey, contentment with the search, and contentment with what is obtained.
There are fifteen kinds of contentment: contentment with receiving, contentment with receiving a moderate amount, contentment with avoiding greediness, contentment with whatever is obtained,
contentment according to one's strength, contentment according to what is suitable, contentment with what is beneficial, contentment with limits, contentment with consumption,
contentment with avoiding hoarding, and contentment with relinquishing.

In that regard, a monk who gathers alms may reflect after washing his face. However, one who wanders with a group of alms-collectors should, at the time of evening attendance upon the elders, think only this much:
"Where shall we go for alms tomorrow? To such-and-such a village, venerable sirs.
After that, he must not reflect further. One who wanders alone, having stood in the reflection-hall, [should likewise reflect only thus].
One should reflect [on this]. Beyond that, if one continues to reflect, one has fallen away from and is excluded from the Noble Lineage (*ariyavaṃsa*).

This is called "contentment with reflection. When entering for alms, one should not go thinking, "Where will I get [something]? but should go with the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) as the primary focus. This is called "contentment with going.
When seeking [food], one should not take just anything, but should seek only from those who are modest and virtuous. This is called "contentment with seeking."
Seeing something being brought from afar, one should not give rise to the thought, "This is pleasing; this is unpleasing. This is called contentment with what is obtained (*paṭilābha-santosa*).

Without thinking, "I will take this pleasing thing, I will not take that unpleasing thing," one should simply take whatever is sufficient for maintenance; this is called contentment in receiving (*paṭiggahaṇa-santosa*).
In this regard, however, if the gift to be given is abundant but the donor wishes to give little, one should take only a little. [If] the gift to be given...
If there is much [to give] and the donor wishes to give much, one should accept only a moderate amount.

If the object to be given is not much and the donor wishes to give little, one should accept little. If the object to be given is not much but the donor wishes to give much, one should accept only a moderate amount.
For one who does not know moderation in receiving defiles the confidence of people.

If one squanders what has been given in faith, does not carry out the Teaching, and is unable to win the heart even of one’s own mother who bore him, then one must accept only after knowing the proper measure.
This is called "contentment in accepting with a sense of measure.

One should not go only to families that have faith, but should go in regular order from door to door. This is called "contentment in avoiding greediness. Contentment with whatever is obtained and the other types are exactly as explained regarding robes.
Having consumed the almsfood with the thought, "I shall maintain the duty of a recluse," and thus consuming it while recognizing its benefit, is called contentment with benefit (*upakārasantosa*).

One should not accept what has been brought in a bowl that is already full; if there is one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*), one should have them take it; if there is none, one should have it removed and then accept only the bare amount required.
This is called contentment with measure (*parimāṇasantosa*). Consuming it with the thought, "The dispelling of hunger is the escape here," is called contentment with use (*paribhogasantosa*).
"Not to consume [food] after having stored it away" is called contentment in avoiding storage.
"Without looking at the mouth, one who stands firm in the qualities conducive to harmony (*sāraṇīya-dhamma*) should offer [the food]"—this is called contentment in offering.

Furthermore, there are five ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) connected with alms-food: the practice of eating only alms-food (*piṇḍapātika-aṅga*), the practice of wandering for alms in regular order (*sapadānacārika-aṅga*), and so forth.

The practice of eating at a single sitting (*ekāsanika-aṅga*), the practice of eating only from the alms-bowl (*pattapiṇḍika-aṅga*), and the practice of refusing food offered after the meal has begun (*khalupacchābhattika-aṅga*). A detailed exposition of these is given in the *Visuddhimagga*.
Thus, a monk who fulfills this Great Noble Lineage of Contentment with Alms-food guards these five ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*).
By guarding these, he is satisfied by the Great Noble Lineage of Contentment with Alms-food. [The passage continues with] "one who speaks in praise," and so forth.
These should be understood in the manner already stated.
Regarding "lodging" (senāsana): here, the lodging itself must be known; the lodging site must be known; contentment with the lodging must be known;
and the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) connected with the lodging must be known. In this context, "lodging" refers to a bed (mañca).

A seat, a mattress, a bolster, a vihāra, an *addhayoga*, a palace, a gabled house, a cave, a rock shelter, a watchtower, a stilt house, a bamboo thicket, the foot of a tree, or wherever else monks go for retreat—these are the fifteen types of lodgings.
Regarding the "field of lodgings," there are six fields: from the Saṅgha, from a group, from relatives, from friends, by means of one’s own wealth, or as a rag-robe.

Contentment with lodgings (*senāsanasantosa*) refers to the fifteen kinds of contentment beginning with contentment with thoughts regarding lodgings. These should be understood in the same manner as those explained in the section on almsfood (*piṇḍapāta*).
Furthermore, there are five ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) connected with lodgings:

the practice of living in the forest (*āraññikaṅga*), the practice of living at the foot of a tree (*rukkhamūlikaṅga*), the practice of living in the open air (*abbhokāsikaṅga*), the practice of living in a charnel ground (*sosānikaṅga*), and the practice of using whatever seat is available (*yathāsantatikaṅga*). An extensive commentary on these is found in the *Visuddhimagga*.
Thus it has been said. In this way, a bhikkhu fulfilling the Great Noble Lineage of Contentment with Lodgings guards these five ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*).
By guarding them, he becomes content through the Great Noble Lineage of Contentment with Lodgings.

As for the requisite of medicine, it is included within almsfood itself; therein, one should be satisfied simply by whatever is obtained, by whatever strength one has, and by whatever is appropriate. The practice of sitting (*nesajjikaṅga*) partakes of the Noble Lineage of Delight in Meditation. And this has also been said:
“Five are spoken of in relation to lodgings, five are dependent on food;
one is associated with energy, and two are dependent on robes.
Thus did the Venerable Sāriputta Thera, the General of the Dhamma, as if spreading out the earth, [fill] the belly of the ocean.
Having first explained the noble lineage of contentment with robes as if filling the sky and expanding it,
and having explained the second noble lineage of contentment with almsfood as if raising up the moon and leaping over the sun,
and having now explained the third noble lineage of contentment with lodgings as if lifting up Mount Sineru— now...
To explain the fourth Noble Lineage, which is adorned with a thousand methods and delights in cultivation, [the Buddha] again began the teaching:
"Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu delights in abandoning.
In this context, *āramaṇa* means "delight"; the sense is "rejoicing. One who has delight (*ārāma*) in the fivefold abandoning is "one who delights in abandoning" (*pahānārāmo*).
"He delights in abandoning sensual desire; he delights in developing renunciation; he delights in abandoning ill will...
[and so on] ...he delights in abandoning all defilements; he delights in developing the path to Arahantship"—thus, because he delights in abandoning, he is "one who delights in abandoning.

By the same method as stated above, one for whom the forest retreat is a delight through development is "one who delights in development" (*bhāvanārāma*); one who delights in development is "one who delights in development" (*bhāvanārata*).

Now, among these four noble lineages (*ariyavaṃsa*), by means of the first three, the entire Vinaya Piṭaka is explained through the thirteen ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) and contentment with the four requisites.
By means of delight in meditation (*bhāvanārāma*), the remaining two Piṭakas are explained.
Furthermore, when a bhikkhu speaks of this noble lineage of delight in meditation, he should do so according to the *Nekkhamma-pāḷi* in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*.

It should be explained. It should be explained according to the method of the *Dasuttara-sutta* in the *Dīgha Nikāya*. It should be explained according to the method of the *Satipaṭṭhāna-sutta* in the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
It should be explained according to the method of the *Niddesa* in the *Abhidhamma*.
Therein, in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, under the section on renunciation (*nekkhamma-pāḷi*), it says: "One who cultivates renunciation finds delight in it; [one abandons] sensual desire..."
While abandoning, he delights: non-ill will abandons ill will; perception of light abandons sloth and torpor;
non-distraction abandons restlessness; discernment of phenomena abandons doubt; knowledge abandons ignorance; gladness abandons discontent;
the first jhāna abandons the five hindrances; the second jhāna abandons applied and sustained thought; the third jhāna abandons rapture; the fourth jhāna [abandons]...

Regarding pleasure and pain: he delights in cultivating the attainment of the base of infinite space; he delights in abandoning perception of form, perception of resistance, and perception of diversity. He delights in cultivating the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness... [and so on] ...he delights in cultivating the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
he delights in abandoning the perception of the base of nothingness.
One delights in developing the contemplation of impermanence; one delights in abandoning the perception of permanence.

One [delights in] the contemplation of suffering [abandoning] the perception of pleasure. The contemplation of non-self [abandoning] the perception of self. The contemplation of disenchantment [abandoning] delight.

The contemplation of dispassion [abandoning] lust. The contemplation of cessation [abandoning] origination. The contemplation of relinquishment [abandoning] grasping. The contemplation of destruction...
The perception of compactness; the contemplation of vanishing, the accumulation [of kamma]; the contemplation of change, the perception of permanence;

the contemplation of the signless, the sign; the contemplation of the desireless, desire; the contemplation of emptiness, misapprehension; the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena, the misapprehension of grasping at a core;
the knowledge and vision of things as they really are, the misapprehension of delusion; the contemplation of danger.
The adherence to the storehouse-consciousness; the contemplation of reflection and the lack of reflection; the contemplation of turning away and the adherence to fetters.
The path of stream-entry [abandons] the defilements associated with views; the path of once-returning [abandons] the gross defilements; the path of non-returning [abandons] the subtle defilements.
One delights in cultivating the path of arahantship; one delights in abandoning all defilements.
Thus it should be explained in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* according to the *Nekkhamma-pāḷi*.
According to the method of the *Dasuttara-sutta* in the *Dīghanikāya*: "One delights in cultivating one quality; one delights in abandoning one quality...
[and so on] ...one delights in cultivating ten qualities; one delights in abandoning ten qualities. Which [qualities]?
By cultivating what one thing does one find delight? By cultivating mindfulness directed to the body accompanied by pleasure, one finds delight in this one thing.
By abandoning what one thing does one find delight? By abandoning the conceit "I am," one finds delight in this one thing. Which two things...
[and so on] ...which ten things does one find delight in by cultivating them? The ten bases of totality (*kasiṇāyatana*).
He delights in cultivating these ten qualities. Which ten qualities does he delight in abandoning? The ten forms of wrongness.
He delights in abandoning these ten qualities. "In this way, monks, a monk delights in cultivation"—thus it should be explained according to the method of the *Dasuttara-sutta* in the *Dīgha Nikāya*.
"According to the method of the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta in the Majjhima Nikāya:

'Bhikkhus, there is one path leading to the purification of beings, for the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation, for the disappearance of pain and grief, for the attainment of the true way, and for the realization of Nibbāna—namely, the four foundations of mindfulness. What are the four?'"
Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body... contemplating feelings in feelings...
contemplating the mind in the mind... contemplating phenomena in phenomena;

or else mindfulness that ‘there are phenomena’ is established in him just to the extent required for bare knowledge and for mindfulness, and he dwells independent, not clinging to anything in the world.
He clings. In this way too, monks, a bhikkhu delights in development and rejoices in development; he delights in abandoning and rejoices in abandoning.
Furthermore, monks, when walking, a bhikkhu understands: "I am walking"... [and so on]...
Furthermore, monks, it is as if a bhikkhu were to see a body discarded in a charnel ground... [and so on].
"Putrid, having become a mass of powder. He compares this very body to that: 'This body, too, is of such a nature, of such a character, and not exempt from this fate.
Thus, he dwells contemplating the body in the body internally... In this way, monks, a monk is one who delights in development (bhāvanārāma).
This is how it should be explained according to the method of the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta in the Majjhima Nikāya."
"In the Abhidhamma, by way of exposition": seeing all conditioned things as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a tumor...
[and so on] ...as phenomena subject to defilement, he delights. "This monk, bhikkhus, is one who delights in development"—thus it should be spoken by way of exposition.

"He does not exalt himself" means that while he is practicing the work of insight—contemplating "impermanence, suffering, and non-self"—for sixty or seventy years today, he does not exalt himself by thinking, "Who is there who is my equal?

"He does not disparage others" means that [others] do not possess even a mere measure of insight into impermanence and suffering; [he thinks], "What are these people, who have abandoned their meditation subjects?"
"Practicing"—thus one does not engage in disparaging others. The rest is exactly as previously stated. 310.
"Exertions" (padhānāni) refers to supreme energies. The "exertion of restraint" (saṃvara-padhāna) is the energy that arises in one who restrains the eye and the other sense faculties.

The "exertion of abandoning" (pahāna-padhāna) is the energy that arises in one who abandons sensual thoughts and so forth. The "exertion of development" (bhāvanā-padhāna) refers to the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga).
The "striving for development" is the energy that arises in one who is developing [the jhānas]. The "striving for protection" is the energy that arises in one who protects the sign of concentration.
Regarding the phrases beginning with "dependent on seclusion": seclusion (*viveka*), dispassion (*virāga*), and cessation (*nirodha*) are all names for Nibbāna.

For Nibbāna is "seclusion" because it is secluded from the substrata of existence (*upadhi*). It is "dispassion" because by resorting to it, lust and the other defilements fade away. It is "cessation" because they cease there.
Therefore, in such passages as "dependent on seclusion," the meaning is that it is "dependent on Nibbāna" either by way of its object or by way of what is to be attained.
Regarding the phrase "tending toward relinquishment" (*vossaggapariṇāmī*): here there are two kinds of relinquishment—relinquishment as giving up and relinquishment as leaping forward.
Among these, insight relinquishes both defilements and the aggregates by way of their partial eradication; thus, it is "relinquishment as giving up."
The path "launches into" Nibbāna by way of its object; thus, there is the "launching relinquishment. Therefore, regarding the phrase "it turns towards relinquishment":
the meaning here is that one develops mindfulness-enlightenment-factor so that, as it is being developed, it turns towards relinquishment and reaches the state of insight and the state of the path.
This same method applies to the remaining terms as well.
"Excellent" means it is auspicious. "The sign of concentration" refers to the very concentration attained by means of the perception of the skeleton and so forth.
"He guards it" means he protects it while purifying it of lust, hatred, and delusion, which are the states that obstruct concentration.
And here, only five perceptions, beginning with the perception of the skeleton, have been mentioned; however, at this point, one should expand upon all ten kinds of foulness (asubha).
These [terms] should be explained. Their detailed exposition is already stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.

"Knowledge of phenomena" (*dhamme ñāṇaṃ*) refers both to knowledge of the phenomena of the Four Noble Truths by way of a single penetration, and to knowledge of the phenomenon of the Truth of Cessation within those Four Noble Truths.
As it is said: "In this context, what is knowledge of phenomena? It is knowledge regarding the four paths and the four fruits..."
"Knowledge. "Subsequent knowledge" (anvaya-ñāṇa) means that after having seen the four truths directly, one follows that knowledge thus:
"Just as it is now, so too in the past and in the future, these same five aggregates are the truth of suffering; this very craving is the truth of the origin;
this very cessation is the truth of cessation; and this very path is the truth of the path. Thus, it is in the following of that knowledge.
Knowledge. Therefore he said: "By means of this Dhamma—known, seen, attained, realized, and fathomed—he applies the method to the past and the future.
Knowledge of others' minds (*pariye ñāṇa*) is knowledge in the discernment of the minds of others. As it is said:
"In this regard, what is knowledge of others' minds? Here, a bhikkhu, with his own mind, [knows] the minds of other beings, of other persons..."

"One understands by way of delimitation"—this should be expanded in detail. However, with the exception of these three types of knowledge, the remainder is called conventional knowledge (*sammuti-ñāṇa*).

As it is said: "In this context, what is conventional knowledge? With the exception of the knowledge of the Dhamma, the exception of the knowledge of inference, and the exception of the knowledge of delimitation, the remainder is conventional knowledge."
Having brought a certain bhikkhu to the state of Arahantship through knowledge of suffering and the other [truths], the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths was taught as his departure-point.
Therein, two truths constitute the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and two constitute the turning away from the round (*vivaṭṭa*). Attachment occurs toward the round, not toward the turning away.

Having mastered the scriptures regarding two of the truths in the presence of a teacher, he practices the work; regarding the other two truths, [he focuses on] the truth of cessation (*nirodhasacca*).
He performs the work by way of hearing, thinking: "The name is desirable, lovely, and pleasing; the Truth of the Path is indeed desirable, lovely, and pleasing.
Regarding the two truths [the Cessation and the Path], comprehension by way of learning, inquiry, hearing, retention, reflection, and penetration is appropriate;
regarding the other two [Suffering and Origin], comprehension by way of hearing and penetration is appropriate. He penetrates three by way of their functions, and one by way of its object.
The two truths are profound because they are difficult to see; the other two are difficult to see because they are profound. 311.
Regarding the "factors of stream-entry": these are the factors for stream-entry, meaning the causes for the attainment of the path of stream-entry.
Meaning: Association with noble persons (*sappurisasaṃsevo*) means approaching and attending upon noble persons such as the Buddha and others.

Hearing the true Dhamma (*saddhammassavanaṃ*) means hearing the beneficial Dhamma consisting of the Three Pitakas. Proper attention (*yonisomanasikāro*) means attention by way of impermanence and so forth.
Practice in accordance with the Dhamma (*dhammānudhammappaṭipatti*) means practicing the preliminary stage of practice which is in conformity with the supramundane Dhamma.
"With resolute confidence" means with unshakable confidence. The phrases beginning with "Such indeed is the Blessed One" have been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*.
The tetrads of fruit, element, and nutriment are clear in meaning. Furthermore, here the grossness and subtlety should be understood by way of coarse and refined objects.
"Bases of consciousness" (*viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo*): consciousness stands in these, thus they are bases of consciousness. This is stated by way of the stability of the object.

It has been said: "Approaching form" means having approached form. For in the five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokārabhava*), the volitionally conditioned consciousness (*abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇa*) stands supported by the aggregate of form; it is with reference to this that it was said.

"Having form as its object" means having the sphere of the aggregate of form as its range, being established in form. "Sprinkled with delight" means being moistened by the very delight associated with greed.

"Having sacrificed. The other [condition] is by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*). "It attains growth, increase, and expansion" means that proceeding in this manner for sixty or even seventy years, it attains growth, increase, and expansion. This same method applies to the acquisition of feeling (*vedanūpāya*) and so forth.

By these three terms, however, the volitional consciousness (*abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇa*) in the four-aggregate existence (*catuvokārabhava*) is described. Its duration lasts as long as its life-span (*yāvatāyukaṃ*).
Its increase, growth, and expansion should be understood by way of its continued occurrence (*pavatta*).
However, because the teaching was presented by way of tetrads (*catukka*), "approaching consciousness" (*viññāṇūpāya*) was not mentioned.

Furthermore, if it were stated in that way, confusion might arise as to "which here is kamma-consciousness and which is resultant-consciousness?"; for this reason also, it was not mentioned. The "wrong courses of conduct" (*agatigamana*) have already been explained in detail.

“On account of robes” means that it arises for the sake of robes, thinking, “I shall obtain a pleasing robe there. Regarding the phrase “on account of this or that state of existence” (*iti bhavābhavahetu*), here *iti* is a particle used in the sense of illustration;
the meaning is: “just as on account of robes and so forth, so too on account of this or that state of existence.
And by “this or that state of existence” (*bhavābhava*) here, superior and more superior things such as oil, honey, molasses, and so forth are intended. Now, of these...
It should be understood that the four noble lineages (*ariyavaṃsa*) were taught in sequence for the purpose of abandoning the four arisings of craving.
The fourfold path has already been explained above. Regarding "intolerance" (*akkhamā*) and the others: at the time of making an effort, one does not tolerate cold and so forth;

thus it is "intolerance. That which is tolerated is "tolerance" (*khamā*). The taming of the faculties is "self-mastery" (*damā*). As it is said: "He does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensual desire," and so on.
"By means of the method for the calming of thoughts.

"Dhammapadāni" refers to sections of the Dhamma. "Non-covetousness" as a dhammapada means non-greed, or alternatively, the jhānas, insight, the path, the fruits, and Nibbāna attained under the heading of non-greed. "Harmlessness" as a dhammapada means non-anger.

Or the jhānas and so forth attained by means of loving-kindness as the heading. Right Mindfulness is called the "Dhamma-footprint," meaning either well-established mindfulness or the jhānas and so forth attained by means of mindfulness as the heading.

Right Concentration is called the "Dhamma-footprint," meaning either meditative attainment (samāpatti) or the jhānas, insight, the paths, the fruits, and Nibbāna attained by way of the eight attainments;
or the jhānas and so forth attained by way of the ten foulness objects (asubha).
Non-covetousness is a footprint of the Dhamma. Through the four divine abodes, non-ill will is a footprint of the Dhamma.

Through the ten recollections and the perception of repulsiveness in food, right mindfulness is a footprint of the Dhamma. Through the ten kasiṇas and mindfulness of breathing, right concentration is a footprint of the Dhamma.
Among the undertakings of the Dhamma, the first is the practice of the naked ascetics; the second is for one with intense defilements to attain arahantship.
The practice of the pure holy life for one who is unable [to obtain requisites], even while weeping with a tearful face; third, the state of being drunk with sensual pleasures;
fourth, the holy life of the Dispensation for one who possesses happiness by way of jhāna and vipassanā, even though they do not obtain the four requisites.

Regarding "aggregates of the Dhamma" (*dhammakkhandhā*), here the meaning of "aggregate" (*khandha*) is the sense of a quality (*guṇa*). "The aggregate of virtue" (*sīlakkhandha*) refers to the quality of virtue; and herein, the virtue of the fruit (*phala-sīla*) is intended. This same method applies to the remaining terms as well. Thus, in all four instances, only the fruit is stated.

Regarding "the powers" (*balāni*), they are called powers in the sense of providing support and in the sense of being unshakable. Their state of being unshakable by their opposites, such as indolence and so forth, should be understood. All of them are described as both mundane and supramundane, according to serenity (*samatha*), insight (*vipassanā*), and the path (*magga*).
Regarding the term *adhiṭṭhānāni*: here, *adhi* is merely a prefix (*upasagga*). As for its meaning: they stand by means of it, or they stand in it;
or rather, that very state is the "basis" (*adhiṭṭhāna*) for persons preeminent in their respective qualities. Thus, wisdom itself is the basis, which is "the basis of wisdom" (*paññādhiṭṭhāna*).
And herein, by the first [basis], there is the wisdom of the supreme fruit (*aggaphala*); by the second, the truth of speech (*vacīsacca*); by the third...
The relinquishing of material things (*āmisa-pariccāga*). It should be understood that by the fourth [verse], the pacification of the defilements (*kilesa-upasama*) is described.
By the first [verse], starting with the wisdom of one’s own karma (*kammassakata-paññā*) or the wisdom of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*), the wisdom of the fruit (*phala-paññā*) is described.

By the second, starting with verbal truth (*vacī-sacca*), the ultimate truth (*paramattha-sacca*), which is Nibbāna, is described. By the third, starting with the relinquishing of material things, the relinquishing of the defilements through the supreme path (*aggamagga*) is described.
The fourth [section] begins with the suppression of defilements by means of meditative attainments and culminates in the pacification of defilements through the highest path.

Alternatively, by means of the foundation of wisdom (*paññādhiṭṭhāna*), the wisdom of the fruit of Arahantship is explained by one [section], while the remaining [sections] explain ultimate truth (*paramatthasacca*).

Or, alternatively, by means of the foundation of truth (*saccādhiṭṭhāna*), ultimate truth is explained by one [section], while the remaining [sections] explain the wisdom of Arahantship; thus says the Elder Mūsikābhaya.
Commentary on the Tetrad of Questions and Answers, etc., 312. The answers to questions have already been explained in detail in the Discourse on the Great Authorities (*Mahāpadesakathā*).

"Black" means dark; it refers to the action of the ten courses of unwholesome kamma. "Black ripening" means having a dark ripening, because it results in rebirth in the states of deprivation (*apāya*).
"White" refers to wholesome courses of action (kusalakammapatha). "White result" refers to a white fruition because of being reborn in the heavenly realms (sagga).
"Black-and-white" refers to mixed karma. "Black-and-white result" refers to a fruition of both pleasure and pain.

For indeed, having performed mixed karma, one may be reborn in the animal realm in such places as the position of a state elephant through unwholesome [deeds], yet during the course of existence [one experiences pleasure] through the wholesome.
It experiences pleasure. Through wholesome [kamma], one is reborn even in a royal family; through unwholesome [kamma], one experiences suffering during the course of existence.
By "neither black nor white," the knowledge of the four paths that brings about the exhaustion of kamma is intended.
For if it were black, it would yield a black result; if it were white, it would yield a white result. It is the exhaustion of both types of results.
But because it does not give [karmic fruit] and its ripening is neither black nor white, the meaning here is that it is "neither black nor white.

"To be realized" means to be realized both by direct perception and by attainment. "By the eye" means by the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*). "By the body" means by the co-nascent mental body (*nāmakāya*). "By wisdom" means by the knowledge of the fruit of Arahantship. "Floods" (*oghā*):

they are called floods because they carry beings away and cause them to sink into the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*). Among these, lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure is the flood of sensuality (*kāmogha*).

The flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*) consists of desire and lust for the realms of form and the formless. Likewise, attachment to meditative absorption (*jhāna-nikanti*) and lust accompanied by the view of eternalism are included.
The sixty-two views constitute the flood of views (*diṭṭhi-ogha*).
They are called "yokes" (*yoga*) because they yoke one to the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*); these should be understood as being like floods.
They are called "disjunctions" (*visaṃyoga*) because they disjoin. In this context, the jhāna of the foul is the disjunction from the yoke of sensual desire (*kāmayoga*).

Taking that as its basis, the path of non-returning attained thereby is exclusively the disjunction from the yoke of sensual desire. The path of arahantship is the disjunction from the yoke of existence (*bhavayoga*).
The path of stream-entry is the disjunction from the yoke of views (*diṭṭhiyoga*). The path of arahantship is the disjunction from the yoke of ignorance (*avijjāyoga*).

They are called "fetterings" (*gantha*) by way of fettering. It is called a "body-fettering" (*kāyagantha*) because it fetters, binds, and entangles both the mental body and the physical body within the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
"Adherence to the view that 'this alone is the truth'" refers to the adherence to views that proceeds in the manner: "Only this is true; all else is false.

"Graspings" (*upādāna*) means acts of seizing and taking hold. "Sensual desire" (*kāma*) is lust; that very same thing, in the sense of grasping, is a "grasping," thus it is sensual-grasping (*kāmupādāna*).
"View" (*diṭṭhi*) means wrong view; since that too is an "clinging" (*upādāna*) in the sense of grasping, it is called "clinging to views" (*diṭṭhupādāna*).

The grasping of those who hold that purity comes through such moral habits and observances is "clinging to rules and observances" (*sīlabbatupādāna*). Because one speaks of and clings to [the self] by means of this, it is "clinging to the doctrine of self" (*attavādupādāna*).
"Wombs" (*yoniyo*) means categories. Those born from eggs are "egg-born" (*aṇḍaja*). Those born from a watery membrane are "womb-born" (*jalābuja*). Those born in moisture are...

*Saṃsedaja* (moisture-born) is a designation for those born from within a bed or from putrid fish and the like. *Opapātika* (spontaneously born) means those who appear as if having arrived with speed.
In this regard, there is this distinction between the moisture-born and the spontaneously born among gods and humans:
the moisture-born are born weak and young; the spontaneously born are born appearing as sixteen-year-olds. Among humans...
For indeed, among the earth-bound deities (*bhummadeva*), all these four modes of birth (*yoni*) are found. Likewise, among animals such as the *supaṇṇas* and *nāgas*.

For this has been said: "In that regard, monks, egg-born *supaṇṇas* carry away only egg-born *nāgas*, not those born from a womb, nor those born from moisture, nor those of spontaneous birth (*opapātika*).
From the gods of the Four Great Kings upward, the higher deities are exclusively of spontaneous birth.
The same applies to those in hell. Among the *petas*, all four types are found. The modes of descent into the womb (*gabbhāvakkanti*) have already been explained in the *Sampasādanīya Sutta*.

Regarding the acquisition of individual existence (*attabhāvapaṭilābha*), the first should be understood by way of the *khiḍḍāpadosika* [gods]; the second, by way of sheep and so forth being slaughtered by butchers and others;
the third, by way of the *manopadosika* [gods]; and the fourth, beginning from the gods of the Four Great Kings (*cātumahārājika*).
By way of deities who arise [in that state]. For those deities do not die through their own volition, nor through the volition of another.
313. Commentary on the Fourfold Purity of the Offering (*Dakkhiṇāvisuddhi*):
"Purities of the offering" means that the offering, which consists of giving, is purified and becomes of great fruit by means of these; thus they are called "purities of the offering."

“It is purified by the giver, not by the recipient” refers to a case where the giver is virtuous and gives a gift acquired in accordance with the Dhamma, while the recipient is immoral. This kind of offering is like the offering of the Great King Vessantara.
“It is purified by the recipient, not by the giver” refers to a case where the recipient is virtuous, while the giver is immoral.
When one gives what has been acquired through unrighteousness, this offering is like the offering of a murderer;
it is purified neither by the giver nor by the recipient—this refers to a case where both are immoral and the gift itself was produced through unrighteous means.
The fourth [offering] should be understood as the opposite of this.
"Bases of conciliation" (saṅgahavatthūni) means causes of conciliation; these have already been analyzed above.
"Ignoble modes of speech" (anariyavohārā) are the modes of speech of ignoble, base people.
"Noble modes of speech" (ariyavohārā) are the modes of speech of noble, true persons.

"Speaking of what has been seen" (*diṭṭhavāditā*) means one who speaks thus: "I have seen it. In this context, the meaning should be understood by way of the volition that originates each respective [action].
Commentary on the Tetrad of Self-Tormenters, etc. (314):

Among the self-tormenters and so forth, the first is the naked ascetic (*acelaka*). The second is one among the sheep-butchers and others. The third is a sacrificer. The fourth is one who practices correctly within the Teaching (*sāsana*).

Among those who practice for their own welfare and so forth, the first is one who is himself endowed with virtue and other qualities but does not encourage others in virtue and the like, such as the Venerable Elder Vakkali.
The second is one who is not himself endowed with virtue and other qualities but encourages others in virtue and the like, such as the Venerable Upananda.
The third is one who is neither himself endowed with virtue and other qualities nor encourages others in virtue and the like.
Like Devadatta. The fourth is one who is himself endowed with virtue and so forth, and encourages others in virtue and so forth, like the Venerable Mahākassapa.
Among these, "dark" (*tama*) means having become darkness. "One whose further destination is darkness" (*tamaparāyana*) means one for whom darkness alone is the further course or goal.
"Having darkness as his ultimate resort. In this way, the meaning should be understood for all the phrases.
Herein, the first person, having been reborn in a low birth such as that of a *caṇḍāla* or similar class, in a difficult life and in a base state of being, fulfills the three types of misconduct.

The second, being likewise [reborn in a low birth], fulfills the three types of good conduct. The third, having been reborn in a noble *khattiya* family with an excellent state of being and abundant food and drink—
Having been reborn, he fulfills the three types of misconduct. The fourth, being similar [to the first], fulfills the three types of good conduct.
“Samaṇamacala” means a recluse who is immovable; the *ma*-sound is merely for the purpose of euphonic junction (*padasandhi*). He should be understood as a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*).
For a stream-enterer is unshakable by the winds of the doctrines of others, like a city gatepost. He is endowed with immovable faith.
The ascetic who is immovable. This is also said: “And what kind of person is the ascetic who is immovable?

Here, a certain person, through the complete destruction of the three fetters... (and so on in detail). However, because lust and hatred have been attenuated, he is called the once-returner, the “ascetic lotus.
Therefore it was said: “And what kind of person is the ascetic lotus? Here, a certain person...”
“Having come to this world only once more, he makes an end of suffering; this person is called a ‘lotus-like ascetic’ (samaṇapuṇḍarīka).
Because of the absence of lust and hatred, he will blossom very quickly; thus, the non-returner (anāgāmī) is named the “white-lotus-like ascetic.
Therefore it was said: “And what kind of person is the white-lotus-like ascetic? Here, a certain person [has abandoned] the five lower fetters... [etc.]”
“This person is called a ‘white-lotus ascetic’ (samaṇapuṇḍarīka).

However, because of the absence of all fetters and defilements, the Arahant is known as the most delicate of ascetics among ascetics. Therefore it was said: “And what kind of person is the most delicate of ascetics among ascetics?
Here, a certain person, through the destruction of the taints... [as before] ...enters and dwells in [that state]. This person is called the most delicate of ascetics among ascetics.”

“‘These, friends,’ and so forth, should be connected in the same manner as previously stated. Thus, by means of fifty-four tetrads, the Elder, in explaining two hundred questions, demonstrated the flavor of harmony.
The commentary on the Tetrads is finished.
The commentary on the Pentads.
315. Having thus shown the essence of harmony by way of tetrads, he now began the teaching again in order to show it by way of pentads.

Therein, among the five aggregates (*khandha*), the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) is mundane (*lokiya*). The remaining ones are both mundane and supramundane (*lokuttara*). The aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*) are exclusively mundane.
A detailed exposition of the aggregates has been stated in the *Visuddhimagga*. The strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*) have already been explained in detail below.

Destinations (*gati*) are so called because one must go there by means of good or bad deeds (*sukata-dukkata*) and the like. "Hell" (*niraya*) is that which is devoid of essence (*nirassāda*). In this context, the aggregates (*khandha*) are mentioned together with their spatial location (*okāsa*). In the three following cases, only the aggregates produced therein are stated; in the fourth, both the location and the aggregates are mentioned.

"Avarice regarding a dwelling" (*āvāsamacchariya*) is stinginess concerning a residence. A monk possessed of this, upon seeing a visitor, says things such as, "The requisites for the shrine or the Saṅgha have been placed here," and thereby prevents even the Saṅgha’s own residence from being used.
Thus, after passing away, one is reborn as a peta or as a python. Stinginess regarding families is "family stinginess.
A monk endowed with this, for those reasons, even prevents others from entering the family of his own supporters.
Stinginess regarding gains is "gain stinginess. A monk endowed with this, being stingy even with gains belonging to the Saṅgha...
He acts in such a way that others do not obtain [these things]. Stinginess regarding praise is *vaṇṇamacchariya*.
Here, "praise" (*vaṇṇa*) should be understood as both physical beauty and the praise of one's virtues. Stinginess regarding the Dhamma of the scriptures is *dhammamacchariya*.
A monk possessed of this [stinginess] thinks, "Having mastered this Dhamma, he will surpass me," and [withholds it] from another.
He does not give. However, when one does not give out of support for the Dhamma or support for a person, that is not stinginess.

They are called "hindrances" (*nīvaraṇa*) because they obstruct and envelop the mind. Sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) has reached the state of a hindrance and is to be abandoned by the path of Arahatship.

The underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) has reached the state of the fetter of sensual lust (*kāmarāgasaṃyojana*) and is to be abandoned by the path of Non-returning. Sloth (*thina*) is a sickness of the mind. Torpor (*middha*)...
The sickness of the three aggregates. Both [restlessness and remorse] are to be abandoned by the path of Arahantship. Likewise is restlessness.
Remorse is to be abandoned by the path of Non-returning. Doubt is to be abandoned by the first path. "Fetters" means bonds.
Among the persons bound by them, those who have been reborn in the fine-material and immaterial realms—namely, stream-enterers and once-returners—[are included].

"Bound within and lying outside" means this: for them, there is bondage in the realm of sense-desire (*kāmabhava*). Non-returners (*anāgāmin*) in the realm of sense-desire are "bound outside and lying inside," for they have bondage in the realms of form and formlessness (*rūpārūpabhava*).
Stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*) and once-returners (*sakadāgāmin*) in the realm of sense-desire are "bound within and lying inside.
Non-returners in the realms of form and formlessness are "bound outside and lying outside. One whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*)...
"Unfettered in every respect.
*Sikkhāpadaṃ* means a training precept; the meaning is "a section of training. Alternatively, *sikkhāpadaṃ* is the basis (*pada*) of training;
the meaning is "the means for attaining the trainings of higher mind and higher wisdom. This is the summary here. But in detail:
The discussion on the training rules (sikkhāpada) is found precisely in the Vibhaṅga section of the Vinaya Piṭaka, within the analysis of the training rules. 316.

The commentary on the pentad beginning with "incapable" (*abhabbaṭṭhāna*)—namely, "Friends, a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is incapable of intentionally killing a living being," and so forth—is merely a summary of the teaching; this applies to stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*) and others as well.
But they are incapable [of such things]. This was said for the purpose of censuring the ordinary person (*puthujjana*) and praising the one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*).

An "ordinary person" is to be blamed, as he even commits such acts as matricide; the one whose taints are destroyed, however, is to be praised, as he does not commit even such acts as killing an ant or a termite.
It is called a "calamity" (*byasana*) because it scatters away; the meaning is that it casts away or destroys welfare and happiness. The calamity of relatives...

*Ñātibyasanaṃ*: the destruction of relatives; the meaning is the ruin of one's kin through thieves, disease, fear, and so forth. *Bhogabyasanaṃ*: the destruction of wealth; the meaning is the loss of possessions due to kings, thieves, and the like.
*Rogabyasanaṃ*: disease itself is the calamity. For disease is called a "calamity" (*byasana*) because it "calamitously destroys" (*byasati*) or ruins health.
*Sīlabyasanaṃ*: the destruction of virtue; this is a name for immorality (*dussīlya*).
A view that has arisen which destroys right view is itself a calamity; thus, it is called "calamity of views" (*diṭṭhibyasana*).

In this context, the three calamities beginning with the calamity of relatives (*ñātibyasana*) are neither unwholesome (*akusala*) nor subject to the three characteristics (*tilakkhaṇa*). The two calamities of virtue and views are unwholesome and subject to the three characteristics.
For this very reason, he said: "Friends, beings do not [suffer] on account of the calamity of relatives," and so forth.
"Perfection of relatives" (*ñātisampadā*) means the perfection, fulfillment, or abundance of relatives. The same method applies to the "perfection of wealth" (*bhogasampadā*).

"Perfection of health" (*ārogyasampadā*) is the perfection of health; its fulfillment is being free from illness for a long time. The same method applies to the "perfections of virtue and view" (*sīladiṭṭhisampadā*).
Here too, the perfection of relatives and so forth are not wholesome (*kusala*), nor are they struck by the three characteristics. However, the perfections of virtue and view are wholesome.
It is struck by the three characteristics. For that very reason, he said: "Friends, it is not for the sake of success among kinsmen," and so forth.
The discussion on the failure and success of virtue has already been explained in detail in the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta.
"By one who reproaches" refers to: pointing out the basis [of the offense], pointing out the offense itself, the refusal of communal living, and the refusal of respectful conduct.

When accusing by means of the four grounds for accusation: "I will speak at the proper time, not at an improper time"—here, the time is stated from the perspective of the one being accused, not the accuser.
For one who accuses another, he should not do so in the midst of an assembly, or at the head of the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā ceremonies, or in places such as the hall of seats or the dining hall.
When sitting in a daytime resting place, [one should not say]: "Venerable sir, are you doing..."
"Please grant me the opportunity; I wish to speak to the Venerable One. Having thus obtained leave, one should then proceed with the censure.
However, after examining the individual, if it is a person of loose character who, by speaking what is untrue, brings infamy upon the monks, he may be censured even without being granted leave.
"In accordance with the truth" means by that which is factual and according to the actual nature of things. "Gently" means smoothly and softly. "Beneficially" means...
[This is] by one endowed with the desire for welfare and the desire for benefit.
317. Regarding the "factors of striving" (*padhāniyaṅga*):
"striving" (*padhāna*) means exertion; one who possesses such striving is called "one characterized by striving" (*padhāniyo*).

The factors for a bhikkhu who is striving are the "factors of striving" (*padhāniyaṅga*). "Faithful" means being endowed with faith. This faith is fourfold: faith as arrival, faith as attainment, faith as conviction, and faith as clarity.
Among these, the faith of the omniscient Bodhisattvas is called "faith as arrival" because it has come from their initial resolve (*abhinīhāra*). [The faith] of the noble disciples...

Faith through realization (*adhigamana-saddhā*) is so called because it is attained through personal penetration. Faith through conviction (*okappana-saddhā*) is the firm settling of the mind characterized by immovability when the words "Buddha, Dhamma, Saṅgha" are uttered.
Faith through serene confidence (*pasāda-saddhā*) is the arising of clarity.
Here, faith through conviction is intended. "Enlightenment" (*bodhi*) refers to the knowledge of the fourth path. One has faith that this was well-penetrated by the Tathāgata.
This is merely the conclusion of the teaching; however, by this factor, faith in the Three Jewels is intended.

For one who possesses strong confidence in the Buddha and the others, the energy of exertion succeeds. "Free from illness" means healthy. "Free from affliction" means free from suffering. "With a well-digesting" means with a well-digestive power.
"Of the stomach" means of the fire-element born of karma (*kammaja-tejo-dhātu*). "Neither too cold" [refers to the digestive heat].
“Neither too cold” means that one who is afflicted by excessive cold is afraid of cold, while one afflicted by excessive heat is afraid of heat;
for such people, striving does not succeed. For one of moderate temperament, it succeeds. Therefore he said: “with a temperance suited to striving.
“To reveal oneself as one really is” means to manifest one’s own lack of virtue as it truly is. “Leading to arising and passing away” means...
"Capable of going to and discerning both arising and passing away"—by this, the knowledge of arising and passing away (*udayabbaya-ñāṇa*), which grasps the thirty-two characteristics, is stated.
"Noble" (*ariyāya*) means purified. "Penetrative" (*nibbedhikāya*) means capable of penetrating those aggregates of greed (*lobhakkhandha*) and so forth that have not been penetrated before.
"Leading rightly to the destruction of suffering" is said because the defilements are abandoned by way of partial penetration (*tadaṅga*).
"Whatever suffering is exhausted, it is [the wisdom] that leads to the exhaustion of each such suffering. Thus, by all these words, only insight-wisdom (*vipassanā-paññā*) is spoken of;
for indeed, the striving of one who lacks wisdom does not succeed.
The Explanation of the Five [Bhikkhus], the Suddhāvāsas, and so forth.

318. "Suddhāvāsā" means those who have dwelt, are dwelling, or will dwell here in purity; thus they are called "Suddhāvāsā. "Pure" (suddhā) means free from the stains of defilements, being non-returners whose taints are exhausted. Regarding what should be said concerning the Aviha and other [heavens], that has already been stated in the Mahāpadāna.

Among the non-returners, one who attains the state of an Arhat through the complete extinction of defilements (*parinibbāna*) in the interval, without exceeding the middle of his lifespan, is called an "antarā-parinibbāyī.
One who attains it after having exceeded the middle and reached the end of his lifespan is called an "upahacca-parinibbāyī."
One who attains parinibbāna without exertion or application, without fatigue, and with ease, is called one who attains parinibbāna without exertion (*asaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī*).
One who attains it with exertion and application, with fatigue, and with difficulty, is called one who attains parinibbāna with exertion (*sasaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī*).

These four types are found among all five pure abodes (*suddhāvāsa*). However, regarding the "one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm" (*uddhaṃsota-akaniṭṭhagāmī*), a tetrad should be understood here.
One who, starting from the Aviha realm, purifies the four deva-worlds, goes to Akaniṭṭha, and attains final nibbāna there is called an "upstreamer bound for Akaniṭṭha.
One who, from Aviha, goes to the second, third, or fourth deva-world and attains final nibbāna there is called an "upstreamer not bound for Akaniṭṭha. One who [from] the sense-sphere existence...
One who, having been reborn among the Akaniṭṭha gods, attains final nibbāna there, is called a non-returner bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm. One who,
having been reborn in each of the four lower deva worlds, attains final nibbāna right there in those very places,
is called a non-returner not bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm.
Commentary on the Five Mental Barrennesses (Cetokhilapañcakavaṇṇanā) 319.
"Mental barrennesses" (*cetokhila*) refers to states of rigidity in the mind. "He has doubt regarding the Teacher" means he doubts either the Teacher’s physical body or his qualities.
One who doubts the body thinks: "How can he truly be adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man?"...
He doubts whether the body exists or does not exist. Doubting regarding qualities, he doubts whether there exists the knowledge of omniscience capable of knowing the past, future, and present.
"For ardor" means for the purpose of exerting energy. "For application" means for repeated application.
"For perseverance" means for constant practice. "For striving" means for the purpose of striving. This is the first.
"Stiffness of mind" (*cetokhila*) refers to this first state of rigidity of the mind, which consists of doubt regarding the Teacher. Regarding "the Dhamma":

there is the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*) and the Dhamma of realization (*paṭivedha-dhamma*). One who is hesitant regarding the Dhamma of the scriptures doubts, thinking: "They say the word of the Buddha consists of the Three Piṭakas and eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dhamma;
does this actually exist, or does it not? Thus he hesitates.
