Summarizing all of that in a single phrase, the Elder said: "Heedfulness regarding wholesome states. Its great utility is also demonstrated in the *Appamādavagga* of the *Dhammapada*.

It should be illustrated. It should also be illustrated by the story of King Aśoka—(Ka) for King Aśoka, upon hearing the verse from the novice Nigrodha, "Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless," was immediately inspired with faith in the novice, saying, "Stop, dear one!
You have recited the Buddha’s word, the Three Pitakas, to me," and he [built] eighty-four thousand monasteries.
Thus, having illustrated with the three Piṭakas how diligence is of great assistance, a bhikkhu endowed with fortitude should speak.
When bringing forward any sutta or verse for the purpose of illustrating diligence, he should not be told, "You bring it forth out of place;
you have leaped across where there is no ford. In this matter, the measure of both fortitude and strength belongs solely to the preacher of the Dhamma.

(Kha) "Mindfulness directed to the body" (*kāyagatāsati*) is a designation for the mindfulness that arises here with respect to: mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna*), the four postures (*iriyāpatha*), mindfulness and clear comprehension (*satisampajañña*), the thirty-two aspects (*dvattiṃsākāra*), the analysis of the four elements (*catudhātuvavatthāna*), the ten foulness subjects (*dasāsubhā*), the nine cemetery meditations (*navasivathikā*), attention to minute particles (*cuṇṇikamanasikāra*), and the four material jhānas regarding the head-hairs and so forth.
"Accompanied by pleasure" (*sātasahagatā*) refers to [mindfulness] elsewhere, excluding the fourth jhāna.
It is accompanied by pleasure (*sāta*) and associated with happiness (*sukha*); it is with reference to this that it was said.

(Ga) "Tainted and subject to clinging" means being a condition for both the taints (*āsava*) and the clingings (*upādāna*); thus, it restricts [the meaning] to phenomena belonging to the three planes of existence.
(Gha) "The conceit 'I am'" (*asmimāna*) is the conceit "I am" regarding form and so forth.
(Ṅa) *Ayoniso manasikāra* is improper attention proceeding by way of such modes as taking what is impermanent to be permanent, and so forth.
(Ca) Proper attention (*yoniso manasikāra*) should be understood as the opposite of that.
(Cha) *Ānantariko cetosamādhi*: elsewhere, the fruit that follows immediately after the path is called "proximate mental concentration" (*ānantariko cetosamādhi*).

[This is] the name. Here, however, "immediate mental concentration" (*ānantariko cetosamādhi*) is intended as the path that follows immediately after insight (*vipassanā*), because it is immediate to insight, or because it yields its fruit immediately after itself.
(Ja) Regarding "unshakable knowledge" (*akuppaṃ ñāṇaṃ*): elsewhere, this refers to the wisdom of the fruit (*phalapaññā*); here, the wisdom of review (*paccavekkhaṇapaññā*) is intended.

(Jha) "Sustained by nutriment" means sustained by conditions. "This is one thing" refers to that condition by which things persist; this one thing is to be fully understood through direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) by means of full understanding through knowledge (*ñātapariññā*).
(Ña) "Unshakable liberation of mind" refers to the liberation of the fruit of Arhatship.

In this section, full understanding through knowledge is explained by way of direct knowledge, while full understanding by scrutinization (*tīraṇapariññā*) is explained by way of what is to be abandoned and what is to be realized.

*Pahānapariññā* (full understanding as abandoning). Here, however, the Path (*magga*) is spoken of by the term "difficult to penetrate. That which is to be realized (*sacchikātabba*) refers to the Fruit (*phala*);
thus, the Path is found in a single expression, whereas the Fruit is indeed found even in many.
"Bhūta" means existing by way of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). "Taccha" means according to reality (*yāthāva*). "Tatha" means having such an intrinsic nature as it has been described.

“Not otherwise” (*avitatha*) means that they are not as they were described; they are not otherwise than what was stated. “Not different” (*anaññathā*) means they are not different from the manner in which they were described.

“Perfectly awakened to by the Tathāgata” (*sammā tathāgatena abhisambuddhā*) means that while seated at the seat of awakening (*bodhipallaṅka*), the Tathāgata himself—by way of cause and reason—has perfectly awakened to, known, understood, and realized them. By this, the Elder [shows] that “these phenomena were by the Tathāgata...”
"Having attained full enlightenment, I am like a messenger bearing a letter for you, O King," he said, generating confidence by showing the *Jinasutta*.
The commentary on the single dharma is finished.
The commentary on the two dharmas.

352. (Ka) "These two qualities are very helpful": these two qualities, mindfulness (*sati*) and clear comprehension (*sampajañña*), are beneficial and supportive in all matters, such as the fulfillment of virtue (*sīla*), just like heedfulness (*appamāda*).

(Kha) "Calm (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*): these two are described in the *Saṅgīti Sutta* as both mundane and supramundane; in this *Dasuttara Sutta*, however, those pertaining to the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*) are discussed.
(Cha) "For the defilement of beings and for the purification of beings": improper attention (*ayoniso manasikāra*) is both the cause and the condition.
And for beings, lack of wise attention leads to defilement, while wise attention leads to purification.

Likewise, being difficult to speak with and having evil friends lead to defilement, while being easy to speak with and having virtuous friends lead to purification. Likewise, there are the three unwholesome roots and the three wholesome roots.
There are four bonds and four releases. There are five mental barrennesses and the five faculties. Six...
Lack of respect and respect; the seven unwholesome qualities and the seven wholesome qualities; the eight bases of indolence and the eight bases for exertion;
the nine grounds for resentment and the nine ways of removing resentment;
the ten courses of unwholesome action and the ten courses of wholesome action—it should be understood that these two categories of phenomena, with such divisions, are difficult to penetrate.

(Jha) "Conditioned elements" (*saṅkhata-dhātu*) refers to the five aggregates produced by conditions. "Unconditioned element" (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*) refers to Nibbāna, which is not produced by conditions.

(Ña) Regarding "true knowledge and liberation": here, "true knowledge" (*vijjā*) refers to the three types of true knowledge (*tisso vijjā*). "Liberation" (*vimutti*) refers to the fruit of Arhatship (*arahattaphala*).

In this section, the supernormal powers (*abhiññā*) and so forth are identical to those in the preceding [section]; however, regarding the terms for what is to be generated, the Path (*magga*) is mentioned, while regarding the terms for what is to be realized, the Fruit (*phala*) is mentioned.
The commentary on the two states is finished.
Commentary on the three states: 353.
Regarding the phrase, "This is the escape from sensual desires, namely, renunciation (*nekkhamma*)," here "renunciation" refers to the path of non-returning (*anāgāmimagga*).
This is what is intended. For that is the complete escape from sensual pleasures.

Regarding the statement, "The escape from forms is this, namely, the formless," here too the path of Arahantship is meant. Because it prevents future rebirth, it is called the complete escape from all forms.
In the phrase, "Cessation is its escape," it is the fruit of Arahantship that is intended here as "cessation. By means of the fruit of Arahantship...

For when Nibbāna is seen, all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) no longer exist in the future; thus, because Arahantship is the condition for the cessation of the conditioned, it is called "cessation" (*nirodha*).
(Ja) "Knowledge regarding the past" means knowledge having the past as its object; the same method applies to the other [two] periods as well.

In this section as well, the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) and so forth are identical to those in the singlefold treatment. However, in the "Difficult-to-Penetrate" section, the path (*magga*) is explained, and the fruit (*phala*) is explained in the "To-be-Realized" section.
The commentary on the threefold categories is concluded.
[Now begins] the commentary on the fourfold categories.
354. (Ka) Regarding "the four wheels": here, "wheel" (*cakka*) is fivefold—namely, the wooden wheel, the jewel-wheel, the Dhamma-wheel, the posture-wheel, and the success-wheel.

Among these, the phrase, "But this wheel, friend chariot-maker, which was completed in six months, [was finished] six days less," refers to the wooden wheel. [The phrase], "Set in motion by the Father... refers to the jewel-wheel.
“‘He sets the wheel in motion’—this refers to the jewel-wheel (*ratana-cakka*). ‘The wheel that has been set in motion’—this refers to the Dhamma-wheel (*dhamma-cakka*).
‘The four-wheeled [body] with nine gates’—this refers to the wheel of postures (*iriyāpatha-cakka*). ‘Bhikkhus, there are these four wheels;
for gods and humans endowed with them, the four wheels roll forth’—this refers to the wheel of prosperity (*sampatti-cakka*). Here too, it is this very one that is intended.”
"Living in a suitable locality" means dwelling in a fitting place where the four assemblies are seen.
"Dependence on true persons" means relying upon, attending upon, and associating with true persons such as the Buddha and others. "Right disposition of oneself" means establishing oneself correctly;
however, if one was previously possessed of lack of faith and so forth, it means abandoning those qualities.
It is the establishing [of beings] in faith and the other [faculties]. Furthermore, "having performed merit in the past" means having accumulated wholesome deeds (*kusala*) previously;

this alone is the measure here. For whatever wholesome deed has been performed with a consciousness associated with knowledge, that very wholesome deed leads that person to a suitable place and causes them to associate with true persons (*sappurisa*). And it is that same individual who establishes themselves rightly.

Among the four nutriments, the first is purely mundane (*lokiya*). However, the remaining three are described in the *Saṅgīti-sutta* as being a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane (*lokuttara*).
Here, in the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*), they are mundane.
Furthermore, the dissociation from the bond of sensual desire (*kāmayoga-viṣamyoga*) and so forth should be understood by way of the path of the non-returner (*anāgāmi-mārga*) and others.

(Cha) Among those conducive to decline (*hānabhāgiya*) and so forth: when one who has attained the first *jhāna* is assailed by perceptions and mental applications associated with sensual desire, that is concentration conducive to decline.
When mindfulness established in accordance with that [attainment] remains steady, that is concentration conducive to stability (*ṭhitibhāgiya*).

When perceptions and mental applications associated with applied thought (*vitakka*) arise, that is concentration conducive to distinction (*visesabhāgiya*). Perceptions and mental applications associated with disenchantment (*nibbidā*)...

The meaning should be understood by expanding upon all the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) according to this method: "They practice concentration associated with dispassion and partaking in penetration.
Furthermore, the detailed exposition of this has already been given in the *Visuddhimagga*.

In this section as well, the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) and so forth are identical to those in the singlefold classification. However, here the path (*magga*) is spoken of under the heading of "direct knowledge," while the fruit (*phala*) is spoken of under the heading of "that which is to be realized."
The commentary on the four states is finished.
Commentary on the five states: 355.
(b) Regarding the pervasion by rapture (*pīti*) and so forth: wisdom (*paññā*) that arises while pervading with rapture is "pervasion by rapture" (*pītipharaṇatā*) in two jhānas.
The wisdom that arises pervading happiness is called the "pervasion of happiness" (*sukhapharaṇatā*) among the three jhānas.
The wisdom that arises pervading the minds of others is called the "pervasion of mind" (*cetopharaṇatā*), which is the wisdom of knowing the minds of others (*cetopariya-paññā*).

The wisdom that arises in the pervasion of light is called the "pervasion of light" (*ālokapharaṇatā*), which is the wisdom of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu-paññā*). The knowledge of reviewing is called the "sign of reviewing" (*paccavekkhaṇanimitta*).
And this has also been said: "Wisdom in two jhānas is the pervasion of rapture; wisdom in three jhānas is the pervasion of bliss.
Wisdom regarding the minds of others is the pervasion of the mind; the divine eye is the pervasion of light.
For one who has emerged from various attainments, the knowledge of reviewing is the sign of reviewing."
In this context, the pervasion by rapture and the pervasion by pleasure are like the two feet; the pervasion by mind and the pervasion by light are like the two hands;
the jhāna that serves as the basis for direct knowledge is like the torso; and the sign for reviewing is like the head.
Thus, the Venerable Sāriputta Thera [described] five-factored right concentration as being complete with its major and minor limbs.
Having fashioned a man, he showed it [to him].
(Ja) In such passages as "this concentration is pleasant in the present," etc., the concentration of the fruit of Arahantship is intended.
For that is "pleasant in the present" because it is pleasant at every moment of absorption. Each preceding [moment] is [the cause] for each succeeding one...
It has a pleasant ripening in the future because it is a condition for the bliss of concentration (*samādhi*).

It is noble (*ariya*) because it is remote from the defilements (*kilesa*). It is unworldly (*nirāmisa*) because it is devoid of the bait of sensual pleasure, the bait of worldly gain, and the bait of the world.

It is not practiced by base men because it is practiced by Great Beings such as the Buddhas. It is so called because of the continuity of its factors, the continuity of its object, and the continuity of the pacification of all the distress of the defilements.
And it is peaceful. It is sublime in the sense of being invigorating.

It is "attained through subsiding" because it is obtained through the subsiding of the defilements, or because it is obtained by one who has attained the state of the subsiding of the defilements; for "subsided" and "subsiding" are identical in meaning.
Alternatively, it is "attained through subsiding" because it is obtained by an Arahant whose defilements have subsided. By way of singleness...
Because it has been attained, it is "attained as a state of singleness" (*ekodibhāvādhigata*).

Unlike weak, mundane concentration (*sāsavasamādhi*), which is accompanied by volitional effort (*sasankhāra*) and application (*sappayoga*), this is not "one who has gone to the state of suppressing and warding off with volitional effort," because it has not been attained by suppressing opposing states or warding off defilements through a mind involving such effort.
Furthermore, one entering that concentration or emerging from it does so because of having reached fullness of mindfulness (*sativipulla*).
One enters attainment mindfully and emerges mindfully; or else, by way of the time previously determined, one enters mindfully and emerges mindfully.

Therefore, when for one who reflects thus, "This concentration is pleasant in the present and has a pleasant result in the future," there arises a knowledge that is personal and independent of others, that constitutes one factor.
This same method applies to the remaining cases as well. Thus, by means of these five kinds of reviewing knowledge, this concentration is called "right concentration consisting of five knowledges.
In this section, the path is explained under the heading of "states conducive to distinction," and the fruit under the heading of "states to be realized. The rest is exactly as before.
Commentary on the Sixfold Dhamma (Chaddhammavaṇṇanā): 356.
Regarding the six groups (chakka), everything is already clear in meaning. However, the Path is explained here in terms of words that are difficult to penetrate. The remainder is the same as before.
Commentary on the Sevenfold Dhamma (Sattadhammavaṇṇanā).
357. (Ña) "Well-seen with right wisdom" means they are well-seen by means of the knowledge of insight (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*), through its cause and method.

"Sensual pleasures" (*kāmā*) refers both to sensual objects (*vatthu-kāma*) and to sensual defilements (*kilesa-kāma*); both are well-seen as being like a pit of glowing coals in the sense that they are burning.
"Inclined toward seclusion" (*viveka-ninna*) means inclined toward Nibbāna. "Sloping" (*poṇa*) and "tending toward" (*pabbhāra*) are synonyms for "inclined. "Brought to an end" (*byantībhūta*)...

"Niyaṭibhūtaṃ" means "free from craving" (nittaṇha). From what? From all things that are bases for the taints (āsava), that is to say, from the phenomena belonging to the three planes (tebhūmakadhamma).
Here, in the word "to be developed," the Path is spoken of. The rest is exactly as before.
This concludes the commentary on the eight factors.
358. (Ka) "By means of the wisdom pertaining to the beginning of the holy life" (*ādibrahmacariyikāya paññāya*) means:

by means of the wisdom of serenity and insight in their initial stage, which constitutes the beginning of the path of the holy life comprised within the three trainings; or, by means of the wisdom of right view, which constitutes the beginning of the eightfold path.

"Intense" (*tibba*) means powerful. "Moral shame and moral dread" (*hirottappa*) means both shame (*hirī*) and moral dread (*ottappa*). "Affection" (*pema*) means affection based on worldly attachment.

"Veneration" (*gārava*) means the state of a heavy mind. For one who dwells depending upon that which is worthy of veneration, the defilements do not arise and one receives instruction and admonition. Therefore, dwelling in dependence upon that is a condition for the acquisition of wisdom.

(6) Since the departed spirits (*petas*) go to the weddings and funerals of the *asuras*, it should be understood that the realm of the *asuras* is included within the sphere of the departed spirits (*pettivisaya*).

"Of one with few desires": here, there are four kinds of fewness of desires—the fewness of desire regarding requisites, the fewness of desire regarding attainments, the fewness of desire regarding the scriptures, and the fewness of desire regarding the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*).
Among these, one who has few desires regarding requisites takes little when much is given, or takes even less when little is given, or does not take at all;
he does not take everything. One who has few desires regarding attainments is like the Elder Majjhantika.
One who is modest regarding one's own attainments does not allow others to know them, as did the Elder Sāriputta.

One who is modest regarding mastery of the scriptures (*pariyatti*), even if they have mastered the Tipiṭaka, does not wish to make known their state of great learning, like the Elder Tissa of Sāketa.

One who is modest regarding the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) does not allow others to know that they observe those practices, like the elder brother among the two brothers. The source for this is in the *Visuddhimagga*.

It has been said: "This is the Dhamma. Thus, by concealing one's existing virtues and by moderation in accepting requisites, this ninefold supramundane Dhamma comes to be accomplished for a person of few desires, but not for one of great desire.
In this way, it should be applied in all instances.
"Of one who is content" means of one who is content with three kinds of contentment regarding the four requisites.

"Of one who is secluded" means of one who is secluded by way of physical seclusion, mental seclusion, and seclusion from acquisitions (*upadhi*). Therein, "physical seclusion" is the state of being alone after having dispelled the company of crowds, by means of the eight bases for exertion.
However, since the task is not accomplished by mere solitude, one should perform the preliminary work (*parikamma*) for the *kasiṇas* and [cultivate] the eight...
One brings about the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*); this is called seclusion of mind (*cittaviveka*).

Since the task is not accomplished by the mere attainment alone, one takes jhāna as a basis, contemplates formations (*saṅkhāra*), and reaches Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*);
this is called seclusion from the substrata (*upadhiviveka*). Therefore the Blessed One said: "There is seclusion of body for those who dwell secluded from the body and delight in renunciation."

“Seclusion of mind belongs to those whose minds are purified and who have attained supreme serenity; seclusion from acquisitions belongs to persons free from acquisitions who have reached the state beyond formations.
“To one who delights in company” means to one who rejoices in both the company of groups and the company of defilements. “To one who has aroused energy” means...

"Of one who has aroused energy" means by way of physical and mental energy (*vīriya*). "Of one whose mindfulness is established" means of one whose mindfulness is established by way of the four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*).

"Of one who is concentrated" means of one whose mind is one-pointed (*ekagga-citta*). "Of one who possesses wisdom" means of one possessing the wisdom of the ownership of kamma (*kammassakata-paññā*).
"Of one free from proliferation" means of one from whom the proliferations (*papañca*) of conceit, craving, and views have departed.
Here, in the section on what is to be developed (*bhāvetabba-pada*), the Path (*magga*) is explained.
The remainder is exactly as before. 359.

(Kha) Purification of Virtue (*sīla-visuddhi*): This refers to the fourfold purification of virtue (*catupārisuddhi-sīla*) which is capable of bringing about purification. It is the factor of striving for purification (*pārisuddhi-padhāniyaṅga*).
Purity of being is a factor of striving. Purity of mind refers to the eight familiar attainments that serve as the proximate cause for insight (vipassanā).
Purity of view is the seeing of mentality-materiality together with its conditions. Purity by overcoming doubt is the knowledge of the mode of conditions;
for one who sees that in all three periods of time phenomena proceed solely by way of conditions, doubt is overcome.
It transcends. Regarding "purification by knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path": light and so forth are not the path;

rather, the knowledge of rise and fall that has entered the proper course is the path—thus there is knowledge of what is the path and what is not the path. Regarding "purification by knowledge and vision of the way": in the *Rathavinīta*, insight leading to emergence was spoken of;
here, it is nascent insight. Regarding "purification by knowledge and vision": in the *Rathavinīta*, the path was spoken of; here, [it is...]
Insight leading to emergence. Furthermore, these seven purifications have been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*.
"Wisdom" refers to the wisdom of the fruit of Arahantship. "Liberation" likewise refers specifically to the liberation of the fruit of Arahantship.
Regarding the statement, "Dependent on the diversity of the elements, there arises a diversity of contacts": this refers to the diversity of the eye-element and so forth.

The meaning is that a diversity of eye-contact and so forth arises. "In dependence on a diversity of contact" means in dependence on the diversity of eye-contact and so forth. "A diversity of feeling" means a diversity of feeling born of eye-contact and so forth.
"In dependence on a diversity of perception" means in dependence on a diversity of perceptions such as the perception of sensual desire and so forth.
"A diversity of intention" means a diversity of intentions such as the intention for sensual desire and so forth. [The repetition of] "a diversity of intention" [is the conclusion].
“Dependent on this, the diversity of desire arises”: through the diversity of intention, there arises the diversity of desire such as “desire for forms” and “desire for sounds.

“The diversity of fever arises”: through the diversity of desire, there arises the diversity of fever such as “fever for forms” and “fever for sounds. “The diversity of seeking arises”: through the diversity of fever...
The diversity of the search for forms and so forth arises. Regarding "the diversity of gains": through the diversity of searches, the diversity of the acquisition of forms and so forth arises.

(Ja) Among perceptions, "the perception of death" is the perception consisting in the knowledge that contemplates death. "The perception of the repulsiveness of food" is the perception that arises in one who is scrutinizing food.
"The perception of non-delight in the entire world" is [the perception] of one who is weary of the whole cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
"Perception has arisen. The remaining [terms] have already been explained above. Here, the Path is explained in the section on "the many benefits.
The rest is exactly like what preceded it. 360.
(Jha) Regarding the "bases for wearing away" (*nijjaravatthu*): these are the causes for wearing away. "Wrong view is worn away" means this [is as stated] below.
By insight (vipassanā) as well, they are indeed worn out and abandoned. Why, then, are they taken up again? Because they have not been completely eradicated.
For although they are worn out by insight, they are not yet eradicated; however, when the Path (magga) arises, it eradicates them and does not allow them to arise again.
Therefore, they are taken up again. This same principle should be applied to all instances.
And herein, with right view as condition, sixty-four states reach the fulfillment of their development.
Which sixty-four? At the moment of the stream-entry path, one fulfills the faculty of faith in the sense of resolution;

one fulfills the faculty of energy in the sense of exertion; one fulfills the faculty of mindfulness in the sense of recollection; and [one fulfills the faculty of concentration] in the sense of non-distraction.
One fulfills the faculty of concentration; one fulfills the faculty of wisdom in the sense of seeing;
the faculty of mind in the sense of cognizing; the faculty of mental joy in the sense of delighting;

and the faculty of life in the sense of predominance over the continuity of existence... [and so on] ...at the moment of the fruit of Arhatship, one fulfills the faculty of faith in the sense of resolution.

The life-faculty fulfills [its function] in the sense of being the dominant factor for the continuity of the process. Thus, occurring eight times each in the four paths and the four fruits, sixty-four factors reach fulfillment.
Here, in the section on what is to be directly known (*abhiññeyya*), the path is discussed; the rest is exactly as before.
Standing here, the questions should be brought together. One hundred questions are stated in the "Tens" (Dasaka). There are one hundred each in the "Ones" (Ekaka) and the "Nines" (Navaka);

one hundred each in the "Twos" (Duka) and the "Eights" (Aṭṭhaka); one hundred each in the "Threes" (Tika) and the "Sevens" (Sattaka); one hundred each in the "Fours" (Catukka) and the "Sixes" (Chakka);
and fifty in the "Fives" (Pañcaka). Thus, five hundred and fifty questions have been stated in total.
“Thus spoke the Venerable Sāriputta; those bhikkhus, being uplifted in mind, rejoiced in the Venerable Sāriputta’s words.
Saying, “Excellent! Excellent! they received it with their heads bowed.

And through that state of uplifted mind, as they reflected upon this very discourse, those five hundred bhikkhus were established in the fruit of Arahantship, the highest fruit, together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
The commentary on the *Dasuttara-sutta* in the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*,
the commentary on the *Dīgha Nikāya*, is completed.
And the commentary on the *Pāṭhika-vagga* is also completed.
The commentary on the Pāṭhika-vagga is finished.
The concluding discourse:
And at this point—
Requested by the Elder Dāṭhānāga Saṅgha, who dwells in a pariveṇa,
possesses steadfast virtues, and belongs to the lineage of the Elders— O Daśabala,
[I have composed] this commentary on the excellent Dīgha Āgama, which elucidates the multitude of your qualities.
That which I have undertaken, O Sumaṅgala, is called by the name *Vilāsini*.
For it has been completed by extracting the essence from the Great Commentary (*Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*),
according to the recitation sections (*bhāṇavāra*) of the eighty-one-fold Pāḷi.
Since the *Visuddhimagga* also consists of fifty-nine recitation sections (*bhāṇavāra*) and was composed for the purpose of elucidating the meaning of the scriptures,
this commentary, together with it, according to the count of recitation sections—
It is precisely delimited as one hundred and forty;
thus is the total measure of one hundred and forty sections from the *bhāṇavāra*.
It proclaims the tradition of those who dwell in the Mahāvihāra.
By me, who has composed this work taking up the essence of the commentaries on the *Mūla-ṭīkā*,
whatever merit has been accumulated— by that, may the entire world be happy.
[This was written] by one adorned with supreme purity of faith, wisdom, and energy, and endowed with a multitude of virtues such as morality, conduct, speed, and gentleness.
To the great poet, the foremost of debaters who speaks with fitting and supreme words, endowed with the analytical discernment of wisdom capable of fathoming both his own and others' tenets;
one whose unimpeded radiance of knowledge shines upon the Teacher’s Dispensation—comprising the Three Pitakas along with their commentaries—as a great grammarian;

one whose speech is graced by the beauty of sweet and noble words flowing forth from the bliss produced by perfection of expression; and one who is adorned with qualities such as the six supernormal powers and surrounded by the four analytical knowledges.
This is the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, the commentary on the *Dīghanikāya*, composed by the Elder named Buddhaghosa—

a name bestowed upon him by his teachers— who was an ornament to the lineage of the Mahāvihāra-dwelling Elders, who were lamps of the Elder tradition and possessed wisdom firmly established in the superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*), and whose intellect was vast and utterly pure.
May he remain in the world for as long as there are seekers of deliverance from the world,
showing to the sons of noble family the method for the purification of view—
even so long as the mere name "Buddha" exists for that Pure-minded One, the Tathāgata.
"In this world, the Great Seer acts for the World-Chief.
Thus ends the commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya named Sumaṅgalavilāsinī.
